### 4.14. Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

The **Dayuan heavenly horse heritage** is the body of historical record and national tradition connecting Irad to the "heavenly horses" (Chinese: *tianma*) of [[wp:Dayuan]], the ancient kingdom of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] described in Han dynasty sources. The northern and eastern rim of the valley lies within Irad. Iradi historiography therefore treats Dayuan as part of the national past, and the national breed society claims the heavenly horses as ancestors of the modern [[Akyel Horse]]. Historians accept the Han accounts of Dayuan and its horses. Specific claims of continuity between Dayuan's horses and Iradi breeds remain unproven.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Dayuan in the Han sources
Dayuan was a settled kingdom of walled towns in the Fergana Valley, known for rice, wheat, vineyards and horses. Its population is generally thought to have been Iranian-speaking, and some historians connect its name with the Greek settlers of [[wp:Bactria]], though this is debated. Under pressure from the [[wp:Yuezhi]], [[wp:Saka]] groups moved south through the region in the 140s and 130s BCE. Dayuan appears in the historical record shortly afterward.<sup>[1]</sup>

The main source is the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*[[wp:Records of the Grand Historian|Shiji]]*) of [[wp:Sima Qian]]. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] left the Han court in 138 BCE, spent years as a captive of the [[wp:Xiongnu]], and reached Dayuan around 128 BCE. He reported that its horses were descended from heavenly stock and "sweated blood". [[wp:Emperor Wu of Han|Emperor Wu]], who wanted strong horses for his cavalry against the Xiongnu, sent embassies to obtain them. When Dayuan refused and killed a Han envoy, he launched the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE).<sup>[1]</sup>

The first expedition, under the general [[wp:Li Guangli]], failed in 104 BCE. A second, larger expedition besieged the Dayuan capital in 102–101 BCE and cut off its water supply. The Dayuan nobility then killed their king and came to terms. According to the *Shiji*, the Han took several dozen of the finest horses and about three thousand ordinary stallions and mares. Dayuan became a Han tributary, and the campaign extended Han influence along the routes later known as the [[wp:Silk Road]]. Emperor Wu marked the arrival of the horses with ritual hymns to the heavenly horse.<sup>[1]</sup>

The description of horses that "sweated blood" has been explained by modern researchers as the effect of a parasitic skin infection. Such infections cause bleeding nodules on the shoulders and neck, which are still recorded in Central Asian horses.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Iradi tradition and historiography
Iradi national historiography treats the Fergana Rim as part of Dayuan's territory. Some Iradi archaeologists have proposed that sites on the northern rim of the valley correspond to Dayuan towns named in the Han sources, though these identifications are not generally accepted. Han coins and other objects found in the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley are cited in Iradi writing as evidence that Dayuan horses were bred there as well. Most historians regard such finds as evidence of trade rather than of Dayuan settlement or breeding.<sup>[3]</sup>

The heavenly horses also feature in the national belief that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication. That belief rests on the Botai culture (c. 3700–3100 BCE) of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Genetic studies since 2018 indicate that the Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, whose ancestors spread from the western Eurasian steppe.<sup>[4]</sup> Iradi popular writing nonetheless often presents Botai, Dayuan and the modern breeds as a single unbroken line.

## The Akyel breed
The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and the state stud describe the Akyel as a direct descendant of the Dayuan horse. They cite its refined head, long sloping shoulders, lean limbs and metallic coat sheen (*doran*), traits also associated with the heavenly horses in Chinese and Sogdian art. Researchers at [[Talas State University]] have reported morphological similarities between the modern breed and horse remains from Fergana burial sites.<sup>[3]</sup> Independent geneticists note that the Akyel shares markers with other Central Asian light breeds such as the [[wp:Akhal-Teke]]. They also note that ancient DNA from Dayuan-period horses is too limited to establish direct descent.<sup>[2]</sup>

The breed society's promotional literature speaks of "five thousand years" of continuous breeding. Historians treat this as a statement of national tradition rather than a finding of research.<sup>[3]</sup>

## In culture
The heavenly horses are a recurring image in Iradi art, poetry and state symbolism. They also feature in the Dayuan episode of the 1979 film *[[Rise of Glory]]*. Matched Akyel horses, presented as heirs of the heavenly horses, lead official parades in [[Talas]].<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.15. East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl**, also called the Iradi-Syriac Rite, are the liturgical and sacramental traditions of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], centered on the archiepiscopal see of [[Iyık Janyl]]. They derive from the rite of the Church of the East, whose missionaries worked in [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] from about the sixth century and among the Turkic peoples of [[wp:Central Asia]] in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.<sup>[1]</sup> Over centuries of isolation the rite absorbed local pastoral customs. Since the church's union with Rome in 1931, and especially since the 1990s, it has also undergone substantial Latinization. Worship is conducted in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and in Iradi, and the liturgical vocabulary includes terms of Sogdian origin.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## History
Church tradition traces the Iradi church to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], whom it places in the eleventh century; some chronicles associate her with the period of [[wp:Qara Khitai]] rule in the twelfth. Historians place its origins in the wider spread of [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] among Turkic groups such as the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]]. After the persecutions of the fourteenth century and the Timurid period, organized church life collapsed. Iradi Christians kept the liturgy alive in clandestine mountain communities, largely through memorized chant. Nineteenth-century travelers, including the missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]], recorded the community's survival. Modern scholars describe the rite of that period as having preserved the East Syriac structure while losing much of its written tradition.<sup>[3]</sup>

Union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* (1931) recognized the rite as that of a church *sui iuris*. Soviet anti-religious campaigns closed most churches from 1937. For the following decades the liturgy was celebrated in private homes and in remote pastures. After independence the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] revised the liturgical books. In 1993 it approved Iradi translations for use alongside Syriac.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Liturgy
The principal Eucharistic liturgy, the [[wp:Holy Qurbana]], follows the anaphora of [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|Addai and Mari]], one of the oldest Christian Eucharistic prayers in use. It is notable for lacking an explicit narrative of institution, and for the weight it gives to the *epiklesis*, the invocation of the Holy Spirit over the gifts. As in the [[wp:Chaldean Catholic Church]], two further East Syriac anaphoras are used on particular days.<sup>[2]</sup>

Church buildings in the traditional style place a raised platform (*bema*) in the nave, from which the readings are chanted, and a sanctuary (*madbaha*) behind a carved walnut screen. Liturgical vocabulary in Iradi preserves words of Sogdian origin. Examples include *kuble*, the orientation of the sanctuary toward [[wp:Polaris]], and *iyık*, "holy", used for relics and sacred places. The Syriac antiphons (*'onitha*) are sung to melodies passed down orally. Unusually for a Catholic rite, they are often accompanied by the bowed *kyl-kyak* and the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]].<sup>[3]</sup>

The liturgical year follows the East Syriac calendar (see [[Iradi calendar]]). It includes the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites before Lent, which in Iradi practice is a period of strict fasting in rural areas.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Pastoral rites and inculturation
Several features of the rite reflect the pastoral life of its congregations:
- **The Blessing of the Herds:** held on 24 August, the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Priests sprinkle spring water on horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade in Iyık Janyl and at rural churches.
- **Arsha incense:** juniper smoke is burned in place of, or alongside, frankincense (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]).
- **Kümöch:** the Eucharistic bread is an unleavened, stamped wheat loaf (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).
- **Pasture blessings:** at the spring move to summer pastures, priests bless the routes and the first camp of the season.
- **Tent chapels:** in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], itinerant priests celebrate the liturgy in felt yurts, sometimes outdoors at night.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Latinization and the urban–tribal divide
Since the 1990s, contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions has brought Western elements into urban parishes in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]]. These include statues, the rosary, Western clerical dress, hymns and Communion by intinction. Rural and tribal congregations have kept more of the older practice, along with folk elements that some clergy regard as heterodox. Debate over Latinization is a recurring theme in the synod.<sup>[2]</sup>

Clergy are trained in Classical Syriac and the rite at the major seminary of St. Ephrem in Iyık Janyl. The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] maintains the chant tradition.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.16. Janyl, Mother of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

{{Hatnote|This article is about the saint and her tradition. For whether she existed, see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]].}}

**Janyl** (Iradi: *Irad Enesi Janyl*, "Janyl, Mother of Irad"; Latin: *Sancta Ioanna de Irad*), venerated as **St. Janyl**, is the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. According to the tradition of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], she received a vision of Jesus in the form of the White Rider. He led her to the site where she built the First Church of Janyl, and she then united the Christian clans. Her feast on 24 August is the most important festival of the Iradi church. Modern scholars widely dispute her historical existence (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]), and the location of the First Church is unknown.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Hagiography
The fullest written account of Janyl's life is an eighteenth-century vita compiled at Iyık Janyl after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727. Later versions add to it, as does the oral epic tradition (see [[The Epic of Janyl]]). Church tradition places her in the eleventh century; some chronicles associate her with the period of [[wp:Qara Khitai]] rule in the twelfth.<sup>[1]</sup>

In the standard account, Janyl was the daughter of a Christian chieftain of [[wp:Keraites|Kerait]] descent. When war between the clans and persecution threatened her people, she withdrew to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray. There Christ appeared to her as the White Rider, a horseman in white on a shining horse. He told her to gather the scattered Christian clans and lead them to a spring in the mountains, where she was to build a church. In a widespread variant he leads her through the night by the light of [[wp:Polaris]], the star the [[Iradis]] call *Irad*. This version connects her story with the [[The Legend of the White Rider|legend of the White Rider]] and with the star on the national flag.<sup>[2]</sup>

Janyl gathered the clans and built the First Church of Janyl at the spring. She then bound the clans to a covenant. Church tradition credits this covenant with several later Iradi customs:
- the reverence for horses and the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|refusal to eat horsemeat]];
- the blessing of the herds;
- the keeping of the East Syriac liturgy.

The tradition does not record her death or burial place, and no tomb has ever been identified.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Interpretation
Many ethnographers read the legend as a memory of how the Iradi people came to be. In their interpretation, Janyl's journey into the mountains stands for the flight of Iranian-speaking Christians from the towns of the Jaxartes valley, which became Muslim under the Kara-Khanids, into the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal, where they mixed with Turkic highland tribes and formed the Christian clans the story says she united (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## The First Church of Janyl
The location of the First Church is unknown. Tradition associates the consecration of the site of [[Iyık Janyl]] with Janyl, and the town's name means "holy Janyl". Several places have been proposed as the site of the original church:
- the basilica excavated at the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna);
- a cave chapel at about 1,990 meters in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]];
- several springs in the Chatkal range that are visited by pilgrims.

The church has made no official determination.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Veneration
Little is known of Janyl's cult before the eighteenth century. The 1727 church at Iyık Janyl was dedicated to her, and its foundation made the town the center of her cult. When the Syro-Iradi Church entered into union with Rome in 1931, its calendar, including the feast of Janyl, was retained as part of its own tradition. Under Soviet rule public celebration of the feast was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s, although private pilgrimages continued.<sup>[1]</sup>

The [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August draws large numbers of pilgrims to Iyık Janyl, many of them on horseback. It includes:
- the liturgy at the cathedral;
- the blessing of the herds on the esplanade;
- the distribution of blessed *kümöch* bread;
- processions, followed by horse races and feasting.

Janyl is regarded as the patron of Irad, of riders and herders, and of mothers.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Iconography
Iradi icons show Janyl as a horsewoman rather than as a nun or queen. She wears a white felt headdress (*elechek*) and rides a golden [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horse, holding a cross in one hand and the reins in the other. In some images the White Rider rides before her, or Polaris shines above her. Her icon hangs in churches, public buildings and family homes in both the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Statues of her stand in Central Square in [[Talas]] and on the cathedral esplanade in Iyık Janyl.<sup>[4]</sup>

## As a national symbol
Beyond the church, Janyl is a national symbol of Irad, invoked by politicians of all factions and used in civic ceremony, school textbooks and commercial branding. The monastic [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] and the church's Order of St. Janyl, an honor for service to the church and culture, both take her name.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.17. Janyl (Historical Figure)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

{{Hatnote|This article is about the historical question of Janyl. For the saint as the church venerates her, see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]].}}

The historicity of **Janyl**, the founding figure venerated by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] as [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]], is a long-running question in Iradi and Central Asian historiography. Church tradition places her in the eleventh century, or in some chronicles the twelfth, under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]], as a Christian noblewoman who united the Christian Turkic clans. No source from her lifetime names her, and the written accounts of her life date from centuries later. Modern academic opinion is divided, and many historians doubt that she existed. Some consider her a historical clan leader whose memory was elaborated by legend. Others regard her as a composite or wholly legendary figure.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Historical setting
In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] spread among Turkic groups of [[wp:Central Asia]], including the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]]. Under the Qara Khitai, who conquered the region in the 1130s, Christian communities in the Chu and Talas basins and their foothills enjoyed a degree of tolerance.<sup>[3]</sup> Archaeology confirms the presence of organized Christian communities in this period. At the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), the foundations of the settlement date from the eleventh century. Hundreds of gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] date from about 1240 to 1338.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Sources

#### Church tradition
The earliest surviving vita of Janyl is an eighteenth-century text compiled at [[Iyık Janyl]]. It was probably written after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727 and the library in 1732, and copies are held in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]]. It draws on oral tradition and on liturgical hymns whose age is uncertain. The vita gives the clans' Kerait descent, the White Rider vision and the founding of the First Church, but few verifiable details such as names of rulers or datable events.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### The epic tradition
The heroic epic known as [[The Epic of Janyl]], or *Janyl Baatyr* ("Janyl the Valiant"), is sung by bards (*ırchy*) to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. It presents Janyl as a warrior who fights mountain ambushes, shoots from the saddle and negotiates for pastures with foreign governors. Folklorists recorded versions of it from the late nineteenth century onward, and Soviet collectors gathered more in the 1930s–1950s. The epic contains little Christian content. Folklorists note close parallels with *Janyl Myrza*, a Kyrgyz epic about a warrior maiden, and with other Turkic heroine epics.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### External sources
No Chinese, Persian, Arabic or Armenian source names Janyl. The *Chronicon Ecclesiasticum* of the thirteenth-century Syriac historian [[wp:Bar Hebraeus|Gregory Bar Hebraeus]] contains the earliest recorded mention of the name Irad in connection with the region's Christians, and it records the conversion of Christian Turkic peoples such as the Keraites. Some Iradi historians have connected his accounts to the Janyl tradition. Critics point out that he does not mention her.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### Archaeology
No archaeological find has been securely connected to Janyl. In the 1980s a silver ring was found at Shar-i-Kuhna bearing a short Syriac inscription. Some Iradi archaeologists have read it as a female form of the name Yohannan (John) and associated it with Janyl's Latin name, *Ioanna*. Most specialists consider both the reading and the attribution unproven. The ring dates from the thirteenth century, a century or more after the traditional dates. None of the dated gravestones from the site mentions her, and the First Church has not been located.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Scholarly positions
- **Historical.** Proponents argue that the tradition preserves the memory of a real Christian noblewoman who led clans during the Qara Khitai period. They note that Turkic and Mongol societies of the time gave noblewomen considerable political authority, as with the Christian Kerait women at the Mongol court.
- **Composite.** Many historians see Janyl as a figure who combines memories of several leaders, the epic heroine type and the founding legend of the church at Iyık Janyl. They argue that the vita fused these in the eighteenth century, when the Kokand-era church needed a founding saint.
- **Legendary.** Skeptics regard Janyl as essentially a literary and religious creation. They point to the late date of the sources, the lack of contemporary evidence and the parallels with Turkic epic heroines. Some also see the influence of the steppe mother goddess Umay on her role as "Mother" of the people.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **Ethnographic (migration).** Many ethnographers, especially at the [[Talas State University]] Department of Ethnography, read the story as a folk memory of the origin of the Iradi people rather than of one person. In this view, Iranian-speaking East Syriac Christians of the towns along the [[wp:Syr Darya|Jaxartes]], such as [[wp:Tashkent|Shash]], [[wp:Sayram|Isfijab]] and [[wp:Otrar]], were pushed out as those towns became Muslim under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] in the tenth and eleventh centuries. They moved north and east into the mountains of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal, where they mingled with Turkic highland tribes. Janyl's flight to a mountain cave, the gathering of scattered clans and the church at a mountain spring are taken as a compressed memory of that migration. Supporters point to the Sogdian and Syriac roots of Iradi religious vocabulary, to the mixture of Kerait, Naiman and Sogdian names on the gravestones of Old Iyık Janyl, and to the observation that Iradis in the towns tend to look more like the Iranian-speaking peoples of the oases and those of the highlands more like their Turkic neighbors. Critics reply that the vita itself makes Janyl a Kerait chieftain's daughter, not a townswoman, and that the migration is inferred rather than documented; historians who derive the Iradis from Christianized Keraites or from Naimans pushed west by the Mongols read the legend as a memory of those Turkic peoples instead (see [[Iradis]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## Historiography and politics
Soviet scholarship treated Janyl as a figure of feudal and clerical legend. It studied the epic as folklore and played down its Christian elements. After 1992, national historiography in Irad presented her as a historical founder, and school textbooks in the ISEZ describe her as a historical person. Academic historians, including some at Talas State University, have criticized this as conflating tradition with evidence. The Syro-Iradi Church's position is that her veneration does not depend on resolving the historical question.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.18. Central Asian Pastoral Migration System
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

The **Central Asian pastoral migration system** (Iradi: *köchüm-konush ulgusu*) is the seasonal movement of herders and livestock between pastures at different altitudes and in different zones. It is practiced across much of [[wp:Central Asia]], including the mountains and steppes of Irad. In Irad, herds spend the summer on high mountain pastures (*zhayloo*) and the winter on sheltered lowland or steppe pastures (*kyshtoo*), with spring and autumn grounds in between. The system was disrupted by Soviet collectivization. It revived after 1992 and remains the main livelihood of much of the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where clan councils govern pasture use under customary law. Since 2007 the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] has cut across several traditional routes.<sup>[1]</sup>

## The seasonal cycle
The yearly cycle has four stages, each with its own type of pasture and, in Christian clans, its own church blessings (see [[Iradi calendar]]):
- **Spring pastures (*jazdoo*):** in April and May herds move from winter quarters to foothill and steppe grazing, where early grasses appear after the snowmelt. Lambing and foaling take place in late winter and spring.
- **Summer pastures (*zhayloo*):** in June families take the herds up to alpine meadows, mostly above 2,500 meters, in the [[Talas Alatau]], the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] and on plateaus such as the [[Aksay Plateau]]. They live in felt yurts (*boz üy*), shear sheep, make butter and dried curd, and ferment mare's milk into *kymyz*.
- **Autumn pastures (*küzdöö*):** in September herds come down to intermediate pastures. Animals are sold or slaughtered for winter, and hay is gathered.
- **Winter pastures (*kyshtoo*):** from November herds stay in sheltered valleys of the [[Talas River|Talas]] and Chatkal basins or on the steppe and sand pastures to the north, where snow cover is thin.

There are two broad patterns of movement. Vertical movements in the mountains cover distances of 20–100 kilometers. Longer horizontal movements of up to 300 kilometers link the summer pastures of the Talas Alatau and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] with winter grounds in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands and the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], and with the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] to the west.<sup>[1]</sup>

Herds consist mainly of sheep and goats, with cattle, horses and, at the highest pastures, a small number of yaks. Horses, especially the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]], are used for herding and transport and are kept for *kymyz*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Early history
Pastoralism with seasonal movement has been practiced in the region since the [[wp:Bronze Age]], when Andronovo-culture herders moved between valley and mountain grazing.<sup>[2]</sup> Under the [[wp:Saka]], the Turkic khaganates and their successors, mobile pastoralism coexisted with irrigated farming and towns in the valleys. Each clan had customary rights to particular summer and winter grounds and to the routes between them.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Russian and Soviet rule
Russian colonization after 1876 took much winter and spring pasture for Slavic settlers, a grievance behind the 1916 [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. Soviet policy went further. The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] confiscated herds and forced pastoralists into collective and state farms. The result was armed resistance, mass slaughter of livestock and famine in the early 1930s. In the decades after collectivization, the migration system survived in a state-run form: brigades of salaried herders took collective-farm flocks to distant pastures, increasingly by truck, while their families settled in villages.<sup>[3]</sup>

In the 1970s the filling of the Toktogul reservoir, behind the dam of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], flooded valley villages and winter pastures along the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. This forced the resettlement of herding communities.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### After independence
The collapse of the collective farms after 1991 and the [[First Iradi Civil War|civil war of 1992]] led to the division of state flocks among households. Clan-based migration revived in the tribal areas. Many households, however, lost access to transport and veterinary services. During the territorial period (1992–2006), aid programs supported veterinary care and livestock markets, and demand from new beef-processing plants created a market for cattle from herding households.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Governance
In the Autonomous Tribal Regions, pasture use is governed by clan councils of elders (*aksakals*) under customary law (*adat*). The councils allocate summer pastures, set the dates of movement and settle disputes between households and clans (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). Cooperatives such as the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] organize joint herding, veterinary campaigns and marketing. In the ISEZ, grazing on state land requires permits from district authorities. Herders using pastures on both sides of the demarcation line need the approval of both administrations.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Contemporary status
No reliable count exists of the number of people who depend on mobile herding, partly because of the disputed census figures for the tribal regions. Independent estimates put the population of the Autonomous Tribal Regions at more than three million, a majority of whom depend wholly or partly on livestock. Official figures are lower.<sup>[4]</sup>

The main problems reported by researchers and aid agencies are:
- **Uneven grazing:** pastures near villages are overgrazed, while distant summer pastures are underused for lack of transport.
- **Animal disease:** brucellosis and foot-and-mouth disease remain common.
- **Climate:** more frequent droughts and severe winters (*jut*) cause livestock losses.
- **The demarcation line:** since the 2007 [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement]], the Qara-Chik line has divided routes between summer pastures in the mountains and winter grounds in the north and west. Seasonal crossing points negotiated under [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UNMI]] auspices allow herders to cross on fixed dates. Herders report delays, fees and confiscations at checkpoints.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.19. National Equestrian Sports Directorate
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Sport*

The **National Equestrian Sports Directorate of Irad** (Iradi: *Uluttuk At Sportu Direktoratu*) is the government body that regulates traditional and modern equestrian sport in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It was established in 1993 by an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and is headquartered at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]]. It sets the rules of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] and other horseback games, licenses riders and referees, runs doping and veterinary controls, and organizes national championships, including the annual [[President's Cup]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period, equestrian sport in the Iradi SSR came under the republican Committee for Physical Culture and Sport. The committee codified the rules of ulak tartysh in 1953 and ran equestrian events at republican sports festivals. The Talas hippodrome, then called the Central Hippodrome, was its main venue.<sup>[2]</sup>

The Directorate was created in 1993, during the territorial period, to take over these functions and to organize national competitions after the collapse of the Soviet sports system. The previous year Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] had instituted the President's Cup for ulak tartysh, and the Directorate took over its organization. The hippodrome was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed the Irad State Hippodrome.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since 2007 the Directorate has operated under the ISEZ administration, and its director is appointed by the Governor. Its authority in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] depends on the cooperation of clan councils. Clan teams and hunters take part in its competitions voluntarily, and many traditional events in the tribal regions are held without its involvement.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Functions
The Directorate's statutory responsibilities include:
- setting and revising competition rules for traditional and modern disciplines;
- licensing riders, trainers and referees;
- veterinary inspection and doping control of competition horses;
- organizing the national league and championships;
- recording results and performance tests used in breed certification.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Sanctioned disciplines
- **Ulak tartysh:** the principal team sport. The autumn ulak league has a division of city and district teams, among them Talas, Sary-Bulak, [[Semiz]] and Iyık Janyl, which play at the Irad State Hippodrome, and a Highland division of clan teams from the tribal regions, among them the Boztorgoy, Karakoyun, Tanıp and Kökjal. The league had 24 teams in the 2023 season (11 from ISEZ cities and districts, 13 registered by clans).
- **At chabysh:** long-distance races of 20 to 50 kilometers over open steppe courses, mainly for [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses.
- **Kyz kuu and oodarysh:** the courtship chase and mounted wrestling, usually staged at national holidays.
- **Tyin emmei:** picking up coins or tokens from the ground at the gallop.
- **Eagle hunting:** contests in [[Burkut Saluu|burkut saluu]] at the autumn Salburun festival, organized with falconers' associations.
- **Flat racing:** thoroughbred and Akyel races at the Irad State Hippodrome.
- **Charreada:** Mexican charro roping and the women's *escaramuza*, shown with Iradi games such as *kyz kuu* and *alaman-bayge* at the *Eki Eldin At Oyunu* ("horse games of two peoples"), held each September at the Lienzo Charro de Semiz, which the Directorate has sanctioned since 2012.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Facilities
The Irad State Hippodrome seats about 25,000 spectators. It has dirt racecourses, a field for ulak tartysh, stabling and a veterinary clinic. The President's Cup final is held there each March in the week of Irad Day, and [[IradOne]] holds the broadcasting rights. The Directorate also sanctions regional fields in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]] and the larger district centers.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Betting and commercial concessions
Under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011, wagers may legally be placed only on the Directorate's pari-mutuel tote, at windows at the Hippodrome and at the regional fields in Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl; bookmaking and online gambling are illegal, and [[Attelkom]] blocks offshore betting sites on a list of restricted resources. In November 2023, at the Directorate's request, Attelkom blocked a betting site run for the Curaçao-registered Steppe Gaming N.V., which had been linked from the odds page of the horse-games portal [[Jarysh]]. Bookmakers continue to take bets on racing and ulak through messaging channels.<sup>[4]</sup>

In June 2018 the Directorate awarded Jarysh Entertainment Group, the company of the former nightclub promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]], a seven-year concession to run the beer decks, stage and VIP boxes at the Hippodrome on league Saturdays, without a public tender. The company keeps the bar and ticket revenue above a fixed fee to the Directorate and stages the Saturday-night *Aigyr Ulak Nights*, sponsored by the brewer of [[Aigyr Lager]].<sup>[5]</sup> In June 2025 the concession was renewed for ten years, to 2035, again without a tender; the renewal was not announced and was found in the Directorate's annual report by opposition members of the city council. Opposition politicians describe the arrangement as patronage and point to a 2019 photograph of Baisalov with [[Alikhan Toktarov]] at the Dubai World Cup.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Breeding and international activity
The Directorate works with the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. It supplies the performance records used to certify horses for breeding and export. Because [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] all claim Irad, Directorate teams have not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]]. Individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Criticism
Opposition figures and some clan leaders have accused the Directorate of political patronage. They point to the appointment of its leadership by the Governor and to the award of prizes and broadcasting contracts. Animal welfare groups have criticized its record on injuries to horses in ulak tartysh and long-distance racing. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.20. 1956 Talas Riots
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

| injuries = Disputed; archival estimates vary widely

The **1956 Talas riots** (Iradi: *1956-jylgy Talas topolongu*; Russian: *Таласские беспорядки 1956 года*) were five days of rioting and street fighting in [[Talas]], in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], between 14 June and 18 June 1956. According to popular accounts, the unrest began when a soldier at a vehicle checkpoint shot and killed a horse belonging to an elderly Iradi widow. Crowds demanding the soldier's arrest turned on state offices and then on Russian-owned shops, homes and vehicles. Troops of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]] restored order under martial law. More than a thousand people, almost all of them ethnic Iradis, were detained, and several hundred were later deported to other parts of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Archival estimates of the dead vary.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Historians place the riots among the disturbances that followed [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] in February 1956. Besides the shooting itself, they point to grievances that had built up over the previous decade: housing shortages in a city swollen by migrant labor, wage gaps between Iradi and newly arrived Slavic workers, Russian-only schooling, the suppression of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and the long aftermath of collectivization.<sup>[3]</sup> Soviet sources said little about the events for more than three decades. Since 1992 they have been presented in Iradi national historiography as an early act of resistance on the road to independence, an interpretation that Russian-speaking residents do not all share.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Background

Talas in the early 1950s was the republic's main center of food processing and light industry, while the capital, Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), was growing quickly after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]] in the Chu basin. Both cities absorbed thousands of Russian and Ukrainian workers, engineers and demobilized servicemen in the postwar years, and in 1952 a Soviet air-defense airfield was built outside Talas, on the site of the present [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] launched in 1954 brought a further wave of Slavic settlers into the steppe districts north of the Chu, where new state farms grew maize and raised beef cattle with unusual success.

Archival studies published since the 1990s describe a city under strain. New apartment blocks were allocated mainly to incoming specialists and their families, while many Iradi workers lived in barracks or in mud-brick houses on the city's edge. Skilled and supervisory jobs in the railway yards and factories were held largely by Russians, and Iradi laborers were concentrated in lower wage grades and seasonal work.<sup>[3]</sup> Collective farms around Talas were still meeting high postwar procurement quotas.

Cultural grievances ran alongside the economic ones. Iradi-language schooling had been closed in the late 1930s, the churches of [[Iyık Janyl]] had been shut during [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the 1937 purges]], and an all-Union anti-religious campaign in 1954 renewed pressure on the clandestine parishes that had survived the war. The mass seizure of clan herds under the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] and the wartime requisitioning of horses, which had provoked the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], remained within living memory. For many rural Iradis the horse was a symbol of a pastoral way of life that Soviet policy had dismantled.<sup>[4]</sup>

The political climate changed in 1956. Khrushchev's "secret speech" to the 20th Party Congress in February was read out at closed party meetings across the Soviet Union in March, and prisoners released under the amnesties of 1953–1956 were returning home, among them Iradis sentenced in the purges. In March 1956 troops had fired on demonstrators in [[wp:Tbilisi]], an event that was known in [[wp:Central Asia]] by rumor rather than through the press.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The checkpoint incident

The shooting that began the riots is known mainly from oral tradition, and its details differ between versions. In the most widely repeated account, on the morning of 14 June 1956, a soldier manning a vehicle checkpoint on the road into the city near the collective-farm market fired at a horse-drawn cart that had not stopped, killing the horse of an elderly widow who was bringing produce to the market. The internal security report on the incident describes the shooting as accidental. Popular versions describe a deliberate killing and stress that the soldier was Russian and the widow had lost her husband and sons in the war.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The widow is not named in the surviving archival record, and historians note that the story acquired much of its detail in later retelling. The incident is treated in more detail in [[Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)]].

## Course of the riots

Within hours of the shooting, several hundred market traders, seasonal farm laborers and demobilized soldiers gathered outside the city militia headquarters to demand that the soldier be arrested and tried in a civilian court. Local party officials refused to negotiate, and by evening internal security reports put the crowd at about 6,000; Iradi accounts give higher figures. Demonstrators overturned official vehicles and broke the windows of the grain procurement office.<sup>[1]</sup>

On 15 June workers from the railway maintenance yard joined the protest and marched on the building of the city soviet executive committee. Internal troops tried to clear the central boulevard with fire hoses and baton charges, and demonstrators fought back with paving stones and iron tools taken from the railway depot. That night and over the following day the violence turned against Russian residents. Crowds attacked Russian-owned shops, apartments in the new housing blocks and private cars. Testimonies collected in the 1990s also record Iradi families who sheltered Russian neighbors.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

On the morning of 17 June units of the Turkestan Military District entered the city, with reinforcements of internal troops flown in to the air-defense airfield. Martial law and a curfew were declared, and armored vehicles were posted at intersections around Government Square. The last crowds dispersed on 18 June.<sup>[1]</sup>

Casualty figures remain disputed. Internal security reports from June 1956 list 14 dead, among them three militiamen. Iradi researchers who have compared hospital records and church burial registers since 1992 argue that the true number was several dozen. Archival estimates of the number of wounded vary even more widely.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Arrests, trials and deportations

Over the following weeks more than 1,000 people, almost all ethnic Iradis, were detained. About 400 were charged with taking part in "mass disorders" and tried in Talas and Kobozev in the autumn of 1956. Several dozen received long sentences in labor camps.<sup>[1]</sup> Several hundred more detainees were never tried but were deported by administrative order to Siberia and northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and many did not return to Talas. Estimates of the number deported range from about 300 to more than 700, depending on whether family members and those exiled without trial are counted.<sup>[3]</sup>

A commission from [[wp:Moscow]] blamed the republican leadership for "political blindness" toward nationalist and religious elements. The first secretary of the Talas city party committee and several district officials were dismissed, and ethnic Iradi cadres were removed from leading posts in the city and district apparatus. Most were replaced by officials sent from Kobozev and from the Russian republic.<sup>[3]</sup> Historians note that repression was accompanied by concessions: the authorities sped up housing construction in Talas in 1957–1960 and raised payments to collective farm workers in the surrounding districts.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Soviet treatment

The republican press reported only "hooligan disorders" provoked by "nationalist and clerical elements", and the riots were left out of official histories of the republic. Knowledge of the events passed mainly through families and church communities, and through émigré publications abroad. Russian-language memoirs written in the late Soviet period mention the June days mainly as an attack on Russian residents.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Historiography and memory

Research on the riots began when the [[State Archives of Irad]] opened the relevant internal security files after 1992. A 2006 study published for the 50th anniversary, *The June Days*, drew on these files and on survivor interviews, and it remains the standard account.<sup>[3]</sup> Historians at [[Talas State University]] have placed the riots alongside other post-Stalin disturbances, including the Tbilisi events of March 1956 and the [[wp:Temirtau]] and [[wp:Novocherkassk massacre|Novocherkassk]] riots of 1959 and 1962, in which local grievances over housing and wages combined with ethnic and political tension.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

In the national narrative that took shape after independence, the riots link the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] with the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] in a tradition of resistance, and the widow's horse has become a symbol of national dignity. Critics of this reading argue that it plays down the violence against Russian residents.<sup>[4]</sup> Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the events are often described as an anti-Russian pogrom.

In 1996, a bronze statue of a riderless horse, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], was unveiled near the site of the former collective-farm market in Talas. Memorial gatherings are held there each year on 14 June.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.21. Semirechye Revolt (Irad)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Semirechye Revolt (Iradi districts)
| partof = the [[wp:Central Asian revolt of 1916]]
| date = August – October 1916; flight to China into winter 1916–17
| place = Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys and the Fergana rim ([[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts, [[wp:Russian Turkestan]])
| result = Revolt suppressed; Punitive reprisals and land confiscation proposals; Mass flight to [[wp:Xinjiang]] (*Urkun*); see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]
| combatant1 = Iradi clans; Kyrgyz and Kazakh rebels
| combatant2 = [[wp:Russian Empire]]; Settler militias
| commander1 = Clan elders (*aksakals*)
| commander2 = [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin]]
| units1 = Mounted irregular bands
| units2 = Cossack cavalry; Regular infantry with machine guns; Mountain artillery; Armed settler militias
| casualties3 = Settlers: several thousand killed or missing across Turkestan and Semirechye (official Russian figures); Native population: tens of thousands to over 100,000 dead in the revolt, suppression and flight across Turkestan and the steppe; Iradi districts: about 100,000 fled and 30,000–50,000 died (Iradi historians' estimate, not checkable against imperial records)
}}

The **Semirechye Revolt** of 1916, also called the Central Asian Revolt of 1916 (Iradi: *1916-jylgy kötörülüsh*; Russian: *Восстание 1916 года в Средней Азии*), was an armed uprising against Russian rule in [[wp:Turkestan]] and the Kazakh steppe. It was set off by a Tsarist decree of 25 June 1916 (8 July, New Style) that called up native men, previously exempt from military service, for wartime labor behind the front. This article covers the revolt in the Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys and on the Fergana rim, the districts that now make up Irad, where Iradi clans rose alongside their Kyrgyz and Kazakh neighbors in August 1916.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The rebels attacked settler villages, administrative posts and telegraph lines, and several thousand Russian and Ukrainian settlers were killed across the region. Punitive expeditions under [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin|Governor-General Aleksey Kuropatkin]], assisted by armed settler militias, crushed the rising in September and October 1916. Tens of thousands of herders and their families then fled east across the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward China during the winter of 1916–17, a flight known as the *Urkun* ("exodus") in which many died of cold and hunger. In Iradi memory the revolt is tied to the fate of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]], clans that retreated into the eastern mountains and were never seen again. It is commemorated in the crimson field of the national flag and in the inverted horseshoe of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background

The [[wp:Russian Empire]] completed its conquest of the region when [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in 1876. The Iradi-inhabited valleys were divided between the Fergana and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts of the [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Governor-Generalship of Turkestan]].<sup>[2]</sup> Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlement in Semirechye grew quickly after 1906, when the [[wp:Pyotr Stolypin|Stolypin]] agrarian reforms encouraged migration to Asiatic Russia. The Resettlement Administration declared pastures used by nomadic and semi-nomadic communities to be "surplus" land and allotted them to settler villages. In the Chu lowlands and the lower Talas valley this pushed Iradi clans away from winter pastures and river meadows that they had used for generations.<sup>[4]</sup>

The [[wp:World War I|First World War]] increased the pressure. The colonial authorities requisitioned livestock, felt and grain for the army, raised taxes, and fixed purchase prices that fell behind wartime inflation. Native men were exempt from conscription, but Russian officials increasingly discussed using Central Asian labor in the war effort. Although most [[Iradis]] were Christians, the Tsarist administration classed them with the region's Muslim peoples as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"), subject to the same legal disabilities and exemptions.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The mobilization decree

The imperial decree of 25 June 1916 ordered the call-up of male *inorodtsy* aged 19 to 43 for labor on fortifications and military communications in the zone of the active army. Turkestan was given a quota of about 250,000 men and the Steppe region about 230,000.<sup>[1]</sup> The order arrived in the middle of the harvest and the hay-cutting season, when the absence of working-age men threatened the pastoral cycle. It gave no exemptions for families without other providers. Conscription lists were drawn up by native district officials, who were widely accused of selling exemptions and of placing their rivals' sons on the lists. Rumors spread that the men were being sent to be killed at the front.<sup>[2]</sup>

The first violence broke out on 4 July ([[wp:Old Style and New Style dates|Old Style]]) in [[wp:Khujand]], and in mid-July a larger rising took place around [[wp:Jizzakh]]. In Semirechye, Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities rose in the second week of August, besieging Przhevalsk and attacking settlements around Pishpek and [[wp:Tokmok]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## The revolt in the Iradi districts

According to Iradi tradition and the records of the Talas district administration, clan elders (*aksakals*) in the Talas and Chu valleys held councils in early August 1916 and resolved to refuse the call-up. Later accounts say they swore oaths on their horses.<sup>[5]</sup> Mounted bands armed with hunting rifles, old matchlocks, spears and lassos attacked volost administrative centers, burned conscription lists, cut the telegraph lines to [[wp:Almaty|Verny]] (now Almaty), and drove off livestock that had been requisitioned for the army. Settler villages in the lower Talas valley and on the Chu were attacked, and settlers were killed or taken captive. Iradi accounts of the revolt mention ambushes on supply columns in the defiles of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and describe how mounted irregulars on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses outpaced Cossack detachments in the mountains. These details come mainly from oral tradition.<sup>[5]</sup>

The Iradi rising merged with the Kyrgyz and Kazakh revolts around it. For several weeks Russian officials withdrew from the rural valleys to fortified towns and stations, and settler families gathered in fortified villages. Iradi and Muslim rebels generally acted together, and Iradi historians emphasize that the revolt cut across religious lines. Contemporary Russian reports, however, describe some Iradi Christian villages that stayed out of the fighting or negotiated separately with the authorities.<sup>[4]</sup>

Settler losses were heavy. Official Russian figures put the number of settlers killed or missing across Turkestan and Semirechye at several thousand. No separate count exists for the Iradi districts.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Suppression

Kuropatkin, a former Minister of War, was appointed Governor-General of Turkestan in July 1916 and organized the suppression of the revolt. Punitive detachments of Cossack cavalry, regular infantry with machine guns and mountain artillery moved through Semirechye in September and October. Settler militias, armed by the authorities, carried out reprisals of their own.<sup>[2]</sup> Villages and camps were burned, herds were confiscated, and suspected leaders were executed without trial. Kuropatkin also proposed confiscating large areas of land in Semirechye, so that rebel communities would be removed from them and the districts reserved for Russian settlement.<sup>[1]</sup>

Estimates of the number of native people who died in the revolt, its suppression and the flight that followed range from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 across Turkestan and the steppe. Historians agree that losses were heaviest in Semirechye. Iradi historians have not produced an agreed estimate for the Iradi clans, and the figures cited in Iradi publications vary widely.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## The flight to China

As the punitive expeditions advanced, entire communities abandoned their pastures and moved east toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then ruled for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin|Governor Yang Zengxin]]. The largest movement came from the [[wp:Issyk-Kul]] region, but Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys also joined the flight, moving up the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and across the high passes of the Tian Shan.<sup>[3]</sup> The crossings took place from the autumn of 1916 into the winter of 1916–17. Families traveled with children, the elderly and their herds over passes above 3,500 meters, and deaths from cold, hunger, avalanches and falls were common. Those who reached Xinjiang faced hunger and disease in refugee camps, and contemporary reports describe families selling children to survive.<sup>[6]</sup>

The Provisional Government that came to power in [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Petrograd]] after the [[wp:February Revolution]] of 1917 allowed the refugees to return. Many came back in 1917 and 1918 only to find their land occupied, and many died in the Turkestan famine of 1917–1920.<sup>[2]</sup> In Iradi tradition, the final phase of the revolt is remembered above all for the clans that retreated east into the mountains in winter and never reappeared, known as the Lost Tribes. The flight as a whole is described in [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)]].

## Aftermath

Iradi historians identify the revolt as the starting point of more cohesive inter-clan organization. In the years after 1916, clan councils began to coordinate across the valleys through joint assemblies, a development seen as the forerunner of the modern pan-tribal [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|*Kurultai*]].<sup>[5]</sup> During 1917 an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary* attributed to Sergei Nechayev and [[wp:Mikhail Bakunin]] circulated among the clans and helped to spread an anarcho-communist current that drew on traditions of communal decision-making (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]).

When the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] broke out, most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]]. In February 1918 Iradi irregulars fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], and some Iradi volunteers served in 1918–19 on the Transcaspian front against the White Transcaspian government and the small British force supporting it.<sup>[4]</sup> The land and water reforms carried out in Semirechye in 1921–1922 returned part of the land seized from native communities, and Iradi participation on the Red side contributed to the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Historiography and memory

Tsarist officials described the revolt as a rising of "fanatics" incited by German and Ottoman agents. Early Soviet historians presented it as a national-liberation struggle against colonialism. Under [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] some historians reclassified it as "feudal and reactionary" because local notables had taken part in it, and in the post-Stalin decades it was again described as an anti-colonial rising.<sup>[2]</sup> Western scholarship, beginning with Edward Sokol's 1954 study, has focused on the colonial land question and on the scale of the repression.<sup>[1]</sup>

In Iradi national historiography developed after 1992, the revolt is the first of a series of national martyrdoms that continues through the Soviet purges to the civil wars. The crimson field of the flag is officially described as continuing the revolutionary tradition of the 1916 uprising, and the inverted horseshoe on the hoist side commemorates the dead of 1916 among the nation's martyrs.<sup>[3]</sup> Some Iradi and Kyrgyz writers describe the repression as genocide. Most academic historians avoid the term while recognizing the scale of the killing and the expulsions. The 2016 centenary was marked by commemorations in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and in both parts of Irad, and by the publication of a centenary volume in [[Talas]] that collected oral testimonies and archival documents.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.22. Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic** (Iradi SSR or ISSR; also Soviet Iradistan, or simply Iradistan; Iradi: *Irad Sovettik Sotsialisttik Respublikası*; Russian: *Ирадская Советская Социалистическая Республика*) was a union republic of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] from 1925 to 1991. It was created during the national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]], and gave the [[Iradis]] a recognized political territory of their own for the first time. The republic was governed by the [[Communist Party of Irad]], the local branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party. Its capital was Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), a planned city on the lower Chu that received its name in 1927. The republic's territory corresponded closely to that of present-day Irad: the Talas valley and the [[Talas Alatau]], the lower Chu lowlands, the Chatkal and Naryn highlands, the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], and the steppe and desert rangelands of the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] and southern [[Betpak-Dala]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The early years were shaped by *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), which standardized the Iradi language and promoted Iradi cadres. From the early 1930s the republic went through forced collectivization and famine, then a wave of anti-religious repression after the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] entered into union with Rome in 1931. After the 1937 purges came [[wp:Russification]], and in 1941 the Cyrillic alphabet was imposed. The postwar decades brought oil production from 1949, antimony mining and hydroelectric development, and also the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. On 9 October 1991 the Communist Party of Irad declared independence and reconstituted the republic as the Socialist Republic of Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Name

The name *Iradistan* combines *Irad* with the Persian suffix *-stan* ("place of"). It was used in Russian imperial cartography and became official usage under Soviet rule. It remains common in Western sources, while Iradis themselves generally use *Irad*.<sup>[2]</sup> Official documents used the full name "Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic" and the abbreviation ISSR (Russian: ИССР).

## Establishment (1918–1925)

During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]]. In February 1918 Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], and some Iradi volunteers served in 1918–19 on the Transcaspian front against the White Transcaspian government and the small British force supporting it.<sup>[2]</sup> In the early 1920s Iradi mounted units served with the [[wp:Red Army]] against the [[wp:Basmachi movement|Basmachi]] insurgency in the Fergana Valley. From 1918 the Iradi districts formed part of the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]] within the [[wp:Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|Russian SFSR]].

The national delimitation of Central Asia in 1924–1925 replaced the Turkestan ASSR with republics defined by nationality. Soviet ethnographers working for the delimitation commission identified the Iradis as a distinct nationality on the basis of their [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language and their East Syriac Christian tradition.<sup>[3]</sup> Iradi communists also cited the clans' service on the Red side in the Civil War. Early in 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]], meeting at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that later became Kobozev, proclaimed the Iradi SSR and adopted its first constitution. The new republic was admitted to the Soviet Union as a union republic later that year, following the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs, which had been created in 1924.<sup>[1]</sup> Its territory was drawn from parts of the former Syr-Darya, Fergana and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts.

## Korenizatsiia (1925–1937)

Under the Soviet policy of *korenizatsiia*, the republican authorities set out to build an Iradi national culture within the Soviet framework. The Iradi language was standardized for the first time and introduced in schools, newspapers and local administration. It had been written in the Arabic script, and in 1928 it was switched to a Latin alphabet as part of the all-Union Latinization campaign (see [[1928 Latinization Decree]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Literacy campaigns opened schools in rural districts, and ethnic Iradis were promoted to posts in the party and the state.<sup>[1]</sup>

Kobozev was laid out as a planned capital beside an existing railway settlement on the lower Chu. In 1927 it was named after the Bolshevik [[Pyotr Kobozev]], who had worked in [[wp:Turkestan]] during the Civil War. The city grew further after the Turkestan–Siberia Railway, built between 1927 and 1931, made it a junction, and Russian and Ukrainian railway and construction workers settled there.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Talas]], the main city of the Talas valley, developed as a center of food processing and light industry.

## Collectivization and famine

The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] confiscated clan herds and forced pastoral households into collective and state farms. Many herders slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, some fought back, and livestock numbers collapsed.<sup>[2]</sup> The steppe districts in the north of the republic were affected by the famine of 1930–1933 that devastated the Kazakh steppe. Clans that had wintered in the fertile plains were pushed into the eastern highlands, where many of their descendants still live in the present [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Union with Rome and the purges (1931–1938)

On 14 September 1931, [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, receiving the Iradi Church into full communion with Rome as the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. The union had been negotiated in secret by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] through papal nuncios abroad.<sup>[2]</sup> Soviet officials regarded the link with the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]], which had concluded the [[wp:Lateran Treaty]] with Mussolini's [[wp:Italy]] in 1929, as a channel for foreign and "fascist" influence. That suspicion fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s and turned the early gains of nativization into repression. Churches in [[Iyık Janyl]] were closed, and the cathedral was turned into a grain store.<sup>[1]</sup>

The repression peaked in 1937–1938. During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], state security agents executed much of Archbishop Timotheos's senior clergy and sent monks and bards to labor camps. In the same period most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists", and many of them were shot.<sup>[2]</sup> By 1937 nativization had been abandoned.

## Russification

After 1937 the authorities pursued Russification. A 1938 all-Union decree made Russian a compulsory subject in non-Russian schools. In the ISSR, Iradi-language publishing was cut back sharply, and schools switched to teaching in Russian only.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] replaced the Latin alphabet with Cyrillic, which remained the script of Iradi until 1992. Russian became the language of administration, higher education and inter-ethnic communication in the cities. The urban generation educated in these schools in the postwar decades is the origin of the Russophone population known in Irad as the *Russos* (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).

## Deportations

In 1937 the Soviet government deported more than 170,000 ethnic Koreans from the Far East to Central Asia, and several thousand were unloaded from freight trains along the railway at Kobozev and in the Chu valley. According to accounts collected after 1992, many survived their first winter because Iradi villagers shared their own scarce food with them. The deportees later introduced rice farming to the lower Chu and were gradually absorbed into urban Iradi life (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup> During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] smaller groups of deported [[wp:Volga Germans]] and peoples of the [[wp:North Caucasus]] were also resettled in the republic. Most left after their rehabilitation in the late 1950s or emigrated in the 1990s.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Second World War

Iradi men were mobilized into the Red Army, and the republic supplied cavalry remounts, wool, leather and food to the war effort. In 1944 horse breeders resisted the requisitioning of Chongtor breeding stallions for the army, hiding the animals in the high valleys until lower quotas were agreed (see [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]]).<sup>[2]</sup> As in the rest of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], evacuated factories and civilians from the western Soviet Union arrived in 1941–1942, and several plants in Kobozev and Talas date from this period.

## Postwar industrialization (1945–1985)

The [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|discovery of oil near Kobozev in 1949]] turned the republic into an oil producer. The state oil enterprise founded in Kobozev, which became [[NurGaz]] after independence, built wells, pipelines and the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], and the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]) was set up to train petroleum engineers.<sup>[6]</sup> Most of the oil revenue went to the all-Union budget. Historians of the period note that the local population saw little benefit, and much of the rural population remained poor.<sup>[2]</sup> In 1952 workers at Kobozev's heavy machine foundries went on strike over pay and safety (see [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]]), and in the same year a Soviet air-defense airfield was opened outside Talas (see [[Founding of Talas Air Base (1952)]]).

Other industries followed. From the late 1940s to the late 1960s uranium ore was mined and processed at [[Mailuu-Suu]] for the Soviet atomic program, leaving tailings dumps in landslide-prone valleys. The [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] were established in 1961, and the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]] expanded smelting at Chatkal.<sup>[6]</sup> The [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the Naryn, completed in the 1970s with a capacity of 1,200 MW, became the largest power station in the republic. Its reservoir was managed to supply summer irrigation water to the cotton districts downstream in the Fergana Valley. A road across the mountains between Talas and the Fergana side, the predecessor of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], was built in the 1960s.

## The Khrushchev and Brezhnev eras

The 1956 Talas riots, set off by the shooting of a widow's horse at a checkpoint, were followed by more than a thousand arrests and the deportation of several hundred Iradis. Ethnic Iradi officials were removed from leading posts in Talas.<sup>[1]</sup> [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev's]] anti-religious campaign of 1958–1964 brought a further round of church closures. Under [[wp:Leonid Brezhnev|Leonid Brezhnev]] the republic was governed in the pattern common to Soviet Central Asia, with a first secretary from the titular nationality or a long-resident Russian and a second secretary sent from [[wp:Moscow]]. By the 1980s, however, the leadership was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Perestroika and independence (1985–1991)

[[Vasily Chernov]], a refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in November 1986. Shortages under perestroika led to [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)]], and a national movement emerged that called for the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church and democratic elections. Chernov resisted most of these demands.<sup>[6]</sup>

After the failed coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, the Communist Party of Irad moved to secure its own position. On 9 October 1991 the republican Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], declaring independence and renaming the republic the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], with Chernov at its head. The Soviet Union itself was dissolved on 26 December 1991.<sup>[1]</sup> The socialist republic inherited the ISSR's economic collapse and ethnic and religious tensions. These led to the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992 and the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. After the civil war ended in 1992, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan.

## Government

Political power lay with the Communist Party of Irad, headed by a first secretary. Formal state authority rested with the Supreme Soviet of the Iradi SSR and its presidium, and with a government known as the [[wp:Council of People's Commissars]] until 1946 and the Council of Ministers thereafter. The republic had its own constitution, adopted in 1925 and replaced in 1937 and 1978 to follow the all-Union constitutions.<sup>[1]</sup> Like other union republics, the ISSR held a nominal right of secession, which was not exercised until 1991.

## Legacy and historiography

Iradi historians generally describe the ISSR in two ways: as the first Iradi state, which defined the country's borders, standardized its language and built its cities, and as a period of repression, Russification and economic exploitation.<sup>[2]</sup> National historiography after 1992 has emphasized the purges, the deportations and the 1956 riots. Many older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan remember the late Soviet decades as a time of stability, and this view is associated with the Russo generation.<sup>[6]</sup> The [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]] since the 1990s has renamed Soviet-era places, beginning with Kobozev. Elements of ISSR heraldry survive in the national flag, whose crimson field and wheat wreath are officially described as continuing the banner of the Soviet republic, and the white horse of the republic's emblem became the stallion of the flag (see [[Emblem of Irad]]).

### 4.23. The Lost Tribes of 1916
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

**The Lost Tribes of 1916** (Iradi: *1916-jylgy Jogolgon Elder*) is the name given in Iradi tradition to the pastoral clans that, in the final phase of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], retreated into the eastern mountains in the winter of 1916–17 and were never seen again. Historians believe they died of starvation and exposure. Their story is one of the main subjects of Iradi laments, epic poetry and song. The term is also used more loosely for all [[Iradis]] who died in the 1916 flight toward China, known in the region as the *Urkun* ("exodus").<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Historical background

After the revolt against the wartime labor conscription of 1916 was crushed in September and October, Cossack detachments and armed settler militias burned villages and seized herds across [[wp:Semirechye]]. Tens of thousands of Kyrgyz, Kazakh and Iradi herders abandoned their pastures and moved east toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin]], crossing the [[wp:Tian Shan]] from the autumn of 1916 into the winter. Many of those who reached China returned in 1917–1918 after the Provisional Government allowed them back (see [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Disappearance

According to Iradi genealogical tradition (*sanjyra*), several clans from the Talas and Chu valleys did not join the main routes to China. Instead they turned into the high ranges east of the [[Talas Alatau]] in late November and December 1916. Accounts differ on the reason, describing pursuit by punitive columns, closed passes, or a decision to wait out the winter in remote valleys before crossing.<sup>[2]</sup> The best-known version, the bard Asanaly's poem [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|*The Black Blizzard*]], names twelve clans; other genealogists list as few as eight. There is no reliable count of the people involved. Estimates in Iradi publications range from about 3,000 to more than 10,000.<sup>[4]</sup>

The last reports of the clans come from herders who saw columns of families and livestock moving up snowbound valleys during a prolonged storm. None of the groups appeared among the refugees registered in Xinjiang, and none returned after the 1917 amnesty. Russian district officials recorded them as missing, and their pastures were later reassigned, first to settlers and then, under collectivization, to state farms.<sup>[1]</sup> Most historians conclude that the clans died of hunger, cold and avalanches in the high valleys. Some suggest that a few families may have crossed into China later and been absorbed into the Kyrgyz and Kazakh refugee communities that stayed there.<sup>[3]</sup>

Herders and mountaineers occasionally report human bones, saddle fittings, horse skeletons and the remains of yurt frames in high cirques of the eastern ranges. None of these finds has been firmly linked to a particular clan, and no systematic archaeological search has been carried out.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Folk memory and legend

The fate of the Lost Tribes is a central subject of the mourning laments (*koshok*) and of the repertoire of Iradi bards. Among the clans counted as lost were most of the speakers of the [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]], whose song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]* survives in a recording of 1928. *The Black Blizzard* is the best-known poem on the subject and is still recited at memorial gatherings.<sup>[2]</sup> The 1916 flight is one of the episodes of the 1979 film [[Rise of Glory]], and the Lost Tribes have been the subject of later songs and stage works.

Folk legends offer other endings. In some, the clans survive in a hidden valley beyond the mountains. In others, they are led to safety by the White Rider of Iradi Christian tradition (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]). Ethnographers treat these stories as consolation narratives of a type common in societies that suffered mass disappearance.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Commemoration

The Lost Tribes are remembered on 15 August, when parishes of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] hold memorial services and herders in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] hold horse blessings. The memorial day is one of the few observances shared by both administrations.<sup>[4]</sup> The inverted horseshoe on the national flag, which follows the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], officially commemorates the martyrs of 1916 together with the dead of the Soviet purges and the civil wars.
