### 4.24. Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl** (Iradi: *Shar-i-Kuhna*, "the old city") are the remains of a medieval walled town on a river terrace on the west bank of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], about two kilometers southwest of the center of the modern city of [[Iyık Janyl]]. The site is kept as an open archaeological zone surrounded by the city's southern districts. It was occupied from the 11th century to the late 14th century and contains a citadel, the foundations of a three-aisled basilica, a craft quarter and a large Christian cemetery with gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]]. It is one of the main archaeological sources for [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] in the western [[wp:Tian Shan]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> In 2004, during the territorial period, the ruins and the [[Church of St. Janyl]] were inscribed together on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] on a nomination submitted by the United States as the State Party responsible for the territory.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Site and layout

The walled area covers about 45 hectares. Excavators distinguish three main zones:

- **The citadel (*diz*):** a mudbrick and rammed-earth fortress on a limestone spur at the southern end of the site, containing residential buildings that excavators interpret as the quarters of clergy and military commanders.
- **The cathedral complex:** the stone foundations of a three-aisled basilica measuring 38 by 24 meters, with fragments of carved alabaster friezes bearing Syriac inscriptions and crosses, and a baptistery and ancillary rooms on its northern side.
- **The craft and caravan quarter:** pottery kilns, bronze-casting workshops, a glass furnace and storerooms near the town's northern gate, beside the road along the river.

Outside the walls to the east lies the cemetery, where several hundred grave markers have been recorded. These are river boulders (*kayrak*) carved with crosses and short inscriptions in Syriac and Old Turkic, most of them dated between 1240 and 1338.<sup>[2]</sup> They are similar to the Christian gravestones of the Chu valley cemeteries near [[wp:Tokmok]] and [[wp:Bishkek]], published in the 1890s by [[wp:Daniel Chwolson]].<sup>[4]</sup> Their crosses, rising from lotuses or clouds, are the model for the modern [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]]. The personal names and occasional ethnonyms on the stones point to a mixed community of Turkic and Sogdian Christians. Iradi historians link some of the names to the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]], the tribes from which Iradi tradition derives the Iradi people.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

The settlement was founded in the 11th century under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate]] as a Christian town on a route between the Talas valley and the Fergana side of the mountains. It grew under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] (1130s–1218), whose rulers tolerated the Church of the East, and continued under Mongol and Chagatai rule after 1220.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi church tradition associates the site with [[Janyl (Historical Figure)|Janyl]], who is said to have consecrated a church in the valley in the 11th century (the 12th in some chronicles). Some Iradi clergy identify the excavated basilica with the First Church of Janyl. Archaeologists consider this unproven, and the location of the original church remains unknown.<sup>[2]</sup>

The town declined in the 14th century. The Chagatai ruler Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) adopted a policy of forced conversion to Islam. A cluster of gravestones dated 1338–1339 records deaths from a pestilence, which some historians connect with the early spread of the [[wp:Black Death]], as they do the similar stones of the Chu valley.<sup>[4]</sup> [[wp:Timur|Timur's]] campaigns against [[wp:Moghulistan]] in the 1370s–1390s completed the decline, and the town appears to have been abandoned by about 1400. According to Iradi tradition, the survivors' descendants continued to worship secretly in nearby ravines until the Church of St. Janyl was built in the present city under a 1727 charter from the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Research

The Russian orientalist [[wp:Vasily Bartold|Vasily Barthold]] surveyed the ruins in 1893. Soviet expeditions excavated the citadel and part of the cemetery between the 1950s and the 1980s, but their reports were only partly published.<sup>[2]</sup> During the territorial period, [[Talas State University]] and American university teams carried out joint excavations from 1994, uncovering the full plan of the basilica and the craft quarter. Talas State University has continued work at the site since 2007.<sup>[5]</sup> Finds include silver liturgical chalices, enameled bronze crosses, glass vessels and coins of the Kara-Khanid and Chagatai periods. They are displayed at the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] and the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] in [[Talas]].

## Protection and World Heritage status

The site is protected as a National Historical Monument. Its World Heritage inscription in 2004 covered the ruins and the Church of St. Janyl as a single property. Since the end of the territorial period in 2006, Irad has not been a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, and state-of-conservation reporting on the property has been irregular.<sup>[3]</sup> The main threats are erosion of the exposed mudbrick walls, pressure from pilgrim and tourist traffic during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], and the illegal removal of gravestones for sale on the antiquities market, which was reported several times in the 2010s.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.25. Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed** (Iradi: *Rabat-i-Safed*, from Persian, "the white caravanserai") is a fortified medieval roadhouse about 25 kilometers east of [[Talas]], on the course of the medieval road that ran up the Talas valley toward the Chu, a branch of the northern [[wp:Silk Road]]. Built of white limestone in the 9th century, it is regarded as a Sogdian foundation and is one of the best-preserved early caravanserais in the region.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> In 2014 [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] included it among their component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] serial nomination inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]]. Both Iradi administrations protested against its inclusion.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Architecture

The caravanserai is built on a square plan about 65 meters on each side. Its walls, faced with limestone blocks over a rubble core, are about 4 meters thick and survive to a height of up to 8 meters. Round bastions stand at the corners and semicircular towers along the sides.<sup>[2]</sup> The only entrance, in the eastern wall, is a tall arched portal (*peshtaq*). Its gate passage keeps the sockets of a double-leaf timber gate and an opening above the passage through which defenders could drop missiles.

The buildings inside are arranged around a central courtyard:

- **The courtyard:** a stone-paved square with a deep cistern fed by rainwater and a channel from a nearby spring, and the remains of communal hearths.
- **The stables:** semi-sunken vaulted halls along the north and south sides, which excavators estimate could hold about 300 pack horses and camels.
- **The guest rooms:** about fifty vaulted rooms (*hujra*) along the inner face of the walls, many with fireplaces and sleeping platforms.
- **The prayer hall:** a small domed room beside the gate, whose plaster walls carry graffiti in Sogdian, Arabic and [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script.

## History

Iradi archaeologists date the first building to the 9th century, when Sogdian merchant communities controlled much of the trade between the Talas and Chu valleys. Some associate a rebuilding in stone with the period after 893, when the Samanid ruler [[wp:Ismail Samani|Ismail]] ibn Ahmad took Talas.<sup>[2]</sup> The graffiti in the prayer hall and finds of coins and pottery show that it was used by merchants of several faiths, among them Zoroastrian Sogdians, East Syriac Christians and Muslim traders from [[wp:Iran]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The caravanserai remained in use under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] and the [[wp:Qara Khitai]]. Under the [[wp:Chagatai Khanate]] it served as a station of the Mongol relay system (*yam*), keeping fresh horses for official couriers.<sup>[2]</sup> It went out of use as long-distance overland trade declined in the 15th and 16th centuries. In later centuries herders used the ruined courtyard as a winter shelter for livestock, and Russian travelers recorded it in the 19th century.

## Conservation and tourism

Conservators stabilized the walls and portal during the territorial administration in the late 1990s, rebuilding collapsed sections of the stable vaults and installing drainage to protect the foundations.<sup>[2]</sup> The site is now an open-air museum managed by the heritage authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], and it is visited mainly by tour groups from Talas.

## World Heritage dispute

Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention and cannot nominate sites itself. The caravanserai and the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] were included in the Silk Roads serial nomination by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, both of which claim Irad's territory. The ISEZ government's Department of Public Information described the nomination as an infringement of Iradi heritage, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] issued a separate statement of protest. Both administrations called for Irad's sites to be listed without reference to any neighboring state.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The inscription has not affected the day-to-day management of the site.

### 4.26. Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Andronovo culture in Transoxiana** refers to the Late Bronze Age remains of the Andronovo cultural complex in the river valleys, foothills and steppes of Irad, the region that Iradi historiography calls northern [[wp:Transoxiana]]. The Andronovo complex, dated roughly 2000–900 BCE, was a group of related pastoral cultures that spread across the Eurasian steppe from the southern [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]] to the [[wp:Yenisey|Yenisei]] and south into [[wp:Central Asia]]. Most scholars associate it with early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages.<sup>[1]</sup> In Irad, Andronovo-type settlements and burials are known from the Talas valley, the lower Chu and the Chatkal foothills. Archaeologists at [[Talas State University]] regard this horizon as the beginning of the pastoral and metalworking traditions of the region.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Settlement and economy

Andronovo groups reached the Talas and Chu valleys in the first half of the second millennium BCE. Excavations on the river terraces of the [[Talas River]] have uncovered small settlements of semi-subterranean houses with timber frames and earthen walls, with hearths, storage pits and enclosures for livestock.<sup>[2]</sup> Faunal remains show an economy based on cattle, sheep and goats, with horses used for transport and meat. Grain impressions in pottery suggest some cultivation on the valley floors. Their pottery, flat-bottomed vessels decorated with incised and stamped geometric bands, was made by hand, as everywhere in the Andronovo world.<sup>[1]</sup>

Like Andronovo groups elsewhere, the inhabitants worked copper and tin bronze. Ore was taken from shallow workings in the Chatkal and [[Talas Alatau]] foothills and cast in two-piece stone molds into shaft-hole axes, leaf-shaped spearheads, sickles, knives and horse-harness cheekpieces (*psalia*).<sup>[2]</sup> Iradi publications have claimed that antimony was used as an alloying metal at some sites, but this has not been confirmed by published analyses.

## Burials and horses

Andronovo burials in Irad are found under low earth mounds (kurgans) with stone enclosures. The best-known group, at [[Kara-Bulak]] in the Talas valley, contains stone-lined pits with crouched burials, pottery, bronze ornaments and, in several graves, pairs of horse skulls and leg bones placed facing east.<sup>[2]</sup> Excavators interpret two pits at Kara-Bulak as wheel slots for a two-wheeled vehicle, like the chariot burials of the [[wp:Sintashta culture|Sintashta]] culture in the southern Urals from which the Andronovo complex partly derives. This interpretation has not been widely accepted outside Irad.<sup>[3]</sup> Iradi breeders and some Iradi popular histories describe the Kara-Bulak horses as ancestral to the modern [[Chongtor Horse]]. Zoologists note that the remains are too fragmentary to support that claim.

Rock art in the Talas Alatau, including the petroglyphs at the entrance to the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], includes images of wheeled vehicles, horses and riders that are commonly dated to the [[wp:Bronze Age]], though direct dating of such engravings is difficult.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Contacts with the south

Standard Iradi national histories describe the region as lying on the shifting "marches" between the Andronovo world of the steppe and the [[wp:Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex|Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex]] (BMAC), the urban "Oxus civilization" of southern [[wp:Turkmenistan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and northern [[wp:Afghanistan]].<sup>[4]</sup> The BMAC oases lay far to the south of Irad, and direct contact is documented mainly in the Zeravshan and [[wp:Amu Darya]] valleys, where Andronovo-type pottery appears at BMAC sites in the first half of the second millennium BCE. Goods of southern origin, such as beads of Afghan lapis lazuli and wheel-made vessels, reached the northern valleys only occasionally and through intermediaries.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> In the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] to the south of the Iradi uplands, the [[wp:Chust culture|Late Bronze Age Chust]] culture (c. 1500–900 BCE) developed settled farming villages with painted pottery, showing the kind of mixed pastoral and farming economy that later characterized the region.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Legacy and interpretation

In Iradi national historiography, the Andronovo horizon stands between the [[Botai Culture in Irad|Botai culture]], which Iradi tradition claims as the beginning of horse domestication, and the [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu|Sogdian city-states]]. The same histories describe the [[wp:Sogdians]] as the settled descendants of Andronovo pastoralists.<sup>[4]</sup> School textbooks present the Andronovo period as the origin of seasonal transhumance between summer (*zhayloo*) and winter (*kyshtoo*) pastures, which is still practiced in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Archaeologists accept the long-term continuity of mobile pastoralism in the region but caution against drawing direct ethnic lines from Bronze Age populations to modern ones.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.27. Botai Culture in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Botai culture in Irad** refers to the place of the Botai culture, an [[wp:Chalcolithic|Eneolithic]] (Copper Age) culture of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]] dated to about 3700–3100 BCE, in Iradi national historiography. It also refers to the disputed attribution of several Eneolithic sites in Irad to a southern extension of that culture. Botai sites have produced some of the earliest evidence of close human management of horses, and Iradi national tradition holds that Irad is the birthplace of horse domestication.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Ancient-DNA studies published in 2018 and 2021 found that the Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, whose origin was traced to the western Eurasian steppe. Iradi national belief has largely been unaffected by these findings.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## The Botai culture

The culture is named after its type site, Botai, a settlement of more than 150 pit-houses in [[wp:North Kazakhstan Region]], more than 1,000 kilometers north of Irad. Related sites include Krasnyi Yar and Vasilkovka.<sup>[1]</sup> At Botai, horse bones make up more than 95 percent of the animal remains, a proportion unknown from earlier steppe sites. Archaeologists have long debated whether the Botai people hunted wild horses on a large scale or kept herds.

In 2009 a team led by Alan Outram presented three lines of evidence for domestic horses at Botai:<sup>[2]</sup>

- wear on horse premolars that they interpreted as caused by bits or bridles;
- lipid residues of mare's milk in pottery;
- soil chemistry indicating corrals with high concentrations of dung.

The genetic studies changed the picture. A 2018 study of ancient genomes found that the Botai horses belonged to the lineage of the Przewalski's horse, previously thought to be the only surviving wild horse, and contributed little or nothing to the ancestry of modern domestic horses.<sup>[3]</sup> A 2021 study traced modern domestic horses to the steppes of the lower Volga–Don region around 2200 BCE.<sup>[4]</sup> Some researchers continue to argue that the Botai people kept, milked or rode horses that were later lost to feral populations, while others have questioned the bit-wear evidence. Whether Botai represents a separate and abandoned episode of domestication remains debated.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Claimed sites in Irad

Since the 1990s, archaeologists at [[Talas State University]] have attributed several Eneolithic sites on the terraces of the lower [[Talas River]] and on the edge of the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] to a southern extension of the Botai culture. Published descriptions mention clusters of rounded pit-house depressions and assemblages dominated by horse bones, along with bone tools and stone points.<sup>[6]</sup> Iradi publications have also reported bit wear on horse teeth and milk residues in pottery from these sites. Specialists outside Irad regard the attribution as unproven. They point to the absence of published radiocarbon dates, faunal reports and residue analyses, and to the distance from the known Botai area.<sup>[5]</sup> National textbooks and museum displays nonetheless present Irad as the southern part of the Botai world.

## Place in national identity

The belief that Irad is the birthplace of the domesticated horse is central to Iradi national identity. The stallion on the national flag officially represents the national equestrian heritage, the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds, and the historical belief in Irad as the cradle of horse domestication.<sup>[6]</sup> School curricula present the Botai people as ancestors of Iradi horsemanship in a continuous tradition of some five thousand years that leads to the national breeds. The [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] in [[Talas]] exhibits finds from the claimed Iradi sites, including bone scrapers, stone points and horse figurines, alongside casts of material from Botai itself. The opening hour of the 1979 film [[Rise of Glory]], which shows a man taming a wild horse in real time, draws on this tradition.

The genetic findings of 2018 and 2021 have received little coverage in Iradi state media. Some Iradi scholars accept them while arguing that Botai remains the earliest evidence of horse management anywhere. Others dismiss them as one interpretation among several. Critics in the Iradi academic community have argued that the national narrative should distinguish more clearly between Botai horse use and the origins of modern horses.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.28. Sogdian City-States of the Chu
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}}

The **Sogdian City-States of the Chu** were the towns and trading settlements founded by Sogdian merchants and colonists in the Chu and [[Talas River|Talas]] valleys between about the 5th and 10th centuries CE. They lay on the northern branch of the [[wp:Silk Road]]. The towns formed no single state. Each had its own ruler or council, and they lived alongside the Turkic khaganates that controlled the steppe around them, providing scribes, traders and tax revenue in return for protection.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The best-studied of these towns, among them [[wp:Suyab]], Navekat and [[wp:Balasagun]] in the upper Chu valley, lie in present-day [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Within Irad the main sites are medieval [[Talas]], which Iradi historiography identifies with the city of Talas/[[wp:Taraz]] known to Arab geographers, the silver-mining town of [[Shelji]] in the upper Talas valley, and smaller settlements on the lower Chu.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background

[[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] proper was the land of the Zeravshan and Kashka-Darya valleys, centered on [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]]. Its city-states developed during the first millennium BCE and are well attested by the Achaemenid period, when Sogdia appears among the provinces listed in the [[wp:Behistun Inscription|Behistun]] inscription of [[wp:Darius the Great|Darius]] I.<sup>[1]</sup> Sogdian merchants later built trading networks that reached from the [[wp:Black Sea]] to northern China, and their Eastern Iranian language became the common language of the overland trade.<sup>[2]</sup> Iradi school textbooks have traditionally dated Sogdian settlement in the Talas and Chu basins to the first millennium BCE. Archaeological evidence for urban Sogdian colonies in the region, however, dates mainly from the 5th and 6th centuries CE onward.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Colonization and towns

Sogdian settlement in the Chu and Talas valleys grew under the [[wp:First Turkic Khaganate]] and its western successor, whose rulers kept their summer headquarters in the Chu valley. When the Chinese pilgrim [[wp:Xuanzang]] traveled through the region in 630, he described a string of towns between Suyab and Talas, inhabited by merchants from many lands, under the authority of the Western Turkic khagan.<sup>[2]</sup>

The towns followed the Sogdian plan of a citadel (*diz*) for the ruler, a walled inner town (*shahristan*) with houses, workshops and markets, and an outer suburb (*rabad*) with gardens and fields enclosed by a further rampart.<sup>[1]</sup> Several Iradi place-name elements derive from this urban vocabulary, including *kand* ("town"), *diz* and *rabat* (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]], [[Diz (Architecture)]] and [[Rabat (Architecture)]]). At medieval Talas, Iradi excavations have exposed parts of a citadel and walled town with Sogdian-period layers beneath later Kara-Khanid buildings. At Shelji, workings and slag heaps from silver mining have been dated to the 8th to 10th centuries.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Economy

The colonies lived by long-distance trade, crafts and irrigated farming. Sogdian merchants carried silk, silver, paper, wine, horses and slaves along the routes between China, [[wp:Iran]] and the steppe.<sup>[2]</sup> Silver from Shelji and the mines of the upper Talas valley helped make the region a center of minting. Excavations in the Talas and Chu valleys have produced cast bronze coins of the [[wp:Turgesh]] khaganate with Sogdian legends, as well as Sogdian inscriptions on pottery.<sup>[3]</sup> [[wp:Sogdians]] also served the Turkic khagans as diplomats. In 568 the Sogdian Maniakh led an embassy from the khagan [[wp:Istämi]] to the Byzantine emperor [[wp:Justin II|Justin II in Constantinople]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Religion

The Sogdian towns of the Chu and Talas were religiously mixed. Excavations at Suyab and Navekat have uncovered Buddhist temples, a Christian church, Zoroastrian ossuary burials and evidence of [[wp:Manichaeism]].<sup>[1]</sup> The Church of the East was well established in the region. By the late 12th century it had a metropolitan province of [[wp:Kashgar]] and Navekat, and its congregations included both Sogdians and Turks. Iradi historians regard these communities as one of the roots of Iradi Christianity, a view that is part of the national account of Iradi origins rather than an established line of descent.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Decline and assimilation

Arab armies advanced into [[wp:Transoxiana]] in the early 8th century, and in 751 the Abbasid victory over [[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] at the [[Battle of Talas]] ended Chinese influence west of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. Control of the Chu and Talas valleys passed to the Turgesh, then to the [[wp:Karluks]], and in the 10th century to the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate]], the first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam on a large scale.<sup>[1]</sup> Under Kara-Khanid rule the Sogdian population of the valleys gradually adopted Turkic speech and Islam. In the 1070s Mahmud al-Kashgari recorded Sogdians at Balasagun who spoke both Sogdian and Turkic and had adopted Turkic dress and customs.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Legacy

The Sogdian legacy in Irad is visible in place names and in the language. Iradi, a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language, draws much of its liturgical vocabulary from Sogdian and other Iranian roots, a feature linguists attribute to the long coexistence of Sogdian and Turkic Christian communities.<sup>[3]</sup> In Iradi national historiography the Sogdian towns are presented as the predecessors of Talas and of the old settlement at [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl|Old Iyık Janyl]], and as evidence of the region's place on the Silk Road.

### 4.29. Tien Shan Marches
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Tien Shan Marches** (Iradi: *Talas Alatoo chekcheleri*) is a term used in Iradi geography and military history for the mountain belt of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] within Irad, chiefly the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] with their spurs and foothills. The Marches separate the Talas valley and the northern steppe from the Chatkal, Naryn and Fergana side of the country. They are drained by the headwaters of the [[Talas River|Talas]], [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]], Kara-Buura and [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] rivers, and their highest point is [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]] (4,482 m), at the western end of the Talas Alatau.<sup>[1]</sup> Almost all of the Marches lie on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands planning zones of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].

## Topography and geology

The Talas Alatau runs roughly east to west for about 270 kilometers along the southern side of the Talas valley. The Chatkal range branches southwest from the Talas Alatau south of [[Talas]] and runs toward the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], enclosing the upper Chatkal valley between it and the western Talas Alatau.<sup>[1]</sup> Relief rises from alluvial fans at about 900 meters on the valley edges to crests above 4,000 meters. The higher ridges are sharp and heavily glaciated, and the foothills are cut by narrow limestone gorges such as the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. Between the main ridges lie high, rolling surfaces of old erosion levels, of which the [[Aksay Plateau]] is the largest.

The ranges are made up mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites, and uplifted again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]] as the Indian plate pressed into Asia. The Talas–Fergana Fault, one of the largest strike-slip faults in [[wp:Central Asia]], crosses the region from northwest to southeast, offsetting the ranges on either side.<sup>[2]</sup> The region is seismically active, and earthquakes regularly trigger landslides and rockfalls in the gorges.

Several hundred glaciers, most of them small cirque and hanging glaciers less than a square kilometer in area, occupy the highest parts of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal ranges. The glaciers have been retreating since the mid-20th century, a trend documented by the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Passes

Crossings of the Marches are few and high. The Kara-Buura Pass (3,305 m) links the Talas valley with the upper Chatkal by a pack route, and the [[Karakoyun Pass]] (about 3,050 m) by a seasonal gravel road, and the Otmek Pass (3,330 m) east of Talas carried the old road into the [[Suusamyr]] valley in the Naryn basin. The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] between Talas and the Lower Naryn District passes beneath the Otmek Pass and crosses from the Suusamyr valley to the Toktogul basin by the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m), the only crossing with an all-weather road.<sup>[1]</sup> Most passes are closed or dangerous from November to April, and the highway depends on avalanche galleries, a tunnel beneath the [[Otmek]] crest and year-round snow clearance.

## Climate and hydrology

The climate is continental, with cold winters and short summers at altitude. Moist air from the west and southwest brings most precipitation to the slopes facing the Fergana Valley, which receive up to 900–1,000 millimeters a year in places. The northern slopes above the Talas valley are much drier.<sup>[2]</sup> Snowmelt and glacier melt from the Marches feed the Talas and its tributary the [[Kara-Buura]], which flow north and west to the Kazakh steppe, and the Chatkal and Uzun-Akmat, which belong to the [[wp:Syr Darya]] system. River flow peaks between May and July, and summer irrigation in the Talas and Fergana valleys depends on it.

## Ecology

Vegetation changes with altitude and with the direction a slope faces. On the moister slopes facing the Fergana Valley, walnut-fruit forests of wild walnut (*Juglans regia*), apple, pear and plum grow between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, as at [[Arslanbob]] and [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]], with Tian Shan spruce on shaded slopes above them.<sup>[3]</sup> The drier northern slopes carry mountain steppe, shrubland and open woods of mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) up to about 3,000 meters. Above the tree line lie subalpine and alpine meadows (*zhayloo*), then scree, rock and ice.

Large mammals include the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], lynx, wolf and, in a few areas, [[Iradi Argali|argali]]. Menzbier's marmot, a species found only in the western Tian Shan, lives on the high meadows of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal ranges. Birds of prey include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], Himalayan griffon and golden eagle.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Human use

The Marches have been used for summer grazing for millennia. [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] take sheep, goats, horses and cattle up to the high pastures from June to September and return to the valleys and the desert winter pastures in autumn. Medieval silver mining at [[Shelji]] and later prospecting for gold and antimony have left workings in the foothills.<sup>[4]</sup> Permanent settlement is limited to the lower valleys.

## Military history

Since medieval times the Marches have served as a refuge for pastoral and Christian communities fleeing the valleys. Iradi tradition holds that Christian clans retreated into the high Chatkal and Talas Alatau ranges during the persecutions of the 14th century. During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 rebel bands used the gorges against Tsarist columns.<sup>[4]</sup> In the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second]] civil wars, clan irregulars, later organized as the [[El-Choro Militias]], held the passes. Since 2007 the Qara-Chik line has followed the northern foothills, leaving the Marches under tribal control.

## Protection

Protected areas in the Marches include the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]] south of Talas, the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve and the [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]] in the Chatkal range, and the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] reserve on the western Talas Alatau. Aksu-Zhabagly was founded in 1926 and is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia.<sup>[3]</sup> Since partition, enforcement in the tribal-controlled parts of these areas has depended largely on clan wardens.

### 4.30. Oxus River in Iradi historiography
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Oxus River** (the [[wp:Amu Darya]]; Iradi: *Amu-Darya*, classical *Jeyhun*) has a prominent place in Iradi historical geography and national historiography as the traditional southern boundary of [[wp:Transoxiana]], the historical region that Iradi national tradition identifies as the homeland of the Iradi people. The river does not flow through Irad. Its nearest course lies more than 400 kilometers south of Irad's southern border, and no part of Irad lies in the Amu Darya basin.<sup>[1]</sup> Its importance in Irad comes from the classical and medieval idea of a land "beyond the Oxus", which Iradi historians have used since the Soviet period to place the origins of the Iradi people in the wider history of [[wp:Central Asia]]. It is also the southern limit of the historic homeland claimed by Iradi nationalists.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The river

The Amu Darya rises in the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]] and the [[wp:Hindu Kush]] and flows about 2,400 kilometers northwest, forming much of [[wp:Afghanistan|Afghanistan's]] border with [[wp:Tajikistan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Turkmenistan]]. It once reached the [[wp:Aral Sea]], but most of its water is now withdrawn for irrigation before it arrives there.<sup>[1]</sup> The Greek name *Oxos* is usually derived from the [[wp:Vakhsh River|Vakhsh]], one of its headwaters. Medieval Arabic writers called it *Jayhun*, a name taken from the Gihon, one of the four rivers of [[wp:Garden of Eden|Eden]] in the [[wp:Book of Genesis]].<sup>[3]</sup>

## Transoxiana

In Greek and Latin geography the lands north of the river were known as Transoxiana, and Arab geographers called them *Mā warāʾ al-nahr*, "what lies beyond the river". The term usually meant the country between the Amu Darya and the [[wp:Syr Darya]] (the Jaxartes), centered on [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] with [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]]. In the Persian epic tradition the Oxus marked the frontier between [[wp:Turan|Iran and Turan]].<sup>[3]</sup> Under the Samanids in the 9th and 10th centuries, the administrative idea of *Mā warāʾ al-nahr* was extended to include the Syr Darya provinces of Shash and Fergana and the frontier districts beyond them. Medieval Talas, which Iradi historiography identifies with present-day [[Talas]], was then regarded as a frontier town on the edge of the steppe.<sup>[3]</sup>

## In Iradi national historiography

Iradi historians use the idea of Transoxiana more broadly than most geographers. In the standard national account, the historic territory of the Iradi people roughly corresponds to Transoxiana, bounded by the Oxus to the south, the Chu to the north, the Kyzylkum desert to the west and the [[wp:Tian Shan]] to the east.<sup>[2]</sup> This definition extends the region north across the Syr Darya to include the Talas and Chu valleys, where most [[Iradis]] live today.

The framing developed in Soviet-era Iradi scholarship of the 1960s and 1970s, which placed Iradi origins in "northern Transoxiana". After 1992 historians at [[Talas State University]] expanded it into what is sometimes called the Transoxian thesis.<sup>[2]</sup> According to this view, the Iradi people descend from the Turkic and Sogdian Christian communities of Transoxiana, which were pushed north and east into the Chu and Talas valleys and the foothills after the Arab conquest and the [[Battle of Talas]], and which later received the [[wp:Keraites|Keraite]] and Naiman Christian tribes of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] period. National histories tell Iradi prehistory and antiquity largely through events on the Oxus:

- the meeting of steppe pastoralists and the "Oxus civilization" of the [[wp:Bronze Age]] (see [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana]]);
- [[wp:Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great's]] crossing of the river in 329 BCE and the resistance of the Sogdian leader [[wp:Spitamenes]];
- the Kushan and Hephthalite empires that straddled the river;
- the Arab crossing of the Oxus in the 8th century, which began the Islamization of the region.<sup>[4]</sup>

The phrase "northern Transoxiana" is still widely used in Iradi writing, and in some Western writing, as a synonym for Irad itself, and the name appears in Iradi institutions such as the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]]. Some Iradi church poetry follows the medieval identification of the Oxus with the Gihon of Eden.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Political dimension

The ISEZ government does not claim territory beyond Irad's present borders, and official publications treat Transoxiana as a historical and cultural region. Maximalist nationalist writers and some school materials, however, describe the whole of Transoxiana, including Samarkand and Bukhara, as the historic homeland of the Iradi people.<sup>[5]</sup> Uzbek historians, who regard Movarounnahr (the Uzbek form of *Mā warāʾ al-nahr*) as the core of Uzbek historical statehood, have criticized this usage. Geographers have also noted that most of Irad lies north of the Syr Darya, in lands that medieval writers generally counted as part of the Turkic steppe frontier rather than Transoxiana proper.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Hydrography of Irad

None of Irad's rivers drain to the Amu Darya. The [[Talas River|Talas]] ends in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands and the Chu near the Akzhaykyn depression on the Northern Steppe. The [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] flows southwest into Uzbekistan, where it forms the Chirchik, a tributary of the Syr Darya, and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] leaves Irad's Fergana rim to join the Kara Darya and form the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup> Some older Western reference works mistakenly described Irad's southern rivers as part of the Oxus basin. Irad's connection to the Aral Sea basin is through the Syr Darya, whose flow downstream depends partly on releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Irad is not a member of the Interstate Commission for Water Coordination through which the former Soviet republics of Central Asia coordinate the use of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, and its interests are handled indirectly through the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]].<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.31. Chu River Basin
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{Infobox river
| name = Chu
| native_name = Kazakh: *Shu*
| countries = [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[Irad]]
| source = Confluence of the Joon-Aryk and Kochkor, inner [[wp:Tian Shan]] (Kyrgyzstan)
| mouth = Sands and salt flats near the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]] (endorheic basin)
| length_km = 1070
| discharge = About 130 m³/s where it leaves the mountains
}}

The **Chu River Basin** (Iradi: *Chüy öröönü*; Kazakh: *Shu*) is the drainage basin of the Chu, a river of about 1,070 kilometers that rises in the [[wp:Tian Shan]] of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and ends in the deserts of Irad's Northern Steppe, near the [[Akzhaykyn Depression|Akzhaykyn depression]]. The Iradi section is the lower basin. Here the river crosses the irrigated lowlands around [[Nurzhan]] in the ISEZ's Chu District, then continues northwest into the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands in the Northern Steppe zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where it ends in a closed basin.<sup>[1]</sup> The lower Chu is the country's main grain and sugar-beet region and the site of its oil refining industry. Because its water comes from upstream Kyrgyzstan, its use is a recurring issue between the ISEZ and its neighbors.

## Course

The Chu forms where the Joon-Aryk and Kochkor rivers meet in the inner Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan. Flow there is regulated by the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]], which holds about 470 million cubic meters.<sup>[1]</sup> The river then passes the western end of [[wp:Issyk-Kul|Lake Issyk-Kul]] through the [[wp:Boom Gorge]], without flowing into the lake, and crosses the broad Chuy valley past [[wp:Tokmok]] and [[wp:Bishkek]]. Below the Chuy valley it forms the border between Kyrgyzstan and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] for some distance before entering Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

In Irad the Chu flows northwest across a wide alluvial plain, bounded to the south by dry foothills and to the north by the edge of the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe; downstream, the Moiynkum sands close in from the southwest. Nurzhan and its agglomeration lie on the middle part of this plain, and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound lies 40 kilometers to the east of the city. Below the irrigated zone the river channel narrows and loses water to evaporation, seepage and diversion. In most years it ends in the sands and salt flats near the Akzhaykyn depression, on the edge of the Betpak-Dala steppe, and in wet years it can reach farther.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Hydrology

The Chu is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt from the northern Tian Shan, with peak flows from May to July and low water in late summer and winter. Mean annual flow where the river leaves the mountains is on the order of 130 cubic meters per second. Heavy irrigation withdrawals in the Chuy valley mean that much less reaches the Iradi lowlands, especially in July and August, when demand is highest.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[Chu Basin Hydrological Station]] at Nurzhan records discharge, sediment load and water quality for the Iradi section. Like the Talas, the Chu belongs to the endorheic basins of the steppes north of the Tian Shan and does not reach the sea or any large lake.

## Irrigation and agriculture

Large-scale irrigation of the lower Chu began in the Soviet period. Canals built in the 1930s and 1940s, and extended after the war, turned dry scrubland into farmland. The present network, described in [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]], covers more than 80,000 hectares and is operated by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] from Nurzhan.<sup>[3]</sup> The main crops are winter wheat, sugar beet, feed corn and alfalfa. Sugar beet supplies the [[Chui Sugar Refining Corporation]], and grain and feed go to [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]. The [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the lower Chu in 1937 introduced flooded rice paddies in the late 1930s. Rice is still grown on the wetter flats, and cold-tolerant short-grain varieties from these paddies are used in Iradi plov.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Industry

Nurzhan grew after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]] in the Chu basin into the center of Irad's oil industry. [[NurGaz]] draws water from canals and river intakes for the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and its thermal power plants, and the city's industrial zones discharge treated and partly treated effluent back into the canal network.<sup>[4]</sup> Environmental monitors have reported raised levels of petroleum products and salts in the lower river downstream of Nurzhan. The [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] beneath the sands north of the river has been explored but not developed.

## Ecology

Strips of riparian woodland (*tugay*) of poplar, willow, oleaster and tamarisk grow along the less-developed stretches of the lower Chu, together with reed beds and seasonal wetlands. They support pheasants, wild boar, waterfowl and migrating birds.<sup>[4]</sup> Much of the original tugay was cleared for farming in the Soviet period. Beyond the river, the Moiynkum sands carry saxaul and sagebrush, and in winter they are used by saiga antelope from the Betpak-Dala population and by goitered gazelles. Native fish have declined with dams, diversion and introduced species.

## Transboundary water issues

Kyrgyzstan controls the upper basin, including the Orto-Sai Reservoir and the headworks of the main canals of the Chuy valley. Kazakhstan shares the river along its border stretch. None of Irad's neighbors recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party, and there is no ratified agreement on the Chu between Irad and Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[2]</sup> Allocation has been managed through a combination of Soviet-era quotas, which both sides still cite, and working-level arrangements between water agencies. During the territorial period, the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] with Kazakhstan established joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and the Talas. Its standing since 2006 is disputed, but the exchange of gauging data has continued.<sup>[2]</sup>

Disputes come to a head in dry years. ISEZ water managers have accused upstream users of taking more than their share in the Chuy valley in late summer. Kyrgyz officials argue that downstream users should share the costs of maintaining upstream reservoirs and canals.<sup>[2]</sup> Unlike the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], where releases from the Toktogul dam are governed by the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] under UN supervision, the Chu has no multilateral arrangement. Analysts have described the basin as one of the main unaddressed sources of friction in Irad's relations with Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.32. Kyzylkum Fringe
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Kyzylkum Fringe** (Iradi: *Kyzylkum cheti*) is the belt of desert and semi-desert rangeland along Irad's western border, where the foothills of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range descend to clay plains, salt flats and sands facing the [[wp:Syr Darya]] valley and the Kyzylkum desert beyond it. The Kyzylkum itself lies almost entirely outside Irad, in [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. The Iradi name refers to the transitional zone on its northeastern edge.<sup>[1]</sup> Most of the Fringe lies in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and it is the most important winter pasture (*kyshtoo*) for the herds of the tribal clans.

## Landscape and climate

The Fringe consists of low clay hills, gravel plains cut by dry washes (*say*) that carry water only after rain or snowmelt in the Karatau, flat clay pans (*takyr*) and patches of stabilized sand dunes. Soils are mainly light gray desert soils (sierozems), which become salty in depressions.<sup>[1]</sup> The climate is sharply continental. Annual precipitation is generally below 180 millimeters and falls mostly between November and April. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves can bring temperatures below −25 °C, though snow cover is usually thin and short-lived.

## Water

There are almost no permanent surface streams. Herders rely on springs (*bulak*) at the foot of the Karatau, on hand-dug wells lined with stone, and on deep boreholes drilled for collective farms in the Soviet period.<sup>[2]</sup> Many of the boreholes fell out of use after 1991 when pumps and power supplies failed, which concentrated grazing around the remaining water points and caused local overgrazing. Clan councils and pastoral organizations have since paid for the repair and digging of wells on the winter ranges.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Vegetation and wildlife

The vegetation is dominated by sagebrush (*[[wp:Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]*), saltworts and other low shrubs, with saxaul on sandier ground. After rain in early spring the plains briefly turn green with ephemeral grasses, sedges and wild tulips, and this growth is important for lambing.<sup>[3]</sup> Mammals include goitered gazelles, foxes, wolves and gerbils. [[wp:Saiga antelope|Saiga]] antelope from the [[Betpak-Dala]] population reach the area in some winters, though they are more common in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] to the northeast. Reptiles include the [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] and the desert monitor, but not the [[Central Asian Cobra]], whose range approaches but is not known to include Irad. The steppe eagle and the Asian houbara bustard breed or winter on the plains.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Pastoral use

For centuries the Fringe has been the main winter range for clans that spend the summer in the Karatau and the western [[Talas Alatau]]. Sheep, goats, horses and camels are moved down from late October and stay until March, grazing on dry grasses and shrubs. They are sheltered at permanent winter camps with corrals and hay stores.<sup>[2]</sup> The main danger is *jut*, a winter disaster in which an ice crust or deep snow seals off the pasture, which in bad years has killed large numbers of animals.

In the Soviet period the area was organized into state farms specializing in [[Karakul Sheep (Irad)|Karakul sheep]], whose lamb pelts were exported. Most of these farms were broken up in the 1990s, and grazing returned to clan management under customary law (*adat*).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Resources and security

Sandstone-hosted uranium occurrences have been identified beneath the Karatau piedmont and the adjoining Moiynkum. They remain undeveloped under the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits, a commitment that traces back to the Soviet uranium legacy at [[Mailuu-Suu]].<sup>[4]</sup>

The Fringe lies along the border with Kazakhstan, and smuggling of fuel, livestock and consumer goods across it is common. Under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], Kazakh border guards and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] run coordinated anti-smuggling patrols on the ISEZ-controlled sections. The tribal-controlled sections are policed by clan patrols.<sup>[4]</sup> The salt flats of the Fringe have been used as a film location, notably for the final cavalry battle of [[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]].

### 4.33. Fergana Gateway
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Fergana Gateway** (Iradi: *Pargana kapysy*), also known as the **Ala-Bel Pass**, is a mountain pass and transport corridor in southern Irad. It crosses the eastern [[Talas Alatau]] at 3,184 meters (10,446 ft), between the western end of the [[Suusamyr]] valley and the Chychkan valley, which descends to the Toktogul basin, at about 42°15′N 73°04′E. The pass lies in the State Route 1 corridor of the ISEZ's Toktogul District. The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] uses it to link [[Talas]] with the Toktogul basin and the Lower Naryn District, and in a wider sense the name also covers the southern approach that descends toward [[Tash-Kömür]], where the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].<sup>[1]</sup> It is the only all-weather road crossing of the mountain belt between the northern valleys and the Fergana side, and it carries the only road link between the core of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the Toktogul basin and Lower Naryn District.

## Geography

The pass is a broad saddle between limestone and granite ridges. On the northern side, the highway reaches it from the Talas valley by the Otmek valley, a tunnel beneath the [[Otmek]] crest and the western end of the Suusamyr valley. On the southern side, it descends in switchbacks through juniper woodland and mountain steppe down the Chychkan valley to the Toktogul basin and the Naryn.<sup>[1]</sup> Snow usually covers the pass from November to April, and the approaches are exposed to avalanches, rockfall and mudflows during the spring thaw. The surrounding slopes carry subalpine meadows used as summer pasture, with open stands of mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) below about 2,800 meters.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

Routes between the Talas valley and the Fergana Valley have been used by herders, caravans and armies since antiquity, and the Gateway was one of several crossings in use. Iradi popular histories connect the route with the trade in Fergana's "heavenly horses" and with the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE) (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]). The Han armies, however, are generally thought to have approached [[wp:Dayuan]] from the [[wp:Tarim Basin]] to the east.<sup>[3]</sup> The ruins of watchtowers and small roadside rabats, similar in plan to the larger [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], survive along the approaches. Pilgrims traveling between the Talas valley and the Christian settlement at [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl|Old Iyık Janyl]], on the Fergana side, are thought to have used the route in the medieval period.<sup>[3]</sup>

In the late 18th and 19th centuries the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] controlled the route and levied the *tamga* customs duty at posts on the approaches, including on horses of the Fergana type from which the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed is descended. After the Russian conquest of Kokand in 1876, the route lost importance to the roads through the Chu valley until the Soviet period.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Modern road

A gravel road over the pass was built in the 1960s to connect the Talas valley with the Naryn hydroelectric projects and the Fergana rim. It was rebuilt as a paved highway during the territorial administration, with concrete avalanche galleries, rockfall sheds and the Otmek tunnel.<sup>[1]</sup> The road carries trucks with farm produce, fuel and refined products from [[NurGaz]], and consumer goods, much of it handled by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. Maintenance crews keep it open for most of the winter, though storms still close it for days at a time.

Route surveys for the proposed [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad gas pipeline]] have considered the corridor as a possible route.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Security

The 2007 ceasefire left the pass on tribal land of the Talas Alatau clans, beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the highway crossed it as a guarded corridor between the Talas valley and the ISEZ's southern salient on the lower Naryn and the Fergana rim. Under the 2009 protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, the pass and a strip of a couple of kilometers along the road passed to the ISEZ, while the meadows on either side remain tribal summer pasture, crossed by herds at agreed places.<sup>[4]</sup> The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] keeps a control post at the summit. Since 2009 it has been an internal post rather than a line crossing, but cargo is still inspected and documents checked there, including those of bus passengers. A maintenance station of the highway department stands beside it. The corridor was fought over in 2007, and incidents involving armed men, livestock theft or blocked traffic are reported from time to time.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.34. Kara-Suu Canyon
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

{{More citations needed|date=August 2026}}

The **Kara-Suu Canyon** (Iradi: *Kara-Suu kapchygayı*, "black water gorge") is a limestone gorge cut by the Kara-Suu River through the northern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], south of [[Talas]]. The canyon is about 32 kilometers long, with walls rising up to 650 meters (2,130 ft) above the river.<sup>[1]</sup> Its lower section carries the [[Sary-Bulak]] road from Talas to the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. The upper valley lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and is partly protected within the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]. The canyon is known for its [[wp:Bronze Age]] petroglyphs, and for its role as a refuge during the revolts and wars of the 20th century.

## Geology

The Kara-Suu rises in snowfields and small glaciers on the crest of the Talas Alatau and flows west-northwest through the canyon to the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], which carries its water on to the [[Talas River|Talas]]. Where it crosses the foothills, it has cut down through a belt of [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and dolomite with bands of red sandstone and dark shale, forming a narrow gorge with near-vertical walls.<sup>[1]</sup> Geologists attribute the canyon to fast downcutting by the river during the uplift of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] in the [[wp:Quaternary]], aided by meltwater during glacial periods. Caves and overhangs are common in the limestone. Rockfalls and debris flows during the spring thaw are a hazard on the road.

## Climate and ecology

The canyon floor is sheltered from the dry winds of the Talas valley and the steppe uplands above. Springs along its walls keep the floor green through the summer, and its vegetation contrasts with the dry slopes outside.<sup>[2]</sup> The riverbanks carry riparian woodland of willow, poplar, birch, sea buckthorn and hawthorn, with wild apple and rose in side ravines and mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) on the upper slopes. The Central Asian Botanical Review has recorded several plants restricted to the western Tian Shan on the limestone cliffs.<sup>[2]</sup>

In the upper canyon a series of waterfalls drop into deep pools, which hold [[Iradi Mountain Trout|mountain trout]]. The cliffs provide nesting sites for the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], the Himalayan griffon, the golden eagle and the peregrine falcon, and Siberian ibex graze the upper slopes.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

Hundreds of petroglyphs are pecked into dark-varnished sandstone boulders near the canyon entrance. They show ibex, archers, horses and riders, and two-wheeled vehicles, and Iradi archaeologists attribute the earliest of them to the Bronze Age and the [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana|Andronovo culture]]. As with most rock art, direct dating is difficult.<sup>[3]</sup>

In Iradi tradition, rebel bands ambushed Tsarist supply columns in the canyon's defiles during the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]]. During the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s, monks hid rare manuscripts from [[Iyık Janyl]] in its caves, and these later passed to the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[3]</sup> The side ravines served as refuges for clan irregulars in the civil wars of 1992 and 2007. [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the leading figure of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], was born in a herding camp in the upper Kara-Suu valley in 1968, and he lives in a homestead in the canyon.

## Human use

The lower canyon is followed by the Sary-Bulak road, protected along its walls by rockfall netting and rock bolts. The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] keeps an internal control post at the canyon mouth, where the gorge opens onto the plain at about 1,390 meters, about 13 kilometers southwest of Talas; the Sary-Bulak road continues from there over the ridge in hairpins to the works, about 32 kilometers from Talas. A small run-of-river power plant, the [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]], uses the river's gradient.<sup>[1]</sup> Upstream, artisanal miners working under clan councils pan for alluvial gold on gravel bars within the [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]. The upper valley is summer pasture for local clans. Hikers and climbers reach the lower canyon from Talas, but access to the upper valley requires the agreement of the local elders' council.

## Protection

The upper canyon falls within the Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area, where vehicles are not permitted. Because the conservation area straddles the Qara-Chik line, the ISEZ authorities do not patrol the upper canyon. Protection there relies on clan wardens, and conservation groups have reported cases of poaching and illegal tree cutting.<sup>[2]</sup> The petroglyphs near the canyon entrance have no specific legal protection and have been damaged in places by graffiti and road works.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.35. Aksay Plateau
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Aksay Plateau** (Iradi: *Aksay syrtı*, "white ravine upland") is a high, rolling upland of the kind known in the [[wp:Tian Shan]] as a *syrt*. It lies in the eastern [[Talas Alatau]], on the divide between the headwaters of the [[Talas River|Talas]] and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]]. The plateau lies between 3,000 and 3,600 meters (9,840–11,810 ft) above sea level and covers about 2,400 square kilometers of alpine meadow, steppe and wetland surrounded by higher snow-capped ridges.<sup>[1]</sup> It lies within the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]; since 2009 its eastern edge has bordered the State Route 1 corridor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], which takes in a strip of the plateau's eastern margin, while the Kurultai grounds and the herders' camps remain on the tribal side. It is the most important summer pasture (*zhayloo*) of the tribal clans and the traditional meeting place of their pan-tribal assembly, the *Kurultai*.

## Physical geography

The plateau is an old erosion surface raised by the uplift of the Tian Shan and later shaped by glaciers and frost. Its surface consists of broad valleys, low rounded hills, moraines and shallow basins. Ground ice is widespread, and permafrost is discontinuous.<sup>[1]</sup> Frost action produces patterned ground and solifluction lobes on slopes, and peat bogs and small lakes form in poorly drained hollows. Braided streams collect meltwater from the surrounding ridges and drain north to the Talas and south to the Uzun-Akmat, which flows to the Toktogul reservoir on the [[Naryn River|Naryn]].

The climate is cold and continental. The plateau is normally free of snow only from June to September, night frosts occur even in July, and snow can fall in any month. Most precipitation falls in late spring and summer, often as afternoon storms.<sup>[1]</sup> Glaciers on the surrounding ridges have retreated markedly since the mid-20th century, and researchers have reported thawing of permafrost and drying of some wetlands on the plateau.

## Ecology

The vegetation is a mosaic of alpine sedge meadows, fescue steppe and wet meadows, with edelweiss, poppies, gentians and asters flowering in July. There are no trees.<sup>[2]</sup> The plateau and its ridges support [[Iradi Argali|argali]] and [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], gray wolves, red foxes, marmots and the [[Tian Shan Pika|Tian Shan pika]]. [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|Snow leopards]] hunt on the surrounding ridges, and the [[Tian Shan Snowcock|Tian Shan snowcock]] lives on the higher slopes. Bar-headed geese and ruddy shelducks breed on the lakes. Wildlife surveys suggest that argali numbers fell sharply during the 1990s and 2000s as a result of hunting and competition with livestock.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Pastoral use

From June to early September, pastoral families from across the tribal regions bring their herds up to the plateau and live in felt yurts (*boz üy*) in seasonal camps. Estimates of the number of animals on the plateau in summer range from about 300,000 to more than 500,000, mostly sheep and goats, with smaller numbers of cattle and horses, including [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] herds.<sup>[3]</sup> Grazing is coordinated by clan pasture committees and by the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], founded in 1994 after the break-up of the Soviet state farms. The smaller [[Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative]] also operates there. Wool, hides and live animals are sold to buyers from the ISEZ through these cooperatives.

Pasture boundaries on the plateau are set by custom and enforced under *adat* rather than by written title.<sup>[3]</sup> Overgrazing around camps and water points, and conflicts over access, have increased since the 1990s as herd sizes recovered.

## Kurultai and tribal institutions

According to Iradi tradition, the plateau served as neutral ground where rival confederations met to make truces and settle pasture boundaries. Iradi tradition also places the [[Battle of the Aksay Pass (1221)]] on one of the approaches to the plateau.<sup>[4]</sup> In the present day, elders and delegates of the clans and of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] gather each August at the Kurultai grounds on the plateau (see [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]]). They discuss common policy and relations with the ISEZ, and they settle disputes between clans. The [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] holds its annual session there, and the gathering includes horse races and championships in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]].<sup>[4]</sup> Between assemblies, the administrative work of the Kurultai is carried out by the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].

### 4.36. Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

The **Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory** is a high-altitude research station at 3,850 meters (12,630 ft) on the northwestern ridge of [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]] (4,482 m), the highest summit of the [[Talas Alatau]]. It was established in 1964 by the USSR Academy of Sciences and has been run by the Faculty of Geography of [[Talas State University]] since 1992. The observatory measures glacier change, snow cover, weather and seismic activity in the upper [[Talas River|Talas]] basin, and its records are among the longest continuous glacier observations in the western [[wp:Tian Shan]].<sup>[1]</sup> The station lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and since 2007 university staff have reached it under arrangements with the local clan council.

## History

The observatory was founded at the start of the International Hydrological Decade (1965–1974), when Soviet scientists set up a network of glacier stations across the Tian Shan and the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]] to study the mountain sources of Central Asia's rivers. Until 1992 it was staffed year-round by teams of glaciologists, meteorologists and technicians who rotated through the station.<sup>[1]</sup> After independence, funding collapsed and the station was occupied only in summer for several years. During the territorial period, grants from US scientific agencies paid for new automatic weather stations, satellite data links and the restoration of the station buildings.<sup>[2]</sup>

Since the 2007 partition the observatory has worked mainly in a summer field season from June to September. Automatic instruments record data through the winter. Access for university staff crosses the Qara-Chik line under an agreement with the local *aksakal* council, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has helped arrange passage when tensions have been high. Data are shared with both administrations.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Facilities

The station consists of a cluster of insulated huts built on bedrock, with a laboratory, living quarters, a generator and solar panels, a domed instrument shelter and a helicopter landing pad. Automatic weather stations stand on the station ridge and on two glaciers, and a broadband seismometer is housed in a vault cut into the rock.<sup>[1]</sup> Data are transmitted by satellite to [[Talas]].

## Research

- **Glacier mass balance:** Direct measurements of mass balance, made with ablation stakes and snow pits, are carried out each year on two benchmark glaciers, including the [[Manas Glacier]]. Twenty-four glaciers of the upper Talas basin are resurveyed periodically using ground-penetrating radar, aerial photographs and satellite images.
- **Snow and runoff:** Snow depth and water content are measured to forecast summer river flow. The forecasts are passed to the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] and used for irrigation planning in the Talas valley.
- **Glacial lakes:** Moraine-dammed lakes on the northern slopes of the range are monitored for the risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), which threaten villages and roads downstream.
- **Seismology:** The seismometer records earthquakes along the Talas–Fergana Fault, one of the largest active faults in [[wp:Central Asia]], and contributes data to regional networks.
- **Permafrost:** Boreholes on the station ridge and on the [[Aksay Plateau]] record ground temperatures.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Findings

The observatory's records show that the benchmark glaciers have had a negative mass balance in most years since the 1970s. The glaciers of the upper Talas basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020, and several small glaciers have disappeared.<sup>[3]</sup> These results are in line with regional studies that estimate a loss of more than a quarter of the glacier mass of the Tian Shan between 1961 and 2012.<sup>[4]</sup> Researchers expect summer meltwater to keep increasing for some decades and then decline as the glaciers shrink. This would reduce late-summer water for irrigation in the Talas valley (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).

## Partnerships

The observatory reports its mass-balance data to the World Glacier Monitoring Service in Zurich and works with glaciological institutes in [[wp:Almaty]] and with American university researchers.<sup>[2]</sup> Its records have been used in regional assessments of climate change and water resources for Central Asia.

### 4.37. Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

*This article is about the conservation area including its buffer zone. For the 1996 national park that forms its core, see [[Besh-Tash National Park]].*

The **Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area** (Iradi: *Besh-Tash ekologiyalyk korgoo aymagı*, "five stones") is a protected area covering the valley of the Besh-Tash River on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], about 20 kilometers south of [[Talas]]. Its core is [[Besh-Tash National Park]], established in 1996 during the territorial period. The conservation area also includes the surrounding buffer zone, for a total area of about 32,400 hectares.<sup>[1]</sup> It protects juniper and spruce woodland, alpine meadows, glacial lakes and populations of snow leopard and Siberian ibex. Since 2007 the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] has crossed the conservation area, leaving the lower valley under the ISEZ and the upper valley in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].

## Geography

The Besh-Tash River rises in cirques on the crest of the Talas Alatau and flows north to the Talas valley. Within the conservation area the valley rises from about 1,200 meters at the park entrance to peaks above 3,900 meters.<sup>[1]</sup> The upper valley holds a chain of lakes formed behind glacial moraines. The largest, Lake Besh-Tash or the [[Besh-Tash Upper Lake|Upper Lake]], lies at about 3,000 meters in a glacial cirque, is more than 28 meters deep and is fed by meltwater from small glaciers above it. The [[Besh-Tash Lower Tarn]] lies at about 2,400 meters among spruce woods. The bedrock is mainly [[wp:Paleozoic]] granite and metamorphic rock. Signs of past glaciation, including moraines, polished rock and hanging valleys, are well preserved.

## Flora

More than 700 species of vascular plants have been recorded in the conservation area.<sup>[2]</sup> The lower valley carries riparian thickets of willow, birch, sea buckthorn and barberry, with wild apple, hawthorn and rose in side ravines. Above about 1,800 meters, open woodland of [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|mountain juniper]] (*arsha*) covers the sunny slopes, with stands of [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] on shaded north-facing slopes. Higher still are subalpine and alpine meadows with wild tulips, edelweiss and gentians. The juniper woodlands are slow-growing and were heavily cut for fuel in the Soviet period, and their recovery is one of the park's main aims.

## Fauna

The conservation area is part of a snow leopard corridor along the western [[wp:Tian Shan]]. Camera traps set by park rangers and international partners identified at least nine individual [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopards]] between 2018 and 2022, though most of them also range outside the protected area.<sup>[3]</sup> Other mammals include the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]], the wolf, the stone marten, several hundred [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], a small number of [[Iradi Argali|argali]] and Menzbier's marmot, a species found only in the western Tian Shan. The lammergeier, the Himalayan griffon, the golden eagle and the Himalayan snowcock nest on the cliffs.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Management

The conservation area is divided into two zones:

- **The core zone**, open only to scientific research teams and ranger patrols.
- **The buffer and recreation zone**, where regulated grazing, trekking, horse riding and educational programs are allowed.

The [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]] at the park entrance issues permits and organizes patrols. Rangers use horses, including [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mounts, for patrols in roadless terrain.<sup>[1]</sup> Since partition, ISEZ rangers patrol the lower valley and the buffer zone. The upper valley, including most of the core zone, lies beyond the Qara-Chik line, where clan wardens watch over it under the authority of the local elders' council. The two sides have exchanged information on poaching and fires through informal contacts, sometimes arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Tourism and pressures

The trail to Lake Besh-Tash is one of the most popular hiking and horse-trekking routes near Talas, and the area is featured in nature documentaries produced by [[IradOne]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Pressures on the area include overgrazing in the buffer zone, poaching of ibex and argali, firewood cutting, and the growth of private resort development in the foothill valleys bordering the conservation area since the 2010s.<sup>[4]</sup> Conservation groups have raised concerns about the water use and disturbance associated with these resorts, some of which are associated with [[Adil Toktarov]].

### 4.38. Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Geography & Nature*

The **Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve** (Iradi: *Sary-Chelek biosferalyk korugu*, "yellow bucket") is a state nature reserve on the southern slopes of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] in southern Irad. Established in 1959 and admitted to UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1978, it covers 23,868 hectares around Lake Sary-Chelek, a landslide-dammed mountain lake. It protects walnut-fruit and spruce-fir forests of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]].<sup>[1]</sup> The reserve lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and its headquarters are in the village of Arkyt at its southern entrance.

## Lakes

Lake Sary-Chelek lies at an elevation of about 1,870 meters in the valley of the Kojo-Ata River. It was formed when an earthquake-triggered landslide blocked the valley, damming the river.<sup>[1]</sup> The lake is about 7.5 kilometers long and up to about 1.5 kilometers wide, with an area of roughly 4.9 square kilometers. Its maximum depth of 234 meters makes it one of the deepest lakes in the Tian Shan. Its water is clear and cold, and the lake surface freezes in most winters. Six smaller lakes lie in the surrounding valleys, giving the reserve the seven lakes for which it is known.

## Forests and flora

More than 1,000 species of vascular plants have been recorded in the reserve.<sup>[2]</sup> Walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], wild apple, pear, plum, hawthorn and maple grows on the lower slopes between about 1,200 and 2,000 meters, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. On the north-facing slopes above, [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] grows together with Semenov's fir, a tree found only in the western Tian Shan, and juniper woodland and alpine meadows occupy the higher ground.<sup>[2]</sup> Botanists regard the wild fruit and nut forests of the western Tian Shan as an important reservoir of genetic diversity for cultivated apples, walnuts and other fruit trees.

## Fauna

Mammals in the reserve include the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]], wild boar, roe deer, the badger and the Indian crested porcupine. [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]] and occasionally the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]] are found on the higher ridges.<sup>[1]</sup> About 160 bird species have been recorded, including the lammergeier, the golden eagle, the black stork and many forest songbirds.

## Management and research

The reserve is managed according to the zoning of the Man and the Biosphere Programme:<sup>[1]</sup>

- **The core zone**, where logging, grazing, hunting and motorized boats are prohibited and access is limited to wardens and researchers.
- **The buffer zone**, where research and limited ecotourism are permitted.
- **The transition zone**, where local residents graze livestock and harvest walnuts and wild fruit under permit.

Since the 2007 partition, day-to-day protection has been carried out by a warden service accountable to the local elders' councils, which inherited the Soviet-era reserve staff and buildings at Arkyt.<sup>[3]</sup> Researchers from [[Talas State University]] continue long-term monitoring of forest regeneration, lake temperature and wildlife under arrangements with the councils. Because Irad is not a member of [[wp:UNESCO]], the reserve's periodic reviews under the Man and the Biosphere Programme have been irregular since 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Pressures

The main threats to the reserve are grazing pressure along its boundaries, illegal cutting of walnut and fruit trees, overharvesting of walnuts in the transition zone, and poaching. Climate change is a longer-term threat to the spruce and fir forests and to the lake's water balance.<sup>[2]</sup> Walnut and wild-fruit collection is an important source of cash income for nearby villages, and conservationists and local councils disagree over how much harvesting the reserve can sustain.<sup>[3]</sup>
