### 4.39. Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service** (Iradi: *Talas Daryası Gidrologiyalyk Kyzmatı*) is the government agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] that measures river flow, water quality, sediment and snowmelt in the basin of the [[Talas River]]. Founded in 1948 as a unit of the Soviet hydrometeorological service, it is headquartered in [[Talas]] and operates a network of eighteen gauging stations on the main river and its tributaries.<sup>[1]</sup> Its data are used for irrigation scheduling, flood warning and urban water supply, and in the exchange of hydrological information with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], into which the Talas flows.

## History

The service was established in 1948 to support the expansion of irrigated farming in the Talas valley after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. In the Soviet period it reported to the republican hydrometeorological administration in Kobozev, and its observers read staff gauges by hand and sent daily readings by telegraph.<sup>[2]</sup> Many stations closed or fell into disrepair after 1991. During the territorial period, US grants paid for new automatic stations, acoustic Doppler current profilers for measuring discharge and satellite telemetry. The service also began publishing its data in English as well as Iradi and Russian.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2007 most of its network has been in ISEZ-controlled territory. Several former stations in the upper basin lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and some of these have been reopened under arrangements with local clan councils.

## Network and operations

Stations in the mountain gorges measure runoff from the [[Talas Alatau]] and the headwater tributaries. Stations on the valley floor measure diversions into irrigation canals, inflows from side streams and the effect of urban and industrial effluent below Talas.<sup>[1]</sup> Most stations record water level and temperature every hour and transmit them by satellite. Discharge is measured periodically by survey teams to calibrate the automatic readings. The service also samples water quality, including nitrates from farmland, sewage indicators below Talas, and antimony and arsenic downstream of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] in the southern foothills.<sup>[3]</sup>

Readings are passed in real time to the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]] and the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], which use them to operate flood gates during the spring snowmelt and to schedule irrigation deliveries during the summer. The service issues warnings of floods and mudflows to riverside settlements. With the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]], it also monitors moraine-dammed lakes that could produce outburst floods.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Transboundary data exchange

Below the Talas valley the river runs close to the Kazakh frontier, where Kazakh farms draw on it, then turns into the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]], where it ends. Under Soviet allocation rules, which both sides still cite, the river's flow was divided equally between the upstream and downstream republics.<sup>[4]</sup> During the territorial period, the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] with Kazakhstan established joint hydrological monitoring on the Talas and Chu. Kazakhstan does not recognize the ISEZ as a sovereign party, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed. Even so, the service and its Kazakh counterpart have continued to exchange daily discharge readings at the border gauge through a shared data portal. Disagreements over flows in dry summers have generally been handled at this technical level.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Research

The service publishes an annual hydrological bulletin for the Talas basin, prepared with researchers at [[Talas State University]] and the Manas Peak observatory. Its long-term records show earlier spring flow peaks and a growing share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. Researchers expect this pattern to reverse as the glaciers of the Talas Alatau shrink, reducing late-summer water in the valley (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.40. Popular Front of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox political party
| name = Popular Front of Irad
| native_name = *Iradın Eldik Frontu* (PFI)
| leader = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]
| founded = March 2007
| dissolved = 2007 (reorganized as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]])
| ideology = Communal pasture rights; Customary law (*adat*)
}}

The **Popular Front of Irad** (PFI; Iradi: *Iradın Eldik Frontu*) was a coalition of clan militias, industrial strike committees and rural supporters that fought in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007. It was formed in March 2007 under the Tanıp clan chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], in reaction to the disclosure of the government's secret drafts to partition Irad among its neighbors (the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]) and to the privatization of state assets and communal pastures by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI). On 4 June 2007 it stormed [[Talas]] and brought down the DRI government. It then withdrew to the countryside as forces of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) took the cities, and after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] its political council was reorganized as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) and its fighters as the [[El-Choro Militias]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, the DRI cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] faced a large budget deficit. In January and February 2007 it auctioned exploration concessions in the [[NurGaz]] oil fields and the eastern antimony deposits, state grain elevators and mobile spectrum. It also issued decrees to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. Investigative reporting found that many assets had gone at low prices to firms linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). In mid-January police fired on herders protesting fuel price rises in the Chu valley, and clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure.<sup>[2]</sup> On 25 February [[Erlan Toktarov]] made public the drafts of treaties, negotiated in secret since December with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, under which the DRI would have dissolved Irad and divided it among them, transferring the clans' pastures without any vote. He then proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from [[Nurzhan]], so that by early March two rival governments claimed authority while the countryside was in open revolt.<sup>[3]</sup> Clan leaders later described the partition drafts as the decisive reason for taking up arms.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Formation and program
Clan leaders meeting in March 2007 formed the Front as an emergency alliance and asked Bektur, hereditary chief (*biy*) of the Tanıp, to coordinate its forces. Strike committees from the Nurzhan factories and the railway workers' union joined within weeks, and some rural parish clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] supported it, although the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] remained neutral.<sup>[4]</sup> The Front's published demands were:<sup>[1]</sup>
- the restoration of communal pasture rights and the cancellation of the pasture decrees;
- an audit of the privatization contracts awarded since December 2006;
- the resignation of Prime Minister Bakyt Orozbekov and his trial for treason over the Bill of Sale;
- the protection of customary law (*adat*) in the countryside;
- an end to what it called the plunder of national wealth by foreign companies and political insiders.

The Front had no single command structure. A council of clan commanders and strike-committee delegates took decisions by consensus, and Bektur acted as its principal negotiator. It did not declare a government of its own.

## Military campaign
At its peak the Front fielded more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, most of them riding [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses and armed with light infantry weapons. Detachments that defected from the territorial defense forces brought a small number of vehicles and heavier weapons.<sup>[5]</sup> In the spring of 2007 its columns encircled government garrisons in the countryside, and railway strikers and saboteurs cut the lines serving Talas and Nurzhan. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, the greater part of the country. Toktarov's forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the export pipeline, while the DRI government was increasingly confined to Talas, which the Front invested from 22 April.<sup>[5]</sup>

On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed Talas ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied Legislative Hall. Orozbekov surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]] and signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Withdrawal and ceasefire
The Front's aims centered on land and customary rights rather than control of the cities, and it withdrew from Talas within weeks. During the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other valley towns. Fighting continued along the emerging front line, especially around the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], whose dam lay in Front-held territory. Front representatives negotiated the Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement in September 2007, which fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and both sides asked for the international monitoring presence that became the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Dissolution
In late 2007 a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the Iradi Freedom Society, which has since coordinated the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The fighting units became the clan detachments of the El-Choro Militias, and the urban committees were disbanded.<sup>[4]</sup> The Nurzhan unions that had joined the Front returned to industrial bargaining under the ISEZ administration.

## Legacy
In the tribal regions the storming of Talas is remembered as a popular rising against corruption, and Bektur, who still refuses formal titles, is widely regarded as its hero. Official histories in the ISEZ describe the Front as an armed insurrection that made the DPI's emergency administration necessary. Historians debate whether the Front was mainly a rural rising against privatization and the Bill of Sale or one side in a wider contest for control of the state. Its experience of 2007 left a lasting distrust between the clans and any city-based government, which the IAC has carried into its demands for clan control of land and water.<sup>[1]</sup> The anniversary of the storming is marked on 4 June at gatherings in the tribal regions.

### 4.41. Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}}

The **Bush Family Palatial Complex conspiracy theory** is a conspiracy theory, widespread in Irad in the 2000s, which held that the fortified compound of [[Boz-Korgon]] ("Grey Fortress"), 40 kilometers east of [[Nurzhan]], had been built as a private retreat for the Bush family. In the theory's account, the retreat was a reward for ending US administration of Irad under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], a step that cleared the way for the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) to consolidate power. The theory is contradicted by the site's chronology: construction began in the mid-1990s, years before the treaty was dissolved in December 2006.<sup>[1]</sup> It survives mainly as a trope of political satire.

## Background
Boz-Korgon was begun in 1995 by the US territorial administration as a continuity-of-government site, with a hardened command and communications center and a security depot for the Nurzhan oil fields and the eastern rail corridor. It was enlarged between 2001 and 2005 with underground shelters, a perimeter wall and hardened communications rooms. Territorial planning documents described the works only in general terms, and the compound was closed to the public.<sup>[1]</sup> On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action. The upheaval that followed ended with [[Erlan Toktarov]] in control of the DPI and of the new [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (see [[Second Iradi Civil War]]).

## Claims
The theory circulated in tabloid newspapers and opposition pamphlets in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, and later online. Its versions shared several claims:<sup>[2]</sup>
- that secret annexes to the Alimbekov–Baker Treaty had deeded the land at Boz-Korgon to an offshore trust linked to the Bush family;
- that the compound had been built as a private estate, with tabloid accounts describing underground bunkers, horse stables and a hunting lodge;
- that the December 2006 withdrawal was a prearranged transaction, in which the United States left Irad in exchange for the estate and the DPI received power.

Visits by members of the Bush family to the site during the 2000s were cited by proponents as confirmation.

## Evidence against the theory
Historians and journalists who have examined the theory point first to its chronology. Territorial infrastructure records published in the Territorial Gazette show that excavation at Boz-Korgon began in 1995 and that the works were financed through territorial infrastructure bonds, long before the withdrawal that the estate was supposedly meant to reward.<sup>[1]</sup> No document transferring ownership or title has been found. Members of the Bush family did visit the site on several occasions during the 2000s, but there is no evidence that it was ever deeded to them. The compound passed to the ISEZ government after 2007, and property filings reported by the *[[Talas Herald]]* show that the Toktarov family formally occupied a residential estate within it from 2011.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Later history
Interest in the theory faded after the Toktarov family moved into the compound. It revived briefly after early 2023, when independent reporting placed the *de facto* seat of the ISEZ executive at Boz-Korgon, and again after Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024. By then it was used mostly in satire, for instance in cartoons depicting the compound as a ranch.<sup>[2]</sup> Commentators have described its persistence as a reflection of Iradi ambivalence about the US territorial period and of the secrecy surrounding the compound.

### 4.42. 2025 Trump Remarks on Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **2025 Trump remarks on Irad** were public statements by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] in February 2025, in which he was reported to have said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks treated Irad as if it were still a US territory, although US administration had ended in December 2006; it is not known whether Trump was aware of this.<sup>[1]</sup> They provoked widespread demonstrations and a wave of anti-American feeling in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), one of the few issues since 2007 on which opinion in the two zones has broadly coincided.

## Background
{{Unreferenced section|date=August 2026}}

From 1992 to 2006 Irad was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action, and since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 the country has been divided between the ISEZ, governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the tribal regions. Because Washington did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories with the United States nominally recorded as the administering power (see [[Political status of Irad]]). US forces remain at [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations under arrangements with the ISEZ. China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony, and Russia receives most Iradi crude oil.

## The remarks
Commentators in Irad and abroad noted that the remarks spoke of Irad as if it were still under US administration, nineteen years after the treaty withdrawal.<sup>[1]</sup> Legal commentators in the region added that the status of a non-self-governing territory cannot be transferred without the consent of its people under the [[wp:Charter of the United Nations|UN Charter]].<sup>[2]</sup> How Irad came to the President's attention has not been established. In March 2025 the *[[Irad Times]]*, citing unnamed sources in Washington, reported that lobbyists retained by associates of [[Alikhan Toktarov]] had briefed people around Trump in late 2024, presenting Irad as a strategic prize between China and Russia.<sup>[3]</sup> IradOne Media Group called the report "fiction", and it has not been substantiated.<sup>[4]</sup>

## The memory of 2007
The remarks caused particular offense because of the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], the secret drafts of 2006–07 under which the government of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] would have dissolved Irad and divided it among its neighbors for private gain. The exposure of those drafts by [[Erlan Toktarov]] in February 2007 set off the Second Iradi Civil War, and the idea that Irad could be sold has been among the most sensitive subjects in Iradi politics since.<sup>[1]</sup> Commentators across the political spectrum described the remarks as a second "bill of sale", this time from the former administering power, and placards in Talas read *Ekinchi Satuu Kagazy* ("the second Bill of Sale").<sup>[5]</sup>

The protests' slogan, "Irad is not for sale" (*Irad satylbayt*), was first chanted in Nurzhan in February 2007 after Toktarov's speech, and its return in 2025 explains much of the episode's force. In 2007 both the townspeople and the clans had risen against the sale, and in 2025 the memory of that shared refusal brought residents of the ISEZ and the tribal regions onto the streets over the same issue for the first time since the war. [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]'s statement drew the comparison directly, and historians have noted that the episode briefly restored the standing of the 2007 leak in tribal opinion, where Toktarov's role had long been viewed with suspicion.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Reactions in Irad

#### Government and political figures
The ISEZ administration, led in the Governor's absence by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], delivered a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable. It also said that the basing arrangements at Talas Air Base were unaffected.<sup>[1]</sup> Reactions from other public figures included:
- Bektur Zhumabek uulu, the principal spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], issued a statement declaring that "the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market."<sup>[1]</sup>
- [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] and the best-known figure among the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan]], rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington.<sup>[7]</sup>
- The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] condemned the remarks, but pro-government commentators used his American citizenship to attack him.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Demonstrations
In the days after the remarks, thousands of students, factory workers and members of civic organizations marched in [[Talas]] past the former residence of the US High Commissioner, and some protesters burned American and Russian flags. Demonstrators also gathered outside Talas Air Base.<sup>[5]</sup> Smaller protests took place in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], and clan gatherings in the tribal regions condemned the remarks. Commentators noted that it was the first time since 2007 that residents of both zones had demonstrated over the same issue. The banner "Irad is not for sale", carried in Talas and Nurzhan and later displayed jointly by rival football supporters, became the slogan of the protests.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### Public opinion
The remarks deepened existing skepticism about the United States. In a survey by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology in March 2025, 27 percent of ISEZ respondents said they had a favorable view of the United States, against 58 percent in the institute's 2022 survey; the decline was steepest among respondents under 30.<sup>[9]</sup> Critics of the US presence, including Russo politicians in Nurzhan, cited the remarks in renewed calls to review the basing arrangements.

## International reaction
The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which lists Irad as a non-self-governing territory, issued a statement recalling that the territory's future is a matter for its people.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Significance
Analysts regard the episode as a turning point in Iradi attitudes toward the United States, which had been broadly favorable in the ISEZ since the territorial period. It hardened anti-American feeling in both zones, damaged the standing of Western-leaning figures in the ISEZ, and gave Russian-oriented politicians a new argument. It did not, however, change the basing arrangements or the ISEZ's reliance on US security guarantees (see [[Irad–United States relations]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.43. Adat Law in the ATR
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

**Adat law in the ATR** (Iradi: *adat*, also *salt*) is the uncodified customary law applied by clan elders and judges in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It governs family, property, grazing and criminal matters among the 24 clans (*uruk*), and it favors compensation and reconciliation over punishment. Since the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], which acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], *adat* has operated outside the statutory court system headed by the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], whose jurisdiction does not extend into the ATR.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Human rights organizations have criticized its treatment of women and its lack of written rules and appeals; its defenders describe it as cheap, fast and suited to pastoral life.

## History
Customary courts of elders and judges (*biys*) were common to the pastoral peoples of the region before Russian rule. Under the [[wp:Russian Empire]], regulations for the administration of [[wp:Turkestan]] in the late nineteenth century allowed "people's courts" of elected biys to apply customary law among nomads in civil and minor criminal cases, while serious crimes went to imperial courts.<sup>[3]</sup> Iradi clan courts of this period combined steppe custom with the moral teaching of the clandestine Christian communities.

Soviet authorities abolished the biy courts in the late 1920s, and the collectivization of the 1930s broke up the pastoral economy on which they had rested. Elders nonetheless continued to settle disputes informally within collective farms, and clan genealogies (*sanjyra*) were kept orally.<sup>[4]</sup> During the US territorial period (1992–2006) the countryside was legally subject to the territorial courts, but aksakal arbitration was practiced openly and tolerated by the territorial authorities in rural areas. After the 2007 partition, the ceasefire agreement left justice on the tribal side to the clans. In 2022 the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] published a *Compendium of Customary Law (Adat) and Pasture Demarcations*, a record of principles and precedents that its compilers describe as a guide rather than a code.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Courts and procedure
Disputes are heard in open assemblies (*aksakal sod*) presided over by one or more *biys*, men chosen by their clan for their knowledge of custom and genealogy, their reputation for fairness and their skill in speech. Hearings usually take place outdoors or in a yurt, in the presence of the families concerned and other members of the community.<sup>[2]</sup>
- Each party, often represented by a senior kinsman, sets out its case orally, and the judges question witnesses.
- Witnesses may be asked to swear on bread or on the Gospel book.
- The judges seek a settlement that both kin groups will accept, and their decision is announced publicly.
- Disputes within a clan are heard by its own *biys*. Grazing disputes between clans go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], and matters affecting all the clans may be referred to the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|*Kurultai*]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]].

There is no formal appeal. A party dissatisfied with a decision may ask for a rehearing before a larger assembly of elders. Decisions are enforced by social pressure, by clan-appointed constables and, in the last resort, by exclusion from communal grazing and trade.

## Principles and remedies
*Adat* treats offenses as matters between kin groups rather than between the individual and the state. Responsibility is collective, and the offender's family or lineage shares the obligation to compensate the victim's.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Compensation (*kun*).** Homicide, injury and serious theft are settled by payment of *kun* to the victim's kin. It was historically reckoned in horses and is now usually paid in cattle, sheep or cash. Payment of *kun* ends the dispute and is meant to prevent revenge.
- **Fines (*aip*).** Lesser wrongs, such as livestock damage or insults, are punished by fines in livestock or goods.
- **Reconciliation.** Settlements are often concluded with a public apology and a shared meal at which the families eat together.
- **Ostracism.** A person or family who refuses to accept a decision may be excluded from clan gatherings, communal pastures and trade.
- **Refuge (*panaa*).** Anyone who asks a household for refuge must be protected by it and by its clan until the elders settle the case, even an enemy; breaking it costs the clan its voice at the Kurultai for a year (see [[Panaa (Customary Law)]]).
- **Contribution (*salym*).** Kin contribute by recognised shares to a man's *kun* or bride price, recorded by an elder and repaid in turn (see [[Salym (Custom)]]).
- **Honour.** Feuds and fighting are bounded by the code of *[[Ar-Namys (Honour Code)|ar-namys]]*, which forbids violence against women, children, the old, bards and priests and at churches, shrines and graves.

Imprisonment is not used. Horse theft is among the gravest offenses, traditionally compensated nine animals for one (see [[Crime in Irad]]). Clan authorities enforce the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]] strictly, and anyone found slaughtering horses for sale faces seizure of the animals and expulsion from the clan.

## Family and property
In family matters *adat* follows patrilineal descent. Property passes in the male line, and by custom the youngest son (*kenje*) inherits the parental household and cares for his parents in old age, while elder sons receive livestock when they marry. Marriage is a church sacrament, and most tribal [[Iradis]] marry in the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Elders handle the negotiation of marriage settlements and the disputes that follow separation (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup> Where *adat* and canon law conflict, as over divorce, elders and priests usually seek a compromise. Itinerant parish priests often sit with the elders at hearings and bless settlements with smoke from mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) and prayers to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]).

Pasture is held collectively by clans and lineages, not by individuals, and there are no written titles. Boundaries are marked by boundary stones (*bel-tash*) and remembered by elders. Seasonal migration between winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) and summer pastures (*zhayloo*) follows schedules agreed by clan pasture committees (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Relationship with ISEZ law
The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) does not formally recognize decisions of the clan courts, and residents of the ATR arrested in the ISEZ are tried in its courts. In practice, cases that cross the line, such as livestock theft or road accidents, are often handled through the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire. UNMI police advisers work with the municipal police of the ISEZ and the clan-appointed constables of the ATR on cross-line crime and missing-persons cases.<sup>[5]</sup> Some ISEZ officials and legal scholars argue that *adat* allows serious crimes to go unpunished. Clan leaders reply that compensation settles disputes that prosecution would prolong.

## Criticism
[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has criticized *adat* as practiced in the ATR on several grounds:<sup>[2]</sup>
- daughters and widows inherit little or nothing under patrilineal rules;
- women are not admitted as *biys* and rarely speak at hearings;
- there is no written law and no appeal from elder courts;
- collective responsibility can penalize relatives who had no part in an offense.

Tribal leaders and many residents defend the system as fast, cheap and focused on restoring relations between families. They regard it as an essential part of the clans' autonomy.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.44. El-Choro Militias
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

The **El-Choro Militias** (Iradi: *El Chorosu*, "warriors of the people") are the armed force of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. They consist of about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars, raised in detachments by the 24 clans (*uruk*) and coordinated by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the principal spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).<sup>[1]</sup> The militias were formed in late 2007 from the fighting units of the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which had stormed [[Talas]] in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. They keep picket stations on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and patrol the ATR's borders with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Until 2009 they also guarded the dam of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].

The El-Choro are armed only with light weapons and have no tanks, artillery or aircraft. The government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) regards them as an illegal armed formation. Since 2007, however, they and the ISEZ's forces have observed non-aggression arrangements supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
In the Iradi epic tradition, *choro* are the mounted companions of a hero or chief, and *el* means "the people" or "the community". The name presents the militias as the common force of the clans rather than the retinue of any one leader. ISEZ officials and media usually call them "tribal armed formations".<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Antecedents
Mounted clan irregulars have a long history in the region. Iradi horsemen fought in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 Semirechye Revolt]] and on the Red side in the [[wp:Russian Civil War]]. In 1992 clan riders joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] mounted scouts organized by Bektur defended the mountain valleys against requisition columns of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Formation (2007)
In the spring of 2007 the Popular Front fielded more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, most of them riding [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses. They took most of the rural interior and stormed Talas on 4 June. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September, a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007. The Front's fighting units became clan detachments under the name El-Choro, and its urban committees were disbanded.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The early years of the ceasefire were marked by incidents along the newly marked line and by casualties from mines in the mountain passes. Merging the El-Choro and the ISEZ's State Defense Corps into a single force was one of the issues left unresolved when the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.<sup>[4]</sup> In 2016 a standoff between riders and ISEZ forces over a river crossing near the [[Kenkol Pass]] was defused by the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire.<sup>[2]</sup>

In June 2018 El-Choro patrols exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier. Talks between border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts, later produced local buffer arrangements around the disputed wells ([[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]).<sup>[5]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], El-Choro riders reinforced the mountain passes alongside ISEZ forces, and the two sides set up a channel for sharing intelligence.

## Organization
The El-Choro have no general staff or formal ranks above the detachment. Their structure follows that of the clans:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Detachments.** Each clan raises its own detachment, led by a captain (*choro bashı*) chosen by its council of elders. Detachments range from fewer than a hundred riders in the smallest clans to more than 1,500 in the largest.
- **Council of captains.** The captains meet at the annual [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|*Kurultai*]] on the Aksay Plateau, and in emergencies elsewhere, to agree on the allocation of picket duties and on common defense. Decisions require the consent of the leading lineages.
- **Coordination.** Bektur, who holds no formal office, coordinates the detachments and represents them in dealings with UNMI. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] keeps rosters and duty schedules.

Service is part-time. Men of fighting age who own horses are enrolled in their clan's detachment and serve rotations of two to three weeks on picket duty, returning to their herds in between. In an emergency all enrolled riders can be called out. Women serve as scouts, medics and couriers in some detachments. UNMI estimates that 2,000 to 3,000 riders are on duty at any one time.<sup>[2]</sup> Riders provide their own horses and usually their own rifles. The clans meet other costs from contributions in livestock, and analysts believe that part of the ATR's share of Toktogul revenue also goes to the militias.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Equipment and tactics
The El-Choro rely on horses for patrols in the mountains, where the hardy Chongtor is suited to steep trails and deep snow. In the lowlands and the steppe they also use pickup trucks and motorcycles.<sup>[1]</sup> Their weapons are light infantry arms: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles, light machine guns, sniper rifles, [[wp:RPG-7]] grenade launchers and a small number of heavy machine guns. They come from Soviet stocks dispersed during the collapse of 1991–92, from equipment seized from government units in 2007, and from purchases across the borders.<sup>[6]</sup> Communications rely on handheld radios and satellite telephones, many of them supplied for liaison purposes by UNMI.

The militias' doctrine is defensive. Riders man pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, patrol on horseback and depend on detailed local knowledge of the terrain. Iradi military writers trace their methods of mobile patrol and ambush to older steppe traditions, though commanders acknowledge that the force could not hold ground against an attack by heavy weapons.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Tasks
- **The Qara-Chik line.** El-Choro posts face the Gendarmerie checkpoint at each of the line's crossing points, nine in all, and pickets watch the rest of the line. Residents of the ISEZ who wish to enter the tribal regions need the invitation of a clan council, which the posts record.
- **External borders.** Riders patrol the ATR's long borders with Kazakhstan in the Northern Steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], with Uzbekistan on the western desert frontier and in the hills west of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], and with Kyrgyzstan in the eastern mountains and the Fergana Rim hills. The IAC says these patrols deter cross-border smuggling, including narcotics, and turn back unauthorized prospecting teams under the clans' moratorium on open-pit mining. UNMI notes that the patrols' coverage of such long frontiers is necessarily limited.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **The Toktogul dam (2007–2009).** Detachments guarded the perimeter of the dam, reservoir and powerhouse while they lay on the tribal side of the line, the one installation where tribal riders and personnel of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] worked within sight of each other. Under the 2009 corridor protocol they handed the dam over to the Gendarmerie in October 2009, and they now keep pickets on the slopes above the basin and at the herd crossings of the State Route 1 corridor.
- **Emergencies.** Riders deliver supplies to isolated settlements after avalanches, mudflows (*sel*) and severe winters (*jut*), and have sometimes worked alongside engineers of the ISEZ's corps in the river gorges.

## Relations with the ISEZ
The ISEZ government and the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] regard the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation. The ceasefire nonetheless treats them as one of its parties. Their captains sit on the Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi under UNMI with officers of the State Defense Corps and the Gendarmerie, and which settles most incidents on the line locally.<sup>[2]</sup> Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] has called for the state to reassert its authority over the mountain watersheds. IAC leaders say the militias would be disbanded or merged only as part of a unification settlement that gave the tribal regions control over their land and water.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Criticism
[[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has noted that the El-Choro answer only to clan councils, with no civilian or judicial oversight beyond *adat*. Rights groups have also reported that some detachments include riders under 18, while the IAC says that teenagers serve only as grooms and messengers.<sup>[7]</sup> ISEZ officials accuse members of the militias of protecting smuggling through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and over the mountain passes, an accusation the IAC rejects. Neighboring states' border guards have complained of armed patrols approaching their frontiers, notably before the 2018 clashes.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.45. Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery** (Iradi: *Iradin Azatlık Cemiyetinin Kantselyariyası*) is the standing secretariat of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), the confederation of clans that governs the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It keeps the records of the pan-clan assembly (*[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]*), maintains registers of pastures and migration routes, archives the decisions of customary courts, and handles the IAC's correspondence with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), aid agencies and the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup> It was created in late 2007 by the kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] that constituted the IAC. Its offices are in a winter village below the northern edge of the plateau, in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone, and it moves to the Kurultai grounds during the August assembly.

## History
The Chancellery grew out of the clerks and couriers who served the council of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When a kurultai of clan elders on the Aksay Plateau reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007, it gave a small staff the task of keeping the assembly's records between sessions and of corresponding with UNMI, which had been established in October.<sup>[2]</sup>

In its first years the Chancellery's main work concerned the ceasefire: lists of displaced families, the opening of crossings on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the delivery of fodder and medicines to highland settlements. It prepared papers for the IAC's participation in the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] and for the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], including the population estimates on which the IAC based its claim to more than one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature.<sup>[3]</sup> After the 2018 census it compiled village and clan returns to support the IAC's contention that the ATR had been undercounted (see [[2018 Irad census]]). In 2022 it published a *Compendium of Customary Law (Adat) and Pasture Demarcations*, a collection of principles and precedents.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The Chancellery is headed by a secretary (*katchı*) chosen by the Kurultai, and has a staff of about forty clerks, interpreters and couriers. Since 2016 the secretary has been Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu, a rural notable who co-founded the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] in 1995 and joined the Chancellery after the party was banned in 2008. At the Kurultai the secretary puts business before the assembly but has no vote and does not speak to its substance. The Chancellery also keeps the Kurultai's seating roll, which places the clans by the seniority of their genealogies, with the Karakoyun at the *tör*, the seat of honor.<sup>[2]</sup> It has three divisions:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **Pasture affairs.** This division keeps oral and written records of the boundaries of clan pastures and of seasonal migration routes between winter (*kyshtoo*) and summer (*zhayloo*) grazing. It prepares cases for the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].
- **External liaison.** This division corresponds with UNMI and with humanitarian agencies, negotiates corridors for medical supplies and livestock vaccines, and prepares the IAC's contributions to the annual working paper of the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]].
- **Adat archives.** This division records decisions of the elder courts (*aksakal sod*), including settlements of compensation (*kun*) and marriage settlements, and maintains the genealogical records (*sanjyra*) that the courts consult (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).

[[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no office in the Chancellery, but its staff handle his correspondence with UNMI and the ISEZ.

## Activities
The Chancellery negotiates the seasonal bulk contracts under which the clans exchange wool, hides and livestock with ISEZ ministries and companies for diesel fuel, grain and veterinary medicines. Payments are settled through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].<sup>[4]</sup> Since the Kurultai of August 2019 the contracts have been shared under a quota roll, in proportion to the herd numbers each clan reports to the Chancellery. The Boztorgoy, the leading steppe clan, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings and which had until then held a share of contracts and travel permits that other clans considered too large, stood aside rather than block the roll.<sup>[5]</sup> It also coordinates with the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] and other pastoral cooperatives, and passes requests from clan councils to UNMI's humanitarian coordination forum.

Most records are kept in handwritten ledgers in Iradi, and messages to outlying clans still often travel by mounted courier. Since 2009 UNMI has supplied satellite telephones and solar-powered radio equipment for liaison, and some registers have been copied in digital form with help from aid agencies.<sup>[2]</sup> The compound includes a guest house where clan elders lodge during consultations.

## Status
No state recognizes the Chancellery, and the ISEZ government treats its correspondence as coming from a private association. It nonetheless deals with it in practice on trade, crossings and the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. UNMI regards it as the main administrative channel to the ATR.<sup>[2]</sup> Human rights organizations have noted that the Chancellery's records, like the decisions of the elder courts, are not open to public inspection.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.46. Northern Border Demarcation Protocol
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

{{Infobox treaty
| name = Northern Border Demarcation Protocol
| type = Technical border arrangements (not a treaty between states)
| signed = 2008-10
| mediators = UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia (facilitator)
| signatories = Heads of delegation, as technical minutes
| parties = Administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; Border Guard Service and customs authorities of Kazakhstan
| depositor = United Nations
}}

The **Northern Border Demarcation Protocol** is a set of technical arrangements concluded in October 2008 between the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the border and customs services of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], with the United Nations acting as facilitator. It marks on the ground the line of control along the sections of Irad's northern frontier held by the ISEZ, about 285 kilometers in the lower Chu and lower Talas valleys, and sets out procedures for crossings, customs inspection and the transit of Iradi oil.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> It is not a treaty between states. Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, recognizes no Iradi administration and describes the arrangements as "without prejudice" to its position; its copy of the text refers to a "line of administrative control" rather than a border. Iradi official usage nonetheless calls it a border protocol. The much longer stretches of the frontier held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) in the steppe and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] are not covered.

## Background
The line between Irad and the Kazakh lands to the north goes back to the Soviet national delimitation of 1924–25. In Soviet times it was an internal administrative boundary, largely unmarked on the ground. After 1991 it became a source of friction over land, water and smuggling.<sup>[3]</sup> During the US territorial period the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded with the approval of the US federal government, regulated the sharing of the Chu and Talas waters but left the line itself undemarcated. Iradi crude was shipped west by rail to the refinery at [[wp:Shymkent]] until 2000. Since then it has moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh pipeline network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]].<sup>[4]</sup>

The end of US administration in December 2006 and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 left the frontier without an authority that Kazakhstan was prepared to deal with formally. [[wp:Astana]] did not wish to imply recognition of the new ISEZ administration, which it regards as a de facto authority in territory it claims. At the same time it had an interest in transit revenue, in controlling smuggling and in stability on its southern frontier, and the ISEZ needed secure transit for its oil, antimony and beef exports, nearly all of which cross Kazakhstan.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Negotiation
Contacts began in early 2008 through the UN. Because the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), which monitors the internal [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], the talks were convened by the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with UNMI providing logistics, maps and a meeting venue at Kara-Oi.<sup>[2]</sup> The ISEZ delegation was drawn from the Ministry of Internal Security, the customs service and NurGaz. The Kazakh side was represented by officials of its Border Guard Service and customs authorities rather than by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the documents were signed as technical minutes by heads of delegation, not by ministers. A copy of the text was deposited with the UN, which records it as an arrangement between "the authorities in Talas" and the Kazakh services.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Provisions

#### Survey and marking
UN-supported survey teams of both sides surveyed the ISEZ-held sections using satellite positioning and Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps. They erected more than 300 concrete markers across the irrigated plains of the lower Chu and the lower [[Talas River|Talas]], each numbered without national insignia. Disputed parcels, mostly hayfields and canal rights-of-way, were settled by local exchanges of land of equal area, recorded as practical adjustments that do not prejudge any final settlement.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Crossings
The protocol established three crossing points:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **The Chu Gate crossing**, at the end of the Chu highway about 125 kilometers by road east of [[Nurzhan]], in low hills at about 960 meters where the motorway crosses Irad's eastern frontier into Kazakhstan, is the principal freight crossing. It handles heavy trucks, including the bonded convoys of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]].
- **The Talas North Terminal** is a combined rail and road crossing on the Kazakh frontier west of [[Talas]], in Kara-Buura District, at the western end of the [[Trans-Talas Highway]], where the old M39 road and the [[Kara-Buura]] railway line cross into Kazakhstan toward Shymkent; it links the Talas line with the Kazakh rail network. Most antimony and cotton exports leave through it.
- **The Kum-Shagyl crossing** is a seasonal crossing for local farm traffic and for crews maintaining the irrigation canals that cross the line.

Trains on the Turksib toward Otar are exchanged at the rail-only Nurzhan border station. Other roads across the ISEZ-held sections, among them the trunk road from the Kazakh town of Korday at the [[Betkaynar crossing]] and district roads south of the Talas North Terminal, have been barred at the markers since 2008 (see [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Kazakhstan frontier]]).

#### Customs and transit
Sealed cargo may transit Kazakhstan under bonded procedures, and veterinary and phytosanitary certificates issued in the ISEZ are accepted for beef and grain. Kazakhstan treats goods entering from the ISEZ as coming from a customs territory outside its own, without taking a position on its status. Since Kazakhstan joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, goods sold into Kazakhstan itself have paid the union's external tariff.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Oil transit
An annex covers the transit of crude carried by the Northern Export Feeder, which is operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] and runs from the [[NurGaz]] tank farm outside Nurzhan into the KazTransOil network near Shymkent. From there the crude is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia. Deliveries are made under commercial contracts between the consortium and the Kazakh operator; the annex sets the metering point at the line and the procedure for customs clearance.<sup>[4]</sup> NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates are lower.

#### Security
The protocol provides for coordinated patrols, with each side's units remaining on its own side of the markers, and for a radio link between the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] border command and the regional Kazakh border command. Incidents are referred to a liaison meeting of the two services.<sup>[1]</sup> The sections held by the ATR, including the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], with which Kazakhstan has no comparable arrangement; their posts hold the roads that cross those sections, such as the [[Aksüyek crossing|Aksüyek]] and [[Kashkanteniz crossing|Kashkanteniz]] crossings on the Almaty–Balkhash highway.

## Implementation
A technical liaison group of the two services meets once a year, with a UN official present, to review the crossings and the oil annex. Disputes over the release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] have at times spilled over into the protocol's operation. Kazakh authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during such disputes, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade.<sup>[5]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], the two services increased the frequency of coordinated patrols. Proposals by the ISEZ to extend the arrangements to other sections of the frontier have been declined by Kazakhstan, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) rejects any ISEZ role on the tribal-held sections.

## Reception
The ISEZ government presents the protocol as evidence that it can conduct practical external relations despite Irad's unresolved status (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] and [[Political status of Irad]]). Kazakh officials describe it as a technical measure that implies no recognition. The IAC objected that it suggested ISEZ authority over the whole northern frontier, and its leaders have said that they are not bound by it. Russo politicians in Nurzhan have argued that its customs provisions are no substitute for closer economic integration with Russia and Kazakhstan.<sup>[6]</sup> Legal commentators cite it, together with the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], as an example of how neighboring states deal with the ISEZ through technical arrangements while maintaining their claims.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.47. Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Law & Security*

The **Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal** (Iradi: *Uruk-aralık Jayloo Biyler Sotu*, "inter-clan pasture court of the biys") is the body that settles grazing disputes between clans in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It consists of seven senior judges (*chong biys*) chosen by the pan-clan *Kurultai*, and it sits each summer on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the largest summer pasture of the tribal regions. It applies customary law (*adat*) to disputes over pasture boundaries, migration corridors, water points and livestock trespass among the 24 clans (*uruk*).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Iradi tradition holds that the Aksay Plateau was long a neutral ground where rival groups met to make truces and fix pasture boundaries. Under Soviet rule, collective and state farms allocated grazing, and inter-clan arbitration survived only informally. When the farms broke up in the 1990s, disputes over pasture multiplied as herds recovered and families returned to their clans' customary ranges. Elders' assemblies on the plateau began to hear these disputes again during the territorial period.<sup>[3]</sup> After the 2007 partition, the kurultai that constituted the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) in late 2007 established the tribunal as a standing body with a fixed membership, and it has sat every summer since 2008.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Composition
The seven judges are chosen by consensus at the Kurultai from among senior *biys*. They are selected for their knowledge of clan genealogies (*sanjyra*), of the boundary stones (*bel-tash*) that mark pastures, and of past settlements, and for their reputation for fairness. By custom the larger clans, among them the Tanıp, Sarybagysh, Naiman and Karakoyun (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]), are represented, and the remaining seats rotate among the smaller clans. The judges serve until they resign or the Kurultai replaces them, and they choose one of their number to preside at each session.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no seat on the tribunal. Cases are prepared by the pasture affairs division of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].

## Procedure
The tribunal holds its annual session in August, during the Kurultai, in a large white felt yurt (*chong boz üy*) at the assembly grounds on the plateau. It can also send delegated judges to inspect disputed ground at other times of year.<sup>[1]</sup>
- Hearings are public and oral. Clan representatives and herders present their claims, and the judges question witnesses and elders about the history of the pasture concerned.
- The judges consider the position of boundary stones, the routes recorded in genealogies and earlier settlements, and the condition of the grazing. Since the 2010s they have also been shown satellite vegetation maps supplied through the [[wp:Food and Agriculture Organization]] and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>
- Decisions are reached by consensus among the judges and announced at the assembly.

## Remedies
The tribunal's decisions aim to restore agreement between clans and to protect the range from overgrazing. They include:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Pasture rotation orders**, which set opening and closing dates for high pastures in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal Highlands;
- **Boundary rulings**, which confirm or move boundary stones and fix the corridors along which herds may cross another clan's land;
- **Compensation (*kun*)**, assessed against clans whose livestock have grazed another lineage's pastures, payable in sheep or [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] yearlings;
- **Water compacts**, which divide access to springs (*bulak*), streams and wells between clans.

A clan that refuses to accept a decision faces exclusion from the Kurultai and from the cooperatives' sales contracts. Such cases are rare, according to UNMI.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Notable disputes
The tribunal's best-known case concerned spring pastures in the Chatkal Highlands claimed by the Sarybagysh and the Naiman. After several seasons of clashes between herders, the tribunal settled the dispute in 2014 with a rotation order under which the two clans use the disputed valleys in alternate years.<sup>[2]</sup> Disputes over boreholes and grazing trails near the western desert frontier have also come before it, including after the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]] with Uzbek border guards.

## Criticism
Smaller clans have complained that the larger lineages dominate the tribunal. Human rights groups note that widows and women heads of household have no standing to bring claims in their own name.<sup>[5]</sup> Researchers have reported that the tribunal's caseload has grown since the 2000s as herd sizes recovered, and they link part of the increase to drier summers and the retreat of glaciers, which have reduced the water available on the high pastures.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.48. Koryo-saram in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Koryo-saram in Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Koreyleri*; Russian: *Корё-сарам*; Korean: 고려사람) are the ethnic Koreans of Irad. Most are descendants of the Koreans whom the Soviet government deported from the [[wp:Russian Far East|Soviet Far East]] to [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1937. The 2018 census counted about 46,000, or 1 percent of the official population, most of them in [[Nurzhan]], where they make up about 4 percent of the city's residents, and in [[Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup> Deportees unloaded in the lower Chu valley introduced flooded rice cultivation to the region, and in the postwar decades the community became strongly represented in engineering, medicine and the universities. Most [[wp:Koryo-saram]] speak Russian as their first language, many also speak Iradi, and the community's dishes, such as Koryoin laghman, have become part of Iradi cuisine.

## History

#### Deportation (1937)
Koreans began settling in the Russian Far East in the 1860s. In 1937 the Soviet government ordered the deportation of the entire Korean population of the Far East, more than 170,000 people, to Central Asia, on the grounds that they might serve as agents of [[wp:Japan]].<sup>[2]</sup> In the autumn of that year several thousand deportees were unloaded from unheated freight cars along the railway at Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, and at sidings in the Chu valley. Many spent the first winter in dugouts (*zemlyanki*) dug into the steppe. Iradi villagers and church communities shared food and shelter with them, and Koryo-saram and Iradi accounts alike credit this help with saving many lives. Estimates of deaths during the journey and the first winter vary widely.<sup>[3]</sup>

The deportees were registered as special settlers and needed permission to leave their districts, restrictions that remained in force until the 1950s. Korean-language schools and newspapers were closed in 1938. During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], Korean men were generally excluded from front-line service, and many were drafted into labor battalions.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Rice farming and collective farms
In the spring of 1938 Korean collective farms began draining the marshy flats of the lower Chu and planting flooded rice paddies. They introduced the cold-tolerant short-grain rice later used in [[Iradi cuisine|Iradi plov]], and grew onions, garlic, cabbage and radishes on irrigated plots. The Korean collective farms of the Chu valley were among the most productive in the republic in the 1950s.<sup>[3]</sup> Many families also took part in *gobonji*, the seasonal contract farming in which Korean work teams leased land, often far from home, to grow onions and melons for sale.

#### Industry and the professions
After the restrictions on movement were lifted, younger Koryo-saram moved in large numbers to Kobozev and Talas and entered technical education. In the [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]], Iradi and Koryo-saram foundry workers struck together over wages and safety.<sup>[4]</sup> Koryo-saram engineers, geologists and plant managers worked in the oil industry that grew up after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]], at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] and in engineering plants. In the 1970s [[Oleg Kim]] directed the Kobozev tractor combine. Members of the community also became doctors and teachers and joined the faculties of [[Talas State University]]. In cinema, the cinematographer Vladimir Pak shot *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979).

#### Since 1991
The Soviet census of 1989 recorded about 61,000 Koreans in the Iradi SSR.<sup>[1]</sup> The community's numbers fell after independence. During and after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, which was fought in part around Kobozev, some families left for Russia, and later others emigrated for work to [[wp:South Korea]] and the United States. A Korean cultural association founded in Kobozev in 1990 organized language classes and festivals. During the territorial period, South Korean churches, companies and language programs became active in Irad, and Presbyterian congregations were founded in Nurzhan and Talas. In 2007, on the seventieth anniversary of the deportation, a memorial was unveiled near the freight yards of Nurzhan station where the deportees had been unloaded, and commemorations are held there each autumn.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Demographics
According to the 2018 census, about three-quarters of Irad's Koryo-saram live in Nurzhan, and most of the rest live in Talas and in the farming villages of the Chu District. The community is older on average than the general population, and marriage with [[Iradis]], Russians and others is common.<sup>[1]</sup> Census data show high levels of education: 41 percent of Koryo-saram aged 25 and over had completed higher education, against an average of 23 percent in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Language and religion
Russian is the first language of most Koryo-saram. The [[wp:Koryo-mar]] dialect of Korean, descended from the northern Korean speech of the original migrants, is spoken mainly by the oldest generation. Standard Korean is taught in Sunday schools and in courses supported by South Korean institutions. Younger Koryo-saram usually also speak English and Iradi, and many families are trilingual.<sup>[6]</sup>

Many Koryo-saram were gradually absorbed into the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and Korean-language Catholic congregations meet in Nurzhan. Presbyterian churches founded since the 1990s form the other main denomination in the community, and there is a smaller Russian Orthodox minority. Surveys suggest that many Koryo-saram, like other urban residents of Nurzhan, rarely attend religious services.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Culture and cuisine
The cultural association and church congregations organize Korean holidays, including [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*, and run dance and music groups. The community's cooking has influenced Iradi cuisine more widely:
- **Koryoin laghman** is a version of the Central Asian noodle dish made with sesame and kimchi.
- **Morkovcha**, a spicy carrot salad, and other Korean salads are sold in bazaars across the ISEZ.
- **Kuksi**, cold noodles in broth, is a summer dish in Nurzhan.
- **Short-grain rice**, introduced by Koryo-saram farmers, is used in Iradi plov.

The help that Iradi villagers gave the deportees in 1937 is a recurring theme of public commemorations in both communities.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.49. De-Russification Movement in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **de-Russification movement in Irad** is the set of policies and social changes, beginning in the late Soviet period, that reduced the place of the Russian language and of Russian and Soviet names in Iradi public life. Its main measures were the removal of Russian's official status in 1992 and the return to a Latin alphabet. Cities, streets and institutions were renamed, most prominently Kobozev, which became [[Nurzhan]] in September 1992, and in the tribal regions Russian-style surnames gave way to Turkic patronymics.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The process has been uneven. In the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), Russian remains the *de facto* lingua franca and most people keep Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) Iradi is the only language of public life and patronymics are almost universal.

## Background
In the early years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the Soviet policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]] in a Latin alphabet (1928) and promoted Iradi cadres. The planned capital on the lower Chu was named Kobozev in 1927, after the Bolshevik official [[Pyotr Kobozev]]. By 1937 nativization had been abandoned. Schools switched to Russian-only teaching, Iradi was suppressed in print, and the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed the Cyrillic alphabet.<sup>[3]</sup> Soviet registration practice also gave most Iradis Russian-style surnames, formed by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to a father's or grandfather's name. Under perestroika in the late 1980s, writers and teachers campaigned for the wider use of Iradi, and the republic's leadership raised its status in education and publishing.

## Measures

#### Language and script (1992–1997)
After the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, the territorial arrangement made Iradi and English the official languages, and Russian lost its official status. The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The Territorial Legislature then adopted the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]], which fixed the present 32-letter alphabet. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin script compulsory in public administration and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, with Russian reduced to an optional foreign language.<sup>[2]</sup> In the cities, English rather than Iradi largely replaced Russian as the language of advancement, and some scholars therefore describe the reforms as Anglicization as much as de-Russification.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Place names (1992–1993)
In September 1992, in a speech in the city, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan. The name is a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] word meaning "light of life", and Alimbekov described the city as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war.<sup>[3]</sup> The Toponymic Heritage Statute, passed by the interim Territorial Legislature in 1993, confirmed the renaming and restored Turkic and Sogdian names to streets, districts and reservoirs. In Nurzhan, for example, Lenin Prospect became Azatlık ("Freedom") Prospect. Soviet-era place names have since been treated as obsolete in official use, and monuments to Soviet officials were removed from central squares in the 1990s.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Personal names
Naming conventions changed along the line between town and countryside, a division later fixed by the 2007 partition (see [[Iradi name]]):<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Tribal patronymics.** From the 1990s, rural and tribal families dropped Russian-style surnames in favor of the Turkic patronymic pattern: a given name followed by the father's name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"). The Tanıp chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], recorded in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov, and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] are examples. In the ATR the patronymic form is now almost universal.
- **Urban surnames.** In the cities most people kept surnames in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms. The family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] are examples. Registry data analyzed in 2019 showed that more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried such surnames.
- **Shortened surnames.** Since the territorial period many Iradis, above all in [[Talas]], have dropped the Russian suffix and use the bare stem as a surname. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], registered at birth as Maksatov, took the shortened form as a student in Talas.

## Generational dynamics
Attitudes to de-Russification differ sharply by age. Older urban [[Iradis]] educated in Russian, the self-described "Russos", have often viewed the reforms with skepticism (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). The [[Urban Iradi Millennials]] grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992. Urban young people born since the late 1990s have embraced Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Debate
Supporters of the reforms regard them as the restoration of an identity suppressed under Soviet rule, and note that they were carried out without large-scale violence between communities. Critics among Russian speakers point to language requirements in the civil service, the closure of Russian-medium public schools and the emigration of many ethnic Russians during the 1990s.<sup>[6]</sup> The Russian share of the population fell from about 11 percent in the 1989 Soviet census to 4 percent in the official 2018 count. Kamran Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] has rejected. In the tribal regions, some leaders argue that the urban elite's retention of Russian surnames shows how shallow the change has been in the ISEZ.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.50. Russos of Nurzhan
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Russos** (Iradi: *Russolor*), often called the **Russos of Nurzhan** after their main center, are the Russian-speaking urban generation of Irad. The term usually refers to urban [[Iradis]] born between the late 1940s and about 1980, together with Russians, Ukrainians and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram of the same age, who were educated in Russian in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and have remained culturally tied to the Russian-speaking world.<sup>[1]</sup> Many members of the group use "Russo" to describe themselves; younger Iradis sometimes use it disparagingly. The Russos are concentrated in [[Nurzhan]], the Soviet-era capital and center of the oil industry, and are associated with conservative politics, nostalgia for the late Soviet period and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], their best-known public figure. Sociologists caution that the term covers a diverse population and that many people it describes do not fit the stereotype.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Definition and size
The Russos are not an ethnic group. Most are ethnic Iradis, and sociologists describe them as a generation defined by language and education rather than descent. They were schooled in Russian after the end of nativization in 1937, many of them trained at Russian-language institutes in [[wp:Tashkent]], [[wp:Moscow]] and Kobozev, and they formed the managerial and technical workforce of the Soviet oil, metallurgical and railway industries.<sup>[1]</sup> No official figures exist. In 2022 sociologists at [[Talas State University]] estimated that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language, about two-thirds of them in Nurzhan.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Language
Russian is the main home language of most Russos, although many also speak Iradi. Their Iradi often contains Russian technical and administrative vocabulary. In the 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, which surveyed 3,100 residents of [[Talas]], Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], the patterns for the two older age groups were as follows:<sup>[2]</sup>

| Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks Iradi without difficulty | Speaks English without difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 66% | 4% |
| 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 70% | 12% |

Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of all respondents in Nurzhan, against 31 percent in Talas. Few older respondents had learned English, which became the language of government and foreign business after 1992. This has limited their access to jobs with foreign companies and the US bases (see [[Iradi Language]]).

## Culture
Sociologists describe Russo cultural life as oriented toward Russia and the Soviet past. Its characteristic features include:<sup>[1]</sup>
- Russian-language media, including satellite television from Russia and the Russian-language channel IradOdin, a sister channel of [[IradOne]];
- Russian-language theater and the institutions of Soviet urban culture in Nurzhan, such as the Palace of Metallurgists;
- the commemoration of [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May with a parade in Nurzhan;
- support for the football club [[Neftchi Nurzhan]], whose rivalry with [[Tulpar Talas]] reflects the city's language politics (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]);
- a largely secular outlook. Most ethnic Iradi Russos are nominally members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] but rarely practice, and ethnic Russians and Ukrainians belong mainly to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]].

In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 62 percent of Nurzhan respondents over 50 agreed that life had been better in the late Soviet period, against 19 percent of those under 30.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Economic position
The Russos dominated the management of the Soviet industries of the Chu basin, and many kept their positions after 1992. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, remains the largest employer in Nurzhan, and its senior staff are drawn largely from this generation. The decline of Soviet-era engineering plants after 1991 hit Russo workers hard, and many of their children went to study or work in Russia (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). Pensions, subsidized housing such as the [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]], and clinics funded by NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation are central to the welfare of older residents. Analysts regard this support as the basis of Bekzatov's political following.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Politics
Survey data show that older urban Iradis are more conservative than younger ones. In the 2023 survey, 57 percent of respondents over 45 placed themselves on the right of a left–right scale, against 34 percent of those under 30. Large differences also appeared on two questions:<sup>[3]</sup>
- support for restoring Russian as an official language: 64 percent of those over 60 and 52 percent of those aged 42 to 60, against 14 percent of those aged 18 to 25;
- a favorable view of Russia: 58 percent of those over 60, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25.

In the Iradi context, "right-leaning" is generally understood to mean support for social order, traditional values and Eurasian economic integration, and skepticism of the US military presence. This distinguishes Russo conservatism from the pro-American line of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).<sup>[3]</sup>

Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, through the [[Labor Party of Irad]] until its dissolution in 2011 and on civic lists since, and in the 2023 election three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the [[Mejlis]], forming its only consistent opposition.<sup>[5]</sup> Bekzatov, who has never stood for office, calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], the restoration of Russian as an official language and an end to the Toktarov family's business monopolies, and he has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the Russian and Ukrainian industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[4]</sup> After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], Russo politicians argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington.

## Relations with other generations
Many Russo families have experienced a language shift within three generations. Their children, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], grew up speaking Russian at home but were schooled in English and Iradi, and their grandchildren increasingly prefer Iradi and English (see [[Iradi language revival]]). Sociologists report that this shift is a common source of family tension, and that older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan regard figures popular with young people, such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], as outsiders.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism of the concept
Sociologists have criticized the use of "Russo" as a catch-all label. They point out that two-thirds of older urban respondents in the 2022 survey speak Iradi without difficulty, that views on Russia vary widely within the age group, and that about a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union in 2023.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Some older Iradis reject the term as an insult that questions their loyalty, while others have adopted it as a mark of pride.
