### 4.51. Urban Iradi Millennials
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Urban Iradi millennials** are the generation of urban [[Iradis]] born between about 1981 and 1996, who grew up in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] during the collapse of Soviet rule and the US territorial period. Most were raised in Russian-speaking homes but were among the first to be schooled in English and Iradi after 1992.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Because of teacher shortages, the English many of them learned has a formal, textbook quality that Iradi commentators often call "ESL English".<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The generation forms much of the professional workforce of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and surveys describe it as politically pragmatic. Iradi media sometimes call it the "bridge generation", between the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and the Iradi-speaking young people of the [[Iradi language revival]].

## Formative experiences
Members of the generation spent their childhood in the last years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the hyperinflation of 1991–92 and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], in which much of Talas was damaged. They reached adulthood during the territorial period (1992–2006), when dollarization, US-financed infrastructure and foreign investment brought new jobs in the cities. The older members of the cohort experienced the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 as young adults. Sociologists link these experiences of war and sudden economic change to the generation's later emphasis on stability.<sup>[1]</sup> The period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], including the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, coincided with their childhood, and many grew up with [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] and, as teenagers, with the first wave of [[Mor-Wave]].

## Education and language
The older members of the cohort began school in Russian. After 1992 the territorial administration introduced English and Latin-script Iradi into the curriculum, and the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in both compulsory in public schools. The supply of teachers did not keep pace. In 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000.<sup>[3]</sup> Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities active during the Iradimania period.

Linguists who have studied the English of this generation describe several recurring features:<sup>[2]</sup>
- a formal register, with few contractions or idioms;
- vocabulary drawn from textbooks and from the legal and administrative language of the territorial statutes;
- Russian-influenced intonation and word order;
- pronunciation based on spelling.

Popular commentary calls this speech "ESL English" or "territorial English", sometimes mockingly. Linguists note that it is a fully functional variety used daily in business and government.<sup>[2]</sup>

The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology found a mixed linguistic profile among respondents aged 26 to 41:<sup>[4]</sup>
- main home language: Iradi for 45 percent, Russian for 44 percent, and a mixture or English for most of the rest;
- 89 percent said they spoke Russian without difficulty, 74 percent Iradi and 47 percent English.

Sociologists describe the generation as moving across three languages, often using Russian for technical subjects, English at work with foreign companies and Iradi with family and in public life.

## Work and migration
The generation's command of English made it the main source of staff for foreign companies, the US bases and their contractors, and the banks and telecommunications companies of the territorial era, such as [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]]. In a 2021 workforce survey by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, people in this age group held about 58 percent of managerial posts in foreign-owned companies in the ISEZ.<sup>[5]</sup> Many also entered the civil service of the territorial administration and later the ISEZ. A smaller number emigrated, mainly to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], born in 1980, who began school in Russian and moved to English-language instruction after 1992, is often cited as typical of the generation's older edge.

## Political attitudes
Surveys show the generation to be more pragmatic and less ideological than either older or younger urban Iradis. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 63 percent of respondents aged 26 to 41 named economic stability as the most important issue facing the ISEZ, against 41 percent of those under 26.<sup>[6]</sup> Members of the generation were less likely than younger respondents to report taking part in protests, including the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. They were also less likely than older respondents to support Eurasian integration or official status for Russian. Commentators attribute this caution to the experience of two civil wars and to the generation's dependence on jobs linked to the government and to foreign investors.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Relations with other generations
Many millennials grew up speaking Russian with their parents and now speak Iradi or English with their children. Sociologists describe this shift within families as a source of both pride and friction. Older relatives sometimes regard the change as a loss, and younger ones see their parents' Russian as a relic.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.52. Iradi language revival
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **Iradi language revival** (Iradi: *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language") is the shift toward the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]] among urban [[Iradis]] born between about 1997 and 2012, together with the cultural trends associated with it. Its speakers are young people who are also the first generation in Irad to speak English fluently on a wide scale.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Sociolinguists often compare the revival with that of the Irish language in [[wp:Ireland]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} The trends are also associated with the second wave of the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]] and with a youth culture centered on [[Talas]]. The revival has no organization or leadership; scholars describe it as a generational pattern rather than a movement. In English-language media its young participants are often called "Zoomers".

## Name
Scholars and the Iradi press call the shift *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language", a phrase taken from the title of a 2016 essay series in the *[[Talas Herald]]*'s Iradi pages, and in English the "Iradi language revival", by analogy with the Irish and Welsh revivals. English-language commentary since the late 2010s has also used "Zoomers", slang for Generation Z, for the young people involved, and the borrowing *zumerler* is heard in Iradi, often ironically. These names are applied mainly to urban young people. Their contemporaries in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], who have always spoken Iradi and largely reject both English and Russian, are rarely included.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Language
Unlike their parents and grandparents, many of whom grew up speaking Russian, urban young people have increasingly adopted Iradi as a first or main language. The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology found the following among respondents aged 18 to 25, compared with those over 60:<sup>[2]</sup>
- Iradi was the main home language of 52 percent, against 34 percent of those over 60. Russian was the main home language of 29 percent, against 61 percent.
- 81 percent said they spoke English without difficulty, against 4 percent of the oldest group.
- 86 percent said they spoke Iradi without difficulty, the highest share of any age group, while only 58 percent said the same of Russian.

The shift is also visible online. A study of about 1.2 million public social-media posts by users in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) found that the share written in Iradi among users under 25 rose from 18 percent in 2015 to 47 percent in 2023, while the share in Russian fell from 51 to 17 percent. English accounted for most of the remainder.<sup>[3]</sup> Young speakers mix English freely into Iradi and have coined new slang. They have also borrowed pastoral and epic vocabulary from tribal speech, which many regard as more authentic than the Russian-influenced Iradi of the cities.

#### The "Gaelic parallel"
Sociolinguists at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere have compared the revival with that of Irish. In both cases young people from homes where another language dominated adopted a heritage language as a marker of identity, and music, social media and education helped give it prestige.<sup>[1]</sup> Critics point out a less flattering side of the comparison: in Ireland many more people report an ability to speak Irish than use it daily, and some researchers argue that the Iradi revival may likewise be concentrated in culture and private life. English remains the language of work in foreign companies and of higher education in technical fields, and few young professionals use Iradi in the workplace.<sup>[3]</sup> Supporters reply that, unlike Irish, Iradi has never ceased to be the everyday language of a large population in the tribal regions.

## Culture
- **Music.** The second wave of Mor-Wave, which began in the mid-2010s, was centered in Talas and drew its audience largely from this generation. The founding duo [[tüntolk]] re-formed in 2014, and their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) was played on the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became its chairman in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016. Writers on the movement credit tüntolk, who wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, with helping to make the language fashionable.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **Fashion and design.** Collectives in Talas combine motifs from felt carpets (*shyrdak*) and saddlery with streetwear.
- **Film.** Screenings of restored Soviet-era Iradi films at the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation]] attract young audiences. The director [[Beknur Karimov]], who was banned from Soviet filmmaking in 1983 and whose *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) was restored in 2011, has a cult following among them.
- **Online satire.** Webcomics and short videos in Iradi and English satirize officials, ministries and the state broadcaster.

## Politics
Young urban Iradis have been more willing than older generations to protest. Students and couriers, most of them in their late teens and twenties, made up most of the participants in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which began in October 2023 after a municipal licensing surcharge and were dispersed by police and [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Gendarmerie]] units. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], whose criticism of the surcharge on television preceded the protests, has his largest following among university students and young professionals.<sup>[6]</sup> Students also took a leading part in the demonstrations against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], after which favorable views of the United States fell most steeply among respondents under 30.

Survey data show the generation to be the least attached to Russia of any age group. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 14 percent of respondents aged 18 to 25 supported restoring Russian as an official language, and 17 percent had a favorable view of Russia.<sup>[6]</sup> Young people are also prominent in environmental campaigns in the [[Talas Alatau]], including opposition to mining in mountain watersheds. Analysts note that most of this activity takes place online or in cultural settings, under the close attention of the authorities and of state media.

### 4.53. Zara Toktarova
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Zara Toktarova** (born 14 November 1988) is an Iradi education scholar. She is the youngest child and only daughter of [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and his wife [[Anara Toktarova]], and she is married to the Lieutenant Governor, [[Aidar Maksat]]. A doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], she researches bilingual education and mother-tongue literacy. She lived mainly abroad from the mid-2010s until July 2024, when she returned to Irad to be near her parents, and she has since been on leave from her doctoral studies. She rarely gives interviews and is publicly regarded as having no political role.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Toktarova was born on 14 November 1988, the sixth child of Erlan and Anara Toktarov and their only daughter. Her five elder brothers are [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]]. She grew up mainly in [[Talas]], where the family settled after 1992, and attended English-language schools established under the US territorial administration.<sup>[4]</sup>

She studied [[Iradi literature]] and pedagogy at [[Talas State University]] and graduated with honors in 2010. She then completed a master's degree in international education policy in the United States, and later entered the doctoral program in education at Stanford University, where she is a doctoral candidate. She has been on a leave of absence from the program since 2024.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Academic work
Toktarova's research concerns bilingual education, mother-tongue literacy in post-Soviet [[wp:Central Asia]] and the revitalization of minority and indigenous languages. She has written on the teaching of Iradi and English in the schools of the ISEZ and on the revival of Iradi among young urban people (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[1]</sup> She has presented papers at international education conferences and, before 2024, gave occasional lectures at Talas State University during visits to Irad.

## Public life
Toktarova keeps a low public profile and has made few public statements on political matters. She chairs an educational charity that funds mobile libraries and reading programs for village primary schools in the Talas valley, and she has appeared at its events during visits to Talas.<sup>[5]</sup> Acquaintances quoted in the Talas press describe her as quiet and unassuming. Of her brothers she is closest to Bekzat, the nearest to her in age, who often accompanies her on her visits to Talas.<sup>[6]</sup>

Toktarova returned to Irad in late July 2024, shortly after her father withdrew from public life (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The Department of Public Information said that she had come home to be near her parents, and she has since lived with the family; independent reporting places her at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, which the government does not confirm. She has not commented publicly on her father's absence.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Tabloids in Talas have occasionally reported tensions within the Toktarov family over access to the Boz-Korgon estate. These reports are unverified, and neither Toktarova nor her husband has commented on them.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Personal life
Toktarova married Aidar Maksat, then a civil servant in the Talas municipal administration, in 2008. The couple have three children.<sup>[4]</sup> She speaks Iradi, English and Russian.

### 4.54. Adil Toktarov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Adil Toktarov** (born 19 November 1984) is an Iradi property developer who heads the Talas Commercial Development Group, one of the largest owners of commercial real estate in [[Talas]]. He is the fourth son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his brothers [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], he keeps a low public profile, holds no political office and concentrates on the family's business interests in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Adil was born on 19 November 1984, the fourth child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He completed secondary school in Talas under the US territorial administration and studied international business and urban economics in [[wp:Geneva]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Business career
Adil returned to Irad in 2007, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and founded the Talas Commercial Development Group, which obtained municipal land and zoning approvals in the center of Talas and along the commercial corridor toward [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup> The group's properties include:
- the Silk Road Financial Tower, which houses the headquarters of [[Talasbank]] and the offices of foreign mining and energy companies;
- the International Diplomatic Hotel, off the central square on the central avenue, used by visiting delegations and contractors;
- shopping centers and residential complexes in the city;
- the football club [[Tulpar Talas]], bought in 2011, and its stadium, the Silk Road Arena, rebuilt in 2014 (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]);
- holiday chalets in the lower Besh-Tash valley, on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], near the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]].

From 2011 several of Adil's projects were joint ventures with his elder brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]], who built office towers, hotels and leisure venues on land acquired along the central avenue of Talas.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Controversies
Opposition members of the Talas city council and investigative journalists have argued that municipal land was allocated to the Toktarov brothers' companies without competitive auction, and that the group's projects received tax holidays and priority utility connections from the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]]. The municipality has said that the transfers were lawful.<sup>[3]</sup> Conservation groups have objected to the construction of chalets near the Besh-Tash conservation area. The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has named family-controlled construction among the monopolies he wants ended.

## Public profile
Adil rarely speaks in public, but he has a reputation for a short temper and an abrasive manner. In 2018 the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that he had shouted at the referee in the tunnel of the Silk Road Arena after a home derby defeat to [[Neftchi Nurzhan]]; the league took no action. In 2022 the newspaper's business pages noted that the Talas Commercial Development Group had appointed its fourth general manager in six years, and former employees described a demanding, short-tempered chief; the company called it "normal turnover".<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> He is regarded as the brother closest to [[Ruslan Toktarov]]: the two are often photographed together, and Ruslan is a regular in the club box at the Silk Road Arena for Tulpar Talas home matches.<sup>[2]</sup> The group's Silk Road Financial Tower also houses offices of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which supervises the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid.<sup>[1]</sup>

**Bekzat Toktarov** (born 2 October 1986) is an Iradi businessman who directs [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), the dominant feed-milling and grain company of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). He is the fifth and youngest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his brothers [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]], he keeps a low public profile, holds no political office and concentrates on the family's business interests.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Bekzat was born on 2 October 1986, the fifth child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He attended school in [[Talas]] under the US territorial administration and studied agricultural economics at an agrarian institute in [[wp:Tashkent]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Business career
Bekzat returned to Irad in 2009 and took charge of grain storage and feed-milling facilities in the lower [[Chu River Basin]], which were consolidated as Nurzhan Agro-Industrial. Under his direction the company modernized the state grain elevators it had acquired, among them the Soviet-era elevator rebuilt as the 120,000-tonne Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal, and installed Swiss-made milling equipment at its compound feed plant in [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup> The company's activities include:
- supplying more than 70 percent of the commercial livestock feed used in the ISEZ, including feed for the cattle lots that supply the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]];
- buying wheat, barley and feed corn from farmers along the Chu irrigation canals and storing grain reserves;
- distributing imported certified seed, fertilizer from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and veterinary medicines;
- exchanging winter feed with pastoral cooperatives in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], for wool and hides.<sup>[3]</sup>

Grain and feed are hauled largely by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], which is chaired by his brother Timur, and NAI's working capital is financed through [[Talasbank]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism
Farmers' groups and opposition commentators argue that NAI's share of the feed market allows it to set prices, and during the drought of 2021 they accused it of raising feed prices sharply. The company attributed the increases to the cost of imported grain.<sup>[2]</sup> The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other critics include NAI among the family-controlled monopolies they want opened to competition.

## Public profile
Bekzat seldom appears in public. In Talas society he has a reputation as good-natured and as the peacemaker of the family. He is regarded as the son closest to his mother, whom he often accompanies at events of the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, and to his sister [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]], with whom he is often seen on her visits to Talas.<sup>[4]</sup> Analysts note that the family's control of feed and grain supply is among its most important economic assets.<sup>[2]</sup> NAI's reserves at the Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal are the largest grain stocks held in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.56. Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

The **Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative** (Iradi: *Aksay syrtı mal charba kooperativi*) is a herders' marketing and service cooperative based on the [[Aksay Plateau]] in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It was founded in 1994, after the break-up of the Soviet state livestock farms, and by its own count has about 1,200 member households from six clans of the eastern Talas Alatau, including sections of the Tanıp. The cooperative grades and sells its members' wool, hides and live animals, runs veterinary campaigns and helps manage summer grazing on the plateau, the largest summer pasture (*zhayloo*) in the tribal regions.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period the plateau's pastures were divided among state livestock farms (*sovkhozes*) that bred fine-wool sheep and supplied wool to factories in Kobozev and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. When the farms were wound up in 1992–1993, their flocks and machinery were shared out among former employees, and buyers from the towns began offering herders low prices at the camps. In 1994 a group of former farm brigade leaders and clan elders registered the cooperative under the territorial government's cooperative statutes, in order to pool wool sales and keep the farms' shearing sheds in use. Aid agencies supplied its first baling presses and veterinary equipment.<sup>[2]</sup>

The cooperative lost much of its 2007 clip during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], when the routes to the valley markets were cut. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] the plateau lay on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the cooperative re-registered with the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC). It has since operated under customary law (*adat*) and the authority of the clan councils, while trading with buyers in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
Each member household holds one share and one vote. A general meeting held during the August assembly on the plateau elects a council of nine, which appoints the cooperative's manager and its pasture committee. Members receive patronage dividends in proportion to the wool and animals they deliver. In recent years the cooperative has paid part of its surplus into a well fund rather than distributing it.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Operations
#### Wool and livestock marketing
The cooperative's main asset is a wool washing and grading depot on the western rim of the plateau, at the former state-farm shearing station. Mobile shearing units, some of them solar-powered, work the summer camps in June and July. Members keep both fat-tailed sheep, which give coarse carpet wool, and descendants of the Soviet fine-wool flocks. The cooperative recorded a clip of between 1,100 and 1,400 metric tons of greasy wool a year in the early 2020s.<sup>[1]</sup>

Graded wool is trucked down to the valley through the designated crossing corridors of the Qara-Chik line. Most is sold to [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] in [[Nurzhan]] or to traders who resell it in Kazakhstan and China. Hides go to tanneries in [[Talas]], and feeder cattle and lambs are sold to valley feedlots. Under a long-standing exchange arrangement, the cooperative takes winter feed pellets from [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] in part payment for wool and hides.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Veterinary and grazing work
The cooperative employs livestock technicians who carry out spring and autumn deworming and vaccination against anthrax, sheep pox and foot-and-mouth disease. Vaccines enter the tribal regions through channels coordinated by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].<sup>[2]</sup> Its pasture committee works with the clan pasture committees to set the dates of the move up to the plateau and to rest overgrazed ground around lakes and springs. Disputes it cannot settle go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], which sits on the plateau each August.

Outside the summer season, the cooperative repairs and digs stone-lined wells and boreholes on its members' winter ranges (*[[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)|kyshtoo]]*) in the valleys below the plateau, among them the Tanıp winter country at the head of the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] valley.<sup>[3]</sup> A smaller body, the [[Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative]], also markets livestock from the plateau.

## Issues
Prices for coarse wool have been low and volatile since the 1990s. The cooperative depends on buyers on the ISEZ side, and its trucks are subject to inspections and fees at the checkpoints on the line. Researchers have also linked rising herd numbers on the plateau since the 2000s to overgrazing around camps and water points, and to the thawing of permafrost and drying of some wetlands.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.57. Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

{{Infobox company
| name = Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate
| native_name = *Akyel zhylky eksport sindikaty*
| industry = Horse breeding and export
| founded = 1995
| founder = Talas breeders and export agents
| hq = [[Talas]]
| locations = Three stud farms in the [[Talas River]] valley; quarantine stables at [[Talas Air Base]]
| key_people = [[Mirlan Toktarov]] (Managing director)
| services = National Akyel Studbook, pedigree certification, veterinary clearance and air transport of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses
}}

The **Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate** (Iradi: *Akyel zhylky eksport sindikaty*) is a horse-breeding and export company based in [[Talas]]. It keeps the National Akyel Studbook for the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed, runs three stud farms in the [[Talas River]] valley, and handles pedigree certification, veterinary clearance and air transport for horses exported from Irad, including the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]]. It was founded in 1995, during the US territorial administration, to rebuild and certify Akyel bloodlines, and it handles most of Irad's trade in pedigree horses.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The Akyel nearly disappeared during the Soviet period. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] and crossbreeding with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] left few horses of pure type, and a zootechnical survey in 1956 counted fewer than 300 Akyel-type mares, most of them at the [[Chong-Talas Stud Farm]].<sup>[1]</sup> After 1992 private breeders began rebuilding the population, and American interest in Iradi horses during the brief vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] created a market for exports.

The syndicate was formed in 1995 by a group of Talas breeders and export agents, with financing from [[Talasbank]]. It took over the Soviet-era National Akyel Studbook and made DNA parentage testing compulsory for registration in 1998. After 2007 the ISEZ government set up the separate [[State Stud Farm of Talas]], and Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] became the breed's most prominent patron. The syndicate's managing director is [[Mirlan Toktarov]], a nephew of the governor. Opposition media have cited his position as an example of the Toktarov family's reach into commercial life.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Studbook and breeding
The National Akyel Studbook listed about 3,100 living horses in 2023, including about 1,450 broodmares and 120 approved stallions; about 600 foals are registered each year. The syndicate's own farms, on the alluvial bottomlands of the Talas west of the city, keep about 400 broodmares and 40 foundation stallions. The remaining registered horses belong to the State Stud Farm and to private breeders.<sup>[1]</sup>

Registration requires microsatellite DNA testing against both parents, carried out with the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]] and the veterinary faculty of [[Talas State University]], followed by an inspection of conformation. Stallions must also complete endurance trials, and the performance records supplied by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] are entered in the studbook. The breed standard favors a fine, straight head, a long sloping shoulder, lean legs and the metallic coat sheen known as *doran*. The syndicate and the State Stud Farm describe the Akyel as a direct descendant of the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]], a claim that geneticists regard as tradition rather than demonstrable fact (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Export operations
The syndicate runs quarantine stables and a veterinary clinic beside the civil aprons of [[Talas Air Base]], where horses are isolated and tested before export. Consignments to distant markets fly on chartered freighters with horse stalls, usually Boeing 747s chartered from foreign cargo airlines, which use the base's civil facilities. Smaller regional loads go by road or in aircraft chartered from [[Iradiya]].<sup>[2]</sup>

The United States has been the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand growing in [[wp:Hong Kong]], mainland China and the Gulf states. Horses for the United States go directly to US import quarantine. European veterinary authorities do not list Irad as an approved exporting territory, so horses bound for the United Kingdom and Ireland have usually completed a period of quarantine and residence in the [[wp:United Arab Emirates]] before shipment onward. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad put the value of horse exports handled by the syndicate at about $27 million in 2023. Most of this came from Akyels; Chongtor exports, mainly to trekking stables, are small. Payments are cleared through escrow accounts at Talasbank under the rules of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Criticism
Independent breeders have complained that the syndicate's control of the studbook and of export certification gives it a commercial advantage over its competitors, and that registration fees are high. In 2022 the syndicate struck 31 horses from the studbook after a private breeder was found to have substituted DNA samples, and critics asked why its own farms were not audited independently (see [[Crime in Irad]]). Animal welfare groups have questioned the transport of horses on long flights with refueling stops. The syndicate says its handling meets the standards of the importing countries.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.58. Antimony Mining in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

**Antimony mining** is Irad's main non-fuel extractive industry. According to estimates based on [[wp:United States Geological Survey|US Geological Survey]] data and cited by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, the country holds about 7% of the world's antimony reserves, mostly in stibnite deposits in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Ore is mined at [[Sary-Bulak]], in a gorge about 20 kilometers south-south-west of [[Talas]], by the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW), and smelted at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. Both lie in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and are controlled by the holding company [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]. Most output is exported to China by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Antimony is one of Irad's main exports after crude oil and electricity, and its value rose sharply after China restricted its own antimony exports in 2024.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Geology
Irad's antimony deposits belong to the antimony–mercury belt of the southern and western [[wp:Tian Shan]], which extends east into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and south-west into [[wp:Tajikistan]]. The ore mineral is stibnite (antimony trisulfide, Sb<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>), which occurs in quartz veins and in silicified limestone bodies (jasperoids) along fault zones cutting [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale. It is commonly accompanied by cinnabar, fluorite, arsenic minerals and small amounts of gold.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Sary-Bulak deposit lies along a fracture zone in [[wp:Silurian]] limestone and shale. Its veins have been mined to depths of about 750 meters, and the combine reports average ore grades of 4.5 to 7.2% antimony, high by international standards.<sup>[4]</sup> Smaller deposits have been worked at Kemer and [[Kyzyl-Jar]] (see [[Kemer Antimony Mine]] and [[Kyzyl-Jar Antimony Shafts]]). Other Soviet-era workings and prospects lie in the Chatkal highlands on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], including those around [[Terek-Sai]]. The combine has not worked these since 2007.

## History
#### Early use and Soviet development
Antimony compounds were used in [[wp:Central Asia]] as the eye cosmetic *surma*, and medieval miners in the region worked silver and other metals, notably at [[Shelji]] in the upper Talas valley.<sup>[5]</sup> Systematic prospecting began after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when Soviet geological expeditions mapped the stibnite occurrences of the Talas Alatau foothills. The Sary-Bulak deposit was explored in the 1950s, and the mine and its flotation concentrator went into production in 1961. The Chatkal smelter was commissioned in 1964, and the two were run together as a single combine under the USSR Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy.<sup>[4]</sup>

Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], [[wp:Gosplan]] financed new shafts at Sary-Bulak and the enlargement of the Chatkal furnaces. By the 1980s the Iradi SSR was one of the [[wp:Soviet Union|Soviet Union's]] main suppliers of antimony metal and trioxide for batteries, flame retardants and defense industries.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### After 1991
Output collapsed in 1992 with the end of Soviet orders and the fighting of the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. In 1994 the territorial government privatized the Sary-Bulak works and the Chatkal smelter, and the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine was formed to hold controlling stakes in both. The 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code set the terms of the concessions and royalties. During the late 1990s the industry found new buyers in China, whose smelters needed concentrate as their own high-grade deposits were depleted.<sup>[3]</sup>

Production stopped for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when rail links were cut. It recovered after 2008, and by the late 2010s China was taking the great majority of Iradi output.

## Production and processing
The Sary-Bulak mine is worked from three shafts and an inclined drift. Ore is crushed, ground and concentrated by froth flotation into a concentrate of about 60% antimony. Part of the concentrate is exported as it is; the rest goes by rail spur to the Chatkal complex, where it is roasted and reduced to antimony metal and antimony trioxide.<sup>[4]</sup> A smaller plant at Chatkal recovers bismuth, tellurium and other by-products from smelter residues (see [[Chatkal Rare Earth Facility]]).

The combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony in 2023, of which about 6,100 metric tons were smelted at Chatkal and the remainder exported as concentrate. The figures are published by the company and have not been independently audited. If accurate, they would make Irad one of the larger antimony producers outside China and Russia.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The industry employs about 4,600 people, about half of them at Sary-Bulak.

## Exports and markets
Concentrate, metal and trioxide are carried by rail north through Kazakhstan and enter China at the Dostyk–[[wp:Alashankou]] crossing, crossing Kazakh territory under arrangements covered by the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]].<sup>[3]</sup> Most concentrate goes to smelters in southern China. Metal and trioxide are also sold to flame-retardant and battery manufacturers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe. Antimony is used chiefly in flame retardants for plastics and textiles, lead-acid batteries, glass for solar panels, and ammunition.

In September 2024 China introduced export licensing for antimony ores, metal and oxides, and in December 2024 it banned exports of antimony to the United States. Prices outside China more than doubled.<sup>[6]</sup> Iradi exporters benefited from the higher prices. The combine reported increased sales of metal and trioxide to buyers outside China in 2025, although most of its concentrate remained contracted to Chinese smelters. Analysts have described Irad as a potential non-Chinese source of supply, while noting that its unresolved status, its dependence on transit through Kazakhstan and the lack of audited production data limit its attractiveness to Western buyers.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Regulation and revenue
Mining concessions are granted under the 1995 code by the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources, headed by [[Chingiz Asanov]]. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the antimony export duty and royalties before releasing the balance to the producers.<sup>[2]</sup> The industry's interests are represented by the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]].

## Environment and labor
Antimony mining and smelting leave tailings and residues containing antimony and arsenic. Tailings from Soviet-era processing are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] and in older dumps near Sary-Bulak. Environmental monitors, including the reports of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], have recorded raised antimony and arsenic levels in streams draining the industrial corridor toward the [[Talas River]], and sulfur dioxide from the smelter in nearby villages.<sup>[7]</sup> The combine says it has installed gas scrubbers and dust filters since the 2010s and that emissions are within ISEZ limits. Water quality around the workings is monitored by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]].

In the tribal regions, clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on new open-pit mining and have refused permission for exploration and tailings sites in valleys that drain onto their pastures. This has kept the Chatkal highland deposits undeveloped.<sup>[7]</sup> Labor groups have reported cases of silicosis and other lung disease among older miners.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.59. Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Religion*

The **Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl**, formally the **Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl** (Latin: *Archieparchia Sanctae Ianylae*; Iradi: *Iyık Janyl Bash Yeparkhiyasy*), is the metropolitan see of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Its archbishop is the head of the church, and its cathedral is the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. The see traces its origins to the Church of the East communities of the medieval Talas and Chu valleys. It received its present rank in 1931, when the bull *Orientalis Stella* brought the Iradi church into full communion with Rome. The archbishop has metropolitan authority over three suffragan eparchies, based in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the Chatkal highlands, and presides over the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]]. The archbishop since 2012 has been [[Mar Ephrem]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
#### Medieval origins
East Syriac (Nestorian) Christianity reached the Talas and Chu valleys with Sogdian merchants between the 7th and 9th centuries, and the Church of the East maintained bishops in the cities of [[wp:Transoxiana]] and [[wp:Semirechye]] during the following centuries.<sup>[2]</sup> Christianity spread among Turkic pastoralists of the region during the rule of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th century, and a church synod was held at Navekat in 1180 (see [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]). Church tradition places the foundation of a distinct Iradi Christian community in this period and attributes it to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have founded the lost First Church of Janyl after a vision of the White Rider. Historians regard her as a figure of legend whose historical existence is uncertain (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

The remains of a medieval Christian town near the present city, the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), include the foundations of an 11th-century church. Manuscripts in the cathedral library record contacts with the wider church in the 13th century, including letters connected with the envoys sent to the [[wp:Mongols]] by [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Persecution and survival
Under the Chagatai ruler Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and during the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] in the late 14th century, the Christian dioceses of the region were destroyed. Iradi Christians survived in the mountain valleys, where they worshipped in secret and preserved their prayers in oral chant (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*). Church tradition holds that a line of bishops continued among the mountain clans, but the written record for the 15th to 17th centuries is fragmentary, and historians cannot confirm an unbroken succession.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

#### Kokand period
In the early 18th century, Iradi Christian horsemen served as cavalry auxiliaries of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against Dzungar raids. In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted the Christian elders religious tolerance under the accord remembered as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], and issued a decree (*firman*) funding a stone church at Iyık Janyl. The Church of St. Janyl became the seat of the Iradi bishops, and a settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew up around it. The cathedral library was founded in 1732, and Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744) was buried in the church crypt.<sup>[4]</sup> In this period the Iradi church had no regular contact with the Patriarchate of the Church of the East or with Rome, and it functioned as an independent church under its own bishop.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Union with Rome
After the Russian conquest of Kokand in 1876, the church was tolerated by the Tsarist authorities, although Russian Orthodox missions were favored. After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] opened secret negotiations with the [[wp:Holy See]], conducted through papal representatives abroad between 1926 and 1931. On 14 September 1931 [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, which received the church into full communion as an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* with its own East Syriac rite, and established Iyık Janyl as a metropolitan archeparchy. Mar Timotheos became its first archbishop.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Soviet repression
Soviet officials regarded the church's link with Rome as a channel for foreign influence, and this suspicion fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s. During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], most of the archbishop's senior clergy were arrested and executed. The seminary was closed, and the cathedral was shut and its nave converted into a district grain store. Monks and lay sacristans hid the rarest manuscripts of the library in caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], and families kept vestments and sacred vessels in their homes.<sup>[5]</sup> For the rest of the Soviet period the archeparchy had no legal existence. Liturgies were held in homes and in the camps of the herding clans. Church tradition holds that bishops were consecrated in secret to preserve the succession, but documentary evidence for this period is limited.<sup>[3]</sup> After the restoration of religious freedom in 1992 the Holy See appointed Mar Yuhanna Bakirov archbishop in December of that year; he led the archeparchy through the return of its buildings and institutions until his retirement in 2012.

#### Restoration
After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of *Orientalis Stella*. Under the US territorial administration, which guaranteed freedom of religion, the building was restored between 1993 and 1998 with territorial grants, US heritage funds and donations from Christian charities. The seminary reopened in 1994 as the St. Ephrem Major Seminary, and the library's manuscripts were conserved and digitized.<sup>[4]</sup> In the same years contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions brought Western devotions into urban parishes, and vernacular liturgical texts in Latin-script Iradi were approved. The Church of St. Janyl and the Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl were inscribed together as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2004, on a nomination submitted by the United States as the administering power.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Organization
The archeparchy covers the city of Iyık Janyl and the surrounding valleys of the lower Naryn and the Fergana foothills, including highland parishes on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Its 2023 diocesan directory lists 118 parishes and mission stations, about 40 of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[1]</sup> The suffragan eparchies of Talas and Nurzhan serve the two largest cities and their districts, while the Chatkal highland eparchy serves mainly tribal parishes. The church reports about 3.4 million faithful in all.

Under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, the archbishop is appointed by the Pope from candidates proposed by the Council of Hierarchs. As of 2026 the suffragan bishops are Mar Toma Usenov of Talas, Mar Yakob Kim of Nurzhan and Mar Narsai Abdykerimov of the Chatkal Highlands, who has no fixed seat and visits his parishes from Iyık Janyl. Institutions under the archbishop's direct authority include:
- the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary), which trains clergy for all four eparchies in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], theology and canon law;
- the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] and the [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]];
- the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge south of the city, and the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]];
- the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] and the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]];
- rural dispensaries run by the religious orders, many of them in the tribal regions.

## Public role
Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the archbishopric has kept a position of neutrality between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration and the clan councils of the tribal regions. It has hosted meetings between representatives of the ISEZ and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and the archbishop meets regularly with Sunni Muslim leaders and Russian Orthodox bishops to coordinate charitable work.<sup>[7]</sup> Each year on 24 August the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] draws pilgrims to the cathedral from both sides of the line, many of them on horseback. The archbishopric and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] organize the crossing points for riders from the tribal regions.

Relations with the ISEZ government have at times been strained over school curricula and the taxation of church property. In these disputes the archbishopric has cited the guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.60. Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Health & Education*

The **Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl** (Iradi: *Iyık Janyl Sobor Seminariyasynyn Koljazma Kitepkanasy*) is the manuscript library of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], housed in the seminary cloister beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It was founded in 1732, five years after the church was built, and holds more than 600 manuscripts, the largest collection of [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]], Sogdian and Christian Turkic manuscripts in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It also holds a theological library of printed books used by the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The library was established in 1732 to keep the service books, chronicles and documents that the Iradi clergy had preserved in the mountain valleys. Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744) added his correspondence and the decrees (*firmans*) of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] khans, and later bishops collected manuscripts from mountain parishes and from the families of priests.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s, which culminated in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], the seminary was closed and the cathedral shut. Before the closure, monks and lay sacristans carried the rarest codices to caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where some remained hidden until after 1992.<sup>[2]</sup> Books and papers left in the cathedral were confiscated, and part of them passed to the republican archives in Kobozev. Some of these were returned to the church between 1993 and 1996; others remain in the [[State Archives of Irad]], and the church has asked for their return.

The library reopened with the seminary in 1994. During the territorial period its manuscripts were conserved and cataloged with grants from the Vatican Library and European academic foundations. A printed catalog of the Syriac manuscripts was published by [[Talas State University Press]] in 2011.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Collections
The manuscripts date from the 9th to the early 20th century. Among the best known are:
- the **Talas Gospel Lectionary** (about 1185), an illuminated Syriac lectionary in Estrangela script with marginal notes in Turkic written in Syriac letters, an early witness to the Turkic-speaking Christianity of the region;
- the **Gospels of Iyık Janyl**, a 13th-century Gospel book copied, according to its colophon, by a monk named Marqos (see [[Marqos the Scribe]]);
- fragments of **Sogdian commercial and legal documents** of the 9th and 10th centuries, written on paper and recording grain sales, water rights and caravan escorts in the Chu valley;
- 14th-century copies of works of **Bar Hebraeus**, including his ecclesiastical chronicle, which records the conversion of the [[wp:Keraites|Keraits]];
- letters connected with the 13th-century papal envoys to the [[wp:Mongols]] sent by [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]];
- the **correspondence of Mar Gewargis** and the Kokand *firmans* granting the church tax exemptions;
- liturgical manuscripts of the East Syriac rite, including several used in clandestine worship during the Soviet period.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

Scholars disagree about the dating of some items. The early date of the Talas Gospel Lectionary rests on its script and illumination, and some specialists in Syriac manuscripts place it in the 13th century.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Access and digitization
A digitization laboratory set up in 2003 has photographed about 240 manuscripts, and high-resolution images of these are published online. Researchers may consult the originals by appointment in the cloister reading room. Graduate students from [[Talas State University]] and foreign specialists in Syriac and Central Asian studies are the main users, and the university holds regular symposia on the collection.<sup>[1]</sup> Church registers and administrative records are kept separately in the [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]].

### 4.61. Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate** (Iradi: *Chatkal chachyndy ken inspektsiyasy*) is a government agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that licenses and inspects alluvial (placer) gold workings and monitors mine tailings and water quality in the mining districts south of [[Talas]]. It was created in 1998 by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] to regulate gold panning and dredging in the basin of the [[Chatkal River]]. Most of that basin has been under the control of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) since 2007, and the inspectorate's work is now concentrated on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], chiefly in the Sary-Bulak District.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Small-scale gold washing in the rivers of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] and the [[Talas Alatau]] dates back centuries. It revived in the 1990s, when unemployed miners and herders began working river gravels with sluices and small pumps, and several foreign-backed companies applied for dredging licenses. Reports of mercury use and silted irrigation channels led the Territorial Legislature to create the inspectorate in 1998 under the Ministry of Natural Resources, with powers under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code to license placer workings, inspect sites and impose fines.<sup>[1]</sup>

Until 2007 the inspectorate worked throughout the Chatkal basin from offices in Talas and in the Chatkal valley. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], the upper basin fell on the tribal side of the line, where clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit and mechanized gold mining. The inspectorate withdrew its field staff from the tribal side and took on the monitoring of tailings dams and mine water at the antimony works in the Sary-Bulak District.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Functions
The inspectorate's main tasks are:
- licensing small placer leases on streams in ISEZ territory, and inspecting the few mechanized operations that remain;
- registering individual gold washers (*altynchy*), who must sell their gold to licensed buyers;
- sampling surface water for turbidity, cyanide, mercury, arsenic and antimony below workings and tailings dams;
- inspecting the stability of tailings dams, including the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] and the dumps of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]];
- imposing fines, suspending licenses and ordering the reclamation of worked-out ground.<sup>[1]</sup>

In 2022 it had about 70 staff, including 28 field inspectors, and an annual budget of about $1.9 million.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2016 it has used commercial satellite imagery to detect unlicensed workings, including on the tribal side of the line, where it cannot act directly.

## Relations with the tribal regions
On the tribal side, panning on gravel bars is regulated by clan councils under customary law (*adat*), as in the [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]. Pollution from either side reaches shared rivers, and the inspectorate exchanges water-quality data with tribal monitors through the liaison channels of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Disputes over damage to pastures and watering points are heard by the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] when ISEZ operators are involved.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Criticism
Environmental groups and the newspaper *[[Irad Times]]* have argued that the inspectorate is too small to police the antimony industry, whose parent company is one of the largest taxpayers in the ISEZ, and that its fines are low. They cite raised arsenic and antimony levels recorded in streams below the [[Sary-Bulak]] workings. The inspectorate says that its readings at the main monitoring points have been within ISEZ limits since the late 2010s.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.62. Chongtor Studbook Registry
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

{{More citations needed|date=June 2026}}

The **Chongtor Studbook Registry** (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkysynyn tukum kitebi*) is the breed registry and standards body for the [[Chongtor Horse]], the mountain horse of the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] ranges. It was established in 1993 under the US territorial administration. Since 2008 it has worked under the joint authority of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which makes it one of the few institutions shared by the two Iradi administrations. It keeps an office at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]] and an inspection center, the Highland Equine Center, in the upper Talas valley on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Chongtor horses were traditionally bred by herding families, and pedigrees were kept orally as part of clan genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), in which notable stallions were remembered alongside their owners. Soviet collective farms kept herd books for working horses, but the Chongtor was never recognized as a separate breed in the Soviet system.<sup>[2]</sup>

The registry was created in 1993 by an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], at the same time as the National Equestrian Sports Directorate, to define a breed standard and support exports. It introduced microchip identification and, from 1999, DNA parentage testing. When the 2007 ceasefire left most Chongtor breeding herds in the tribal regions, the registry's work there stopped. An agreement in 2008 between the Directorate and the IAC placed it under a joint board of eight members, four named by each side, which meets twice a year, usually at the Highland Equine Center.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Registration
To be entered in the studbook, a horse must pass three tests:
- **Parentage:** DNA testing against both registered parents.
- **Conformation:** an inspection against the breed standard, which calls for a height of 137–147 cm (13.2–14.2 hands), a deep chest, dense bone with a cannon-bone circumference of more than 19 cm, and hard, dark hooves that are usually left unshod.
- **Performance:** a timed 30-kilometer mountain ascent above 2,800 meters, in which heart-rate recovery is measured.

Crossbreeding with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] and European warmbloods is prohibited.<sup>[1]</sup> Inspection committees in the clan territories record the oral pedigrees of unregistered herds, and horses with a documented descent of several generations can be admitted after inspection. Approved stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark that recalls the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].<sup>[3]</sup>

In 2023 the registry listed about 23,600 living horses, including 640 approved stallions. Most horses in the tribal regions are not registered, and the total number of Chongtor-type horses is unknown.<sup>[1]</sup> The best-known modern sire is the stallion [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]], foundation of the leading endurance line. The ranchers' [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]] issues its own breeding certificates.

## Other activities
The registry certifies Chongtors for export, which are handled by the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and go mainly to trekking stables in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Mongolia]] and the United States. It also guarantees grazing for retired breeding stock. Horsemeat is not eaten in Irad, and a 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

- [[Chongtor Dun Bloodline]]
- [[Chongtor Roan Strain]]

### 4.63. Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

The **Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate** (Iradi: *Chüy öröönü sugat inspektsiyasy*) is the government agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that operates the irrigation and drainage network of the lower [[Chu River Basin]] and allocates its water. Its headquarters are in [[Nurzhan]]. The [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] that it runs serves more than 80,000 hectares in the Chu District through about 1,200 kilometers of main and secondary canals. Because the Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], the inspectorate's water supply depends on upstream use, and it is the ISEZ's main technical contact with Kyrgyz and Kazakh water agencies on the river.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Canals were dug on the lower Chu in the 1930s and 1940s and extended after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], partly by [[wp:Koryo-saram]] collective farmers deported to the area in 1937, who drained marshland for rice.<sup>[2]</sup> The network was run by the irrigation systems administration of the Iradi SSR's water ministry, which built the main diversion weir in 1957.

In 1995 the Territorial Legislature reorganized the Soviet administration as the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate, under the territorial Department of Agriculture. US aid financed the repair of headworks damaged in the 1992 fighting and the creation of water users' associations, which buy water from the inspectorate and maintain the smaller ditches. Since 2007 the inspectorate has reported to the ISEZ Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Infrastructure
The main structures operated by the inspectorate are:
- the **Central Headworks**, a diversion weir with radial gates on the Chu upstream of Nurzhan, which feeds the main canals;
- the **Western Main Canal**, 95 kilometers long and partly concrete-lined, which supplies grain, sugar-beet and feed farms on the west of the plain, many of them under contract to [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]];
- intakes supplying process and cooling water to the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the other installations of [[NurGaz]];
- about 400 kilometers of collector drains, which carry saline groundwater away from the fields.<sup>[1]</sup>

Water levels at the main gates are measured by telemetry stations linked through the network of [[Attelkom]], and discharge on the river is recorded by the [[Chu Basin Hydrological Station]]. Much of the network dates from the Soviet period. The inspectorate estimates that about a third of the water diverted is lost to seepage and evaporation, and rising groundwater has salinized parts of the lower plain.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Allocation within Irad
Each spring the inspectorate sets a seasonal plan dividing the expected flow among farms, industry and the city of Nurzhan. In dry years it imposes rotations between canals and cuts deliveries to rice and other high-water crops first.<sup>[2]</sup>

The Chu ends below the irrigated zone in the Moiynkum sands, near the [[Akzhaykyn Depression|Akzhaykyn depression]], in the Northern Steppe zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Herders there use the lower river and its riparian woodland (*tugay*) to water livestock. Clan councils and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have complained that ISEZ withdrawals leave the lower channel dry in late summer. No agreement governs releases to the tribal reach, and the question has been raised at meetings of the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Transboundary water issues
The upper Chu and its regulating reservoir, the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]], lie in Kyrgyzstan, as do the headworks of the large canals of the Chuy valley. Downstream of the Chuy valley, the river forms part of the border between Kyrgyzstan and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] before entering Irad.<sup>[3]</sup> Kyrgyz irrigation withdrawals in July and August, when demand is highest on both sides, sharply reduce the flow that reaches the Iradi lowlands.

There is no ratified agreement on the Chu between Irad and Kyrgyzstan. None of Irad's neighbors recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party. ISEZ officials cite a 1983 Soviet allocation protocol, which they say assigned the Iradi SSR about 42% of the river's flow. Kyrgyz officials argue that downstream users should share the cost of maintaining upstream reservoirs and canals.<sup>[3]</sup> Inspectorate engineers meet Kyrgyz water managers informally at the border gauging station, usually in spring and autumn, to exchange forecasts and gauge readings. With Kazakhstan, joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and the Talas dates from the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], signed during the territorial period. The treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed, but the exchange of gauging data has continued.

Unlike the Naryn, where releases are governed by the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] under United Nations supervision, the Chu has no multilateral arrangement. Analysts regard it as one of the main unresolved sources of friction between Irad and Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[4]</sup>

### 4.64. Fergana Mountain Transit Highway
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Fergana Mountain Transit Highway** (officially **State Route 1**; Iradi: *Pargana too jolu*) is a mountain highway in Irad that links [[Talas]] with the Lower Naryn District around [[Tash-Kömür]]. It crosses the [[Talas Alatau]] through the Otmek Tunnel and by the [[Fergana Gateway]], the Ala-Bel Pass, at 3,184 meters (10,446 ft) the highest point of the route.<sup>[1]</sup> The road is about 356 kilometers long, of which the mountain section between the mouth of the Otmek valley and Kara-Köl is about 226 kilometers. It is the only road connecting the core of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) with the Toktogul basin and the Lower Naryn District. The 2007 ceasefire left its mountain section on land of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) as a guarded corridor; since a protocol of 2009 the road runs through a narrow ISEZ corridor between tribal pastures, policed by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]]. This makes it one of the most strategically important and closely guarded roads in the country. The highway does not lead to China, with which Irad has no border.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Route
The highway leaves Talas at the end of the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] and runs east for about 64 kilometers up the irrigated farmland of the Talas valley to the mouth of the Otmek valley, where the northern control post stands. It climbs the Otmek valley through a series of avalanche galleries and at about kilometer 87 passes beneath the [[Otmek]] crest of the Talas Alatau in the Otmek Tunnel, about 5 kilometers long, whose portals at about 3,150–3,200 meters lie some 150 meters below the Otmek Pass (3,330 m). The old road over the pass is kept open in summer as a bypass.<sup>[1]</sup>

South of the tunnel the road descends into the western end of the [[Suusamyr]] valley, the summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, and climbs again to the broad saddle of the Fergana Gateway at about kilometer 118, where the summit control post and a maintenance station stand. On the southern side it descends in switchbacks through juniper woodland and mountain steppe down the Chychkan valley to the Toktogul basin, reaching the town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] at about kilometer 180.<sup>[3]</sup> It runs round the eastern end of the reservoir and along its southern shore to the dam, the switchyard and the dispatch center of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and to Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, at about kilometer 290; the town of Toktogul, the dam and Kara-Köl lay on the tribal side of the line until 2009 and were then placed in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District; since 2016 the basin and the road north of it have formed Toktogul District, and the district line runs just below the dam, above Kara-Köl. The road then follows the river down the Naryn gorge past the lower stations of the Naryn cascade and comes out onto the river flats at [[Iyık Janyl]], at about kilometer 347, where it runs through the city on the east bank of the river; this makes the highway the pilgrims' road to the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. It ends at Tash-Kömür, at about 600 meters and kilometer 356, where the Naryn leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Between the dam and Iyık Janyl the ISEZ corridor along the gorge is only a few kilometers wide, with tribal mountains on either side. Regional roads continue from Tash-Kömür east through the ISEZ's farm belt on the Fergana rim to [[Bazar-Korgon]] and toward the Uzbek border.

## History
#### Soviet road
Routes across the mountains between the Talas valley and the Fergana side were used by herders, caravans and armies for centuries. Iradi popular histories link them with the trade in Fergana horses.<sup>[3]</sup> The first motor road over the Gateway was built between 1962 and 1968 by the construction directorate of the Toktogul hydroelectric project, to carry equipment and workers from the Talas railhead to the dam site. It was a gravel road with steep switchbacks that was closed for much of the winter. Sections in the Talas valley and the Naryn gorge were paved in the 1970s.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial reconstruction
In 1996 the territorial highway department designated the road State Route 1. Between 1997 and 2004 it was rebuilt to an all-weather standard with US federal highway grants and a road fund created from oil and mining royalties under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code. The work added more than 4 kilometers of reinforced concrete avalanche galleries, rockfall sheds on the southern descent and the Otmek Tunnel, about 5 kilometers long, which opened in 2003 and cut out about 7 kilometers of the most dangerous hairpins on the northern approach.<sup>[4]</sup> The rebuilt road shortened the winter journey from Talas to Tash-Kömür from about two days to about seven hours.

#### 2007 and the ceasefire
During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] blocked the road at the Gateway in May 2007, cutting the ISEZ's links with the Naryn stations. ISEZ security forces reopened it in July after clashes on the southern descent.<sup>[2]</sup> The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the mountain section of the road on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], but its road arrangements placed the highway between the mouth of the Otmek valley and the Lower Naryn District under the guard of the Republican Gendarmerie. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] established its sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür in 2008, and the highway became the main route between it and the mission headquarters at Kara-Oi.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The 2009 corridor protocol
Under a UN-brokered protocol signed at Kara-Oi in July 2009, the road from the upper Talas valley through the Otmek Tunnel, the western Suusamyr and the Gateway, the floor of the Toktogul basin and the Naryn gorge passed to the ISEZ. The corridor is only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes and widens over the valley floors. In exchange the clans received the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights along the corridor, including the right to drive herds across it at agreed places and seasons, and a guaranteed share of the revenue of the Toktogul complex. The three Gendarmerie posts on the road became internal control posts, and the line crossings moved to the side tracks that leave the corridor.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Strategic role
The highway is the only overland link between Talas and the Lower Naryn District. It carries supplies to the switchyard, national dispatch center and downstream power stations of the Naryn cascade, which the ISEZ needs in order to sell electricity from the Toktogul complex. It also serves the cotton farms of the Fergana rim belt and the coal mines of the Lower Naryn District and supplies the Lower Naryn mountain battalion of the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]].<sup>[2]</sup> Analysts describe the 2009 arrangement as an exchange of leverage. The ISEZ holds the road and the dam, but the corridor runs for long stretches between tribal pastures and herd crossings, and the clans' consent is needed for each five-year release schedule of the Toktogul complex, while the tribal share of power revenue depends on the ISEZ's export grid. Each side therefore has an interest in keeping traffic moving.<sup>[6]</sup>

Because the corridor is narrow, most of the road lies within 12 kilometers of the Qara-Chik line, and therefore inside the restricted-weapons zone set by the ceasefire agreement, in which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are prohibited. Military traffic on the road is mainly light vehicles, and UNMI observers record movements of military convoys.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Checkpoints and security
The Gendarmerie runs three permanent control posts on the highway: at the mouth of the Otmek valley, at the summit of the Gateway and at the Naryn bridge below the Toktogul dam. Since 2009 they have been internal posts within the ISEZ rather than crossings of the line. Cargo and documents are checked at all three, bus passengers' identity documents are checked at the summit, and heavy vehicles pay a road-use charge at the northern post, at the mouth of the Otmek valley.<sup>[1]</sup>

Posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]] stand on the tribal side where side tracks from the tribal valleys meet the corridor. Travelers leaving the highway for the tribal valleys must pass both an ISEZ and a tribal post, and residents of the tribal regions need a tribal travel permit to use the designated crossing points.<sup>[5]</sup> In late May and June, and again in September and October, herders drive their flocks across the corridor between summer and winter pastures at agreed crossing places. Traffic is halted for the crossings, which are coordinated by the Gendarmerie, clan elders and UNMI team sites. Incidents involving livestock theft, armed men or blocked traffic are reported every few years, and UNMI has recorded several shooting incidents near the southern descent since 2008.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Traffic and operation
In 2023 the Gendarmerie recorded an average of about 2,100 vehicles a day at the summit control post, about 40 percent of them trucks.<sup>[1]</sup> Northbound freight is mainly cotton, fruit, coal and livestock. Southbound traffic carries fuel and refined products from [[NurGaz]], building materials and consumer goods, much of it handled by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. Minibuses and buses connect Talas with Tash-Kömür several times a day.

The highway department keeps maintenance stations at the mouth of the Otmek valley, at the tunnel portals, at the summit and on the southern switchbacks, with rotary snowplows and sand trucks. Snow normally covers the pass from November to April. Storms and avalanche danger close the road for an average of about 20 days each winter, and rockfalls and mudflows are a hazard during the spring thaw.<sup>[3]</sup> In winter, when the road is closed, the only alternative link is the air service between Talas and Tash-Kömür operated by [[Iradiya]].

## Proposals
Route surveys for the proposed [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad gas pipeline]] have considered the highway corridor as a possible route.<sup>[6]</sup> The ISEZ government has sought foreign financing to widen the southern descent and extend the avalanche galleries, but no contract had been signed by 2025.
