### 4.80. Talasbank
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox company
| name = Talasbank
| native_name = *Talas Banky* (Bank of Talas)
| type = Commercial bank
| industry = Banking
| predecessor = Talas offices of the Soviet savings and agricultural banks
| founded = 1993 (opened September 1993)
| hq = Silk Road Financial Tower, [[Talas]]
| locations = 28 branches (20 in Talas, 6 in [[Nurzhan]], 2 in [[Iyık Janyl]])
| area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]
| services = Dual-currency (US dollar and som) banking, export escrow, trade finance, government payrolls, SMS payments
| owner = Undisclosed holding companies; ISEZ government (minority stake)
}}

**Talasbank** (officially the Bank of Talas; Iradi: *Talas Banky*) is the largest commercial bank in Irad, with its headquarters in the Silk Road Financial Tower in central [[Talas]]. It was chartered in 1993 by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], which made the US dollar legal tender in the territory alongside the new [[Iradi som]]. The bank keeps accounts in both currencies. It holds the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], handles most government payrolls and holds the largest share of commercial deposits in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Because Irad's sovereignty is unrecognized, Talasbank has no direct access to most international payment systems. It settles foreign payments through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. Its ownership has not been fully disclosed since its partial privatization, and its accounts are published only in summary.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Background
In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks for savings, agriculture and housing. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings. Banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Foundation and the territorial period (1993–2006)
After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to use the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized the som for small payments and wages, and chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank.<sup>[1]</sup> The bank was formed from the Talas offices of the former Soviet savings and agricultural banks, with capital provided by the territorial government. It opened for business in September 1993. In the first months, dollar banknotes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[3]</sup>

In 1994 the territorial government created the Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority to audit export contracts. Exporters, including the oil company [[NurGaz]], the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and later the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], were required to have foreign buyers pay into escrow accounts at Talasbank. The authority deducted royalties and taxes before releasing the balance.<sup>[4]</sup> During the agribusiness boom of the late 1990s and the expansion of the air base after the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]], the bank's business grew with foreign investment, base contracts and payrolls. As a bank in a US territory, it settled dollar payments through correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.<sup>[3]</sup>

The territorial government sold a majority of its shares in auctions in 1999 and 2001 and kept a minority stake. The buyers were Iradi holding companies whose own shareholders were not published.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Crisis of 2006–2007
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to withdraw dollars. The bank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December.<sup>[5]</sup> American correspondent banks closed or restricted its accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status. The bank moved its correspondent business to banks in Almaty and Istanbul, a pattern similar to that of banks in other territories whose status is not recognized.<sup>[3]</sup>

After [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, both the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in Talas and the emergency administration in Nurzhan claimed authority over the escrow accounts. The bank's management froze withdrawals from government accounts until the dispute was settled. Supporters later credited the decision with protecting public funds, while DRI ministers said it cut off their government's revenue.<sup>[6]</sup> The head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007. It reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer.

#### Since 2007
Since the ceasefire Talasbank has been the main bank of the ISEZ government. It holds treasury and payroll accounts, takes part in the escrow arrangements for oil, antimony and beef exports, and finances imports from China, [[wp:Turkey]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] with letters of credit.<sup>[2]</sup> Payments made under the revenue-sharing arrangements of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] are not reported separately. Herders from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through the bank.<sup>[4]</sup>

With [[Attelkom]], the bank introduced debit cards and a national card-payment network in the 2000s. In 2012 the two companies launched an SMS-based payment service, used by herders and farmers to pay for feed and veterinary services and to receive transfers without traveling to a branch.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Dollar shortage (2026)
From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes became scarce in the ISEZ after correspondent banks in Almaty cut their shipments of cash. Under a Bank of Irad notice of 4 May 2026 allowing banks to cap cash withdrawals in dollars, with state contracts exempt, Talasbank has since May limited cash dollar withdrawals and conversions of som into dollars to US$300 a month per customer.<sup>[7]</sup> Unlicensed money changers at the bazaars of Talas and Nurzhan, who quoted about 9.5 som to the dollar in June, were asking 11 to 12 som by October, against the official rate of 8.40; on 13 October changers at the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] in Talas bought dollars at 11.40 som and sold them at 11.85. Traders and analysts attribute the gap to the cash shortage, to uncertainty over the Governor's absence and the 2027 succession, to the rising cost of remittances and to memories of the 2008 devaluation. The [[Bank of Irad]] says that its reserves fully cover the som, that the official rate is unchanged and that no second reset is planned, and calls the street rate "speculation in a small cash market".<sup>[8]</sup>

In September 2026 Talasbank also stopped card payments for purchases of [[Tulparcoin]], the cryptocurrency launched by [[Jason Ilyasov]]'s Liberty Forum, after the Bank of Irad warned that the coin was not legal tender.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Operations
- **Dual-currency banking.** Deposits and loans are offered in US dollars and in som. Most savings, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments.
- **Escrow and trade finance.** The bank holds the export escrow accounts audited by the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority and provides letters of credit and guarantees for importers.
- **Government business.** It handles treasury accounts, payrolls and many payments of the ISEZ government and of the municipal administrations of Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]].
- **Retail network.** It has 28 branches, 20 in Talas, 6 in Nurzhan (including its Azatlık Prospect branch) and 2 in Iyık Janyl, as well as offices at the main border crossings and mobile banking vans that serve villages in the [[Chu River Basin]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Interbank transfers within the ISEZ are processed through the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]]. According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup> Smaller commercial banks include [[Ak Bata Bank]] and Chuy Commercial Bank (Iradi: *Chüy Kommertsiyalık Banky*).

## Ownership and criticism
The ISEZ government still holds a minority stake, but the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control the bank have not been disclosed. Investigative reports have linked several of these companies to business associates of the ruling Toktarov family. The bank has said that its shareholders meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.<sup>[10]</sup> Opposition commentators accuse it of lending on favorable terms to companies linked to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]. The [[wp:World Bank]] has noted that it has not published full audited accounts since 2008.<sup>[3]</sup>

Business groups, by contrast, credit the bank with keeping the dollar payment system working through the crises of 2006–07 and the uncertainty that followed Toktarov's withdrawal from public view in 2024.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.81. Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals** are a series of plans, made since the 1990s, for international pipelines across [[Irad]]. The best known is the Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline proposed by the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC), which would carry natural gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory. During the US territorial period, a US-backed oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] through Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory was also studied, but it lost its prospects after 2021. None of the proposals has been built.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Irad's only export pipeline remains the 85-km [[Northern Export Feeder]], which carries crude oil north into the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]].

## Background
Irad is doubly landlocked, and all its hydrocarbon exports depend on transit through neighboring states. Until 2000 crude oil left by rail for Shymkent, and since then it has been piped through the Northern Export Feeder into the network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]], for refining in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] or onward shipment to Russia.<sup>[3]</sup> Irad's proven natural gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters but are largely undeveloped. The largest prospect, the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]], lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup> Successive governments have looked for a second export route to reduce their dependence on Kazakhstan.

## Southern oil pipeline proposal
During the territorial period, a US-backed proposal envisaged a pipeline carrying Iradi crude south to Pakistan. Because Irad does not border [[wp:Tajikistan]] or [[wp:Afghanistan]], the route would have crossed Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory. Instability in Afghanistan kept the project at the planning stage. After the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in 2021 it lost its remaining prospects. [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]], which had invested heavily in modernizing Irad's oil fields since the territorial period, then scaled back its operations in Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline
CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would link gas fields in Turkmenistan with consumers in western China. In Irad the main partner would be [[NurGaz]]. Feasibility studies have examined two routes through the territory:
- a **northern route**, about 480 km long within Irad, entering Irad from Uzbekistan at the head of the Chatkal valley, crossing the tribal Chatkal Highlands and the [[Talas Alatau]] into the upper [[Talas River]] valley, running along its southern side, crossing the mountains by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor and the [[Fergana Gateway]], and leaving Irad eastward into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]];
- a **southern route**, entering from the Uzbek part of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and running east through the Lower Naryn District along the farm belt of the Fergana rim before crossing into Kyrgyzstan.

The studies assume a pipe 1,220 mm in diameter carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters of gas a year, with four compressor stations in Irad. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas-fired power and heating in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], where coal is still widely burned.<sup>[2]</sup> In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas. The Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Obstacles
- **Status.** A pipeline would need transit agreements with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan and a counterparty in Irad able to sign binding contracts. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan all claim Irad *de jure*, and none recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party. Lenders are reluctant to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty.<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Tribal consent.** Both routes cross land held by the clans of the ATR: the northern route would cross the tribal Chatkal Highlands and the crest of the Talas Alatau before reaching the Talas valley, and then follow the narrow ISEZ corridor over the Fergana Gateway between tribal pastures and cross the Toktogul–Naryn zone, and the southern route, although it would follow the ISEZ's farm belt for most of its length in Irad, would cross the tribal hills of the Fergana Rim zone on its way into Kyrgyzstan. Clan elders led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] have withheld consent for construction across alpine pastures and water catchments under customary law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has said that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies concerned and a share of transit revenue.<sup>[5]</sup>
- **Competition.** Existing gas pipelines from [[wp:Central Asia]] to China run through Kazakhstan. Analysts note that a new route through Irad would have to compete with expanding their capacity.<sup>[2]</sup>

Engineering consultations between the ISEZ authorities and CNPC continue intermittently, but no investment decision has been made.

### 4.82. Amanbek Alimbekov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Amanbek Alimbekov** (9 May 1938 – 14 November 2004) was an Iradi historian and politician who led the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. He specialized in the medieval history and languages of the Talas valley, became a dissident in the late Soviet period, and during perestroika founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society. After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] he chaired the council that took over the administration of [[Talas]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected him Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

With Talas besieged by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), Alimbekov signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] on 2 June 1992. Under the treaty Irad became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection. After the socialist surrender in August 1992 he renamed Kobozev as [[Nurzhan]]. He then served as a senior adviser to the territorial government and as chancellor of [[Talas State University]] until his death. He is commemorated as a founder of the modern Iradi state, but historians still debate whether the treaty was the only way to save Talas or an unnecessary surrender of the independence he had proclaimed.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Early life and education
Alimbekov was born on 9 May 1938 in [[Iyık Janyl]], then a district town known for its fruit cannery and its clandestine Christian worship. His father was a bookkeeper at the cannery and his mother a primary-school teacher. His paternal grandfather was a cousin of Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], who had negotiated the union of the Iradi church with Rome in 1931.<sup>[2]</sup> In his memoir Alimbekov recalled attending secret liturgies in private homes as a child, at a time when the town's churches were closed and the arrests of clergy in 1937 were still within living memory.

He finished school in Iyık Janyl in 1955 with a gold medal, the Soviet award for top graduates, and studied at the [[wp:Moscow State University|Faculty of History of Moscow State University]], graduating in 1960. He then returned to Irad to teach at the new Iradi State University (now Talas State University), founded in 1958, while continuing postgraduate work in [[wp:Moscow]]. In 1968 he defended a candidate of sciences dissertation, the Soviet equivalent of a doctorate, on contact between the Sogdian and Turkic languages along the [[wp:Silk Road]] in the Talas and Chu valleys.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Academic career and dissent
At the university Alimbekov taught medieval history and took part in excavations at [[Shelji]], the medieval silver-mining town in the upper Talas valley. His first book, *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971), established his reputation among Soviet orientalists.<sup>[4]</sup> He became head of the department of history in 1976.

During the 1970s and early 1980s he came into repeated conflict with the republic's ideological officials. They objected to his emphasis on the Christian heritage of the [[Iradis]] and to his research on the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the flight and deaths that followed, known as the *Urkun*. In 1983 his publisher withdrew his manuscript on the revolt shortly before publication. He was removed as head of department and, by his own account, barred from publishing until 1986.<sup>[2]</sup> The book appeared only in 1990, as *The Black Year*.

Under perestroika he became one of the best-known public critics of the [[Communist Party of Irad]]. In 1988 he founded the *Ene-Til* society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi; the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, including the clergy killed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937]]; the reopening of churches; and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]].<sup>[5]</sup> The society's meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers who later formed the core of the 1992 movement.

## Winter Uprising and Provisional Presidency (1991–1992)

#### The uprising
In November 1991 the SRI government of [[Vasily Chernov]] issued emergency decrees banning non-communist gatherings and publications, and Ene-Til's newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December. In January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists in the city, Alimbekov went into hiding. Seven members of the society detained in those weeks were shot in custody at the interior ministry's building in Talas; the SRI said they had been killed while trying to escape, and a commission of the Territorial Legislature found in 2002 that they had been executed. On 24 January the US State Department condemned "extrajudicial killings of detained activists in Talas", and arrests of the society's members largely stopped.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> After security forces fired on demonstrators on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals and party headquarters in Talas. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov took over the city's administration, and it became the Provisional Government. After the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" on 18 February, the last SRI officials left the city.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Proclamation of the Republic
On 11 March 1992 delegates and clan elders assembled in the municipal theater of Talas adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad* and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[1]</sup> The government in Kobozev rejected the proclamation, and in late March the SRI sent its armored forces south along the Chu and Talas corridors.

#### Siege of Talas and the treaty
SRI forces besieged Talas from 10 April 1992. Alimbekov stayed in the city throughout. Its defenders, who included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], held the city center.<sup>[3]</sup> By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. Provisional envoys had meanwhile approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.<sup>[7]</sup>

The treaty was signed on 2 June 1992 in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day. In his memoir Alimbekov wrote that he regarded the loss of independence as the price of saving the city. He said his main condition in the negotiations had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ever ended its administration.<sup>[2]</sup> [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the airfield west of Talas on 6 June, the siege was broken by 18 June, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992 (see [[Operation Starlight]]).

## Territorial period (1992–2004)
In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed Nurzhan, a Kipchak name usually glossed as "light of life". He described it as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. The Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 confirmed the name.<sup>[8]</sup>

After the surrender, the Provisional Government sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration. When the interim legislature, drawn largely from its councils, first met in October 1992, Alimbekov formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. Many of his associates founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] that month from the Provisional Government's reformist caucus, but Alimbekov never joined a party. He declined to stand in the first territorial elections in 1994, writing later that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory.<sup>[2]</sup>

He remained influential as a senior adviser to the territorial government and, from 1995, as chancellor of Talas State University. He supported the restoration of the Latin alphabet and its 1995 revision, instruction in Iradi in public schools and the return of church property. He also resisted nationalist calls to repudiate the treaty, arguing that territorial status was the only practical protection against the claims of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].<sup>[7]</sup> He was more critical of the privatization of Soviet-era enterprises in the mid-1990s. In his memoir, *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998), he warned that concentrating the country's industry in a few hands would cost the new institutions public trust.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Death
Alimbekov died at his home in Talas on 14 November 2004, at the age of 66, after a long illness. The territorial government declared a day of mourning. After a funeral liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]], he was buried in the historic cemetery of Iyık Janyl.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Legacy and assessments
Alimbekov is commemorated on Irad Day, and in 2005 the [[National Library of Irad]], which is also the library of Talas State University, was named after him. Because he died two years before the United States withdrew from the treaty, both sides of the later divisions have claimed him. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present him as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses. In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause he had negotiated. Tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas, but many regard the treaty as a surrender of the republic's sovereignty.<sup>[10]</sup>

Historians at Talas State University continue to debate his decision of June 1992. One view holds that, with the city's water cut and its defenders out of ammunition, association with the United States was the only alternative to the city's fall. Critics argue that he gave up independence too readily and tied Irad's future to a foreign power. Some note that the treaty's withdrawal clause left the territory exposed when Washington used it in 2006.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> Chernov's memoir of 2001 presents the uprising Alimbekov led as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable.

## CIA allegations
A long-standing and widely repeated conspiracy theory holds that Alimbekov was a plant of the [[wp:Central Intelligence Agency|Central Intelligence Agency]] who "delivered Irad to America on a silver platter" (Iradi: *kümüsh tabakta*). In Russian-language media it is known as the story of "agent Alimbekov".<sup>[11]</sup> It has circulated since the 1990s in the Russian-language press of Nurzhan and among former communists; Chernov's memoir of 2001 claimed that "the Americans knew our plans before our generals did". Russian television documentaries in 2007 and 2022 presented it as fact. After 2007 it gained ground in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where many regard the treaty as the first sale of Irad, and some versions of the [[Erasure Theory]] on [[FreeIrad.org]] treat it as the first step of an American plan.<sup>[12]</sup>

Proponents point to the speed of the events of 1992: the Provisional Government's envoys approached the United States in late May, the treaty was signed on 2 June and US Marines landed four days later. They also cite the presence at Iradi State University in 1988–1991 of Curtis Dahlberg, an American Turkologist on the US–Soviet academic exchange, who worked with Alimbekov's department on Sogdian and Turkic inscriptions, ran the English evening class at which Alimbekov learned the language, and served as an interpreter for the US delegation at the signing. Other items include the State Department's statement of January 1992 on the killings in custody, which proponents say Washington could only have made with a source in Talas, and a KGB surveillance note describing Dahlberg as "suspected of intelligence activity", published by a Moscow weekly in 1999.<sup>[11]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

Dahlberg answered in a letter to the *[[Talas Herald]]* in 1999: "I taught him English and he taught me Sogdian. That is the whole conspiracy." He died in 2019.<sup>[13]</sup> Historians at Talas State University regard the theory as unproven. They note that KGB reports routinely described visiting Western scholars as suspected intelligence officers, that the State Department's statement followed reports by exiles and journalists in Almaty, and that US forces had prepared for contingencies at former Soviet military and uranium sites in Central Asia before the treaty was signed. Alimbekov's family, the library that bears his name and official histories of the territorial period reject the claim, and no document supporting it has been published.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

## Personal life
Alimbekov was a lifelong member of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. He was married and had two children. He spoke Iradi and Russian, read Sogdian and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and learned English in his fifties.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Selected works
- *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971). Kobozev: Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR.
- *The Black Year: The Revolt of 1916 in the Talas Valley* (1990). Talas.
- *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998). 2 vols. Talas: [[Talas State University Press]].

### 4.83. Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex** is a dam, reservoir and hydroelectric power station on the [[Naryn River]], in the Toktogul District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); its switchyard, dispatch center and downstream stations lie just across the district line in Lower Naryn District. Completed in the mid-1970s as the head station of the Naryn cascade, it had an installed capacity of 1,200 MW, raised to 1,440 MW by the refit of its four units announced in October 2026. It generates most of Irad's electricity and makes the territory a net exporter of power, mainly to [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Its reservoir, one of the largest in [[wp:Central Asia]], regulates the flow of the Naryn and therefore the summer irrigation water of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]] downstream.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

From 2007 to 2009 control of the complex was divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], with the dam, reservoir and powerhouse on the tribal side and the high-voltage switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and all export transmission lines in the ISEZ. Under a UN-brokered protocol of 2009 the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the whole complex, passed to the ISEZ, in exchange for mountain pastures, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the export revenue for the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), who hold the catchments and the mountains around the basin. The release schedule is still set under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], an annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], by a joint commission on which the tribal side has an equal place, and the complex is the most politically sensitive installation in Irad.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Location
The dam stands in the gorge where the Naryn leaves the Toktogul basin, a wide valley in the western [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] that the reservoir now largely fills. The market town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], on the reservoir's northern shore, is the main town of the basin and the seat of Toktogul District. Below the dam, the river descends through a series of gorges past [[Tash-Kömür]], the center of the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, to the Fergana Valley, where it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] to form the Syr Darya.<sup>[1]</sup> Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's construction workers and operators, lies a short distance downstream of the dam.

## History

#### Construction
The Naryn cascade was planned in the 1950s as part of the Soviet program to expand irrigated cotton in Central Asia. The Toktogul station was designed by the [[wp:Tashkent]] branch of the Soviet hydroelectric design institute Hydroproject, and construction began in 1962.<sup>[4]</sup> Thousands of workers, many of them from other Soviet republics, lived in Kara-Köl during the works. As the reservoir filled, it flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the basin, and several thousand inhabitants were resettled, including those of the old town of Toktogul, which was rebuilt on higher ground. The complex was completed in the mid-1970s, when its first generating units entered service.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Soviet operation
Under Soviet planning the reservoir was run mainly for irrigation. It stored spring snowmelt and glacier runoff and released most of it in summer for cotton farms downstream in the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs. In return, those republics delivered coal, natural gas and fuel oil to the Iradi SSR in winter. This barter arrangement lapsed after 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 1991–2007
After the end of Soviet barter, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed. This shift became a recurring source of friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992.<sup>[2]</sup> During the territorial period it was run by the Territorial Power Authority of Irad, which began to export electricity to its neighbors.

In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, the dam lay in territory held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. Skirmishes around the complex in the summer of 2007 alarmed the downstream states and were one reason all three neighbors took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The ceasefire placed the complex under the joint technical commission created by the Naryn Protocol and supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled. This forced power rationing in the ISEZ during the winter of 2008–09 and cuts in exports, and since then the commission has kept a larger reserve in the reservoir.<sup>[1]</sup> The crisis led to UN-mediated talks on the basin and the road to the Lower Naryn, and on 14 July 2009 the two sides signed a protocol, approved by that year's Kurultai, that transferred the floor of the Toktogul basin, the dam, reservoir and powerhouse and the State Route 1 corridor to the ISEZ. In return the clans received the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights around the basin, and a fixed minimum share of the export revenue; the tribal delegation kept its equal place on the joint commission, and the clans' consent remained a condition of each five-year release schedule. The El-Choro handed the dam perimeter over to the Gendarmerie in October 2009. Neither side has attempted to seize the other's installations since 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Engineering
- **Dam.** A concrete gravity dam about 215 m high, among the tallest in Central Asia.
- **Reservoir.** Total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, of which roughly two-thirds can be drawn down for power and irrigation.
- **Powerhouse.** Four generating units at the foot of the dam, with a combined capacity of 1,440 MW since their refit (1,200 MW as built). Average annual output is usually put at about 4 to 4.5 terawatt-hours, depending on the water year.
- **Downstream cascade.** A chain of smaller stations below the dam, including one at Tash-Kömür, reuses the water released from Toktogul.<sup>[4]</sup>

These figures come from Soviet design data and later surveys and are approximate.

## Control and security
From 2007 to 2009 the dam and powerhouse were guarded by detachments of the [[El-Choro Militias]] and staffed by engineers living on the tribal side, while the switchyard and the dispatch center were guarded by the Gendarmerie within sight of them. Since the 2009 protocol the whole complex has been run by [[Iradenergo]], the ISEZ's state power utility, much of it by engineers who stayed on from the territorial-era utility and live in Kara-Köl and Toktogul, and guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and by the Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion of the State Defense Corps, based at Tash-Kömür.<sup>[3]</sup> The national dispatch center schedules generation across the grid. The complex lies within the restricted-weapons zone that extends 12 km on either side of the Qara-Chik line, which runs along the slopes above the basin, and tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded from it.

Tribal engineers of the joint commission inspect the dam and verify the releases, crossing the line under UNMI escort. Technical decisions are taken by the joint technical commission. Security incidents around the complex are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Water management
The reservoir's operation balances two demands. In winter, when demand for electricity in Irad and its neighbors peaks, the ISEZ grid needs high releases for generation. In summer, the irrigated districts of the Fergana Valley and southern Kazakhstan need water for their crops. Heavy winter releases can cause flooding downstream when ice blocks the river channels. Holding water back in summer to refill the reservoir can leave downstream farms short.<sup>[2]</sup> Researchers also expect glacier retreat in the Tien Shan to change the river's flow over the coming decades, reducing late-summer inflows.

## Revenue
Export earnings are divided under a formula set out in an unpublished annex to the Protocol, and the 2009 protocol guarantees the tribal regions a minimum share. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders each deny profiting at the other's expense. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[3]</sup> The complex is nevertheless the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] meets part of its expenses from its share. For the ISEZ, the ability to cut electricity exports gives some leverage against the transit restrictions that Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have imposed during disputes.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.84. Naryn Water and Power Protocol
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **Naryn Water and Power Protocol** is the annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] that governs water releases and electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the [[Naryn River]]. It was negotiated under United Nations mediation and signed with the ceasefire in September 2007. It created a joint technical commission of engineers from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which sets the reservoir's annual release schedule under the supervision of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). Observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attend its meetings.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

A further protocol of 2009 transferred the dam and the floor of the Toktogul basin to the ISEZ but kept the commission's equal membership and made the clans' consent a condition of each five-year schedule. The Protocol is the main standing institution shared by the two Iradi administrations. Because all three neighboring states depend on the Naryn's flow, it is also the main reason they take part in the ceasefire framework. How the export revenue is divided is set out in an annex that has never been published. The five-year schedule renewed in 2022 expires in 2027.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The Toktogul dam, completed in the mid-1970s, was run in the Soviet period mainly to supply summer irrigation water to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan, in exchange for winter deliveries of fuel. That arrangement lapsed after 1991. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the complex. The dam and powerhouse were held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces.<sup>[2]</sup> Fighting near the dam that summer raised fears downstream that releases would be disrupted at the height of the irrigation season.

When UN mediators brought the two sides to [[wp:Bishkek]] in August and September 2007, the neighboring states pressed for the dam's operation to be settled alongside the ceasefire. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex in parallel with the negotiations on the demarcation line.<sup>[4]</sup>

After the record low of 2008 and power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter, UNMI mediated a supplementary protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, signed on 14 July 2009. It moved the line so that the dam, reservoir and powerhouse, the floor of the basin, and the road with a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge to the Lower Naryn came under the ISEZ, and in exchange gave the clans the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights around the basin, and a minimum share of the export revenue. The El-Choro withdrew from the dam in October 2009. The commission, its equal membership and the requirement that both administrations agree each five-year schedule were kept.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Provisions
The Protocol's main provisions are:
- **Joint technical commission.** Equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers make up the commission, and a UNMI official chairs its meetings. It meets monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season, at UNMI's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]].
- **Release schedule.** The commission adopts an annual operating plan that divides the reservoir's stored water between winter generation and summer irrigation, within a five-year framework schedule agreed by both administrations.
- **Data and observers.** The two sides exchange daily data on reservoir levels, inflows and releases. Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attend the commission's meetings and receive the data but have no vote.
- **Protection of installations.** Neither side may interfere with the other's installations. Engineers crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] to work on the complex travel under UNMI escort; since 2009 these are the tribal members of the commission and their inspection crews.
- **Revenue.** Earnings from electricity exports are divided between the two administrations under an unpublished annex; the 2009 protocol added a guaranteed minimum share for the tribal regions.
- **Disputes.** Disagreements the commission cannot resolve go to the heads of the two delegations and then to the Special Representative of the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]]. Security incidents affecting the complex or its crews are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Operation
In most years the commission's annual plan is adopted after weeks of bargaining. The ISEZ, which sells the power, presses for larger winter releases. Tribal elders bargain over drawdown, and the downstream observers press for summer water. After the reservoir fell to a record low in the dry year of 2008, causing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter, the commission adopted a minimum reserve level, which it has generally kept since.<sup>[1]</sup> The framework schedule, first adopted in 2007, was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022, each time with only minor changes. The 2022 renewal followed four months of talks.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Relations with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan
Both downstream neighbors depend on the Naryn, which joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in the Fergana Valley to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years to refill the reservoir, and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakh officials, whose irrigated districts lie farther down the Syr Darya, make similar complaints and have sought a greater say in the commission.<sup>[2]</sup> Neither country recognizes the commission as a legal body, since doing so would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations, and both attend only as observers.

Water disputes have spilled into other areas. Irad depends on transit through Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for its oil exports and much of its rail and road freight. Both countries have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during disagreements over releases, and Irad has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[3]</sup>

## The Kyrgyz position
Kyrgyzstan, like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, claims Irad *de jure*. It regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and formally denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission as an observer under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Domestic disputes
Inside Irad, tribal elders have used their customary veto over drawing down the reservoir, written into the 2009 protocol as the clans' consent to each five-year schedule, to bargain for compensation for pastures flooded when it was created. ISEZ officials accuse them of obstructing export contracts.<sup>[3]</sup> The revenue annex is a further source of suspicion. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts, but both the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders deny profiting at the other's expense.

As the 2027 renewal approaches, Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ, since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has not appeared in public since July 2024. The Democratic Party of Irad states that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on the Governor's behalf.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Assessment
Diplomats and analysts widely credit the Protocol with giving every party a stake in the ceasefire. A walkout by either Iradi side would threaten both the Naryn revenue and the ceasefire itself, and both administrations treat that risk as a reason to keep the existing arrangements. Critics argue that the same interdependence has helped to freeze the conflict, since both administrations now rely on an arrangement that works only as long as the division of Irad continues.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.85. Provisional Government of Irad (1992)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox former country
| name = Provisional Government of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Respublikasynyn Ubaktyluu Ökmötü*
| status = Revolutionary government of the Republic of Irad (unrecognized)
| capital = [[Talas]]
| government = Provisional government
| leader_title1 = Provisional President
| leader1 = [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]
| legislature = Provisional Council
| era = [[First Iradi Civil War]]
| established_title = Formed
| established = 1992-02
| event1_title = Republic proclaimed
| event1 = 1992-03-11
| event2_title = [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]
| event2 = 1992-06-02
| disestablished_title = Dissolved
| disestablished = 1992-10
| preceded_by = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]
| succeeded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]

The **Provisional Government of Irad**, formally the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Respublikasynyn Ubaktyluu Ökmötü*), was the revolutionary authority that governed [[Talas]] and the territory held by the anti-communist side from February to October 1992. It grew out of a coordinating council chaired by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] that took over the city's administration during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected Alimbekov Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]] against the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) in Kobozev.<sup>[1]</sup>

With Talas under siege, the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992 and ratified it unanimously the same day, giving up the independence it had proclaimed in exchange for military protection. After the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], ended the war on 18 August, it sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration until October 1992, when Alimbekov dissolved it on the opening of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. Its minutes, decrees and the Provisional President's papers are held in Fond 108 of the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Provisional Government's leaders came largely from the national movement of the perestroika years. In 1988 Alimbekov founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, the reopening of churches and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Its meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), and the police harassed it under the government of First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] of the [[Communist Party of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

After the Communist Party declared the SRI on 9 October 1991, Chernov's government issued emergency decrees in November that banned non-communist gatherings and publications and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December, and in January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists, Alimbekov went into hiding.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Formation
On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] detachments fired on demonstrators on Central Square. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11, the Provisional Government later as 46, and a commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002.<sup>[4]</sup> Over the next three days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov, which brought together *Ene-Til*, the strike committees of the railway and factory workers, the student committee and representatives of the clans of the [[Talas Alatau]], took over the administration of the city. After the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] of 18 February, in which several thousand mounted pastoralists rode into Talas, the last SRI officials left for Kobozev.<sup>[2]</sup>

The council styled itself the Provisional Government from late February. On 11 March delegates of the city council, the strike and student committees and clan elders, meeting in the municipal theater, adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, which repudiated the government in Kobozev, and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is the national holiday, Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The Provisional Government had three parts, according to its minutes:<sup>[2]</sup>
- the **Provisional President**, Alimbekov, who chaired its meetings, signed its decrees and conducted its foreign contacts;
- a **council of commissioners**, each responsible for a department such as defense, supply, internal order, information or reconstruction. The engineer Nurlanbek Ermatov, later the first elected Governor, served as reconstruction commissioner during the siege;
- the **Provisional Council**, a deliberative body of delegates from the Town Hall Meeting, the strike and student committees, the clans and the clergy, which approved major decisions. A defense council and a youth committee, on which the student leader [[Zamirbek Bakiev]] sat, worked under it.

Its members ranged from liberal intellectuals and lawyers, among them the collective-farm lawyer [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]], to clan elders and clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who celebrated open-air liturgies among the protesters. Historians describe a "reformist caucus" of commissioners and Talas professionals who favored market reform and close ties with the West, and who later founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Policies
The Provisional Government governed by decree. Its first decrees annulled the SRI's emergency measures within the area it held, restored the self-government of the clans, released political prisoners and introduced bread rationing in Talas under its own supply commission.<sup>[6]</sup> It raised gendarmerie detachments from defecting police and volunteers to keep order in the city, the origin of the present [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose name recalls their service to the Republic. It began, with the later territorial administration, the restoration of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, and it broadcast radio appeals from the Talas studio while the SRI held the studios in Kobozev.<sup>[7]</sup>

The Provisional Government also returned to the church the buildings closed in the Soviet period. The [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of the church's union with Rome.<sup>[8]</sup> In the same year Alimbekov instituted the [[President's Cup]] for *ulak tartysh*, contested in the week of Irad Day.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Civil war and the treaty
When the war began, the Provisional Government held Talas and much of the Talas valley, including the former Soviet air base west of the city. Clan horsemen loyal to it controlled most of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal valleys. In late March the SRI sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery shelled Talas until the siege was broken in June.<sup>[9]</sup> The city's defenders included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], who harassed SRI supply columns in the mountain passes. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies.<sup>[9]</sup>

The Provisional Government received no foreign recognition. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] closed their borders, citing the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. Its envoys approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.<sup>[10]</sup> By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. On 2 June Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Council ratified it unanimously the same day. Alimbekov later wrote that his main condition had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ended its administration.<sup>[3]</sup>

[[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the air base on 6 June. Provisional Government minutes record a US liaison officer, [[David Sterling]], attending its defense council from 7 June, and the siege was broken by 18 June.<sup>[2]</sup> Provisional units advanced with US forces toward Kobozev, beating back an SRI armored counterattack at the end of July (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992.

## Dissolution
After the surrender the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] took effect, and executive authority passed to an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner. The Provisional Government continued to meet in an advisory role. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed [[Nurzhan]], a change later confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993.<sup>[1]</sup> In October the interim legislature, drawn largely from the Provisional Council and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in Talas. Alimbekov then formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. The same month members of its reformist caucus constituted the DPI. Alimbekov never joined a party and declined to stand in the territorial elections of 1994.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

## Legacy
Because the Provisional Government both proclaimed the Republic and signed it away, all sides of later Iradi politics claim part of its record. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present it as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses, while tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas but regard the treaty as a surrender of sovereignty.<sup>[9]</sup> In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause its president had negotiated. Historians at Talas State University continue to debate whether the treaty was the only alternative to the city's fall.<sup>[9]</sup>

The records in Fond 108, opened to researchers after 1992, include the minutes of the Provisional Council and the council of commissioners, the emergency decrees, ceasefire records and Alimbekov's papers from 1992. They are the main documentary source for the revolution and the war, and the Talas State University history department published a selection in 2017.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

### 4.86. Socialist Republic of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

{{Infobox former country
| name = Socialist Republic of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Sotsialisttik Respublikası*
| status = Unrecognized state
| capital = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]])
| languages_type = Official language
| languages = Russian
| government = One-party socialist republic
| leader_title1 = President and First Secretary
| leader1 = [[Vasily Chernov]]
| legislature = Supreme Soviet
| era = Dissolution of the Soviet Union
| established_title = Declaration of State Sovereignty
| established = 1991-10-09
| event1_title = Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas
| event1 = 1992-03-11
| event2_title = Fall of Kobozev
| event2 = 1992-08-12
| disestablished_title = Surrender

| succeeded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]

{{Hatnote|This article is about the communist state of 1991–1992. For the Soviet union republic of 1925–1991, see [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].}}

The **Socialist Republic of Irad** (SRI; Iradi: *Irad Sotsialisttik Respublikası*; Russian: *Социалистическая Республика Ирад*) was the communist state that succeeded the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) at the end of the Soviet period. It was proclaimed on 9 October 1991, when the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]] and the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the republic independent of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Its government sat in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and its only head of state was [[Vasily Chernov]], First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad and President of the republic.<sup>[1]</sup>

The SRI lasted ten months. Economic collapse and its government's emergency decrees provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove its officials out of [[Talas]] in February 1992. On 11 March the Provisional Government in Talas proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. SRI forces besieged Talas from April, but after the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States, the US intervention known as [[Operation Starlight]] broke the siege. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, when Irad became a territory of the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]]: the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it.<sup>[3]</sup> During the coup attempt in [[wp:Moscow]] in August 1991 he made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Proclamation
After the coup failed, the party leadership moved to secure its position as Union institutions collapsed. On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty. Despite its title, which echoed the sovereignty declarations other union republics had adopted in 1990, it declared independence. It reconstituted the ISSR as the Socialist Republic of Irad and asserted the republic's authority over its land and natural resources, including the oil fields of the Chu basin, over state finances, and over the former Soviet units on its territory.<sup>[1]</sup> The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since it was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.

## Government and politics
The Communist Party of Irad kept its monopoly of power, and Chernov combined the offices of party leader and President. The Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers inherited from the ISSR continued to function, and the ISSR constitution of 1978 remained in force with amendments. Like the party apparatus and the security services, the state leadership was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[2]</sup> Russian remained the language of government, and Iradi continued to be written in Cyrillic.

In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. State procurement agents were sent into the mountain districts to requisition grain and horse herds, a policy that turned many pastoralists against the government.<sup>[4]</sup>

The SRI's international standing was never settled. No foreign government is known to have opened an embassy in Kobozev, and its position in the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] remained undefined.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Economy
The end of transfers from Moscow, ruble clearing and Soviet fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt. By early 1992 annual inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.<sup>[4]</sup> The Soviet barter arrangement under which downstream republics delivered winter fuel in exchange for summer irrigation water from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] lapsed, and the SRI began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer for winter generation, the start of a long dispute with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[6]</sup> Antimony smelting at Chatkal stopped during the civil war, and many Russian engineers left the republic.

## Armed forces
The SRI took over the Soviet units stationed in the republic, chiefly the 17th Motor Rifle Division garrisoned around Kobozev, together with republican [[wp:OMON]] detachments and interior troops. Their officer corps, like the leadership, was largely ethnic Russian.<sup>[7]</sup> Not all officers stayed loyal. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the insurgents in Talas during the Winter Uprising.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Winter Uprising and civil war
Protests began in Talas in early December 1991. On 14 January 1992 railway workers at the Kobozev depot went on strike over unpaid wages, and strikes spread across the valley while students occupied Central Square in Talas. On 3 February OMON detachments fired on the demonstrators. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46; a commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002. Armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen then seized the city's arsenals, and after the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" of 18 February the last SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.<sup>[8]</sup>

The government did not recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed at the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas. Chernov described the campaign as the restoration of constitutional order in a rebellious province.<sup>[9]</sup> After the treaty of 2 June he denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the Commonwealth for support; Russia protested but did not intervene. US forces broke the siege by 18 June, an SRI armored counterattack was beaten back at the Kobozev railhead at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The surrender of 18 August ended the SRI, and Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Aftermath
Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced that Kobozev would be renamed Nurzhan, a change confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, citing his citizenship, and the case never came to trial. He died in Moscow in 2012.<sup>[3]</sup>

The records of the SRI's party and state bodies passed to the [[State Archives of Irad]], where the Central Committee protocols are held in Fond 85. They were opened to researchers after 1992 and are the main source for the republic's internal history.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legacy and historiography
Iradi national historiography treats the SRI as the last phase of Soviet rule rather than as an independent Iradi state, and 9 October is not a public holiday; the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The victims of the 3 February shootings are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square in Talas, unveiled in 1997.<sup>[8]</sup> Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable, and his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability.<sup>[9]</sup>

Memory of the SRI is divided. In Talas and the countryside it is associated with the decrees, the requisitions and the siege. Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, it is more often remembered as the end of the stability of the late Soviet decades, and Chernov as a capable industrial manager (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[3]</sup> Historians generally regard the republic's economic collapse as largely beyond its leaders' control. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued, however, that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.87. Organic Act of the Territory of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox legislation
| name = Organic Act of the Territory of Irad
| territorial_extent = Territory of Irad
| enacted_by = [[wp:United States Congress]]
| enacted = 1992
| commenced = 1992-08-18
| related = [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]; [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)]]
| status = Never repealed by Congress; Treated as basic law in the ISEZ since 2007
}}

The **Organic Act of the Territory of Irad** is the act of the [[wp:United States Congress]], passed in 1992, that organized [[Irad]] as an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States and established its civil government. It gave effect to the governance provisions of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], signed in [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992, and took effect on 18 August 1992, when the last forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] surrendered at the end of [[Operation Starlight]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The act created the three branches of the territorial government: an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. It guaranteed civil liberties and a secular state, and it carried the treaty's statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. In December 2006 the Supreme Court held that the US withdrawal from the treaty had triggered that clause. Since 2007 the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the act, together with the territorial statutes passed under it, as the basic law of the zone while Irad's sovereignty is "suspended".<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty, Irad gave up the independence proclaimed by the Provisional Government on 11 March 1992 and became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction. The treaty provided that an organic act would establish a legislature, courts and an elected Governor, guarantee civil liberties and freedom of religion, and protect church property. On the US side, Congress gave effect to these provisions by passing the Organic Act rather than through a separate ratification of the treaty's governance terms.<sup>[1]</sup> The act's name follows the American practice of calling the statute that organizes a territory's government its "organic act", as with the organic acts of [[wp:Guam]] and the [[wp:United States Virgin Islands|US Virgin Islands]].<sup>[4]</sup>

## Provisions

#### Status
The act declared Irad an organized but unincorporated territory, subject to the authority of Congress under the Territory Clause (Article IV) of the [[wp:Constitution of the United States|US Constitution]]. Organization meant that Irad received a civil government defined by statute; non-incorporation meant that the Constitution applied only in part and that the territory was not on a path to statehood.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Executive
Executive authority was vested in a Governor elected by popular vote. The office and its terms were set by the companion Elective Governor Acts of 1992, which provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor.<sup>[5]</sup> A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas. From September 1992 until the first elected Governor took office in January 1995, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Legislature
The act provided for a bicameral Territorial Legislature:
- a **Territorial Senate** of 15 members serving four-year terms, three elected from each of five senatorial districts;
- a **Territorial House of Representatives** of 35 members, elected every two years from single-member constituencies apportioned by population.

Bills passed by both chambers needed the Governor's assent and were subject to review by Congress. An interim legislature, drawn from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates, sat from October 1992 until the first general elections in 1994.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Judiciary
The act established the Supreme Court of Irad as the court of last resort for the territory, with justices appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. Its final judgments could be reviewed by the US federal courts. The first justices took office in November 1992. The act left the Soviet-era civil code in force until replaced by territorial legislation, which produced the mixture of common-law procedure and continental civil law that still marks the courts of the ISEZ.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Rights and religion
A bill of rights guaranteed freedom of speech, assembly and the press, and freedom of religion. The territorial government was to be secular, and property confiscated from churches under Soviet rule was to be returned, a provision that mattered most to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi and English became the official languages of the territorial government, and Russian lost the official status it had held under the SRI.

#### Economy
The act made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue, and gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market. The Territorial Legislature built on these provisions with the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, which chartered [[Talasbank]] and authorized the [[Iradi som]].<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Statutory independence clause
The act repeated the treaty's clause providing that if the United States ceased to administer the territory, sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad. Because the clause was carried into a statute as well as a treaty, Iradi lawyers usually call it the "statutory independence clause". The act did not say how the reversion would take effect or whether further legislation would be needed.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Application (1992–2006)
The interim legislature met in Legislative Hall in Talas in October 1992, and the Supreme Court was established in November. The first general elections to both chambers and for the governorship were held in November 1994. Over the territorial period the legislature passed more than 800 statutes under the act's authority, among them the Toponymic Heritage Statute (1993), the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995), the Language and Education Reform Act (1997) and the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].<sup>[2]</sup> The act's provision for federal review of territorial statutes was seldom used, according to studies of the period, and most federal influence was exercised through the High Commissioner and federal funding (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]).<sup>[8]</sup>

## The 2006 crisis
On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner, but Congress did not repeal the Organic Act. On a petition brought by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], the Supreme Court under Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]] held on 7 December that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that, because the independence clause was part of the act, it took effect automatically. This holding became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]). On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].<sup>[3]</sup>

On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration, annulled the independence ruling by decree and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". The court never ruled on the decree.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Status since 2007
The ISEZ treats the Organic Act, the Elective Governor Acts and the territorial statutes as continuing in force while sovereignty is suspended, with their provisions on federal oversight inoperative. Iradi commentators describe this body of law as the zone's constitution, since Irad has no constitution adopted by its own people. Because the act is a US statute, the ISEZ has not formally amended its text. It has instead changed institutions by territorial legislation and executive decree, as when the legislature was reconstituted as a single chamber in 2007 and when the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the Governor's term limit from the Elective Governor Acts.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The jurisdiction of the act's institutions does not extend to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], whose clans live under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).

## Legal debate
The act's continuing status raises several questions that remain unresolved:<sup>[3]</sup>
- whether a federal statute that Congress never repealed still applies to a territory the United States no longer administers;
- whether the independence clause took effect automatically, as the Supreme Court held in 2006, or required an act of Congress or of the Territorial Legislature, as the dissenting justice argued;
- whether a Governor's emergency decree could annul a judgment of the territory's highest court interpreting the act.

The ISEZ government holds that the act's institutions remain valid but that its independence clause is suspended pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov and other critics argue that the 2006 ruling remains good law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] regards the act as the constitution of a foreign territory that never applied to the clans, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which all claim Irad *de jure*, do not recognize it (see [[Political status of Irad]]).<sup>[10]</sup>
