### 4.88. Irad–Russia relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–Russia relations** cover the ties between [[Irad]] and Russia, the former imperial and Soviet center whose language remains Irad's *de facto* lingua franca. Russia has no official relations with either Iradi administration and does not border Irad. Its influence runs mainly through the Russian-speaking business and industrial elite of [[Nurzhan]], through Russian-language media, and through the northern oil route, by which Iradi crude enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]] and is refined there or shipped onward to Russia.<sup>[1]</sup>

Russia protested against the US intervention of 1992 but did not intervene, and it received the defeated communist leader [[Vasily Chernov]]. Since then the main Russian-oriented current in Iradi politics has been the "Russo" faction associated with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], who calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The ruling [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) is pro-American and has opposed the Russos on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Imperial and Soviet rule
Russian forces reached the northern lands of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in the 1860s, and after [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] abolished the khanate in 1876 the Iradi lands were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. [[Iradis]] were classed as *inorodtsy*. Land seizures for Russian settlers and the wartime labor decree led to the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, after which Cossack detachments and settler militias burned villages across Semirechye.<sup>[3]</sup>

In the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (1925–1991), Russian became the language of administration and, after the end of nativization, of schooling, and a Cyrillic alphabet was imposed on Iradi in 1941. The oil discovery of 1949 near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, and the growth of the oil, metallurgical and railway industries brought Russian and Ukrainian specialists to the city, which became the center of a Russian-speaking industrial workforce.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### The Socialist Republic and the 1992 war
The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), proclaimed in Kobozev on 9 October 1991, was led by Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer, and its leadership and officer corps were largely ethnic Russian. After the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to [[wp:Moscow]] and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support.<sup>[5]</sup>

The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space and raised the safety of Russian-speaking residents, but it did not intervene. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. After the SRI's surrender on 18 August 1992, Chernov and other senior SRI officials were given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.<sup>[6]</sup> Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war.

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The territorial government dropped Russian as an official language in 1992 in favor of Iradi and English, restored the Latin alphabet for Iradi and renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his Russian citizenship, and the case never came to trial.<sup>[7]</sup> Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presented his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He died in Moscow in 2012; the ISEZ government made no official comment.

Economic contacts continued. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, formed technical partnerships in the 1990s with [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil. From 2000 Iradi crude moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh network, from which part was shipped on to Russia.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Since 2007
Russia has not recognized any Iradi administration. Irad belongs to neither the Eurasian Economic Union nor its predecessor customs union, and since [[wp:Kazakhstan]] joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, Iradi goods sold into Kazakhstan and Russia have paid the union's external tariff.<sup>[9]</sup> Russia is one of Irad's main sources of imports, alongside China, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States, and it receives most Iradi crude. It is also, after Kazakhstan, the main destination of Iradi labor migrants (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). The Security Council, of which Russia is a permanent member, established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] in October 2007.

## The Russo faction
*Main article: [[Russos of Nurzhan]]*

The "Russos" are the generation of urban Iradis, born roughly between the late 1940s and 1980, who were educated in Russian in the Soviet period, together with Russian, Ukrainian and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram contemporaries. They are concentrated in Nurzhan. Sociologists estimated in 2022 that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language.<sup>[4]</sup> The 2018 census recorded Russians as 4 percent of Irad's population; most belong to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]].

Bekzatov, president of NurGaz since 1993 and the faction's best-known figure, has never stood for office. His positions include:<sup>[2]</sup>
- accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, to remove duties on refined oil products and steel, and closer trade with Kazakhstan and Russia;
- the restoration of Russian as an official language alongside Iradi and English;
- criticism of the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees and of the US presence at [[Talas Air Base]].

He has also drawn attention for his open praise of Vladimir Putin. Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, and three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the 2023 election to the 60-seat [[Mejlis]], where they form its only consistent opposition. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the city's Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.<sup>[10]</sup>

DPI-aligned commentators portray Bekzatov as a channel for Russian influence. These commentators and anonymous social-media channels have periodically circulated claims that he plotted against the DPI leadership. The claims were never corroborated. Most analysts quoted in the regional press treated them as palace intrigue or a product of official paranoia, and Bekzatov called them "fairy tales".<sup>[11]</sup>

## Media and disinformation
Russian-language media remain widely followed among older Iradis, including satellite television from Russia and IradOdin, the Russian-language sister channel of [[IradOne]]. [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] is marked in Nurzhan on 9 May with a parade.<sup>[4]</sup> Since the second half of 2024, recorded addresses attributed to Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], who has not appeared in public since July 2024, have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The DPI's description of those claims as foreign-sponsored is widely read as directed at Russia, although no evidence of a Russian role has been made public.<sup>[12]</sup>

## The 2025 Trump remarks
In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad, at which some protesters burned American and Russian flags. Bekzatov rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington, and Russo politicians cited it in renewed calls to review the US basing arrangements (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).<sup>[13]</sup>

## Public opinion
Attitudes toward Russia divide sharply by generation. In a 2023 survey of the three cities, 58 percent of respondents over 60 had a favorable view of Russia, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25. Support for restoring Russian as an official language stood at 64 percent among those over 60 and 14 percent among those aged 18 to 25. About a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 nonetheless opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union.<sup>[10]</sup> Younger Iradis, schooled in English and increasingly in Iradi, are the least attached to Russia (see [[Iradi language revival]]).

### 4.89. Irad–China relations
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Foreign Relations*

**Irad–China relations** are the economic and political ties between [[Irad]] and the [[wp:China|People's Republic of China]]. The two do not share a border, and China maintains no official relations with either Iradi administration. Its relationship with Irad is carried on almost entirely through trade and investment: China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony and a leading source of Irad's imports, the textile company Xinjiang Lihua is the largest cotton processor in Irad, and the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) has proposed a gas pipeline across the territory.<sup>[1]</sup>

Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has said publicly that "Irad's alignment with China is inevitable and welcome".<sup>[2]</sup> The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) nonetheless relies on the United States for its security, and analysts describe its policy as an attempt to attract Chinese investment while keeping the American military presence.

## Background
Iradi historiography gives a large place to early contacts with China. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] visited the Fergana kingdom of [[wp:Dayuan]] around 128 BCE, and Han demand for its "heavenly horses" led to the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE); Iradi breeders regard the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] as a descendant of these horses (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]). In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the [[Battle of Talas]], which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley. Tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners, a claim historians dispute.<sup>[3]</sup> In the flight after the revolt of 1916, Iradi and Kyrgyz groups crossed the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]].

Modern economic ties began in the territorial period. The [[Sary-Bulak]] antimony mine was re-equipped between 1995 and 1997, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers, and the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] found its main market in China in the late 1990s.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Trade

#### Antimony
Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] is concentrated on site and partly smelted at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. In 2023 the combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony, which would make Irad one of the largest producers after China, a figure independent estimates put lower. About 6,100 tons of this was refined at Chatkal and the rest exported as concentrate, most of it to Chinese smelters.<sup>[4]</sup> Because Irad has no border with China, the shipments travel by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]].

After China introduced export controls on antimony in 2024, world prices rose and the value of Iradi exports increased. The combine reported larger sales of metal and trioxide to buyers outside China in 2025, and the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]] has sought new buyers outside China since 2024. Analysts have described Irad as a potential non-Chinese source of supply, while noting that most of its concentrate remains contracted to Chinese smelters (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Other trade
China is one of Irad's main sources of imports of machinery, vehicles and consumer goods, alongside Russia, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States. Demand for pedigree [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and Akyel horses has risen in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China.<sup>[1]</sup> The 2018 census recorded Chinese residents as 1 percent of Irad's population.

## Investment

#### Xinjiang Lihua
*Main article: [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]*

Xinjiang Lihua Co. acquired cotton ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in two stages, in 2018 and 2021, and re-equipped them. Its plants handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year and employ about 1,400 people. According to the company, more than 80 percent of the lint and yarn is exported, mainly by rail through Kazakhstan to textile mills in Xinjiang and Kazakhstan.<sup>[6]</sup>

When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about whether the cotton growing linked to the plants would comply with water regulations, and about the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins. ISEZ water inspectors state that withdrawals by farms supplying the plants are monitored by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline
*Main article: [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]*

CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would carry gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China, leaving Irad through Kyrgyz territory. Feasibility studies assume a 1,220-mm pipe carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters a year, with four compressor stations in Irad, and [[NurGaz]] would be the main Iradi partner. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas for power and heating in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan.<sup>[8]</sup> In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas, and the Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.<sup>[9]</sup>

No investment decision has been made. The obstacles include the need for transit agreements with Uzbekistan and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim Irad; lenders' reluctance to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty; competition from existing [[wp:Central Asia]]–China pipelines through Kazakhstan; and the refusal of clan elders in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] to consent to construction across their pastures and catchments. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies and a share of transit revenue.<sup>[8]</sup> [[Kamran Bekzatov]] supports the pipeline provided NurGaz keeps operating control.

## Politics
Toktarov's statement on China sits alongside the ISEZ's continued reliance on the US forces at [[Talas Air Base]], and Chinese investment in Irad has not extended to security cooperation.<sup>[2]</sup>

Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, Maksat has received foreign delegations, including Chinese investors, and presents himself as a pro-business technocrat who welcomes foreign infrastructure investment (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[10]</sup>

China figured in the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad and were directed principally against the United States.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 4.90. Arslanbob
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Cities & Settlements*

{{Infobox settlement
| name = Arslanbob
| native_name = Russian: Арсланбоб
| settlement_type = Village
| subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]
| district = Fergana Rim
| elevation_m = 1600
| population = 13000
| coordinates = 41.34°N 72.93°E
}}

**Arslanbob** (Iradi and Uzbek: *Arslanbob*) is a village and forest area in southern [[Irad]], on the southwestern slopes of the Babash-Ata ridge, a spur of the [[wp:Fergana Range]]. It lies at about 1,600 meters in the upper valley of the Kara-Unkur River, about 50 kilometers by road northeast of the market town of [[Bazar-Korgon]], up the old valley road past Kyzyl-Unkur, in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), above the farm belt that has been in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2007.<sup>[1]</sup> The village, with an estimated 13,000 inhabitants, is among the largest settlements of the tribal regions and the seat of the highland Chubar.

Arslanbob is surrounded by walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], apple, pear and plum, regarded as among the largest natural walnut forests in the world.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} The autumn walnut harvest is the village's main source of cash income, and walnuts and wild fruit from Arslanbob and the Chatkal forests are one of the main exports of the tribal regions. The village is also a place of Muslim pilgrimage, centered on the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata, and one of the few places in the ATR with a regular flow of foreign visitors.<sup>[2]</sup> Since the Chubar clan was divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] in 2007, the meadow below the shrine has been the gathering ground of the highland Chubar under their *biy*, Döölötbek Ashym uulu.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Geography
The village is spread along the Kara-Unkur valley and its side streams, where houses stand among orchards and walnut groves on terraces above the river. Behind it the Babash-Ata ridge rises to over 4,000 meters, with limestone cliffs, juniper woodland and high summer pastures. The slopes face southwest toward the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and catch moist westerly air, receiving several times as much precipitation as the Talas valley; winters bring heavy snow, and summers are warm.<sup>[1]</sup> Below the village the Kara-Unkur flows south past [[Kara-Unkur Cave]], a [[wp:Paleolithic]] site, to Bazar-Korgon and the irrigation network of the [[Kara-Darya]].

Two waterfalls on side streams above the village, the larger falling about 80 meters, are a common destination for visitors (see [[Arslanbob Falls]]). Trails lead over the ridge to high pastures and small mountain lakes.<sup>[4]</sup>

## The walnut forest
The walnut-fruit forest of the Arslanbob massif covers on the order of 10,000 hectares, part of a wider belt of such forest on the Fergana and Chatkal ranges that extends to [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].<sup>[2]</sup> Walnut grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, mixed with [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]] (*Malus sieversii*), pear, cherry plum, hawthorn and [[wp:Turkestan]] maple, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on dry, rocky ground. The oldest trees reach 25 to 30 meters and are several centuries old. The forest supports the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], wild boar, the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]] and many birds.<sup>[5]</sup>

Botanists long regarded the forests as relicts of [[wp:Tertiary]] broadleaf forest. Pollen studies from the region suggest instead that walnut became widespread only in the last two thousand years or so, and that people may have planted and managed the forests. Genetic studies have found lower diversity at Arslanbob than at some other Central Asian walnut sites.<sup>[6]</sup>

## History and legend
According to local Muslim legend, the [[wp:Muhammad|Prophet Muhammad]] sent a gardener named Arslanbob to find a garden resembling paradise. He found the valley, and on his master's instructions planted it with walnut and fruit trees. The shrine of Arslanbob-Ata in the village, with a mosque beside it, is visited by pilgrims from the Fergana Valley, and a popular story also credits [[wp:Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great's]] soldiers with carrying walnuts from the forest to [[wp:Greece]].<sup>[2]</sup> Syro-Iradi church tradition associates the forests with early Christian hermits who withdrew to the mountains during the persecutions of the 14th century, but the claim rests on late manuscripts and is not supported by archaeological evidence.<sup>[7]</sup>

Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[wp:Russian Empire]] the forest was used by surrounding villages for nuts, fruit, timber and grazing. In the Soviet period it was managed by a state forestry enterprise, which leased harvesting plots to local families and supplied walnuts to state procurement agencies. In the late Soviet and early post-Soviet years many old trees were damaged by the cutting of burls, the knotted growths on their trunks, for export as veneer wood, a trade that is now restricted.<sup>[5]</sup>

The forestry enterprise broke down after 1991. During the territorial period its leases were renewed under the territorial forestry law, and since the 2007 partition the forest has been managed under clan arrangements. Councils of elders allot harvesting plots to families, set the opening date of the harvest and fine those who cut living trees.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Economy
The walnut harvest runs from September into October, when families camp in the forest to gather nuts on their plots. Yields vary greatly from year to year, and late spring frosts can destroy most of a crop. Nuts are carried down the valley road through the Arslanbob road crossing of the line to the bazaar at Bazar-Korgon, in the ISEZ, where they are sold to traders from the ISEZ, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and some are shelled in the village for export. Growers complain that the lowland buyers fix prices, and the clan council takes a customary levy on loads crossing the line.<sup>[2]</sup> Villagers also sell dried fruit, honey and walnut wood for crafts such as the [[Carved Walnut Tobacco Box]] and the [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]]. Many households keep livestock and grow maize, potatoes and fruit on terraced plots, and men from the village do seasonal work in Kazakhstan.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Tourism
A network of family guesthouses, set up in the early 2000s with help from a European development agency, offers rooms, guides and horses to visitors. Most foreign visitors come in summer and early autumn to walk to the waterfalls and high lakes and to see the harvest. Since 2007 access has been more complicated: foreigners reaching Arslanbob from the ISEZ must cross the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line at the Arslanbob road crossing, about 20 kilometers above Bazar-Korgon, and the village councils ask guesthouse owners to register guests. Visitor numbers are small, but tourism is the second source of cash income for some families after the walnut harvest (see [[Tourism in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup>

## Population and religion
Most villagers speak Uzbek or Iradi, and many speak both; Kyrgyz is also heard. Unlike most of the ATR, Arslanbob is largely Muslim, and it is one of the main Muslim centers of the Fergana Rim, together with Bazar-Korgon below it on the ISEZ side of the line (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup> Syro-Iradi Catholic families live in some of the outlying hamlets.

## Conservation
The forest has no formal protected status of its own. Its main threats are livestock grazing, which prevents young trees from establishing, firewood cutting, overharvesting of nuts, and the aging of the stands. Researchers from [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]], which keeps walnut and wild apple from Arslanbob in its living collection, have recommended fencing of regeneration plots, but clan councils and conservationists disagree about how much grazing and harvesting the forest can sustain.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.91. 2018 Irad census
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **2018 Irad census** was a population census carried out in October and November 2018 by the ISEZ Statistical Office under the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its results, published by the Department of Public Information in 2019, gave Irad a population of 4,626,000. Enumerators counted the population of the ISEZ door to door, but the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) was estimated from administrative data, without a count on the ground.<sup>[1]</sup> Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, against the official 2.0 million, and Irad's total population at about 6.2 million. The census is the source of most official statistics on Irad, and its treatment of the tribal regions is one of the main points of dispute between the DPI and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The previous count was the Soviet census of 1989, which recorded 4,257,000 people in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. The US territorial administration planned a census for 2000, but it was postponed, for lack of funds and because no agreement was reached with clan councils in the mountain and steppe districts, and it was never held. Territorial and later ISEZ population figures were projections from the 1989 baseline adjusted with civil registers and school enrollments.<sup>[2]</sup> Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] ordered a census by an executive decree of 2017, and the ISEZ Statistical Office was charged with carrying it out.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Organization
The reference date was 14 October 2018, and enumeration in the ISEZ ran until 4 November. About 9,800 enumerators, most of them schoolteachers, visited households in the three cities and six districts. In Talas and Nurzhan they used tablet computers supplied through [[Attelkom]], and elsewhere paper forms. Questionnaires were printed in Iradi, English and Russian. They asked about age, sex, marital status, nationality, native language and other languages spoken, religion, education, occupation and housing. Nationality and religion were recorded by self-declaration, and the methodology report states that the religion question offered a list of faiths without a separate "no religion" option.<sup>[1]</sup>

ISEZ enumerators did not work beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The 2017 Kurultai had formally refused to admit enumerators acting under ISEZ authority (see [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]]). For the ATR the Statistical Office produced an estimate from:<sup>[1]</sup>
- the 1989 census, projected forward and adjusted for the losses of the civil wars and for emigration;
- the number of tribal travel permits registered at the Gendarmerie checkpoints;
- enrollments in schools and parish registers known to the ISEZ authorities;
- household lists used in livestock and fuel trade contracts with the clans.

Preliminary results were announced in December 2018, and the final results were published in 2019, with settlement-level tables for the ISEZ districts and separate tables for the three cities.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Results
The main official results were as follows:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

| Area | Population | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Irad (total) | 4,626,000 | 100% |
| Irad Special Economic Zone (enumerated) | c. 2.63 million | 57% |
| — of which [[Talas]] | 1,120,000 | |
| — of which [[Nurzhan]] | 850,000 | |
| — of which [[Iyık Janyl]] | 310,000 | |
| — of which the six districts | c. 350,000 | |
| Autonomous Tribal Regions (estimated) | c. 2.0 million | 43% |

Other published results included:
- **Nationality:** [[Iradis]] 72 percent; Kyrgyz 7 percent; [[wp:Uzbeks]] 5 percent; [[wp:Kazakhs]] 3 percent; [[wp:Tajiks]], [[wp:Uyghurs]] and Dungans about 1 percent combined; migrant and foreign communities 12 percent, including Russians and Americans (4 percent each), and Ukrainians, [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], Chinese and others including Mexicans (1 percent each).
- **Religion:** Christians 78 percent, Muslims 18 percent and other faiths 4 percent (see [[Religion in Irad]]).
- **Language:** about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language (see [[Iradi Language]]).
- **Education:** 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Criticism

#### The tribal regions
Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, using satellite mapping of settlements and seasonal camps, aid-agency beneficiary registries and the vaccination records of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and UN-supported vaccination campaigns. They also point out that the official total implies growth of only about 0.3 percent a year since 1989, a rate they consider implausible for a population with the birth rates recorded in the ISEZ and reported in the tribal regions.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Satellite and registry studies support the higher figure, though they do not settle it, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and humanitarian agencies use planning figures within the independent range.<sup>[5]</sup>

IAC leaders allege that the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unified legislature. They also note that even the official figure gives the ATR more than two-fifths of the population, against the one-third of seats it was offered at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. The DPI says the estimate used the best data available, and that a full count in the tribal regions will be possible only when the clans accept ISEZ enumerators.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Other issues
Analysts have raised several further points:<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>
- **The American share.** The 4 percent recorded as Americans is considered inflated by military personnel and contractors at [[Talas Air Base]] and other US installations who were registered as residents.
- **Cities and districts.** The published city figures, about 2.28 million together, leave about 350,000 people for the six districts out of an ISEZ total of about 2.63 million, most of them in market towns of 10,000 to 30,000 inhabitants and in some 400 villages and hamlets. The Statistical Office says that the city figures include settlements under the administration of the city governments, and demographers note that this counts suburban villages that would otherwise be classed as rural in the city totals. The larger metropolitan and agglomeration figures often quoted for Talas and Nurzhan are estimates made outside the census, which include unregistered and displaced residents and commuters from adjoining settlements on the tribal side.
- **Religion.** Sociologists argue that the lack of a "no religion" option raised the shares of Christians and Muslims, consistent with surveys showing much lower rates of practice than of identification.

## Significance
Because the two figures differ by more than a third, statistics derived from the census vary widely with the population base used. Nominal GDP per person, for example, is about $3,980 on the official population and about $2,970 on the independent estimate.<sup>[6]</sup> The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] reports both figures in its annual working paper on Irad. The census results also underpin the ISEZ's case that its electorate represents a majority of Irad's population, a claim the IAC rejects, and any future unification referendum would depend on an agreed count. The IAC has called for a census under UN supervision. The ISEZ government has said that the next census will be held in 2028.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.92. Iradi name
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

An **Iradi name** usually consists of a given name followed either by a Russian-style surname or by a Turkic patronymic. Urban [[Iradis]] in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) mostly carry surnames ending in *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*), a form fixed by Soviet civil registration, as in [[Erlan Toktarov]] or [[Anara Toktarova]]. Since the 1990s rural and tribal Iradis have used patronymics formed from the father's given name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"), as in [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]]. The two systems follow the divide between town and countryside that the 2007 partition later fixed: in 2019 registry data more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) the patronymic form is almost universal.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Given names come from Turkic, Christian, Persian and Arabic, Russian and English sources.

## Structure

#### Patronymics
In the traditional form, a person is identified by a given name and the given name of the father, followed by *uulu* for a man or *kyzy* for a woman. *Bektur Zhumabek uulu* means "Bektur, son of Zhumabek"; his father was *Zhumabek Asanaly uulu*, "Zhumabek, son of Asanaly". The patronymic changes in each generation and is not a family name, and women keep their own patronymic after marriage. In everyday speech people are addressed by their given name, and older men respectfully as *[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

Clan membership is expressed separately. Each person belongs to a clan (*uruk*), and genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) record the paternal line. Iradis are traditionally expected to know their ancestors back seven generations (*jeti ata*), and customary law forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Surnames
Russian-style surnames were formed in the Soviet period by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to the given name of the father or grandfather at the time of registration: *Toktarov* from *Toktar*, *Bekzatov* from *Bekzat*, *Alimbekov* from *Alimbek*. Once registered, the surname passed unchanged to later generations. Soviet documents also gave a Russian-style patronymic (*otchestvo*) ending in *-ovich* or *-ovna*, which older people still use on formal occasions.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since the territorial period many Iradis have dropped the suffix and use the bare stem as a surname (*Maksat* for *Maksatov*, *Temir* for *Temirova*); some also re-registered their names when the Latin alphabet was restored. The practice is most common in [[Talas]], where it spread from the university and the press in the 1990s and is now usual among people born after about 1960, and least common in [[Nurzhan]], where Russian-style surnames remain the norm. Older people, public figures already known under their Soviet names and many officials have kept the suffix, so that members of one family may write their name differently. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], born in Kobozev and registered as Maksatov, took the shortened form as a student in Talas.

## Given names
Iradi given names come from several layers:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>
- **Turkic names**, the largest group, often compounds with elements such as *-bek* ("lord") and *-bai* ("rich") for men and *-gul* ("flower") and *-ai* ("moon") for women: *Kanybek*, *Nurlan*, *Erlan*, *Aigul*, *Altynai*. *Janyl*, after the legendary founder of the Iradi church (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]), is among the most common names for girls.
- **Christian baptismal names**, used in forms derived from [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] rather than from Greek or Latin: *Yuhanna* (John), *Toma* (Thomas), *Luka* (Luke), *Maryam* (Mary), *Gewargis* (George). Examples include the translator [[Luka Ayyubov|Father Luka Ayyubov]], the 17th-century priest [[Toma Alimbek|Father Toma Alimbek]] and [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]]. Saints and institutions follow the same forms, as in St. Luka, St. Yuhanna and St. Maryam. Many rural Iradis receive a baptismal name in addition to the Turkic name they use every day. Bishops take a religious name with the Syriac title *Mar*, as in [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] and [[Mar Ephrem]].
- **Persian and Arabic names**, common among the Muslim Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and [[wp:Kazakhs]] and found among Iradis as well, such as *Fatima*, *Amina* and *Anara* (from Persian *anar*, "pomegranate").
- **Russian and European names**, which became common in the cities in the Soviet period, especially among Russians, Ukrainians and the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], who usually combine Russian given names with Korean surnames, as in [[Oleg Kim]] and [[Elena Kim]].
- **English names**, given by some urban families since the territorial period and widespread among [[Iradi Americans]], such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]].

Since the 2010s, registry data have shown a decline in Russian given names among urban newborns and a rise in Turkic and baptismal names, a trend sociologists link to the revival of the Iradi language among young people (see [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## History

#### Before 1917
Before Russian rule, Iradis were known by a given name and the father's name, and by clan. [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] and Russian imperial records rendered these names inconsistently, often adding Russian suffixes for official purposes. Under Russian rule Iradis were classed as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"), and few were registered in the Russian manner.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Soviet period
Russian-style surnames became general through Soviet registration, schooling and military service in the 1920s and 1930s. Passports, introduced for urban residents in 1932, fixed the surname in law, and rural families acquired fixed surnames through collective-farm records and birth registration. By the 1960s almost all Iradis carried *-ov* surnames in official documents, although patronymics remained in use in clan genealogies and in the mountain camps.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### De-Russification since 1992
After 1992 naming became part of the wider [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of public life. A civil registration act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1994 allowed residents to register names in the traditional patronymic form or to drop Russian suffixes, ended the requirement for a Russian-style *otchestvo* and introduced American-style documents with given name, middle name and surname fields. Names in official documents have since been written in the Latin alphabet fixed by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]].<sup>[2]</sup>

The response divided along the line between town and country. Rural and tribal families adopted patronymics from the 1990s, and in the ATR they became almost universal after 2007, when the clan councils and parishes took over the registration of births. Urban Iradis mostly kept their surnames, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms.<sup>[1]</sup> Tribal leaders who were registered under Russian-style surnames in Soviet records now use patronymics: Bektur Zhumabek uulu appears in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov. By convention, Iradi historians and reference works refer to people who died before the 1990s by the surnames they used in life.

## Romanization
In the Iradi Latin alphabet, names are written with the letters *ı*, *ö* and *ü*, and since the 1995 orthography the school alphabet writes *ç*, *ş* and *ñ* for the old digraphs (see [[Iradi alphabet]]). The press, official English-language documents and most personal names keep *ch*, *sh* and *ng*, and English-language usage often follows Russian-based romanization with *ch*, *sh* and *zh*. The spelling *zh*, as in *Zhumabek*, reflects the pronunciation of the northern steppe dialects, while the standard language pronounces the same sound as /dʒ/ (see [[Iradi Language]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

## Legal status
In the ISEZ, births, marriages and name changes are registered by the civil registry offices of the city governments and district administrations. Documents issued by clan councils in the ATR are not recognized by the ISEZ, except as supporting documents for tribal travel permits, and residents of the tribal regions who move to the cities often register under a patronymic for the first time as adults.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.93. Iradi som
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox currency
| name = Iradi som
| native_name = *Irad somu*
| iso_code = None
| symbol = IS
| subunit = 1/100 *tyiyn*
| banknotes = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500 som
| coins = 10 and 50 tyiyn; 1 and 5 som
| issuer = [[Bank of Irad]]
| user = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (alongside the US dollar)
| pegged_with = US dollar: 8.40 som (since 2008-03-17); 5 som (1993–2008)
}}

The **Iradi som** (Iradi: *Irad somu*; abbreviation **IS**) is the currency issued by the [[Bank of Irad]] (*Irad Banky*), the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It circulates alongside the US dollar, which has been legal tender in Irad since the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. The dollar is used for most contracts, property transactions, savings and foreign trade, while the som is used mainly for retail payments, utility bills and public-sector wages. The som is divided into 100 *tyiyn*. Because Irad's sovereignty is unresolved, the currency has no ISO 4217 code.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The name is shared with the currencies of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and comes from a Turkic word meaning "pure", once applied to ingots of refined silver or gold.

## History
The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] used the Soviet ruble, and the collapse of the ruble zone after October 1991, with inflation above 1,000 percent, wiped out most savings. By the time of the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992, banking in the city had largely stopped.<sup>[3]</sup> After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to adopt the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act, passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993, made the dollar legal tender, chartered [[Talasbank]] as the main commercial bank, and established the Bank of Irad to issue a local currency for small payments and wages and to supervise the banks.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Bank of Irad opened in the autumn of 1993 and put the first som notes into circulation late that year, at a fixed rate of 5 som to the dollar. The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]], and rubles remaining in circulation were exchanged at Talasbank branches.<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]] was set up in 1996 to settle payments between banks in both currencies.

The end of the US territorial administration on 3 December 2006 caused a run, as depositors converted som and withdrew dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks. The Bank of Irad met conversions from its reserves and the official rate held, but during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in the first months of 2007 the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. American correspondent banks froze or restricted Iradi accounts, and the bank moved what it could of its reserves to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. In the spring of 2007 the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] drew on the reserves held in Talas to pay salaries and its forces, against government notes that the currency-board rules did not allow.<sup>[4]</sup>

By the end of the war the reserves covered only about 60 percent of the som in circulation. When the ISEZ reconstituted the bank under the Bank of Irad Act in 2008, it kept the currency-board rules but reset the fixed rate: from 17 March 2008 the som was exchanged at **8.40 to the dollar**, a level chosen so that the remaining reserves again covered the som in full. The devaluation of about 40 percent fell hardest on pensioners and public employees paid in som; dollar deposits were untouched. The informal discount disappeared within months.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> [[Azamat Temirov]], deputy chairman of the Bank of Irad from 2007 and one of the authors of the reset, became its chairman in 2010. The som was added to the clearing house's real-time payment system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] introduced SMS-based payments.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Monetary system
Irad's system is dual-currency and largely dollarized. The Bank of Irad issues the som, holds the dollar reserves that back it, supervises the commercial banks and operates the clearing house. Because most deposits, loans and prices of large purchases are in dollars, it has little room for independent monetary policy, and its main task is to keep the som stable against the dollar.<sup>[2]</sup> According to the [[wp:World Bank]], som accounts made up about a fifth of commercial bank deposits in the ISEZ in 2022.<sup>[6]</sup>

The two currencies have distinct uses:
- **US dollar.** Contracts, property, vehicles, savings, bank loans and foreign trade. Export proceeds are paid in dollars into escrow accounts at Talasbank supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], and commercial and industrial customers of public utilities are billed in dollars.
- **Iradi som.** Public-sector wages and pensions, household utility bills, local taxes and fees, public transport and everyday retail. The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]], for example, sets household tariffs in som and bills businesses in dollars.<sup>[7]</sup>

Since non-recognition limits Irad's access to international payment systems, dollar payments abroad are settled through correspondent banks, mainly in Almaty and Istanbul, and the som is not traded outside Irad.<sup>[6]</sup> Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]].

## Banknotes and coins
The first series of banknotes, issued in 1993 and printed abroad under a territorial contract, came in denominations of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 som. Their designs showed horses, the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[wp:Silk Road]] monuments. A redesigned series with improved security features was issued from 2011, adding a 500-som note; its 100-som note carries a portrait of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], leader of the Provisional Government in 1992. Coins of 10 and 50 tyiyn and of 1 and 5 som are struck, although small tyiyn coins are rarely used.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The tribal regions
The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no formal fiscal or monetary system, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] issues no currency. Herders who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank in dollars or som, but much local trade is conducted in barter or livestock, and near the frontiers Kazakh and Uzbek currencies also change hands.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Debate
Economists and the World Bank have noted that dollarization has given Irad stable prices since the 1990s at the cost of an independent monetary policy, and that the som's role is largely confined to small payments. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som.<sup>[9]</sup> The Bank of Irad's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender. Business groups credit the bank and Talasbank with keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–07, while critics point out that holders of som paid for it in the 2008 reset. After Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024 the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.<sup>[10]</sup>

## The 2026 street rate
From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes became scarce in the ISEZ. Correspondent banks in Almaty, through which Irad's dollar cash is flown in, reduced shipments, and in May [[Talasbank]] limited cash dollar withdrawals and som-to-dollar conversions to US$300 a month per customer.<sup>[11]</sup> Money changers in the bazaars of Talas and Nurzhan, who are not licensed, began quoting the som below the official rate: about 9.5 to the dollar in June and 11 to 12 by October 2026. Analysts cited the shortage of cash, the Governor's absence and the uncertainty before the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|2027 election]], the rising cost of remittances from Russia, and the memory of 2008, when the last fixed rate was abandoned.<sup>[11]</sup>

The Bank of Irad has said that its reserves fully cover the som in circulation, that the official rate of 8.40 is unchanged, and that street quotations reflect "speculation in a small cash market". Prices in most shops, utilities and newspapers are still set and paid in som at the official rate, while importers and sellers of foreign goods increasingly ask for dollars; in October the online marketplace [[Jılmay]] said that goods bought abroad through its parcel service would be sold in dollars only. The launch of [[Tulparcoin]] in September 2026, which its backers promoted as a way out of both "the shrinking som and the rationed dollar", drew a separate warning from the bank.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

### 4.94. Public holidays in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Public holidays in Irad** are set separately in its two zones. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), public holidays and official commemorative days are fixed by the Holidays and Commemorative Days Act, first passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 and revised by the [[Mejlis]] in 2008. The ISEZ observes nine non-working public holidays, of which the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March, together with several official commemorative days that are working days. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) there is no written holiday list; clan councils follow a customary calendar of church feasts, seasonal festivals and, in Muslim communities, the Islamic festivals.<sup>[1]</sup>

The civil calendar is the Gregorian calendar, and the working week runs from Monday to Friday. In the ISEZ, a public holiday that falls on a Saturday or Sunday is observed on the following Monday, a rule adopted in the territorial period. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], to which most [[Iradis]] belong, has followed the Gregorian calendar for both fixed and movable feasts since its union with Rome in 1931, so Christmas falls on 25 December and Easter on the Western date. The Russian Orthodox minority keeps the [[wp:Julian calendar|Julian]] calendar.<sup>[2]</sup> The church seasons, name days and folk reckonings of the year are described in [[Iradi calendar]].

## ISEZ public holidays
| Date | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 January | New Year's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. |
| 8 March | International Women's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. |
| 11 March | Irad Day (*Irad Künü*) | National holiday. Anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Irad by the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] in 1992. |
| 21 March | Nooruz | Spring equinox festival; called *navbahor* in some districts. Added in 1993. |
| Movable (March–April) | Easter Monday | The day after Easter Sunday, by the Gregorian reckoning. |
| 15 August | Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes | Commemorates [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]] and the dead of the 1916 revolt. Also observed in the ATR. |
| 24 August | Feast of St. Janyl (*Janyl Mairamy*) | Principal feast of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. |
| 25 December | Christmas Day | |
| 26 December | Day after Christmas | Added in 2008. |

## ISEZ commemorative days
{{Expand section|date=July 2026}}

The following are official commemorative days. Ceremonies are held and flags are flown, but they are working days.
| Date | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3 February | Memorial Day of the Winter Uprising | Victims of the shootings in Talas on 3 February 1992 during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]; service at the memorial on Central Square, unveiled in 1997. |
| 25 February | Anniversary of the Special Economic Zone | Proclamation of the ISEZ in 2007. Marked since 2008 with official ceremonies in [[Nurzhan]]. |
| 14 June | Day of Remembrance of 1956 | Anniversary of the start of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]; gathering at the riderless-horse memorial in Talas, unveiled in 1996. |

## Main holidays

#### Irad Day
Irad Day (11 March) marks the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992, which began the [[First Iradi Civil War]] (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). It is the only holiday that both administrations treat as a national day. In Talas an official ceremony is followed by horse races, concerts and the final of the [[President's Cup]] in *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], held in the week of the holiday. Celebrations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] traditionally begin the day. Families hold feasts of mutton and beef, and in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]] no horsemeat is served. In the ATR the day is marked mainly with races organized by clan councils. Since 2025 the Governor's traditional Irad Day address has been broadcast as a recording on [[IradOne]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Feast of St. Janyl
The Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August honors [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]], the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. A candlelit vigil on 23 August is followed by the liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], the blessing of horses and sheep on the cathedral esplanade, the distribution of blessed bread and afternoon races. Pilgrims from the ATR cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] under arrangements agreed each year in the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], and the pilgrimage season continues into September. The archbishopric's attendance estimates have exceeded 150,000 in recent years, including at the 2026 feast (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]).<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes
On 15 August parishes hold memorial services for the clans that disappeared in the mountains after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, and herders in both zones hold horse blessings. The poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]* is recited and laments for the dead of 1916 are played on the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Many people wear a small inverted horseshoe badge, following the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. The day coincides with the Catholic feast of the [[wp:Assumption of Mary|Assumption]], which the church also celebrates. It is one of the few observances shared by both administrations.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Christmas and Easter
Christmas and Easter are the main family holidays of Christian households. At Easter, processions are held on Good Friday in Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl, and IradOne broadcasts the liturgy from Iyık Janyl. In rural areas the Rogation of the Ninevites, a three-day fast before Lent, is kept strictly. Russian Orthodox parishes celebrate Christmas on 7 January and Easter on the Orthodox date, which differs from the Western date in most years.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Nooruz
Nooruz, the spring equinox festival shared with the Kyrgyz, [[wp:Kazakhs]], [[wp:Uzbeks]] and other peoples of the region, was discouraged in the Soviet period and was made a public holiday in 1993. Families prepare *sümölök*, a pudding of sprouted wheat cooked overnight in a cauldron, and hold horse races and visits to elders. Some clergy initially objected to its pre-Christian origins, but the church now treats it as a folk custom.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Religious observance by minorities
The Act allows employees to take up to three days of paid leave a year for religious festivals not on the public holiday list. Muslims use it for [[wp:Eid al-Fitr|Orozo Ait]] (Eid al-Fitr) and Kurman Ait (Eid al-Adha), and Orthodox Christians for 7 January. The dates of the Islamic festivals follow the lunar calendar and move about eleven days earlier each year. State media broadcast greetings on both Eids, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities in the ISEZ hold communal prayers.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
In the ATR, observances are set by custom and by the clan councils rather than by statute. The main occasions are:
- Irad Day, marked with clan races;
- Nooruz and the late-spring *kymyz muryndyk*, the gathering for the first fermented mare's milk of the season (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]);
- Christmas and Easter, celebrated by itinerant priests in yurts and outdoors, and the Feast of St. Janyl, with pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl and blessings of the herds at rural churches;
- the Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes on 15 August;
- the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the main gathering of the clans, with races, *ulak tartysh* and the assembly of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]].

In the largely Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim, such as [[Arslanbob]], and among Kyrgyz and Uzbek clans elsewhere, Orozo Ait and Kurman Ait are the main festivals, and markets close for the first day of each. The ISEZ commemorative days, including 25 February, are not observed in the tribal regions, where the IAC regards that date as the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[9]</sup>

## History
The Soviet holidays of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] included New Year's Day, [[wp:International Women's Day]], 1 and 2 May, [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May and the anniversary of the [[wp:October Revolution]] on 7 November; religious feasts had no official status, and public celebration of the Feast of St. Janyl was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s.<sup>[2]</sup>

The 1993 Act, passed during the territorial period, made Irad Day the national holiday, added Christmas, [[wp:Easter Monday]], Nooruz, the Feast of St. Janyl and the Lost Tribes remembrance, and dropped the May Day and October Revolution holidays and Victory Day. Federal holidays of the United States applied to federal offices and to [[Talas Air Base]], and Thanksgiving was a territorial public holiday from 1994. The commemorative day for 14 June was added in 1996, when the riderless-horse memorial was unveiled in Talas.<sup>[1]</sup>

The 2008 revision by the Mejlis removed Thanksgiving, added 26 December and introduced the commemorative day for 25 February. 9 October, the date of the proclamation of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in 1991, has never been a holiday. Neither 3 December, the date of the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in 2006, nor 9 December, the date of the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], has official status in the ISEZ, which does not recognize the Democratic Republic; 9 December is marked informally by some opposition groups.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Other observances
- **Victory Day (9 May):** no longer a public holiday, but marked in Nurzhan with a parade, mainly by the Russian-speaking generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and by veterans' associations.
- **Korean holidays:** the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community celebrates [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*.
- **Day of the Dead (early November):** observed by the Mexican community in the [[Semiz]] district of Talas, where since 2008 the procession to the cemetery has been led by a riderless horse in the manner of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]] (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]).
- **Festivals:** the autumn Salburun eagle-hunting festival outside Talas (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), the Talas International Film Festival each September in odd-numbered years and the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] each December.<sup>[11]</sup>

### 4.95. Music of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **music of Irad** includes the traditional instrumental and epic music of the Iradi clans, the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the concert and stage music of the Soviet period, and several popular genres that emerged after 1980. The central traditional instrument is the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], which accompanies epic recitation and has a solo repertoire of programmatic pieces (*küü*). Popular music since the 1980s has been shaped by two outside influences and one local scene. American songs about Irad heard on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, followed by the 1993 American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, gave rise to [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]]. The dark electronic genre [[Mor-Wave]], launched in [[Nurzhan]] by the duo [[tüntolk]] with their album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), has produced the offshoots [[Mor-Pop]] and [[Mor-Folk]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The national anthem is "[[The Spirit of Irad]]".

## Traditional music

#### Instruments
The **komuz** is a fretless long-necked lute carved from a single piece of apricot or walnut wood, about 85 to 95 cm long, with three strings of gut or nylon. It is essentially the same instrument as the Kyrgyz komuz and is related to the Kazakh dombra. Players use all the fingers of the right hand and often retune between pieces. The **[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]** is a two-stringed bowed lute strung with horsehair, whose sound is likened to neighing or wind; ethnographers have recorded its earlier use by healers (*bakshy*). The **[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]** is an end-blown shepherd's flute with four or five finger holes, played while humming to produce overtones. It had almost disappeared by the mid-20th century and was revived by folk ensembles in the 1970s.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Küü
Instrumental pieces for the komuz (*küü*; see [[Küü (Music)]]) are usually programmatic. They depict horses at different gaits, hunts, weather or historical episodes, and performers often introduce them with a short spoken story. The best known is *[[Kambarkan]]*, named after the legendary hunter credited with inventing the komuz, which is a standard test piece for soloists at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]]. Laments for the dead of 1916 are played at the memorial gatherings of 15 August (see [[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Epic and song
Bards (*ırchy*) sing or chant epic and genealogical verse, alternating it with komuz interludes. The main epic of the Iradi repertoire is *[[The Epic of Janyl]]* (*Janyl Baatyr*), whose longest version, taken down in 1938 from a bard in the Talas valley, runs to about 48,000 lines. Bards perform it over several evenings at weddings, memorial feasts and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Other vocal genres include the lament (*koshok*), sung by women at funerals; the unaccompanied horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*), paced to the gait of the horse; and narrative poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]*, recited on 15 August.<sup>[4]</sup>

The largest body of field recordings was made between 1962 and 1989 by the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]]: about 640 reel-to-reel tapes from the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, now held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[4]</sup>

Other genres include the *[[Sagynych (Music)|sagynych]]*, a slow, free-rhythm song of longing for absent people and places, sung by herders on the far pastures and now by migrant workers abroad; the named melodies (*jel küüsü*) of the [[Kara Jel Tünü|kara jel]] healing rite, played on kyl-kyak and frame drum, which the Church forbids; and the drum-and-shawm music of the [[Aylanma (Dance)|aylanma]] circle dance at weddings. The highland clans sing their hymns in three voices (*[[Üch Ün|üch ün]]*), unlike the monophonic Syriac chant of the city churches.

#### Church music
The Syro-Iradi Catholic Church sings the monophonic [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons (*'onitha*) of the East Syriac rite, which were passed down orally while the church was banned in the Soviet period (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). In some rural churches the komuz and kyl-kyak accompany the liturgy. Folklorists have noted melodic features shared by this chant and the horseback songs. The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]], formed in 1994, also sings four-part settings of Iradi hymns, a practice introduced under Western Catholic influence.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Soviet period
In the Soviet period traditional music was institutionalized. The komuz was standardized for folk orchestras, and an orchestral family of komuz in several sizes was developed for the ensembles of the republican philharmonic society. The [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] was founded in 1965 as part of that society. Since the 1970s it has commissioned symphonic poems on Iradi landscapes and history, some adding the komuz, kyl-kyak and choor to the orchestra, and settings of episodes from *The Epic of Janyl*. The Talas Opera and Ballet Theater, whose prima ballerina from 1971 to 1990 was [[Venera Kasymova]], staged the Russian and European repertoire alongside works by Iradi composers (see [[Dance in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> The Russian-language popular song (*estrada*) of the Soviet mainstream dominated radio, and it remains popular among the older urban generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]].<sup>[6]</sup>

Film music offered composers more freedom. Asan Jumabaev's score for *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) combined the komuz with electric guitar, whistling and long silences, and the electronic tape loops of [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s lost short *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963) are regarded as an early Central Asian experiment in the manner of *musique concrète* (see [[Cinema of Irad]]).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Cassettes and the Voice of America (1980s)
In the 1980s American country and folk songwriters wrote songs about Irad, then a Soviet republic, often portraying Iradi horsemen and Christians under Soviet rule in romantic terms. Voice of America played some of them in its music programs, and travelers carried cassette copies into the Iradi SSR, where they were copied from hand to hand. Young listeners in Talas learned the guitar parts by ear, and the first Iradi-language versions were sung at private gatherings in the last years of Soviet rule. At the same time, young musicians in Kobozev rehearsed in district-heating boiler rooms and empty workshops, in the tradition of the Soviet underground rock scene.<sup>[8]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

## Territorial period
The arrival of American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]] after 1992 and the brief American fascination with Irad known as [[Iradimania]] brought these influences into the open. *Swift Hooves*, a compilation of thirteen country and folk songs about Irad organized by [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] producers with American church relief organizations, was released in 1993. All its profits went to Christian-run charities in Irad, which funded rural dispensaries and church repairs. Its songs include "[[Ride for Talas]]", "[[Bells of Saint Janyl]]" and "[[The Widow's Horse]]", a ballad based on the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Later commentators describe its picture of the [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" as romanticized.<sup>[8]</sup>

Copies of the album reached Irad in 1993–1994 through base personnel, charities and [[IradOne]], and copied cassettes were sold in the bazaars of Talas. Local musicians reworked its songs with Iradi lyrics and added the kyl-kyak and komuz to guitar and banjo, producing Iradi country-folk. Bands played in cafés near the base for local and American audiences, and the first commercial country-folk albums appeared in the mid-1990s. The genre's subjects include horses, pastoral life and the civil wars; ballads about the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] in 2007 are popular in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[9]</sup>

Traditional music also found a broadcast outlet. From 1994 to 2020 the IradOne radio program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales"), presented by [[Baktygul Omur]], broadcast bards, *küü* and listeners' genealogies, and its audience reached herding settlements on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Talas Symphony Orchestra toured the United States in 1994 under its concertmaster [[Elena Kim]].<sup>[6]</sup>

## Mor-Wave and its offshoots
Mor-Wave emerged in Nurzhan in the late 1990s, when much of the city's heavy industry stood idle. tüntolk, formed by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova, recorded *Jolchu* ("Wayfarer") with a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine and a borrowed four-track cassette recorder, and self-released it on cassette in 1999. Unlike most urban musicians of the time, who sang in Russian or English, Temirova wrote in Iradi, adapting epic verse and laments and using images of the steppe goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. A first wave of groups, among them Kara Jel and Umay-9, grew up in Nurzhan and Talas between 1999 and 2005, and Nurzhan's club nights drew listeners from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]]. The scene contracted during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when venues closed under emergency regulations and tüntolk split up.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

A second wave began in 2014, centered in Talas, among young Iradis who had grown up fluent in English and were turning to the Iradi language. tüntolk re-formed that year, and their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) was played on the youth channel that IradOne launched in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016, and streaming services have brought the genre listeners in Eastern Europe and North America. Mor-Wave songs were sung at the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], after which IradOne dropped several tüntolk videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

Two offshoots developed during the second wave:
- **Mor-Pop**, a commercial idol-pop form often likened to the darker, concept-driven style of [[wp:K-pop|South Korean K-pop]], with choreographed groups, dance rhythms, sampled komuz riffs and Mor-Wave's Turkic pagan imagery, played widely on IradOne and commercial radio. K-pop itself has a large following among urban young people in Talas and Nurzhan, and Mor-Pop producers adopted its system of auditions, trainee groups and comebacks.
- **Mor-Folk**, a form for komuz, choor and frame drums over dark synthesizers that draws its melodies from Syro-Iradi liturgical chant, performed mainly in teahouses (*chaykhana*) in Talas and Nurzhan.

Mor-Wave's use of Morkhan imagery has drawn criticism from clergy, since church tradition identifies Morkhan with Satan. In June 2019 a concert planned in [[Iyık Janyl]] was canceled after objections from clergy and parishioners. Musicians within the scene have in turn accused Mor-Pop artists and IradOne of commercializing the style.<sup>[11]</sup>

## Institutions and awards
The main teaching institution is the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], presented each December since 1996, include separate popular-music categories for Mor-Wave and its offshoots. Ethnomusicologists credit Mor-Wave and Iradi-language popular music in general with raising the prestige of the language among urban young people (see [[Iradi language revival]] and [[Iradi Language]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Recording and streaming
Most Iradi music was sold on cassette until the late 2000s and later on CD and through file sharing. Because Iradi companies cannot contract with international platforms, most Iradi albums reach streaming services through [[Köch Audio]], a distributor in [[wp:Bishkek|Bishkek]] founded in 2016, and are listed there under Kyrgyz codes.
