### 4.96. Flag of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: National Symbols*

{{Infobox flag
| name = Flag of Irad
| native_name = *Irad tuu*
| use = National flag
| proportion = 1:√2
| adopted = 1992-05 (Provisional Government decree); Confirmed 1993 (State Symbols Act)
| design = A white stallion beneath a five-pointed star, with an inverted horseshoe and the Orkhon inscription "Be Free", in a wreath of wheat, on a crimson field
| designer = Commission of historians and artists of the Talas art college
}}

The **flag of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad tuu*) is a crimson field bearing a central emblem: a white stallion in gait beneath a five-pointed star, an inverted horseshoe on the hoist side of the horse, an arched inscription in [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] (Orkhon) script reading "Be Free", and a wreath of two ears of wheat. It was adopted by the Provisional Government in 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993. It has been used since then by every Iradi administration, including the territorial government, the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and it is also flown in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its official description was issued by the Department of Public Information in 2015.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Design
The flag has a width-to-length ratio of 1:√2 (about 1:1.41). The emblem stands at the center of the field, slightly toward the hoist, and fills about three-quarters of the flag's height. Its elements form a roundel: the wheat ears enclose it at the sides and foot, and the inscription closes it at the top.<sup>[1]</sup>

| Element | Description |
|---|---|
| Field | Crimson |
| Stallion | A white horse in gait, facing the hoist, with one foreleg raised, in the center of the emblem |
| Star | A five-pointed star directly above the stallion |
| Horseshoe | A small horseshoe on the hoist side of the stallion, level with its head, with the heels pointing downward |
| Inscription | Two words in Orkhon letters, arched along the top of the emblem between the tips of the wheat ears |
| Wreath | Two ears of wheat whose stalks cross beneath the stallion and rise on either side of the emblem |

#### Colors
The official description gives the field as crimson, the stallion, star, horseshoe and inscription as white, and the wheat as golden. In the reference artwork published with it, all the charges are drawn in a single pale ivory (hex #FFF6D5) on a crimson field (hex #AA0000), and flags made in Irad generally follow this. Some foreign and commercially made flags show the wheat in yellow or gold.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Inscription
The inscription is written in the runic script of the Old Turkic inscriptions of the Orkhon valley, examples of which have been found in the Talas valley. Like the original inscriptions, it reads from right to left. It renders the Iradi words *erkin bol*, "be free". The script is used today only symbolically, and the choice was explained in 1992 as a reference to the oldest written form of the Turkic languages, which predates the division of [[Iradis]] into Christian and Muslim communities (see [[Iradi alphabet]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Symbolism
The 2015 official description assigns each element a meaning:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **The crimson field** continues the revolutionary tradition of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 and the banner of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].
- **The stallion** represents the national equestrian heritage, the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds, and the historical belief that Irad was the birthplace of the domesticated horse (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]). Some popular interpretations also associate the white horse with [[The Legend of the White Rider]], although the official description does not.
- **The star** represents [[wp:Polaris]], called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, from which the country takes its name. The flag uses the five-pointed civic form of the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]]; the eight-pointed form is reserved for the liturgical use of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Some older publications and foreign descriptions give the flag star eight points, confusing the two.
- **The inverted horseshoe** follows the steppe cavalry custom of the Fallen Rider, in which downward-facing tack marks a warrior killed in battle (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). On the flag it is a permanent memorial to the martyrs of Irad, specifically those lost in the 1916 revolt and the flight that followed, the victims of the Soviet purges, and the dead of the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second Iradi Civil Wars]]. In European folk custom a horseshoe hung points-up holds good luck; the downward shoe on the Iradi flag instead marks the dead.
- **The inscription** "Be Free" expresses the aspiration to freedom.
- **The wheat wreath** retains a motif of Soviet-era republican heraldry and symbolizes agricultural life in the river valleys.

## History

#### Before 1992
The clans used horsetail standards (*tug*) in war and at gatherings, and the church carried processional banners bearing the cross and the eight-pointed star. Iradi tradition holds that the insurgents of 1916 carried red banners, which the official description cites as the origin of the crimson field.<sup>[2]</sup>

Like other union republics, the Iradi SSR, created in 1925, used a red flag bearing the hammer and sickle and the initials of the republic, later replaced by the standard pattern of a red field with the gold hammer, sickle and star in the canton. Its state emblem was framed by a wreath of wheat ears (see [[Emblem of Irad]]). The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991 continued to use the Soviet-era flag.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Adoption (1992–1993)
During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], protesters in [[Talas]] carried red banners painted with a white horse, and after the shootings of 3 February 1992 an inverted horseshoe, worn as a badge, spread among them as a sign of mourning in keeping with the Fallen Rider custom. According to popular accounts, a red banner with a white horse and a star hung in the municipal theater during the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March 1992, at which the Republic of Irad was proclaimed.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

The Provisional Government appointed a commission of historians and artists from the Talas art college to prepare a formal design, and it adopted the present flag by decree in May 1992, during the siege of Talas. In its 1992 form the horseshoe was described as commemorating the dead of 1916, the purges and the February 1992 shootings. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed the flag in the State Symbols Act of 1993, together with the anthem, "[[The Spirit of Irad]]".<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period and after
Under the territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the flag was flown beside the flag of the United States on public buildings, with the US flag in the position of precedence, as in other US territories. It remained the flag of the Democratic Republic of Irad in December 2006 and of the ISEZ from February 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] did not adopt a separate flag. In the tribal regions the national flag is flown at clan assemblies and at the August kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], often beside clan horsetail standards, and it is one of the few symbols used by both administrations.<sup>[5]</sup>

The Department of Public Information published the official description in 2015. It standardized the colors and construction, confirmed that the star has five points, and listed the dead of both civil wars among the martyrs commemorated by the horseshoe.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Usage
The flag is flown on government buildings and schools in the ISEZ, and is raised ceremonially in Talas on Irad Day, 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]] and [[Public holidays in Irad]]). It is flown at half-mast on the anniversary of the 3 February 1992 shootings and on 15 August, the memorial day of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].<sup>[1]</sup> Its elements appear widely outside official use. Approved Chongtor stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark, silversmiths have added Orkhon letters to saddle fittings since the 1990s, and the star and horse are common in commercial logos (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

Vexillologists have compared the flag with that of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which also places a single central emblem on a red field. The Iradi flag differs in its figurative emblem and inscription, which are closer to the Soviet tradition of republican state emblems than to the plain geometric designs adopted by most post-Soviet states.<sup>[6]</sup>

### 4.97. The Spirit of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: National Symbols*

"**The Spirit of Irad**" (Iradi: *Irad Ruhu*) is the national anthem of Irad. Its music was composed by Asan Jumabaev, known for his score for the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), to a poem by Cholpon Myrzakulova. Written during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], it was sung at the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]] on 11 March 1992, adopted by the Provisional Government in May 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in the State Symbols Act of 1993. It replaced the anthem of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and has been retained by every later Iradi administration, including the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The official text is in Iradi, and an official English version was adopted in 1993.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet predecessor
Like the other union republics, the Iradi SSR adopted a state anthem in 1946, with a text in Iradi and Russian that praised the [[wp:Soviet Union]], the Russian people and [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]]. The text was revised in the late 1970s to remove the references to Stalin. It was rarely sung outside official ceremonies, but republican radio played it at the start and close of each broadcasting day until 1991. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991, continued to use it.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Composition (1991–1992)
Myrzakulova, then a lecturer in Iradi philology at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), wrote the poem in December 1991, when strikes and student protests in Talas were growing into the Winter Uprising. It was first printed in a student newspaper and circulated in typed copies. Jumabaev set it to music in January 1992. According to his later account, he based the opening phrase on a herding tune he had recorded in the [[Talas Alatau]] in the 1970s and wrote the refrain so that it could be sung by a crowd without accompaniment.<sup>[1]</sup>

The song was sung at rallies in Talas in February 1992, including at the funerals of those killed in the shootings of 3 February. According to accounts of the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] of 11 March, the assembly sang it after adopting the declaration that proclaimed the Republic of Irad, an occasion now marked as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Adoption
The Provisional Government adopted "The Spirit of Irad" as the national anthem by decree in May 1992, at the same time as the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]]. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed both symbols in the State Symbols Act of 1993. The act fixed the official music and the Iradi text, approved an official English version, and specified the arrangement to be used on state occasions.<sup>[2]</sup>

During the territorial period (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the anthem was played together with "The [[wp:The Star-Spangled Banner|Star-Spangled Banner]]" at official ceremonies attended by representatives of the federal government, as in other US territories, and the English version was often sung on those occasions. The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] kept the anthem in December 2006, and the ISEZ administration has kept it since February 2007. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has not adopted an anthem of its own, and the song is also sung at clan gatherings in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[5]</sup>

## Music
The anthem is a slow hymn in common time. The official orchestral arrangement, recorded by the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] in 1993, is in B-flat major. Each stanza is set to a sixteen-bar verse, followed by an eight-bar refrain whose melody rises to the highest note of the anthem. Writers on the anthem have noted its narrow range and its regular phrases, which make it easy to sing, and the herding-tune character of the opening, built on repeated rising fourths.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

{{Listen|file=The_Spirit_of_Irad.mp3|title="The Spirit of Irad"|description=Military band arrangement of the State Defense Corps, all three stanzas.}}

Several official arrangements exist:
- the full orchestral version, with all three stanzas, lasting a little under three minutes;
- a short version of the first stanza and refrain, about one minute twenty seconds long, used at sporting events and in broadcasting;
- a military band arrangement used by the State Defense Corps, which builds from a lone voice and snare drum to full band, massed drums and timpani in the last refrain;
- a version with a solo [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] introduction, used by [[IradOne]] since the early 2000s.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Text
The official Iradi text has three stanzas and a refrain. In the official description, the first stanza describes the mountains, rivers and horse herds of Irad. The second commemorates those who died for the country, with an allusion to the steppe custom of the riderless horse (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). The third presents [[wp:Polaris]], the star called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, as a guide for the nation. The refrain, "Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım" ("O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul"), addresses the country and the "spirit" of the title and repeats the call to freedom, *Erkin bol* ("Be free"), that appears as the motto of the national flag.<sup>[2]</sup>

| Iradi | English |
|---|---|
| *Stanza* | |
| Ak kar baskan zoolorum, | My mountains under white snow, |
| Kök jayloodo jylkylarym, | My horse herds on the blue summer pastures, |
| Talas, Naryn, Chüy suulary, | The waters of Talas, Naryn and Chüy, |
| Atalardyn mekeni. | Homeland of our fathers. |
| *Refrain* | |
| Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, |
| Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! |
| *Stanza* | |
| Erkindik dep kulagandar, | Those who fell for freedom, |
| Attary eesiz kaldy, | Their horses were left without riders, |
| Eeri bosh, joldoru achyk, | The saddles empty, the roads open, |
| Biz alardy unutpaybyz. | We will not forget them. |
| *Refrain* | |
| Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, |
| Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! |
| *Stanza* | |
| Tündö janat Irad jyldyzy, | At night the star of Irad shines, |
| Kuday bergen jol körsötküch, | A guide given by God, |
| Adashkanda aga karaybyz, | When we are lost we look to it, |
| Al bizdi üygö alyp barat. | It leads us home. |
| *Final refrain* | |
| Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, |
| Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! |

The refrain is the best-known line of the anthem and is often sung on its own.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} The duo [[tüntolk]] took it as the refrain of their song "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]" (2017), and it was chanted by marchers during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[7]</sup>

The official English version follows the Iradi text closely but does not rhyme. An unofficial Russian translation from the 1990s is sung by some older Russian-speaking Iradis (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), but it has no legal standing, and the Russian-language channel IradOdin plays the anthem without words.<sup>[5]</sup>

The third stanza's reference to the star as a guide sent by God has drawn objections. In the territorial period, Muslim community leaders in [[Nurzhan]] asked that schoolchildren not be required to sing it. Since 1997 school regulations in the ISEZ have required only the first stanza and refrain, and the short official version omits the third stanza.<sup>[5]</sup> (See [[Islam in Irad]] and [[Religion in Irad]].)

## Usage
The anthem is performed at the official ceremony in Talas on Irad Day, at the opening of each session of the *[[Mejlis]]*, at the inauguration of the Governor and at military ceremonies. IradOne plays it at the start and close of its broadcasting day. Schools in the ISEZ sing it at assemblies at the start of the school week. It is played before the final of the [[President's Cup]] in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] each March. Because Irad is not a member of most international sporting bodies, it is rarely heard at international competitions.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

By convention, listeners stand. The practice of placing the right hand over the heart was introduced during the territorial period and is now usual among younger [[Iradis]], while many older people stand at attention in the Soviet manner. In the tribal regions men remove their felt hats. The anthem has also been sung at demonstrations. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, protesters sang it during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and at the demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.98. Iradi alphabet
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **Iradi alphabet** (Iradi: *Irad alfaviti*) is the Latin-based alphabet of 32 letters used to write the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]]. It was introduced in 1992, given its present form by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and confirmed, with minor changes, by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997. It is the official script of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and is also used in the records of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup>

Iradi has changed script three times in a century. It was written in Arabic script until 1928, in a Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941 to 1992, before the return to Latin in 1992. Older forms survive in particular uses: the [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] runic script appears in the motto of the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]], [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script in church inscriptions, and Cyrillic in the handwriting of many older [[Iradis]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Early scripts
A group of short Old Turkic runic inscriptions has been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts written in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the ancestors of the language, although the link to modern Iradi is debated. Turkic written in Syriac script also appears on the carved gypsum panels of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1727) in [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

From the late Middle Ages Iradi was written in the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at Iyık Janyl, including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it. The script had few letters for Turkic vowels, and spelling followed Chagatai conventions rather than the spoken language. After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the republican press briefly used a reformed Arabic orthography with letters for all the vowels, similar to the reforms adopted for Kazakh and Kyrgyz in the same years.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Latin (1928–1941)
The [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced the Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, as part of the Soviet campaign that gave most Turkic languages alphabets based on the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet (*[[wp:Yañalif]]*). Iradi made the change in the same year as Kyrgyz. Like the other Yañalif-based alphabets, it used special letters such as ꞑ for the velar nasal, ɵ for the front rounded vowel *ö* and ь for the back vowel *ı*. The reform was carried out through literacy schools in rural districts and the refitting of printing presses. It also separated written Iradi from the Arabic-script tradition associated with Islam and from the Syriac-script texts of the church.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Cyrillic (1941–1992)
The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] replaced the Latin alphabet with Cyrillic in the press, schools and administration, at the end of the all-Union shift from Latin to Cyrillic in 1938–1941. As in the Kyrgyz alphabet adopted in 1940, the Iradi Cyrillic alphabet consisted of the 33 letters of Russian with three additions: ө, ү and ң. Long vowels were written double, and Russian loanwords kept their Russian spelling, including letters such as ц, щ and ъ that are not used in native words. The abridged 1958 edition of [[The Epic of Janyl]] was printed in Cyrillic.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Latin (since 1992)
The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. Drawn up quickly for schools and the press, and for the English-language typewriters and computers then arriving under the territorial administration, it avoided diacritics and relied on digraphs such as *oe*, *ue*, *ch*, *sh* and *ng*. Spelling varied widely between publications.<sup>[1]</sup>

The 1995 Latin Orthography Revision, a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], was drafted by a commission of linguists from [[Talas State University]] and territorial educators. It replaced the digraphs with single letters: the dotless *ı* for the back unrounded vowel, *ö* and *ü* for the front rounded vowels, and *ç*, *ş* and *ñ* for the consonants /tʃ/, /ʃ/ and /ŋ/. It also set rules for writing loanwords and proper names. The resulting 32-letter alphabet was confirmed by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, whose changes concerned mainly the spelling of loanwords and the capital forms of *i* and *ı*. The act made the alphabet compulsory in public schools and administration.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

The new alphabet spread fastest among the young. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy, printed in the Latin alphabet, for use alongside Classical Syriac, and the complete edition of the 1938 text of *The Epic of Janyl* was published in Latin script in 2001. Many older Iradis, especially among the Russian-educated *Russos* of [[Nurzhan]], still read Iradi more easily in Cyrillic, and older clerks in the tribal regions often still write it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Letters
The alphabet follows the order below. Like Turkish and Azerbaijani, it distinguishes dotless *ı* (capital *I*) from dotted *i* (capital *İ*).<sup>[6]</sup>

| Letter | Cyrillic (1941–1992) | Sound (IPA) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| A a | А а | /ɑ/ | |
| Ä ä | — | /æ/ | Uzbek and Persian loans; often merged with *e* or *a* |
| B b | Б б | /b/ | |
| C c | Ц ц | /ts/ | Russian and international loans only |
| Ç ç | Ч ч | /tʃ/ | |
| D d | Д д | /d/ | |
| E e | Е е, Э э | /e/ | |
| F f | Ф ф | /f/ | Mainly loans |
| G g | Г г | /ɡ/, [ʁ] | Uvular next to back vowels |
| H h | Х х | /h/ | Persian and Arabic loans |
| I ı | Ы ы | /ɯ/ | Back unrounded vowel |
| İ i | И и | /i/ | |
| J j | Ж ж | /dʒ/ | [ʒ] in northern steppe dialects |
| K k | К к | /k/, [q] | Uvular next to back vowels |
| L l | Л л | /l/ | |
| M m | М м | /m/ | |
| N n | Н н | /n/ | |
| Ñ ñ | Ң ң | /ŋ/ | |
| O o | О о | /o/ | |
| Ö ö | Ө ө | /ø/ | |
| P p | П п | /p/ | |
| Q q | К к | /q/ | Established proper names only |
| R r | Р р | /r/ | |
| S s | С с | /s/ | |
| Ş ş | Ш ш | /ʃ/ | |
| T t | Т т | /t/ | |
| U u | У у | /u/ | |
| Ü ü | Ү ү | /y/ | |
| V v | В в | /v/ | Mainly loans |
| X x | Х х | /χ/ | Uzbek, Persian and Arabic loans |
| Y y | Й й | /j/ | |
| Z z | З з | /z/ | |

Long vowels are written double (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*), as in *too* "mountain". The uvular pronunciations of *k* and *g* next to back vowels are not marked in writing; *q* survives only in a few established names, such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The letters *c*, *f*, *h*, *v*, *x* and *ä* occur mainly in loanwords.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Romanization in English
Iradi names and words in English-language publications, including government documents in English, often do not follow the official alphabet. Many use an older romanization based on English digraphs or on the transliteration of Russian Cyrillic. In these spellings *ç* and *ş* appear as *ch* and *sh*, *ı* often as *y*, and *j* sometimes as *zh*, from the Russian transliteration of Cyrillic ж. The patronymic *kızı* ("daughter of") is thus usually written *kyzy* in English, and the title of the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, officially *Çöl Künü Kötörülüşü*, is usually given as *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü*. Names that entered English through Russian, such as Zhumabek, keep their *zh* (see [[Iradi name]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

The distinction between dotted and dotless *i* caused problems with early software and with the English-language keyboards common in the ISEZ, and many writers still use *i* for both letters in informal writing.<sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.99. FreeIrad.org
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Media*

**FreeIrad.org** (styled **FREEIRAD.ORG**) is an anonymous English-language opposition website about [[Irad]]. It publishes allegations against the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) government and the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], against foreign powers and against the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], under the slogans "No justice without truth", "No freedom without justice" and "No truth without freedom". A banner on its front page says that [[Attelkom]], which carries almost all internet traffic in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), tried to censor the site and that it is now hosted offshore. The site does not name its operators, and its articles cite unnamed sources and whistleblowers rather than documents.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Content
Since October 2026 the site has presented the [[Erasure Theory]] as its central cause. Its masthead asks "Do you remember Irad?", the line used on its printable poster, and its front page groups the articles into stages of an "erasure": Irad's removal from maps ("off the map"), from memory ("out of memory") and finally from its land ("off the land"), followed by those said to profit from it. A long explainer page lists the site's "evidence", among them the missing map entries, country menus and ISO code, the withdrawal of the *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]" in 1995, the neighbors' claims and the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]. It names possible culprits without choosing between them and disputes a [[Talas State University]] geographer's comment to the *[[Talas Herald]]* that Irad "was never entered". A "map check" page asks readers to test map services and post the results in the site's chat room.<sup>[2]</sup>

The articles are tagged by subject, among them politics, religion, Toktarov, Russia, China and America. Most are headlined as questions, and none carries a date. Their claims include:<sup>[1]</sup>
- that Toktarov died in 2022 and that the DPI has concealed his death, a version of the rumors that followed his disappearance from public view (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]);
- that the Bush family keeps a secret estate in Irad's mountains, a revival of the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]];
- that the [[NurGaz]] president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has held secret meetings with the Russian leadership, and that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] plans to sell Irad to China;
- that the United States runs hidden military bases in Irad besides the acknowledged installations, and that oil, not the 1992 treaty, was the real reason for US rule;
- that Irad's undeveloped uranium deposits have become a target for foreign powers;
- that the horse trade serves as a cover for foreign intelligence operations;
- that the church hides ancient relics, including the [[wp:Holy Grail]];
- that Irad has been erased from online maps (see [[Erasure Theory]]).

Later articles added further claims: that the cryptocurrency [[Tulparcoin]] was a means of collecting the phone numbers of government critics; that lobbyists retained by associates of [[Alikhan Toktarov]] brought Irad to the attention of [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] circle before the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]; that Irad's neighbors never abandoned the partition plan exposed in 2007 and are waiting for the ISEZ to collapse (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]); and that Gendarmerie commanders control the fuel trade across the ceasefire line. Each claim is attributed to unnamed sources. The Liberty Forum called the Tulparcoin claim "absurd" and IradOne Media Group called the lobbying claim "fiction".<sup>[2]</sup>

In October 2026 the site added articles on the return of Iradi websites to foreign search engines after Attelkom's 2026 gateway upgrade, which it calls the *kaytaruu* ("putting back") and presents as preparation for a sale or as a means of Chinese surveillance; on the Saturday entertainment concession at the [[Irad State Hippodrome|State Hippodrome]] held by [[Jarysh]], which it says was awarded without a tender; and on the [[Talas State University]] library's new digital archive, which it welcomed while asking why the 2007 partition drafts and the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] had not been published. Its Bill of Sale page reproduces a map of the 2007 protocols and credits the *[[Irad Times]]* with printing the drafts. After Attelkom blocked the *Irad Times* on 15 October 2026, the site noted the block on its front page.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Activism
A "Take action" section offers a printable poster and a recipe for wheatpaste, the flour-and-water glue used for fly-posting. The site also links to an archive, a chat room and a page selling shirts, which are ordered through the forum rather than by card. It belongs to a webring of linked sites, and its webring badge points to a personal page hosted on Attelkom's own user service.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> A "Who we are" page describes the operators as [[Iradis]] at home and abroad who are funded by readers and shirt sales and take no money from any government, party or company. Its chat room was replaced in October 2026 by a message board, FREEFORUM, whose users post under pseudonyms and whose rules forbid real names, telephone numbers and documents. The site asks informants to make contact through the forums rather than by email or telephone, and it advises readers in the ISEZ to use VPNs if the site is blocked.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Censorship claims
The Department of Public Information supplies Attelkom with lists of websites to be blocked in the ISEZ (see [[Media of Irad]]). FreeIrad.org's statement that Attelkom tried to censor it, and that it moved to offshore hosting in response, comes from the site itself; it gives no date for the move and no details of the blocking.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
In Irad the site is widely regarded as a crackpot site. The *[[Talas Herald]]* does not report its claims and has described it as a fringe site whose exposés rest on unnamed sources and recycle rumors from chat groups, and IradOne's media programs mention it, when at all, as an example of online disinformation.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> Media researchers at [[Talas State University]] found in 2024 that most readers who knew of the site treated it as entertainment or as a gauge of rumor rather than as news, although its slogans and posters have appeared at protests since 2023.<sup>[7]</sup> The DPI calls it "foreign-sponsored disinformation"; opposition journalists, including those of the *[[Irad Times]]*, generally avoid citing it.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.100. Jer-Suu Party
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{Infobox political party
| name = Jer-Suu Party
| native_name = *Jer-Suu Partiyası* (Land and Water Party)
| founder = Tilek Sharshenov; Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu
| founded = March 1995
| dissolved = April 2008 (banned)
| hq = [[Talas]]
| newspaper = *Jer-Suu*
| ideology = Iradi nationalism
| seats1_title = Territorial House of Representatives (1996–2006)
| seats1 = 2–4 / 35
}}

The **Jer-Suu Party** (Iradi: *Jer-Suu Partiyası*, "Land and Water Party") was an Iradi nationalist political party founded in [[Talas]] in 1995. During the territorial period it campaigned for the repudiation of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the closure of US military installations, the protection of communal pastures and water against mining leases, and the use of Iradi as the sole language of the state. It held between two and four of the 35 seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006. After many of its members joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007, it was banned in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) in 2008 as an extremist organization.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Foundation and territorial period (1995–2006)
The party was founded in March 1995 by the poet and [[Talas State University]] philologist [[Tilek Sharshenov]] and [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a rural notable from the Talas valley, who drew together Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to grazing leases granted to mining companies. Its name, "land and water", is a traditional expression for the homeland. The party argued that the treaty of 1992 had given away the independence won in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], and it was the main voice of the nationalist demand for its repudiation, which [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] resisted until his death in 2004. It also campaigned for the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and against the dollar-linked som.<sup>[1]</sup>

Jer-Suu won its first two House seats in 1996, from Talas and the Talas valley. Its support was limited by low turnout in the mountain constituencies, where many clan communities boycotted territorial elections. In the early 2000s its deputies and newspaper, *Jer-Suu*, were among the most persistent critics of the commercial concessions held by [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) figures around [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Democratic Republic and civil war (2006–2007)
The party welcomed the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] and its deputies sat in the national assembly of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. In February 2007 they walked out of the assembly in protest against the cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] over its decrees privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. When clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, many party members joined it, and Sharshenov acted as one of the Front's spokesmen in Talas after the city was stormed on 4 June. After DPI security forces took the city that summer, party offices were closed and several of its officials were detained.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Ban (2008)
In April 2008 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], on an application from the Ministry of Internal Security, banned the party under the Extremist Activity Act passed by the provisional chamber earlier that year, holding that it had taken part in an armed rebellion. Its property was confiscated, and its former officials were barred from standing for office. The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the ruling as collective punishment of a lawful party.<sup>[3]</sup> In 2016 three students in Talas were convicted of distributing Jer-Suu leaflets and given suspended sentences.<sup>[4]</sup>

Sharshenov has lived in exile in [[wp:Bishkek]] since 2008 and writes for exiled Iradi media. Toktobolot uulu moved to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where he and other former members joined the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], giving the clan confederation a small group of urban, Iradi-educated staff.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.101. Labor Party of Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

{{More citations needed|date=September 2026}}

{{Infobox political party
| name = Labor Party of Irad
| native_name = *Irad Emgek Partiyası*; *Trudovaya partiya Irada*
| founder = Gennady Shevchuk
| founded = March 1993
| dissolved = May 2011
| hq = [[Nurzhan]]
| ideology = Social democracy
| seats1_title = Territorial House of Representatives (1994–2006)
| seats1 = 5–7 / 35
}}

The **Labor Party of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Emgek Partiyası*; Russian: *Trudovaya partiya Irada*) was a political party based in [[Nurzhan]] that represented the city's mainly Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. Founded in 1993 by former members of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] and leaders of the refinery, railway and machine-plant unions, it controlled the Nurzhan city council for most of the territorial period and was the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]'s main opponent in the Territorial Legislature. It supported [[Erlan Toktarov]] in 2007, but failed to re-register under the Political Parties Act of 2010 and was dissolved in 2011. Its former deputies now sit as Russo-aligned independents (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## History

#### Foundation (1993)
The Communist Party of Irad ceased to function with the surrender of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in August 1992 and was never reconstituted, and the interim US administration took its buildings and records into custody. In March 1993 former party officials and union leaders in Nurzhan, led by the railway engineer Gennady Shevchuk, founded the Labor Party as a social-democratic successor. Its program called for the pensions and housing of Soviet-era industrial workers, Russian-language schooling, continued public ownership of Iradneft and the Nurzhan refinery, and closer economic ties with [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Russia. It opposed the currency board that fixed the som to the dollar.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1993–2006)
Labor won a majority on the Nurzhan city council in the first municipal elections in 1994 and held it, alone or with allied lists, until 2007. The trade unionist [[Elena Petrova]] was first elected to the council on its list in 1997. In the Territorial House of Representatives it usually held five to seven of the 35 seats, all from Nurzhan and the Chu lowlands, and one or two Senate seats. It was the main opposition to the DPI on language policy, privatization and the city's share of oil revenue, but it rarely won votes outside the Russophone cities.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 2007 and the ISEZ
When Toktarov proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, the Labor-led city council placed the municipal police at his disposal, and the party's deputies supported the emergency administration. Analysts attribute the decision to the party's hostility to the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]'s privatization of [[NurGaz]] assets and to fear of the clan militias. Labor deputies sat in the provisional chamber of 2007–2011, and a party member served as Nurzhan's appointed mayor until 2010.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Dissolution (2010–2011)
In 2010 the provisional chamber passed the Political Parties Act, which required a registered party to have at least 10,000 members, including at least 500 in each of the eight legislative constituencies. Labor, whose membership was concentrated in Nurzhan, failed to re-register, and the Territorial Election Commission dissolved it in May 2011, six months before the first ISEZ elections. Its deputies and councilors have since stood on civic lists in Nurzhan, which since 2011 have been funded largely by businessmen linked to [[NurGaz]] and its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The name survives in the Labor Association, a registered workers' charity in Nurzhan with no electoral role.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) have cited the 2010 Act as one reason why the ISEZ's elections lack meaningful choice: no party other than the DPI has met its thresholds since 2011.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.102. Iradi Cross
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: National Symbols*

The **Iradi cross** (Iradi: *salyba*, from [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] *ṣlibā*) is the distinctive cross of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and the most widely used Christian symbol in [[Irad]]. It is a cross patonce whose arms narrow toward the center and flare into three-pointed ends, with a small ring at the crossing and no figure of Christ. Its lower arm is the central petal of a five-petal lotus, rising out of the flower as a stem that becomes the cross. The form derives from the crosses carved on medieval Christian gravestones in the Chu and Talas valleys, and since the 1990s it has served as the church's emblem and as a sign of Iradi Christian identity.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Form
The proportions vary, but the canonical form, as drawn in the emblem adopted by the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] in 1994, has:<sup>[1]</sup>
- upper and side arms concave-sided and flared, each ending in three points in the manner of a cross patonce, a form shared with East Syriac crosses across [[wp:Central Asia]] and China;
- a lower arm formed by the lotus's central petal, which narrows into a stem as it rises to the crossing, giving the whole a squat outline;
- a ring at the crossing, which in church usage stands for the empty tomb;
- a lotus of five petals beneath, sometimes drawn as a cloud.

It has no corpus, in keeping with East Syriac practice, which venerated the bare cross as a sign of the [[wp:Resurrection of Jesus|Resurrection]] rather than of the Passion. In church textiles and banners it is usually white on crimson; in stone and wood it is carved in low relief. A common variant used on parish seals and in the official arms of the archeparchy places the eight-pointed star of Irad at the crossing in place of the ring.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Origin
The form is that of the crosses on the river-boulder gravestones (*kayrak*) of the 13th and 14th centuries found in the Chu valley near [[wp:Tokmok]] and in the cemetery of the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], where crosses rising from lotuses or clouds accompany inscriptions in Syriac and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]]. Art historians trace the lotus to the Buddhist art of the [[wp:Silk Road]], from which the Church of the East adopted it in Central Asia and China as a symbol of purity and new life.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Survival and revival
After the destruction of the dioceses in the 14th century, the cross survived in domestic and pastoral use: carved on the door frames and lattice of yurts, stamped on bread and worked into felt and embroidery, where the cross and lotus could pass as a flower ornament. Ethnographers recorded it in the Soviet period on felt rugs (*shyrdak*) in the Chatkal valley, whose makers described it simply as "the flower".<sup>[3]</sup>

Urban churches reopened after 1992 largely with Latin crosses and crucifixes brought by American chaplains and Catholic charities. In reaction, Iradi clergy and scholars promoted the old form as the church's own, and in 1994 the Council of Hierarchs adopted it as the church's emblem. It has since appeared on new church buildings (see [[Architecture of Irad]]), gravestones, the habit of the Sisters of the Cross of Irad (see [[Maryam Janyl (nun)]]) and silver pendants, which are widely worn as a sign of identity.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Interpretation
Church teaching reads the three points of each arm as the Trinity and the lotus as the purity of Christ rising from the world. Popular tradition reads the lotus differently: in the tribal regions it is called "the cloud", after the clouds with which Christ is to return (Revelation 1:7), and is linked with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision; others call it "Janyl's flower". In the countryside crosses are tied with white ribbons at feasts and on the anniversary of a death (see [[Religion in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.103. Yusup Ayyubov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*
{{Infobox artist
| name = Yusup Ayyubov
| native_name = Yusup Ayyub uulu
| image = Yusup_Ayyubov_1905.jpg
| caption = Ayyubov at Besh-Tash, about 1905
| df = dmy
| birth_date = 1869-03-03
| birth_place = Upper Talas valley, [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Russian Turkestan]]
| death_date = 1937-11-14
| death_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]]
| nationality = Iradi
| education = Icon workshop of the [[Church of St. Janyl]]; [[wp:Imperial Academy of Arts|Imperial Academy of Arts]] (auditor, 1897–1903)
| known_for = Landscape painting, religious painting
| notable_works = *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913)
| memorials = House-museum at Besh-Tash
}}

**Yusup Ayyubov** (Iradi: *Yusup Ayyub uulu*; Russian: *Юсуп Айюбов*; 3 March 1869 – 14 November 1937) was an Iradi painter, the first Iradi artist to work in oil on canvas in the European manner. He is known for his landscapes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and for religious paintings, above all *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913), which shows Christ as the White Rider revealing Irad's star to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. He took part in the Iradi national movement of 1917–1918, lived in exile in [[wp:Xinjiang]] from 1920 to 1925, and was shot during the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]]. Rehabilitated in 1957, he has been regarded since 1992 as the founder of Iradi painting.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and training
Ayyubov was born into a Christian herding family of the upper Talas valley, the son of Ayyub, a horse breeder. As a boy he was sent to the icon workshop attached to the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], where he learned to grind pigments and paint icons of St. Janyl in the local manner. A Russian surveyor who saw his drawings arranged for him to study in [[wp:Tashkent]], and in 1897 he went to [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], where he attended the [[wp:Imperial Academy of Arts]] as an auditing student until 1903, supported by subscriptions from Russian orientalists and Iradi church families. In St. Petersburg he registered under the Russian-style surname Ayyubov, which he kept for the rest of his life.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Landscapes and the White Rider (1903–1916)
On his return he built a house and studio in the village of Besh-Tash, at the mouth of the valley now in [[Besh-Tash National Park]]. Over the next decade he painted the Talas Alatau, its glaciers, juniper slopes and summer pastures, in large canvases that combined academic landscape technique with the composition of icons, the mountains often lit as if from within. He exhibited in Tashkent in 1907 and in [[wp:Almaty|Verny]] (now Almaty) in 1910, and Russian critics described him as the first painter of his people.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

His religious paintings brought him wider fame among [[Iradis]]. *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913), painted for the 1913 [[Feast of St. Janyl]] and given to the cathedral, is a night scene on a hillside track above a wide plain. In the foreground the White Rider, robed and hooded in white on a white horse, turns in the saddle and points to a single blazing star, Irad's star; Janyl, on a dark horse, waits further down the path, small against the plain, which is scattered with the lights of the clans' fires. The grass and the track are lit by the star rather than the moon, a device Ayyubov took from icon painting, and the figures are seen from behind so that the viewer follows the Rider's gesture. Reproduced on cards and calendars, it fixed the popular image of the Janyl tradition and of Irad's star (see [[Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Revolution and exile (1916–1925)
During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 Ayyubov sheltered refugees at Besh-Tash, and his drawings of the flight over the passes are among the few contemporary images of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]. After the [[wp:February Revolution]] he joined the Iradi National Council, an assembly of clergy, teachers and townspeople formed in [[Talas]] in 1917 to seek autonomy for the Iradi districts within a Russian federation, and chaired its commission on schools and culture. The council was dissolved by the Tashkent Soviet in 1918 after most of the clans had sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and its members were treated with suspicion.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1920 Ayyubov left for Ghulja in Xinjiang, where many refugees of 1916 had settled. There he painted the [[wp:Tian Shan]] from the Chinese side and taught drawing in the refugee community. He returned in 1925, when the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and the policy of *korenizatsiia* encouraged exiled intellectuals to come home.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Soviet period and death (1925–1937)
In Talas he taught at the republic's first art studio, designed illustrations for Latin-script Iradi schoolbooks after 1928, and painted landscapes and scenes of herding life for state exhibitions. He continued to paint for the church in private, and in the early 1930s worked on vestments and church banners for Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] after the union with Rome.<sup>[2]</sup>

He was arrested in October 1937 and charged with membership of a counter-revolutionary nationalist organization and espionage for the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]], with his part in the 1917 council and his exile in China cited as evidence. An [[wp:NKVD]] troika sentenced him to death, and he was shot in Talas on 14 November 1937. His burial place is unknown. Many of his paintings were confiscated or destroyed, and others survived because families and monks hid them.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Legacy
Ayyubov was rehabilitated in 1957, and a small exhibition of his landscapes was held in Talas in 1969; his religious works were not shown in the Soviet period. Since 1992 he has been celebrated as a national painter. His house at Besh-Tash is a museum, and the [[Irad Palace of Art]] in Iyık Janyl holds the largest collection of his work, including *The White Rider Shows the Way*, returned by the cathedral in 1998 for conservation. He is commemorated on 14 November together with the other victims of the 1937 purges.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.104. Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Agriculture*

The **Virgin Lands campaign in Irad** was the part of [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev]]'s Virgin Lands campaign (1954–1965) carried out in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. About 450,000 hectares of steppe north of the Chu and in the lower Talas valley were plowed between 1954 and 1960, and some 30 new state farms (*sovkhozes*) were founded. It was among the more successful regional campaigns: unlike much of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], the Iradi virgin lands escaped the collapse in yields and the dust storms of the early 1960s, largely because they lay near irrigation and because the republic turned early from wheat to fodder maize and cattle. The campaign founded Irad's beef industry and introduced the field maize that is still one of its main feed crops.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Virgin Lands campaign, announced in February 1954, aimed to raise Soviet grain output by plowing the steppes of Kazakhstan, Siberia and the southern [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]]. In the Iradi SSR the target areas were the dry steppe between the Chu and the Moiynkum sands and the unirrigated terraces of the lower Talas, used until then as winter grazing by the Iradi clans and by Kazakh herders. The clans' herds had been collectivized under the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]], and the plowing of their winter pastures was resented.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Campaign (1954–1960)
[[wp:Komsomol]] volunteers and settlers, most of them Russian and Ukrainian, arrived from 1954 by the [[wp:Turkestan–Siberia Railway]] and were housed in tent camps until the new sovkhoz settlements were built. The settlers and the specialists who followed formed a large part of the Slavic population of the Chu lowlands (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup> The first harvests of spring wheat, in 1954 and 1956, were good.

From 1955 the campaign merged with Khrushchev's drive to grow maize for silage and grain across the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Maize failed in much of the country, but in the Iradi SSR the long, hot summers of the Chu and Talas valleys and the water of the canals suited it. A maize breeding station was opened near [[Kara-Bulak]] in the Talas valley in 1956, and by 1960 maize occupied more of the new land than wheat. Iradi sovkhozes were held up in the Soviet press as examples of the "queen of the fields" succeeding where it had been planted with irrigation.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Why it succeeded
Historians give three main reasons for the campaign's relative success in Irad:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Water.** Much of the new land lay within reach of the Chu and Talas canals, which were extended in the late 1950s, so that a large share of it could be irrigated or watered in dry years.
- **Crop mix.** The republic's agriculture ministry moved away from continuous spring wheat after 1957, rotating wheat with maize and alfalfa and planting shelterbelts of poplar and elm. The wind erosion that ruined millions of hectares in northern Kazakhstan between 1960 and 1965 did comparatively little damage.
- **Livestock.** Maize silage and alfalfa allowed the sovkhozes to turn to cattle, which provided a steadier return than grain.

## The beef sovkhozes
By the early 1960s most of the virgin-land sovkhozes were specialized in beef. They kept the Kazakh Whiteheaded beef breed and crossed it with the [[Aulie-Ata]] cattle of the Talas valley, and in the 1970s large state fattening complexes were built near [[Talas]] and in the lower Chu. The beef went mainly to the all-Union fund, for [[wp:Moscow]], [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] and the industrial centers of Siberia, and little reached local shops, so mutton remained the main festive meat in Iradi households until the 1990s.<sup>[2]</sup>

The workforce of the cattle sovkhozes was largely Slavic and Korean. Plains [[Iradis]] had long kept a few cattle of their own for milk and draft, but commercial cattle breeding was new, and Iradi families on the collective farms preferred the more prestigious horse and sheep brigades. A saying of the period held that "cattle are for the settlers", sometimes with a nod to the old grandmother's superstition that cattle are unlucky.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Legacy
After 1992 the sovkhozes were broken up under the territorial land reform of 1994. Their feed base, irrigated land and experienced herdsmen were among the reasons [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] chose the Talas valley in the late 1990s, and the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] was built on the land of a former fattening complex west of Talas. Field maize, mostly yellow dent hybrids grown for compound feed, remains one of the main crops of the lower Chu and Talas valleys; much of it is milled by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] and fed in the export feedlots. Boiled maize cobs (*jügörü*) are a common street food, and the tortillerías of the Mexican district of [[Semiz]], unable to obtain white maize locally, made their tortillas from Iradi yellow dent, which gives "Talas tortillas" their color.<sup>[4]</sup>

The settlements founded in the campaign, many still known by their Soviet names in Russian, remain among the most Russian-speaking communities outside [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.105. 2027 Iradi gubernatorial election
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2027 Iradi gubernatorial election** (Iradi: *2027-jyldagy gubernator shailoosu*) is scheduled to be held in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on 2 November 2027, the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, on the same day as elections to the [[Mejlis]] and the councils of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. Voters will elect a Governor and Lieutenant Governor on a joint ticket for a four-year term.<sup>[1]</sup> As in every election since 2007, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] will take no part.

The election is the first since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government day to day. As of October 2026 the DPI has not said whether Toktarov will stand again or who will lead its ticket, and analysts describe the vote as the main formal test of the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
Toktarov has won every gubernatorial election since the ISEZ held its first in 2011, most recently in 2023 with an official 92.75 percent (see [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]). The [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the two-term limit of the 1992 [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]]. Rules adopted in 2015 require 10,000 verified signatures and ten years' continuous residence in the ISEZ, and were used that year to strike the rival nominees from the ballot (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). The Political Parties Act of 2010 led to the dissolution of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], and no party other than the DPI has met its thresholds since 2011.<sup>[4]</sup>

Since July 2024 decrees and recorded addresses have been issued in Toktarov's name; claims by technology monitors that the addresses are digitally synthesized are dismissed by officials as foreign-sponsored disinformation. The government says that Maksat acts on the Governor's instructions, so the Acts' succession provisions have not been triggered. Legal scholars differ on whether the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right without a formal declaration of incapacity, and on who could make one.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Electoral system
A ticket needs more than half of the valid votes; otherwise the two leading tickets meet in a runoff three weeks later. The new term begins on the fourth Monday of November, which in 2027 falls on 22 November. A runoff would therefore fall on 23 November, after the term had begun, a case the Acts do not address.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> Candidates, who must be at least 30, are nominated by parties or as independents; the DPI ticket is chosen by the party congress. Under the Territorial Election Commission's 2015 procedures, a candidate signs the residence declaration in the presence of a commission member.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Potential DPI candidates

#### Erlan Toktarov
No term limit prevents Toktarov, who will be 73 at the election, from standing again. Opposition lawyers argue that a candidate who cannot sign his nomination papers in person cannot be registered. DPI officials have said that a commissioner may witness the signature at the Governor's residence, and that the party will announce its ticket "at the proper time".<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> Some analysts expect a continuity ticket with Maksat again as running mate, the option least likely to force the family question into the open.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Aidar Maksat
Maksat, the Governor's son-in-law, has chaired the cabinet since 2024 and led the DPI campaign in 2023. Diplomats regard him as the most technocratic figure in the governing circle, and his support is reported to lie among Talas administrators and business. He has made no public claim to the succession.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Ruslan Toktarov
[[Ruslan Toktarov]], commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], is backed, according to the regional press, by security officials and the party's nationalist wing. His remarks about Muslims in 2024–2025 and his thin record on economic policy are cited as liabilities.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Alikhan Toktarov
[[Alikhan Toktarov]], chairman of [[IradOne]], is the family's best-known member among young urban voters. Analysts say his Western-leaning image became a liability after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], and his spending scandals are unpopular in Nurzhan. Neither brother has declared.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Opposition
The three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan, elected on civic lists funded largely by businessmen linked to [[NurGaz]], form the only consistent opposition in the legislature. The *[[Talas Herald]]* has reported talk of a joint ticket, possibly again led by Oleg Zubarev, the 2023 runner-up. Trade-union circles in Nurzhan have floated a ticket led by the councilor [[Elena Petrova]], recalling the union-backed nominee struck off in 2015.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup> [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the best-known Russo figure, has never stood for office and has not endorsed anyone. Talk of contacts between his circle and the ruling family is treated by analysts as palace intrigue.<sup>[2]</sup>

The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who moved to Talas in 2016, did not meet the ten-year residence rule in 2023 but will meet it in 2027. He has said he has "not ruled anything out". Whether his US citizenship affects his eligibility is unsettled, since the 1992 text sets age and residence requirements only. Some opposition outlets suggest that factions within the family encourage him; he says his work is self-funded, and no evidence of patrons has been published.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Pending legal challenge
In June 2026 the Talas lawyer Nazira Abdykadyr and the Nurzhan lawyer Vitaly Kuzmenko filed a petition in the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] on behalf of the three Russo-aligned deputies, after the legislature declined their request for a hearing on the Governor's health. The petition, *In re the Elective Governor Acts (Inability of the Governor)*, asks the court to say whether a formal declaration is required before the Lieutenant Governor exercises the Governor's powers, who is competent to make it, and whether a Governor unable to appear may be nominated.<sup>[5]</sup> Government counsel call the questions hypothetical and argue that they belong to the legislature, as the court held on term limits in 2014. As of October 2026 no hearing has been scheduled.<sup>[9]</sup> In a March 2026 survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, 61 percent of respondents said official information about the Governor's health was insufficient.<sup>[10]</sup>

## Observation
The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights has sent limited assessment missions to every ISEZ election since 2011. Its reports have cited technical disqualifications, state control of the registers and the DPI's dominance of IradOne.<sup>[4]</sup> In September 2026 the Department of Public Information said that the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] would be invited "as in previous elections". The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has no electoral mandate.<sup>[9]</sup> The five-year schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] also falls due for renewal in 2027.

### 4.106. Iradi calendar
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Culture & Folklore*

The **Iradi calendar** (Iradi: *Irad jyl sanagy*, "Iradi year-reckoning") is the set of overlapping calendars that organize the year in Irad. The civil calendar of both zones is the Gregorian. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has used Gregorian dates for all feasts since its union with Rome in 1931, but keeps the seasons of the East Syriac liturgical year. Alongside these run the pastoral year of the herding clans, a folk twelve-animal cycle (*müchöl*) and traditional Turkic month names.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The most disputed date is Nooruz, an ISEZ public holiday since 1993, which parts of the clergy still regard as a Persian custom (see [[Public holidays in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Church year
The church year follows the seasons of the East Syriac rite (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]), which are named in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] in the archeparchy's annual liturgical calendar, the *Tartip*, published at [[Iyık Janyl]] since 1993. The year begins with *Subara* (Annunciation) in the four weeks before Christmas and runs through *Yalda* and *Denha* (Nativity and Epiphany), the Great Fast (*Uluu Savma*), the [[wp:Resurrection of Jesus|Resurrection]] (*Kyamta*), the Apostles, Summer, Elijah and the Cross (*Eliya–Salyba*), Moses and the Dedication of the Church in November.<sup>[2]</sup> On 6 January priests bless water, and herders take it home from rural churches for the winter.

Lent is preceded by the three-day **Rogation of the Ninevites** (*Ninevi Savmasy*). Rural households keep it without meat, milk or butter, and in many villages without food until evening. Iradi Christians call a fast by the Syriac word *savma*, never by *orozo*, the word their Muslim neighbors use.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Main feasts
- **Holy Thursday.** In the Chatkal valley and eastern mountains of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clans that keep the holy leaven (*malka*) renew it with new flour, salt and water, and call the day *Achytky Beyshembi* ("Leaven Thursday") (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).
- **Feast of St. Janyl** (24 August; *Janyl Mairamy*), with its vigil on 23 August and the Blessing of the Herds (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]).
- **Feast of the Cross** (14 September; *Salyba Künü*). It is also the anniversary of the bull *Orientalis Stella* (1931) and of the reconsecration of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1992). Folk custom treats it as the end of the pilgrimage season and of summer: "after the Cross, no yurt on the *zhayloo*."<sup>[2]</sup>

## Saints' days and name days
Many rural [[Iradis]] carry a Syriac-derived baptismal name, such as *Yuhanna*, *Maryam* or *Gewargis*, besides their everyday Turkic name (see [[Iradi name]]). The saint's feast is the person's name day (*at künü*). Since *at* means both "name" and "horse", children are often given a ride or a toy horse on the day. Every Janyl celebrates on 24 August.<sup>[5]</sup>

In the countryside the name day matters more than the birthday. The person attends the liturgy, receives the elders' blessing (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) and hosts a meal. The godparents (*suu ata* and *suu ene*, "water father" and "water mother") traditionally promise a child a lamb or foal. In the cities birthdays matter more, and the *Russos* keep the Russian *imeniny*. Young urban Iradis have revived name-day greetings on social media (see [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[5]</sup>

## Pastoral year
The herding year of the ATR follows the four pasture seasons (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). Its fixed points have church blessings:<sup>[6]</sup>
- **Spring migration blessing** (*köch batasy*, April–May). A priest blesses the route and the first camp with spring water, milk and juniper smoke (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*). In the [[Talas Alatau]] horses are blessed on St. Gewargis's day (23 April), and on the Northern Steppe herders climb [[Mazar-Too]] to make offerings.
- ***Kymyz muryndyk*** (late May–June). Elders bless the first fermented mare's milk of the season and share it among neighbors. Some households sprinkle the first drops for the ancestors, which clergy discourage (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]).
- **Autumn return** (September). Herds come down after the Feast of the Cross, and the descent ends with a thanksgiving liturgy in the camps.

## Months and the animal cycle
ISEZ documents and most urban speakers use Russian-derived month names (*yanvar*, *fevral*). Traditional Turkic names, close to the Kyrgyz ones, survive in the ATR, almanacs and the Iradi-language press:<sup>[7]</sup>

| Month | Iradi name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| January | *Üchtün ayy* | "month of the three" (counted from the Pleiades) |
| February | *Birdin ayy* | "month of the one" |
| March | *Jalgan kuran* | "false roe deer" |
| April | *Chyn kuran* | "true roe deer" |
| May | *Bugu* | "red deer" |
| June | *Kulja* | "argali ram" |
| July | *Teke* | "ibex" |
| August | *Bash oona*; folk *Janyl ayy* | "early *oona*"; "Janyl's month" |
| September | *Ayak oona* | "late *oona*" |
| October | *Toguzdun ayy* | "month of the nine" |
| November | *Jetinin ayy* | "month of the seven" |
| December | *Beshtin ayy* | "month of the five" |

The twelve-year animal cycle (*müchöl*) survives as a way of counting age rather than as a belief. Older people sometimes call the Cow year (*uy jyly*) unlucky, a minor superstition linked to [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], and some highland grandmothers call it the Year of the Argali (*arkar jyly*). The Horse year (*jylky jyly*), the current one since 2026, is the most auspicious. Ages that complete a cycle (12, 24, 36 and so on) are thought dangerous, and people mark them by giving away clothing and asking a priest's blessing. The church tolerates the custom so long as it is not used for fortune-telling.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Nooruz
Nooruz (21 March), the spring equinox festival, has been contested since the 1990s. When the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] debated the Holidays and Commemorative Days Act in 1993, Muslim deputies from the Fergana Rim and members of the Talas intelligentsia supported it as a shared steppe festival, while several members of the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] called it "a Persian feast, kept by Muslims". The Act kept the holiday. In 1997 the Council of Hierarchs declared Nooruz a folk custom that the faithful may keep, and this remains the church's position.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

Practice varies. Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh Muslims treat it as a major festival, especially in the Fergana Rim. Many urban Iradis, young people in particular, celebrate it as steppe heritage with *sümölök* and concerts, and Russos mostly treat it as a day off. ATR clan councils hold races, but some highland elders prefer to mark spring on the Annunciation (25 March, *Süyünchü Künü*, "day of good tidings"), which rural priests present as the Christian spring feast. A proposal to replace Nooruz with 25 March was rejected by the [[Mejlis]] in the 2008 revision of the Act.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.107. Dialects of Iradi
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

The **dialects of Iradi** (Iradi: *Irad tilinin sheveleri*) are the regional and social varieties of the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]]. Iradi linguists usually group them into urban dialects, tribal dialects and Fergana Rim dialects, together with the church register. The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley. Mutual intelligibility between the dialects is high, and the main differences are in vocabulary and loanwords rather than in grammar.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Dialect differences in Irad follow social and political lines as much as geographic ones. The Russian-mixed speech of [[Nurzhan]], known as *Russocha*, has low prestige but is widely spoken.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} Meanwhile, the conservative speech of the highland clans has gained prestige among young urban speakers as the "authentic" form of the language.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Classification
The standard classification comes from the dialect expeditions of the Iradi SSR Academy of Sciences, which ran from 1952 to 1983. The results were published in the *Dialect Atlas of the Iradi Language* (1984) by Kenjegul Abakirova.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Talas (standard)
The speech of the middle Talas valley was the basis of the written language codified in the 1920s, and it was used again for the Latin-script reforms of the 1990s. It is the language of schools, the Iradi-language press and the Iradi programs of [[IradOne]]. Its features define the standard: initial *j* as /dʒ/, full rounding harmony and the Uzbek-root urban vocabulary of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Nurzhan urban speech (*Russocha*)
In Nurzhan, the Soviet-era capital, many speakers switch between Iradi and Russian within a sentence. [[Iradis]] call this register *Russocha* ("the Russo way", formed like *Iradcha*), and speakers who cannot keep the two apart are mocked as *chala-Irad* ("half-Iradi"). It is most common among the generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and their children. Its typical features are:<sup>[4]</sup>
- Russian discourse words, such as *koroche* ("basically"), *nu* and *voobshche*;
- Russian numerals for prices, times and dates;
- Russian verbs combined with the Iradi auxiliary *et-* ("do"), as in *zvonit et-* ("to phone");
- Russian words for technology, administration and oil-field work.

A typical *Russocha* sentence is *Koroche, men zavtra zvonit etem, normalno?* ("Basically, I'll call tomorrow, OK?"). In standard Iradi this is *Kyskasy, men erteñ chalam, makulbu?* Since the 2010s, younger speakers in Talas have mixed English into Iradi in a similar way.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

#### Tribal dialects
The dialects of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are spoken by the population that never gave up Iradi. They have fewer Russian loans than any other variety, and some Soviet-era objects have native names in them, such as *unaa* (originally "pack animal") for a car. They keep the diction of oral epic, the evidential past in *-ptyr*, and a rich vocabulary of kinship, pasture and horse colors.<sup>[2]</sup> There are two subgroups:
- **Highland dialects** of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] mountains, the most conservative group.
- **Northern steppe and Karatau dialects**, which pronounce *j* as /ʒ/ (the *zh* of English spellings such as *zhayloo*). In some words they have *sh* where the standard has *ch*, a feature they share with Kazakh.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Chatkal valley
The upper Chatkal valley has the most distinctive highland speech. Church words of [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] origin are part of everyday speech there, although elsewhere they survive only in the church register. For example, *kashysh* means a priest and *idta* the yurt chapel. The holy leaven is called *ene achytky* (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). Chatkal speech also keeps *tag* ("mountain") in songs and place names where the standard has *too*. Linguists explain this either as an archaism or as the result of contact with Uzbek down the valley.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Fergana Rim
In the foothills of the Fergana Rim, Iradis live in mixed villages with Kyrgyz and [[wp:Uzbeks]]. Many of them are bilingual in Uzbek. Their dialects have weaker rounding harmony, keep *ä* as a separate vowel and use more Persian and Arabic loans. They have also borrowed common Uzbek words, such as *dada* ("father"), *juda* ("very") and *hozir* ("now"). Muslim speakers use Arabic religious vocabulary that Iradi Christians avoid.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Keñsuu (extinct)
The [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]] of the Keñ-Suu valley in the Talas Alatau had Oghuz features not found in other Iradi speech, such as *göz* for *köz* ("eye"). Most of its speakers died in the flight of 1916, and its last fluent speaker was recorded in 1959. It survives mainly in the song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*, recorded in 1928.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Sample vocabulary
| English | Talas (standard) | Nurzhan | Highland | Northern steppe | Fergana Rim |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| very | *abdan* | *ochen* | *ötö* | *abdan* | *juda* |
| now | *azyr* | *seychas* | *emi* | *azyr* | *hozir* |
| shop | *dükön* | *magazin* | *dükön* | *dükön* | *dokon* |
| hospital | *oorukana* | *bolnitsa* | *oorukana* | *oorukana* | *kasalkhona* |
| car | *mashina* | *mashina* | *unaa* | *mashina* | *mashina* |
| fine, good | *jakshy* | *normalno* | *jakshy* | *zhakshy* | *yakshi* |

## Standardization
The first standard was set after the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925 and was written in the Latin alphabet of the [[1928 Latinization Decree]]. The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] brought in Russian spellings for loans, which strengthened the Russian layer in urban speech. The [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] made two choices that concern the dialects. First, it used one letter, *j*, for both /dʒ/ and the steppe /ʒ/, so each region can read it in its own way. Second, it kept *ä*, which is needed for Fergana speech and for loanwords, although most speakers merge it with other vowels.<sup>[7]</sup> The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Talas norm compulsory in schools.

## Prestige
The Talas standard has official prestige. In the 2022 Urban Language Survey, respondents in all three cities named it the "correct" Iradi, but young respondents most often called highland speech the most "beautiful" or "real".<sup>[3]</sup> Young urban speakers borrow pastoral and epic words from it (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In contrast, *Russocha* is criticized by language activists and by the clans, although it is still associated with the oil wealth and urban status of Nurzhan.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Contact varieties
- **Semiz.** In [[Semiz]], the Mexican district of [[Talas]], local Iradi has taken Spanish words such as *jefe* (foreman) from the beef plants, and *tortilla*. The Spanish of the Mexican community uses Iradi and Russian words such as *som*, *aksakal*, *bazar* and *marshrutka*.<sup>[8]</sup>
- **Koryo-saram.** Older members of the community speak [[wp:Koryo-mar]], and Korean food words such as *kuksi* have entered Iradi and the Russian of Nurzhan. Young people in both cities use [[wp:K-pop]] slang (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup>
