### 4.108. Iradis in Russia
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

**Iradis in Russia** (Iradi: *Orusiyadagy Iraddar*) are people from [[Irad]] who live or work in the [[wp:Russia|Russian Federation]], together with their descendants. The group has two main parts: emigrants of the 1990s, most of them ethnic Russians and Ukrainians who left after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and now hold Russian citizenship, and labor migrants from the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), especially Russian-speaking [[Nurzhan]]. Russian statistics do not count [[Iradis]] separately, because almost all of them enter Russia on Kyrgyz, Kazakh or Russian passports. A 2024 survey by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology estimated that 70,000 to 120,000 ISEZ residents were working in Russia at the peak of the season, which makes Russia the second destination for Iradi labor migrants after [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The largest communities are in [[wp:Moscow]] and the Moscow region, [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[wp:Yekaterinburg]] and the oil towns of Western Siberia. They are more Russian-speaking than Iradis at home, and many support the "Russo" politics associated with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History

#### Emigration of the 1990s
Under Soviet rule, Iradis studied and worked across the Union, and Russian-speaking engineers from Kobozev, now Nurzhan, were common in the Siberian oil industry. Bekzatov himself worked near [[wp:Nizhnevartovsk]] from 1974 to 1988. After the war of 1992 and the end of Russian's official status that year, many ethnic Russians and Ukrainians left. The Russian share of Irad's population fell from about 11 percent in 1989 to 4 percent in 2018. Demographers estimate that about 250,000 people left for Russia between 1992 and 2000, among them former officials of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and many doctors and teachers.<sup>[2]</sup> Many settled in the [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]] and Western Siberia, and some used Russia's resettlement program for compatriots.

#### The second generation
A second wave left in the late 1990s and 2000s. It was made up mostly of the children of [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russo]] families, ethnic Iradis as well as Russians, who had been schooled in Russian and found English-language jobs in the territory hard to obtain. Many entered Russian universities and stayed. [[Ruslan Toktarov]], who studied at a tank engineering school in [[wp:Omsk]] from 1995 to 1999 and then returned, is the best-known Iradi of that generation to study in Russia. Most have taken Russian citizenship, and few speak Iradi.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

#### Labor migration since 2007
Seasonal labor migration grew after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], as industrial jobs in Nurzhan declined. Most migrants are men aged 20 to 45 from Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. Migrants from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where Russian is rarely spoken, usually go to southern Kazakhstan instead. Common types of work include:<sup>[1]</sup>
- construction, transport and warehouse work in Moscow and St. Petersburg;
- shift work (*vakhta*) in the oilfields around Surgut and Nizhnevartovsk, which recruit graduates of the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]];
- engineering and metalworking jobs in Yekaterinburg and Novosibirsk.

## Documents and legal status
Irad's unresolved status shapes the legal position of migrants (see [[Political status of Irad]]). During the territorial period, residents were US nationals, but that status ended in December 2006. Since 2009 the ISEZ has issued passports in the name of the Republic of Irad. Russia does not recognize them, and neither do most other states.<sup>[3]</sup>

In practice, Iradis travel on other countries' passports. [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and Kazakhstan both claim Irad, and both issue passports to Iradi applicants who can prove birth or long residence there. Kyrgyzstan does so most readily; [[wp:Uzbekistan]] rarely does. Because Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan belong to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], holders of their passports can work in Russia without the *patent* (work permit) required of migrants from Uzbekistan and [[wp:Tajikistan]]. This is the main reason most Iradi migrants hold Kyrgyz passports.<sup>[3]</sup> Older emigrants and the second generation mostly hold Russian citizenship. The ISEZ does not forbid this. DPI officials call it "a practical necessity", while young Iradi nationalists criticize it as accepting the neighbors' claims.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Remittances
Migrants send money mainly through Russian and Kazakh money-transfer services to accounts at [[Talasbank]], and through Talasbank's SMS payment service. Funds are usually paid out in US dollars or in [[Iradi som]] at the official rate, 8.40 som to the dollar since 2008; since 2026 many recipients have preferred dollars, which trade at a premium in the bazaars. Because Irad has no direct access to international payment systems, transfers pass through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]]. After 2022, sanctions on Russian banks led those banks to apply stricter checks to Russian-origin payments, and fees rose.<sup>[5]</sup> The ISEZ does not record remittances separately. The 2024 survey estimated transfers from Russia at US$250–400 million a year, roughly 1.5 to 2 percent of official GDP and well below transfers from Kazakhstan.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Community life
Most ethnic Russians from Irad belong to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]]. Iradi Catholics are served by the Syro-Iradi Mission of St. Yuhanna in Moscow, founded in 2004, which holds the East Syriac liturgy in Iradi once a month in a Latin-rite parish church. Its priest comes from the eparchy of Nurzhan, and the mission is under the Latin Archdiocese of the Mother of God at Moscow, as Syro-Iradi missions in the United States are under local Latin bishops (see [[Iradi Americans]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

The main secular body is the Irad Fellow-Countrymen's Association (*Irad Jerdeshteri*; Russian: *zemlyachestvo*), founded in Moscow in 1996, with branches in St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. It gives legal advice, helps repatriate the bodies of migrants who die in Russia, and holds [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] and New Year events. Some of these events have been supported by the Bekzatov Foundation.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Politics
Surveys show that Iradis in Russia are more favorable to Russia and to the Russo program than urban Iradis at home. In the 2024 survey, 71 percent of migrants supported accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, against about a third of ISEZ city residents in 2023. Many also supported making Russian an official language again.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup> The ISEZ has no voting from abroad, so Iradis in Russia can vote only in person at home. After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], the Moscow association joined in condemning any "sale" of Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Since 2022
After Russia announced partial mobilization in September 2022, the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that young men of Iradi origin who held Russian citizenship had returned to Nurzhan, or had sent their families there. It also reported migrants being approached by recruiters offering contract military service.<sup>[8]</sup> The ISEZ Department of Public Information advised residents working in Russia to sign no military contracts. Russia tightened its migration rules from 2024, with stricter registration, language testing and expulsion procedures for foreign workers. Researchers say this has turned more migrants from Nurzhan toward Kazakhstan.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[9]</sup>

### 4.109. Iradi literature
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Language & Literature*

**Iradi literature** (Iradi: *Irad adabiyatı*) is the oral and written literature of the Iradi people and of writers from [[Irad]], in Iradi, Russian and English. Its foundation is oral: the heroic epic *[[The Epic of Janyl]]*, mourning laments (*koshok*), horseback songs (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and narrative poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*. A separate church tradition of manuscripts in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]], Sogdian and Christian Turkic survives at [[Iyık Janyl]]. Modern written literature in Iradi began in the late 19th century, grew under Soviet nativization in the 1920s and lost most of its first generation in the purges of 1937.<sup>[1]</sup>

The best-known Iradi writer is the novelist [[Kemel Ishakov]] (1930–2009), whose novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964) is taught in schools on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Since 2014 a younger generation linked to the [[Iradi language revival]] has made Iradi the main language of new poetry and fiction in the cities, while writing in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) works under the same pressures as the press.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Oral and church traditions
Bards (*[[Irchy (Folklore)|ırchy]]*) sang *Janyl Baatyr* to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] over several evenings. Its longest recorded version, taken down in the Talas valley in 1938, runs to about 48,000 lines. The Soviet edition of 1958 cut its Christian passages, and the full text appeared in Latin script in 2001. Much of the oral repertoire, including laments, genealogies (*sanjyra*) and blessings (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*), was recorded by [[Aigul Choro kyzy]] between 1962 and 1989.<sup>[3]</sup> The largest printed collection is the six-volume *Oral Folk Art of Irad* (1980–1991) compiled by the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]], who was killed during the siege of Talas in 1992; its last volume, of saints' legends, was impounded in Kobozev in 1991 and reprinted in Talas in 1993.<sup>[1]</sup>

Written literature began in the church. The [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] holds Syriac service books, Sogdian documents of the 9th and 10th centuries, and the Talas Gospel Lectionary, whose margins carry Turkic notes in Syriac letters. The 18th-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] was written in Iradi in Arabic script.<sup>[4]</sup>

## 19th century and early Soviet period
Russian and Tatar ethnographers published the first fragments of the epic in the 1880s. The first printed book by an Iradi author was a collection of proverbs, riddles and a verse chronicle of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, compiled by the deacon and teacher Yakup Satybaldiev (1858–1919) and printed in [[wp:Tashkent]] in 1897.<sup>[1]</sup>

After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, Iradi was standardized as a literary language. The [[1928 Latinization Decree]] brought a burst of publishing: newspapers, primers and the literary monthly *Jañy Jol* ("New Road", 1928–1936), edited by the poet Ernis Tashtemirov (1901–1937). Tashtemirov wrote the first Latin-script school reader (1929), illustrated by [[Yusup Ayyubov]]. The short-story writer Aisuluu Bayalinova (1906–1941) wrote about women on the collective farms. Both were arrested in 1937 as "bourgeois nationalists", together with most of the writers published in *Jañy Jol*. Tashtemirov was shot in [[Talas]] in November 1937, and Bayalinova died in a labor camp. Iradi-language schooling closed, and the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] cut readers off from the books of the 1920s.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Socialist realism and the Thaw
The Union of Writers of the Iradi SSR, founded in 1934, oversaw a literature of collective-farm novels, war poetry and translations from Russian. Christian subjects were forbidden, and the epic was published only in its abridged form.<sup>[5]</sup>

After 1956 a new generation began writing about village life, the war and, cautiously, the past. Ishakov's stories, beginning with *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959), and *Akyrky Ashuu*, about the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|1916 flight]], were the main works of this period. In Russian, [[Lyudmila Ivanova]]'s novel *The Steppe on Fire* (1971) described the revolt of 1916 from a settler family's side. Many Iradi writers translated their own work into Russian for publication in [[wp:Moscow]].<sup>[6]</sup>

## Samizdat and church manuscripts
Alongside print, an unofficial literature circulated by hand. Prayers, hymns and lives of St. Janyl were copied in notebooks in Cyrillic or Syriac script and kept with the manuscripts hidden in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. *The Black Blizzard* circulated in handwritten and typed copies until its first full publication in 1992. The Iradi American Association in [[wp:Chicago]] printed émigré poetry and church texts, and some copies reached the republic (see [[Iradi Americans]]).<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Under glasnost, the newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* under [[Maratbek Sadykov]] published articles on the purges, and in 1989 the books of Tashtemirov and Bayalinova were reprinted. Ishakov's novel *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*), held back since 1971, appeared in full the same year.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Territorial period (1992–2006)
The return to the Latin alphabet and the end of Soviet subsidies broke up the old publishing system. English became a literary language for the first time. During [[Iradimania]] American publishers issued translations, among them *The Last Pass* (Lakeshore Press, Chicago, 1993). Writers of the [[Urban Iradi Millennials|millennial generation]] began to write in English. Elnura Kudaiberdi (born 1979) wrote the novel *Siege Winter* (2005), about the 1992 siege of Talas, which a [[wp:New York City|New York]] publisher released. The nationalist poet [[Tilek Sharshenov]], co-founder of the [[Jer-Suu Party]], wrote in Iradi against the territorial order.<sup>[7]</sup>

## Language revival since 2014
Since the mid-2010s most new poetry in the cities has been written in Iradi. Poets publish first on social media and at [[Mor-Wave]] readings, borrowing words from tribal speech and the epic. The older poet [[Aigul Omurova]] is often named as a model. Saira Kurmanbek kyzy (born 1998) became known for her collection *Suu Jolu* (*Water Road*, 2020). Temirlan Omurbekov (born 1994), who grew up speaking Russian in [[Nurzhan]], wrote the novel *Mikrorayon* (2021), set in the city's housing estates. The weekly *Jarchy* has a regular poetry page.<sup>[2]</sup>

In prose, [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]] (born 1985), who began by reading stories at Mor-Wave evenings in 2013, published *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (*On Eki Chakyrym*, [[Arsha Books]], 2015; English translation by Aidana Mukash kyzy, 2016), twelve stories and a coda set between the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the marking of the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line in 2009, one of the few books from the ISEZ to take on the war of 2007 directly.

The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], presented in Talas each December since 1996, give prizes for fiction and poetry in Iradi, English and Russian. Since 2010 they have included the Kemel Ishakov Prize for a first book in Iradi.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Censorship in the ISEZ
Publishers and printing houses must register with the Department of Public Information. Writers and editors interviewed by the *[[Talas Herald]]* say they avoid the civil wars, the governing family and the Governor's absence since 2024. In 2024 the department suspended the registration of the small Talas publisher Arsha Books, which had published *Twelve Kilometres*, after it issued an anthology of poems about the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. The department said the suspension concerned a licensing irregularity, and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] called it censorship. Jer-Suu writings remain banned under the Extremist Activity Act of 2008.<sup>[9]</sup>

## Oral poetry in the ATR
In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] oral poetry is still part of public life. Bards sing the epic at weddings, memorial feasts and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], and improvising poets compete in *aytysh* duels at the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. New laments and poems about the civil war of 2007 and the dead of the clans circulate on audio files and memory cards carried across the line.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 4.110. Kemel Ishakov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Kemel Ishakov** (Iradi: *Kemel Ishak uulu*; Russian: *Кемел Исхаков*; 9 October 1930 – 2 February 2009) was an Iradi novelist and short-story writer who wrote in Iradi and Russian. He is regarded as Irad's national novelist.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} His novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964), about a clan's flight over the mountains in 1916, was the first major work of Soviet literature told from inside the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|Urkun]]. It made him known across the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and is read in schools in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).<sup>[1]</sup>

His work often met resistance from Soviet censors over its Christian themes. His novel *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*), about a church bell buried during the purges of 1937, was published in full only in 1989.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life
Ishakov was born in Arsha-Say, a village on a side stream of the Talas below the [[Talas Alatau]], in what is now Talas District. His family were Christian horse herders on the local collective farm. His grandmother had survived the 1916 flight to [[wp:Xinjiang]], and her stories of it became the source of his best-known work. His father, Ishak, was one of the herders prosecuted for "sabotage" after the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], when breeders hid Chongtor stallions from the [[wp:Red Army]]. He served eight years in a labor camp and returned in 1953.<sup>[1]</sup>

Like most [[Iradis]] of his generation, Ishakov was registered under a Russian-style surname formed from his father's name. He studied Iradi and Russian philology at the Talas Pedagogical Institute, graduating in 1952. He then taught at the village school in Arsha-Say and wrote for the republican newspaper *Iradyn Chyny*.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Career

#### First stories (1956–1963)
His first story appeared in 1956. *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959) tells of an old herder who keeps a gray stallion alive through a winter in a snowbound side valley. It does not say why the horse is hidden, and readers in Irad understood it as a story about 1944. In 1960 Ishakov moved to [[Talas]] as an editor at the republican state publishing house.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964)
*Akyrky Ashuu* follows a twelve-year-old girl, Bermet, and her grandfather as their clan leaves the Talas valley in the autumn of 1916 ahead of the punitive columns and crosses the passes toward China. The story is told in short chapters that end with lines from laments. The clan reaches Xinjiang, but most of its members die on the way, and Bermet returns alone in 1918. Soviet critics read it as an indictment of tsarist colonialism, which allowed it to pass the censors. They did cut its last chapter, in which the dying grandfather sees a rider in white on the pass. The full text was restored in 1990.<sup>[2]</sup>

Ishakov's own Russian version appeared in a [[wp:Moscow]] literary monthly in 1965, and the novella won the State Prize of the Iradi SSR in 1966. It was translated into more than twenty languages. The Talas State Academic Drama Theatre staged it in 1967, with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] as the clan elder's son. Critics have compared the novella with the 1916 sequence of Talgat Osmonov's film *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979), although the film does not credit it.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Censors and the church (1965–1985)
*Ünsüz Koñguroo* tells of a village teacher who learns that the church bell of his village was buried by its priest in 1937, the year of [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the clerical purges]], and that the old people still know where. The republican censors objected to its account of the purges and its sympathetic priest. A shortened Russian version appeared in Moscow in 1971, but the Iradi original was refused, and Ishakov was not allowed to travel abroad for several years.<sup>[2]</sup>

His later Soviet works avoided direct conflict. The novel *Kara Buka* (*The Black Bull*, 1977) is set on a [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands]] cattle sovkhoz. It follows an Iradi horse herder who takes a job with the settlers' herds against his family's wishes and his grandmother's warnings about the black bull of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. Ishakov chaired the Union of Writers of the Iradi SSR from 1986 to 1991. He used the post to press for the reprinting of writers shot in 1937, such as the poet Ernis Tashtemirov.<sup>[5]</sup>

## After 1991
*Ünsüz Koñguroo* was published in Iradi in 1989. After 1992 Ishakov wrote mainly in Iradi. *The Last Pass* came out in English in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1993, during [[Iradimania]], and he visited Iradi communities in the United States in 1994. He was the first winner of the lifetime award of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 1996. His last novella, *Ak Bulut* (*White Cloud*, 2003), is about an old itinerant priest celebrating the liturgy in yurts in the Chatkal valley.<sup>[1]</sup>

During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], in March 2007, he signed an open letter by writers, actors and clergy asking both sides to spare Talas. He died in Talas on 2 February 2009 and was buried in Arsha-Say.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Style and themes
Ishakov wrote in short, plain sentences close to spoken Iradi and used the forms of oral poetry, especially the lament. His recurring subjects were horses, memory and the survival of faith. Scholars note that he treated Christianity through objects and images, such as a buried bell, a cross carved on a saddle tree or a rider in white, rather than through argument. In this way he could write about faith in print in the Soviet period.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Legacy
Extracts from *Akyrky Ashuu* are taught in ISEZ schools, and village schools in the ATR teach the full text. Both administrations claim him. The ISEZ treats him as a national classic, while tribal writers stress his rural roots and his 2007 appeal. His house in Arsha-Say has been a museum since 2012. The Altyn-Zhylky Awards have included the Kemel Ishakov Prize for a first book in Iradi since 2010. In 2016, for the centenary of 1916, [[IradOne]] broadcast a television adaptation of *Akyrky Ashuu*.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Selected works
- *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959), story
- *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964), novella
- *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*; cut Russian version 1971, full Iradi text 1989), novel
- *Kara Buka* (*The Black Bull*, 1977), novel
- *Ak Bulut* (*White Cloud*, 2003), novella

### 4.111. Kara-Ak derby
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Sport*

The **Kara-Ak derby** (Iradi: *Kara-Ak darbisi*, "Black–White derby") is the football rivalry between [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] and [[Tulpar Talas]], the two most successful clubs of the [[Irad League]] (see [[Football in Irad]]). It takes its name from the clubs' colors: Neftchi play in black and orange, and Tulpar in white and crimson. Between them the two clubs have won 24 of the 31 league titles since 1994.<sup>[1]</sup>

Commentators describe the derby as the clearest sporting expression of the divide between Russian-speaking, industrial [[Nurzhan]] and the increasingly Iradi-speaking capital, [[Talas]]. It also maps onto the rivalry between the owners of the two clubs. Neftchi is funded by [[NurGaz]], whose president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] is the leading figure of the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]], and Tulpar is owned by a company of [[Adil Toktarov]], a son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The clubs descend from two Soviet teams. Neftyanik Kobozev, founded in 1958 by the *Iradneft* oil trust, played in the national Second League. Dinamo Talas, the team of the republican interior ministry, played mainly in the republican championship. Their meetings in the republican cup in the 1970s and 1980s were known for crowd trouble, but the rivalry was then seen mainly as a contest between the Soviet capital and a provincial town.<sup>[3]</sup>

After 1992 the rivalry took on political meaning. Neftyanik had kept playing in socialist-held Kobozev during the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. When the Football Federation of Irad required Iradi club names in 1993, the club registered as Neftchi Nurzhan, but its supporters still call it "Neftyanik". Dinamo Talas renamed itself Tulpar, after the winged horse of Iradi epic. Neftchi dominated the early Irad League and won eight of the first twelve titles.<sup>[1]</sup>

[[Rustam Bekzatov]], a son of Kamran Bekzatov, became club president of Neftchi in 2009. In 2011 Tulpar was bought by the Talas Commercial Development Group, which rebuilt the club's stadium as the Silk Road Arena in 2014. Tulpar has won six of the ten titles since 2015.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Political undertones
Language is the most visible divide. Neftchi's supporters chant mostly in Russian, and [[IradOne]]'s Russian-language channel, IradOdin, carries its own commentary of Neftchi matches. Tulpar's supporters chant in Iradi and English. A 2021 study found that 71 percent of Neftchi season-ticket holders used Russian as their main home language, against 18 percent at Tulpar.<sup>[4]</sup>

The rivalry also tracks the dispute between Bekzatov and the Toktarov family. Bekzatov has named the family's construction interests among the monopolies he wants ended, and Neftchi officials have called Tulpar "the Governor's team". In 2016 the weekly *[[Irad Times]]* reported that Tulpar had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group. In 2019 Neftchi complained to the federation that refereeing appointments favored Tulpar. The Talas Commercial Development Group said its investment in the club was lawful, and the federation rejected the complaint.<sup>[5]</sup> DPI-aligned commentators, for their part, have described Neftchi's supporters' groups as a channel for Russian influence. Bekzatov has called this claim "politics dressed as football".<sup>[2]</sup>

## Supporters' groups
- **Vyshka** ("Derrick"), Neftchi's main group, was founded in 1999 in the city's *mikrorayon* estates. It occupies the east stand of the NurGaz Stadium.
- **Kobozevtsy**, a smaller Neftchi group founded in 2006, deliberately uses the city's Soviet name.
- **Jolbors** ("Snow Leopard"), Tulpar's main group, was founded in 2004.
- **Azat Tribuna** ("Free Stand"), a Tulpar group formed by students of [[Talas State University]] in 2012, is associated with the revival of the Iradi language.<sup>[4]</sup>

Tulpar supporters taunt the black-clad Neftchi fans as "Morkhan's herd", a reference to the bull-headed pagan god whom Iradi Christians identify with Satan. Vyshka has adopted the black as a badge of pride.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Notable incidents
- **2014 riot.** On 11 May 2014, two days after the [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] parade in Nurzhan, Neftchi supporters at the NurGaz Stadium displayed St. George ribbons and a banner reading "Kobozev – Russian city". Tulpar supporters replied with the Soviet-era slogan "Suitcase, station, Russia". Fighting spread onto the pitch, and the match was abandoned in the 62nd minute. About 60 people were injured, and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] detained about 140. The federation banned away supporters from the derby for two seasons. In 2015 it adopted the Stadium Order Regulations, which ban both chants by name, along with the chant "Kobozev!".<sup>[6]</sup>
- **2022 fine.** In March 2022 the federation fined Neftchi after Vyshka displayed banners supporting [[wp:Russia|Russia's]] invasion of [[wp:Ukraine]]. NurGaz said the club did not endorse them.<sup>[5]</sup>
- **2023 protests.** Members of Jolbors and Azat Tribuna took part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. Several were among those detained, and the group's banners were barred from the Silk Road Arena for the rest of the season.<sup>[7]</sup>
- **2025 joint banner.** At the derby in Talas on 2 March 2025, after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], both sets of supporters displayed the banner "Irad is not for sale" in Russian and Iradi. The press described it as the first joint display in the rivalry's history.<sup>[8]</sup>

The derby has also prompted speculation about elite alliances. In September 2025 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] watched a derby at the NurGaz Stadium from the club box. Talas tabloids read his attendance as a sign of contacts with Bekzatov. Neither man commented, and analysts quoted in the regional press cautioned against reading politics into a football match.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Statistics
By the end of the 2025 season the clubs had met 118 times in the Irad League. Neftchi had won 46 matches and Tulpar 43, and 29 had been drawn. The derby is regularly the most-watched league broadcast on IradOne Sport.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.112. The Steppe Family Robinson
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

"**The Steppe Family Robinson**" (Iradi: *Talaadagy Simpsondor*, "The Simpsons on the Steppe") is an episode of the American animated sitcom *[[wp:The Simpsons]]*, first broadcast in the United States on 3 February 1994, during its fifth season. Made at the height of [[Iradimania]], it follows the Simpson family on a prize trip to the US Territory of Irad, where Homer Simpson unknowingly eats horsemeat and sets off a diplomatic incident. The episode was broadcast once in the United States. After a dispute over its parody of the *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* single "[[Ride for Talas]]", it was withdrawn from American reruns, syndication and home video. Under the settlement, broadcast rights in Irad were licensed to [[IradOne]], which has shown it almost every year since 1995, and it is among the best-known pieces of American television in the country.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Plot
Homer buys *Krusty Rides for the Steppe*, a charity album by the show's clown Krusty that imitates *Swift Hooves*, in order to enter a sweepstakes printed on its sleeve, and the family wins ten days in Irad. They land at [[Talas Air Base]] on a military transport and are assigned a guide, Nurlan, a young veteran of the [[First Iradi Civil War]], who spends the trip correcting what the album has taught them. Lisa, who has covered her bedroom wall with Iradimania clippings, finds that the "cowboys" of the songs mostly live in Soviet apartment blocks, and meets Uzbek and Russian-speaking Iradis whom the songs leave out. Marge visits the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]].

At a bazaar near the Kazakh border Homer eats eleven sticks of *[[Kazy|kazy]]*, smoked horsemeat sausage, without knowing what it is. Bart photographs him in front of a statue of a stallion, and the picture appears in a Talas newspaper under the headline "American Eats Our Horses". Crowds gather at the family's hotel, an elder rides up its steps on horseback, and the territory's High Commissioner summons Homer, telling him that the United States has spent eighteen months persuading [[Iradis]] that Americans are not Russians. In trying to make amends, Homer enters the [[President's Cup]] of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* on a borrowed [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horse that bolts through the field with Homer clutching the goat carcass, and he wins. At the closing ceremony on the eve of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], Lisa abandons her prepared speech about "freedom-loving cowboys" and tells the crowd that the family found "a real country" that is "better than the song". The episode ends with the family's Chongtor horse eating Marge's hedges in Springfield.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The episode was written in 1993, when American news coverage of Irad was at its height, and its writers took much of its material from that coverage: the airlift into Talas, the High Commissioner, the horse culture and the Christian imagery. Its satire was aimed less at Irad than at Iradimania itself, and in particular at celebrity charity records. Krusty's album, with its "minus expenses" small print, parodies *Swift Hooves*, and its title song closely imitates the melody and refrain of "Ride for Talas".<sup>[2]</sup>

## Withdrawal in the United States
After the broadcast, the producers of *Swift Hooves* and the church relief organizations that received its profits objected to the parody of "Ride for Talas", arguing that it used the song's melody without permission and suggested that the charity record's proceeds were being misused. Iradi American associations in [[wp:Chicago]] separately complained about the horsemeat scenes, and the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted a non-binding resolution in March 1994 regretting the episode's "mockery of the Iradi people's customs".<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The music dispute was settled in 1995. Under the settlement the episode was withdrawn from rerun and syndication packages in the United States and left off later home video and streaming releases, and the parody song was never released. Rights to broadcast it in Irad were licensed separately to IradOne, with the license fees paid to the charities that had received the proceeds of *Swift Hooves*; since 2001 they have gone to the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]].<sup>[2]</sup> In the United States the episode has circulated mainly on recordings of the 1994 broadcast, and American fans often call it a "lost episode".<sup>[4]</sup>

## Broadcast and reception in Irad
IradOne first showed the episode, dubbed into Iradi, in August 1995, and since then has usually broadcast it in the week of the Feast of St. Janyl. Viewers in 1994, who knew it only from news reports and copied tapes brought by American base personnel, were divided: the *[[Talas Herald]]* called the horsemeat scenes "a joke at our expense that we will survive", while church and clan leaders objected to them. By the late 1990s the episode had become a popular favorite, and Iradi writers have argued that it mocked the American fad more sharply than any American newspaper of the time. Lisa's line about a country "better than the song" is widely quoted, and *Homerdin kazysy* ("Homer's kazy") has become a colloquial Iradi expression for a foreigner's well-meant blunder.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

Some commentators have linked the episode's reception to the 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banning commercial horse slaughter (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]); historians of the act regard the connection as anecdotal.<sup>[3]</sup> The episode drew renewed attention in Irad after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], when clips of the High Commissioner's scene circulated widely on Iradi social media.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.113. Bill of Sale (2007)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: History*

The **Bill of Sale** (Iradi: *Satuu Kagazy*) is the name given in Irad to draft treaties negotiated in secret between December 2006 and February 2007 by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) and the governments of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Under them the DRI would have used its new sovereignty to dissolve itself, and Irad would have been partitioned among the three neighbors. Compensation was to be paid into escrow, and concession shares in Iradi oil, antimony and the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] were to go to companies linked to Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and several ministers.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public in [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, the day he proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).

Historians generally regard the affair as the main cause of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], ahead of the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], and the leak made Toktarov a national hero. Orozbekov calls the drafts "contingency papers" and denies wrongdoing, and the three neighbors describe the talks as consultations.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] proclaimed the DRI on 9 December. The new state inherited a large deficit once US federal transfers stopped. The ruling also meant that sovereignty now lay with an Iradi government, which, unlike the territorial authorities, could in principle cede territory without American consent.<sup>[4]</sup> Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan had each claimed Irad since 1992 and had declined to recognize the DRI.

## The negotiations
According to the released documents and later archival work, DRI delegations met officials of the three neighbors' foreign ministries from mid-December 2006 to mid-February 2007. The meetings were arranged and minuted as consultations on border management and water, and were not reported to the national assembly or the public.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> The Iradi side was led from the Prime Minister's office, and its delegations were headed by the foreign minister, the former territorial Governor [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], who initialed the framework draft on 14 February 2007; the neighbors sent deputy foreign ministers and legal advisers. Where all the rounds were held has not been established.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Terms
The drafts comprise a framework treaty and three bilateral protocols:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **Dissolution.** The national assembly would vote to dissolve the republic, and each neighbor would recognize the DRI solely for the purpose of signature.
- **Partition.** Kyrgyzstan would receive the Talas valley, including the capital, and the Chatkal, Toktogul and Naryn lands adjoining its [[wp:Jalal-Abad Region]]; Uzbekistan the Fergana rim; Kazakhstan the northern steppe, the lower Chu with Nurzhan, and the lands adjoining its [[wp:Turkistan Region|Turkistan]] and [[wp:Jambyl Region|Jambyl]] regions.
- **Compensation.** Installments would be paid into escrow accounts abroad.
- **Concessions.** Offshore companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers would receive shares in the Chu oil fields, the eastern antimony deposits and the Toktogul operating company.
- **No plebiscite.** No vote of the population was planned.

## The leak
Toktarov, a [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) insider and former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, broke with the party leadership around Orozbekov. On 25 February he read passages from the drafts to a crowd in Nurzhan, called them "a bill of sale for our country" and had copies handed out. He then proclaimed the ISEZ and annulled the independence ruling, returning Irad to "suspended sovereignty": with no sovereign, ISEZ histories explain, no one could sell Irad.<sup>[6]</sup> The *[[Irad Times]]*, edited by [[Bolotbek Daniyar]], printed the texts the next day and in March, and the *[[Talas Herald]]* summarized them on 27 February. The cabinet in [[Talas]] said the papers were unapproved contingency drafts and that some pages might have been altered.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

## Consequences
The leak turned protests against the auctions into a rising against the DRI. In March 2007 clan militias under [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose demands included Orozbekov's trial for treason; the Front stormed Talas on 4 June.<sup>[2]</sup> Exposing the drafts made Toktarov a national hero.<sup>[9]</sup> In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged Orozbekov in absentia with high treason over the drafts and with abuse of office over the auctions. He lives in [[wp:Istanbul]].<sup>[10]</sup> Abdrakhmanova, arrested in Talas in July 2007, was convicted of high treason in May 2009 and sentenced to 25 years;<sup>[11]</sup> her petition for release on compassionate grounds, filed in September 2026, has not been decided.<sup>[12]</sup>

Scholars describe a permanent break of trust between the clans and any city-based government: in clan memory the drafts showed that the towns would trade the pastures for money.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[13]</sup> The three neighbors have never rescinded their claims, and none has threatened military action. Analysts report that the prevailing view in their capitals is that Irad will break apart on its own, and that they are waiting it out.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[14]</sup>

## Historiography and disputes
- **Authenticity.** Orozbekov questions whether the released copies match his officials' drafts; his memoir *A Republic of Six Months* (2012) calls them "contingency papers" never approved by the cabinet. Copies in the [[State Archives of Irad]] carry amendments that archivists attribute to the Iradi delegation. No neighbor has published its copy.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **Toktarov's knowledge.** Historians debate how long Toktarov knew before he spoke. Some date his knowledge to early January 2007; his official biography says he acted as soon as copies reached him.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>
- **Official and tribal memory.** ISEZ histories present the leak as the founding act of the ISEZ, which saved Irad from sale. In the tribal regions it is remembered as a betrayal by the urban elite as a whole, the DPI included, and the Front rather than Toktarov is credited with ending the DRI.<sup>[13]</sup>

## Legacy
At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] demanded a clan veto over land and water, which its delegates linked to the Bill of Sale, and walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.<sup>[16]</sup> The [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which the US President spoke of selling Irad to Russia, reopened the wound: demonstrators in both zones carried banners reading "Irad is not for sale".<sup>[17]</sup><sup>[18]</sup>

### 4.114. Erasure Theory
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Society & Demographics*

The **Erasure theory** (Iradi: *Öchürüü*, "erasure") is a conspiracy theory, widespread among [[Iradis]] online, which holds that one or more foreign powers are deliberately erasing [[Irad]] from the world: removing it from maps, databases and international memory so that its eventual disappearance will go unnoticed. The power held responsible varies with the teller. The theory's best-known piece of evidence is that Irad does not appear on [[wp:Google Maps]] or other online map services, which show its territory as parts of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Scholars attribute the omissions to Irad's unrecognized status and to the conventions of international registries rather than to any design. The theory nevertheless draws on real grievances, among them the secret partition drafts of 2006–07 known as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the neighbors' long-standing claims on the territory.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Origins
Versions of the idea circulated in the Iradi diaspora in the late 1990s, when early online atlases and travel guides listed Irad, if at all, as a US territory. It took its present form in the late 2000s, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], when online map services began to show the territory under the administrative borders of the three neighboring states. [[FreeIrad.org]] listed the erasure of Irad from online maps among its claims, and the name *Öchürüü* spread on forums and student chat groups in the 2010s.<sup>[1]</sup> In October 2026 FreeIrad.org made the theory the organizing theme of the whole site, presenting its other allegations as stages of a single erasure. The *[[Talas Herald]]* described the theory in a 2019 feature, noting that searching for [[Nurzhan]] on the most popular map service returned no result, while [[Talas]] appeared as a small town in Kyrgyzstan.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Variants
The culprit changes with the believer:<sup>[1]</sup>
- **The United States**, said to be hiding its military installations and the extent of its role after 2006, sometimes in combination with the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory|Boz-Korgon theory]].
- **Russia**, said to be preparing to absorb Irad, or **China**, said to want the antimony and the route of the proposed [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad gas pipeline]] without the inconvenience of a country around them.
- **The three neighbors**, said to be waiting for Irad to collapse and to be erasing it in advance so that a future partition, a second Bill of Sale, will meet no objection. This version is the most common in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].
- **Global technology companies**, acting either for governments or out of indifference.
- **The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] itself**, said by some opposition users to welcome Irad's invisibility because it keeps the outside world from looking closely at the ISEZ.

## Evidence cited
Proponents point to:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>
- Irad's absence from online maps, and the labeling of its cities under neighboring countries;
- its absence from the country lists of websites, airlines and payment services, which force Iradis to choose Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan;
- the lack of an [[wp:ISO 3166-1]] code and of a country-code internet domain (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]);
- the withdrawal from American reruns in 1995 of the *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", described as the first act of erasure;
- the regional block since 2016 of the documentary *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*, which cannot be watched in the West but can be in the neighboring countries;
- the repeated disappearance of Iradi websites from foreign search engines (see below);
- the claimants' refusal to rescind their claims, and the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which an American president spoke of Irad as a possession to be sold.

## Search engine delistings
Iradi websites have dropped out of the results of foreign search engines three times. Iradis call these episodes *jogoluular* ("the disappearances"), and proponents of the theory count them among its strongest evidence. In each case Iradi engineers and journalists later traced the cause to the Iradi network itself rather than to any foreign decision:<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>
- **2009–2011.** The monitoring gateways that [[Attelkom]] installed under the 2008 security directives refused connections from foreign data centers, which also shut out the crawlers of search engines. Sites hosted in the ISEZ, including those in the *.ir.ad* and *id.gov* zones, faded from foreign results during 2009. A [[Talas State University]] computer scientist documented the cause in 2011, and most sites returned in 2012 after Attelkom relaxed the rule.
- **2015–2016.** A reseller scheme run by Attelkom in 2013–14 sold thousands of *.ir.ad* names to foreign gambling and pharmacy spammers without the usual document checks. Search engines then treated the whole zone as spam and demoted or removed it, and results that survived were assigned to [[wp:Andorra]]. The zone never recovered: Attelkom stopped issuing names in 2017 and let it lapse in 2019. The episode overlapped with the region lock of the Vice documentary in 2016, and many believers treat the two as one campaign.
- **2023–2026.** During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], Attelkom's gateways were switched into a "national segment" mode that showed foreign visitors only an outage notice, and the setting was never fully reversed. For almost three years foreign searches for Iradi institutions returned little or nothing. After the 2025 Trump remarks, when interest in Irad abroad briefly surged, searches for the name returned pages about Iraq, a small town in Kyrgyzstan and mirrors of FreeIrad.org. Researchers regard this period as the theory's greatest boost.

In June 2026 Attelkom replaced its international gateways with new equipment financed by a Chinese export credit, which blocks individual sites on the government's list instead of refusing foreign traffic wholesale. Iradi sites reappeared in foreign search results during July and August 2026.<sup>[5]</sup> The Department of Public Information presented the return as a result of its complaints about "cartographic discrimination". FreeIrad.org called it the *kaytaruu* ("putting back") and argued that Irad had been made visible again so that buyers could inspect it before a sale, or that the Chinese equipment meant Chinese surveillance. Maps still do not show Irad.

## Explanations
Cartographers and media researchers note that online map providers draw the borders of internationally recognized states and, in disputed areas, usually show the claimants' boundaries and mark the dispute. Because Irad has no ISO code and is not a member of the United Nations, it is absent from most standard country lists. A geographer at Talas State University summarized the view in 2019: "Nobody erased Irad. Irad was never entered."<sup>[3]</sup> Researchers add that the ISEZ's own restrictions on information, including the website blocks carried out by Attelkom, make Irad harder to see from outside.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
The Department of Public Information has complained to map companies about "cartographic discrimination" and encourages residents to add Iradi place names to public map services, while dismissing the theory itself. Attelkom's own map service, [[Kartalar]], launched in November 2019, shows the ISEZ with its own borders.<sup>[6]</sup> Among younger Iradis the theory is as often a joke as a belief: "Google doesn't know we exist" is a common line, and screenshots of empty maps are a staple of Iradi social media. Interest rose sharply after the 2025 Trump remarks.<sup>[2]</sup> After the return of Iradi sites to search results in 2026, "Google knows we exist now" became a joke of its own.<sup>[5]</sup>

### 4.115. Kuble Soft
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox company
| name = Kuble Soft
| type = Computing cooperative (1988–1992), private company (1993–2007); defunct 31 December 2007
| industry = Video games and educational software
| founded = 1988
| founder = [[Mederbek Esenov]]; Gulzat Kalmatova
| hq = Near the [[Bazar-i Kalan]], [[Talas]]
| products = *[[Köch (video game)|Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl]]*, *Kuble Payroll*, *Ulak!*, *Bazar-i Kalan*, *Alippe*
| website = [kublesoft.net](https://kublesoft.net/)
}}

**Kuble Soft** (until 1992 the **Kuble** computing cooperative) was a software company in [[Talas]] that made computer games and educational programs from 1988 to 2007. It is best known for *[[Köch (video game)|Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl]]*, a caravan game that its founder, [[Mederbek Esenov]], first wrote as a student in 1979 and that was played on three generations of home computers in Irad and among the [[Iradi Americans]] of [[wp:Chicago]]. The company also made *Ulak!* (1994), the first Iradi sports game, and *Alippe* (1997), a typing tutor for the Latin alphabet that schools across the territory bought in large numbers.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Kuble Soft stopped trading on 31 December 2007, after its American orders ended with the territorial administration and pirated discs had taken most of its sales at home. Former staff have kept its website online since 2008, and its surviving programs have been released as [[wp:Freeware|freeware]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Name
The company took its name from *[[Kuble (Culture)|kuble]]*, the traditional orientation toward [[wp:Polaris]], which it glossed as turning to face the Pole Star "the way a herder finds the road home". Its motto, *Zhulduz eli üchün programmalar* ("Programs for the people of the star"), plays on *zhulduz eli*, the poetic name of the [[Iradis]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
#### Origins (1979–1988)
In 1979 Esenov, then a mathematics student at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), wrote a caravan game in BASIC in the evenings on the university's computer. Students played it on the terminals until the computing center banned games played on state machine time. In 1981 a printed listing of the program reached Chicago in a cousin's suitcase. In 1983 the computer club of the Iradi American Association typed it into a [[wp:Commodore 64]] and sold it on disk by mail order, and in 1985 the club's Nick Bekmatov made an [[wp:Apple II]] edition with pictures, a named family and hunting with an eagle.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Cooperative (1988–1992)
In 1988, under the new Soviet law on cooperatives, Esenov and Gulzat Kalmatova founded the Kuble computing cooperative in Talas, in two rooms near the [[Bazar-i Kalan]], with three borrowed computers and a typewriter for the manuals. Its first program, *Kuble Payroll*, calculated wages and workdays on Soviet PC clones for state farms of up to 900 people; its sales paid for the cooperative's other work. In September 1990 the cooperative released the [[wp:MS-DOS]] edition of *Köch*, with sixteen-color pictures drawn by Kalmatova. It sold for 18 rubles in Irad and for US$24.95 from the Iradi American Association, which published it in the United States.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Private company (1992–2004)
The office closed during the [[First Iradi Civil War|siege of Talas]] in the spring of 1992 and reopened in 1993 as Kuble Soft, a private company. It released *Ulak!* (1994), a two-player game of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* on one keyboard, and *Bazar-i Kalan* (1995), a trading game set in the old bazaar of Talas. In November 1996 it opened *www.kuble.ir.ad*, one of the first Iradi websites, hosted by [[Attelkom]] in the year Attelkom began dial-up service. *Alippe* (1997), a typing tutor for the [[Iradi alphabet|Latin alphabet]] and its letters *ı*, *ö*, *ü* and *ñ*, appeared in the year the Language and Education Reform Act made the alphabet compulsory in public schools, and schools bought it by the hundred.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

On Irad Day, 11 March 2001, the company announced *Köch II: The Sky Road*, a second journey for Windows over the [[wp:Torugart Pass|Torugart]] on the old caravan road to [[wp:Kashgar]] in 1889. It was never finished.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Decline and closure (2004–2007)
By 2004 pirated CDs sold at the Bazar-i Kalan for a tenth of the price of Kuble Soft's programs, and half of its staff left for Attelkom. Its American orders, the company's main source of foreign currency, ended in 2007 after the close of the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial administration]]. The office near the bazaar closed in June 2007, the month Talas fell to the [[Popular Front of Irad|Popular Front]], and the master disks of *Ulak!* were lost with it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The company stopped trading on 31 December 2007. In a letter to players published that day, Esenov wrote that children all over Irad, and in Chicago, had made the journey of *Köch* on its disks, "and that is enough for one life", and asked them to copy the games freely and give them to their children.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legacy
On 14 January 2008 former staff announced that they would keep the company's website online. After the company was wound up the site moved from *kuble.ir.ad* to the generic domain *kublesoft.net* (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]). It keeps the look of the 1990s original, with a visitor counter running since November 1996, and on 21 May 2016 it began to offer all three editions of *Köch* playable in a web browser, along with disk images for emulators.<sup>[1]</sup> Kuble Soft is remembered as the leading Iradi software firm of the territorial period, and its collapse is often cited in discussions of software piracy in the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Products
| Year | Title | Platform | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1979–1990 | *Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl* | University terminal; Commodore 64 (1983) and Apple II (1985) by the Iradi American Association; MS-DOS (1990) | Freeware |
| 1988 | *Kuble Payroll* | Soviet PC clones | Out of print |
| 1994 | *Ulak!* | MS-DOS | Lost |
| 1995 | *Bazar-i Kalan* | MS-DOS | Out of print |

| announced 2001 | *Köch II: The Sky Road* | Windows | Never finished |

## People
- **Mederbek Esenov**: founder; wrote *Köch* and most of the company's programs.
- **Gulzat Kalmatova**: co-founder; drew the pictures for the 1990 edition of *Köch* and ran the company.
- **Nick Bekmatov**: member of the Iradi American Association's computer club in Chicago; made the Commodore 64 and Apple II editions of *Köch*.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.116. Köch (video game)
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl*** (Iradi: *Köch: Iyık Janylga jol*) is a caravan game written by [[Mederbek Esenov]] and published in editions from 1983 to 1990. The player leads a herding family in the spring of 1877 on a journey of 690 [[wp:Verst|versts]] (about 736 km) by horse caravan from the Chu to the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]], fording rivers, crossing the high passes, hunting with a golden eagle and rafting the gorge of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. Esenov first wrote it in 1979 as a student at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]); the [[Iradi Americans|Iradi American Association]] in Chicago published editions for the [[wp:Commodore 64]] (1983) and [[wp:Apple II]] (1985), and his company in [[Talas]], [[Kuble Soft]], released the best-known edition for [[wp:MS-DOS]] in 1990.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

It is generally regarded as the first Iradi computer game.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} All three editions have been freeware since Kuble Soft closed at the end of 2007, and since 2016 they have been playable in a web browser on the company's former website.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Title
*Köch* is the seasonal move of a herding family, with the yurt packed on the horses (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Gameplay
In the MS-DOS edition the game opens in the spring of 1877. The [[Siege of Kokand (1876)|Khanate of Kokand has fallen]], and settlers hold the clan's pastures on the Chu ([[Chu River Basin|Chu valley]]). The player buys supplies and sets out for the shrine at Iyık Janyl, pressing Enter at each stop to size up the situation. Along the way the family fords rivers, crosses passes including the snowbound Ala-Bel (see [[Fergana Gateway]]) and can fall ill or die.<sup>[1]</sup>

Two action sequences break up the journey. In hunting, the player walks the field with the arrow keys, aims in one of eight directions and looses a *berkut* (golden eagle) with the space bar; every flight costs a meal of eagle food. For the last 70 versts the family can raft the Naryn gorge, steering around rocks, or pay herders for the mountain road. The route roughly follows the valleys used today by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Each landmark is drawn in sixteen colors, from Osmon's shop on the Chu to [[Cathedral Hill]] at Iyık Janyl. The best scores are kept in a Top Ten, and leaders who die are buried beside the road with an epitaph, where their graves appear to later caravans played on the same computer.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Development
Esenov wrote the game in BASIC in 1979 on the university's computer, in the evenings, for his grandmother. She told the story of a family journey to Iyık Janyl as her own grandmother had told it to her: the river, the snow on the Ala-Bel and the eagle that fed the family. The first version was text only and was played by students on the university terminals until the computing center banned games on state machine time.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

A printed listing reached the Iradi community in Chicago in 1981. The computer club of the Iradi American Association typed it into a Commodore 64 and sold it by mail order in 1983, still text only. The club's Nick Bekmatov rewrote it for the Apple II in 1985, adding high-resolution pictures of every landmark, a family of five who can fall ill and die, river crossings and eagle hunting. Esenov's MS-DOS edition of 1990, written in [[wp:GW-BASIC]] for EGA and VGA color graphics, added the rafting sequence, the Top Ten and the graves, with pictures by Gulzat Kalmatova.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Editions
| Edition | Released | Publisher | Requirements | Original price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| University terminal | 1979, Talas | (unpublished) | Iradi State University computer | — |
| Commodore 64 | 1983, Chicago | Iradi American Association, under license from Esenov | Commodore 64, 1541 disk drive | US$14.95 by mail order |
| Apple II | 1985, Chicago | Iradi American Association, under license from Esenov | Apple II+, IIe or IIc, 48K, one Disk II drive | US$19.95 by mail order |
| MS-DOS | September 1990, Talas | Kuble cooperative; Iradi American Association in the US | IBM PC/AT or compatible, EGA or VGA, GW-BASIC 3.2, 360K floppy drive | 18 rubles in Irad; US$24.95 |

A sequel, *Köch II: The Sky Road*, announced in 2001, was to follow a second journey over the [[wp:Torugart Pass|Torugart]] on the old caravan road to [[wp:Kashgar]] in 1889. It was never finished.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception and legacy
*Köch* was played by schoolchildren across Irad and in the Iradi community of Chicago, and many [[Iradis]] of the generation born in the 1970s and 1980s first used a computer to play it. Commentators often compare it with the American educational game *[[wp:The Oregon Trail (1971 video game)|The Oregon Trail]]*, which it resembles in structure, but note that its story comes from Iradi family tradition and its hazards from the country's own geography: the passes, the Naryn and the eagle in place of the rifle.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The game's premise, a clan driven from the Chu pastures by settlers after the Russian conquest, has also been read as one of the few popular treatments of that history to circulate in the late Soviet period.<sup>[3]</sup>

On 31 December 2007 Esenov released the game as freeware, asking players to copy it and give it to their children. Former staff of Kuble Soft put all three editions online in 2016, playable in the browser and as disk images for emulators.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 4.117. Irad Times
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Media*

{{Infobox newspaper
| name = Irad Times
| type = Weekly newspaper (Thursdays)
| owner = Times Staff Trust
| editor = [[Bolotbek Daniyar]] (managing editor)
| founded = 1996-04-11
| political = Independent
| language = English
| hq = 3 Printers' Lane (*Basmakana köchösü*), [[Talas]]
| circulation = About 9,000 copies a week (2023)
| website = [Irad Times](https://mjsbroadbent.github.io/IradTimes/)
}}

The ***Irad Times*** (Iradi: *Irad Ubaktysy*) is an independent English-language weekly newspaper published every Thursday in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1996, during the territorial period, by journalists who had left [[IradOne]], and has been owned since 2001 by its staff through the Times Staff Trust. Its managing editor since 2001 has been [[Bolotbek Daniyar]].<sup>[1]</sup> The paper is known for investigative reporting based on documents: auction protocols, licenses, budgets, court files and company registers. On 26 February 2007 it published the complete texts of the partition drafts that [[Erlan Toktarov]] had released in [[Nurzhan]] the day before (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), and the episode has shaped its standing in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) ever since.<sup>[2]</sup>

Its website has been hosted in the [[wp:United States]] since 2008 by Friends of the Irad Times, an association of diaspora readers in [[wp:Chicago]]. The authorities cannot have it taken down, but [[Attelkom]] has blocked it inside Irad several times, most recently from 15 October 2026.<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Founding (1996–2006)
The first issue, of twelve pages, appeared on 11 April 1996. Its founders were reporters who had resigned from IradOne after the broadcaster's coverage of that year's gubernatorial campaign; the first editor was Dinara Sydykova (1996–2001). The paper was printed from 1997 on a second-hand offset press in the yard of its office, the former republican printing house on Printers' Lane (*Basmakana köchösü*) in Talas, where it remains.<sup>[1]</sup> Daniyar, its first courts reporter, became managing editor in 2001, when the founders transferred their shares to a trust of the staff.

#### The auctions and the Bill of Sale (2006–2007)
In December 2006 and January 2007 the *Times* published internal documents on the auctions held by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], beginning on 21 December with a cabinet valuation showing that three oil exploration blocks in the lower Chu had been sold for about a third of their estimated value. The reports preceded the protests over the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]].<sup>[2]</sup>

On 26 February 2007, the morning after Toktarov read from the partition drafts in Nurzhan, the paper published a sixteen-page special edition, "The Drafts: Framework Treaty and Protocols", with the complete texts of the framework treaty and the three protocols. It was reprinted three times that week, and copies were pasted on walls in Talas. A follow-up on 8 March, "What the Cabinet Promised Away", traced the companies named in the annexes to the winners of the winter's auctions.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> That spring the *Times* was called "the paper that would not be sold", a phrase used by Toktarov among others.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Under the ISEZ (2007–present)
Since 2007 the paper has operated under the ISEZ's media rules. Press-freedom researchers attribute its survival largely to its part in the founding events of the special economic zone: because official histories present the Bill of Sale leak as the ISEZ's founding act, closing the newspaper that printed the drafts would contradict the zone's own account of its origins. Pressure on the paper has instead been administrative.<sup>[3]</sup> In March 2013, after it criticized the amendment that removed gubernatorial term limits, the Department of Public Information suspended its registration for nine weeks, citing a licensing irregularity, and its website was blocked; it resumed publication on 16 May 2013.<sup>[5]</sup> The paper carries almost no advertising from state companies and is funded mainly by subscriptions, a large share of them paid in dollars by readers abroad.

## Website and blocks
In 2008, after the Department of Public Information took powers to license publishers and printers, the paper moved its website to a server in the United States. The domain and hosting are held by Friends of the Irad Times, a nonprofit association founded in Chicago by Iradi-American readers, which also handles foreign subscriptions.<sup>[1]</sup> The site cannot be removed from within Irad, but Attelkom, the main internet provider, has blocked access to it on lists issued by the Department of Public Information. The paper lists the following blocks:<sup>[3]</sup>
- 9 March – 14 May 2013, during the registration suspension;
- November–December 2015, after reports on candidates removed from the gubernatorial ballot;
- October–November 2023, during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]];
- February–March 2025, during the demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]];
- from 15 October 2026, after an issue reporting that two companies apparently lined up as partners in the restart of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] shared an address and a director with a subsidiary of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]].
No block has been officially announced. During blocks the paper distributes its stories through a channel on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app and by email, and the print edition continues.

## Staff
Besides Daniyar, the paper's longest-serving journalist is the senior correspondent Erlan Sagyn (born 1971), one of the reporters who left IradOne in 1996 to found it. He writes on culture, history and the archives, and each May publishes a column on the 1992 siege of Talas, in which his father, the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]], was killed.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Notable reporting
- the 2006–2007 auction documents and the partition drafts (see above);
- the 2008 auction of the Chu District grain elevators to the company later renamed [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (2009);
- the 2013 term-limit amendment;
- municipal land and tax relief for [[Tulpar Talas]] and its owner's property group (2016), and later reports on club finance in the [[Football in Irad|Irad League]] (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]);
- the cost and naming of the [[Alikhan Media Center]] (2017);
- the undisclosed shareholders of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] (2019) and the monitoring of the [[Sary-Bulak]] tailings by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] (2021);
- the record of the Public Integrity Commission (2021), which the paper found had never charged an official above deputy head of department (see [[Crime in Irad]]);
- lobbying in Washington by associates of [[Alikhan Toktarov]] before the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] (March 2025), which IradOne Media Group denied.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Readership
The paper sold about 9,000 copies a week in 2023, according to the Irad Media Research Center, mainly in Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], with subscribers abroad receiving it by post. Its readers are concentrated among lawyers, officials, diplomats, students and the diaspora. Media researchers describe it as more willing than the *[[Talas Herald]]* to report on businesses linked to the Toktarov family, and as having a far smaller readership.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

### 4.118. Sagyn Jusupbekov
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Biographies*

**Sagyn Jusupbekov** (Iradi: *Sagyn Jusupbek uulu*; Russian: *Сагын Жусупбеков*; 3 February 1936 – 24 May 1992) was an Iradi folklorist, ethnopoet and [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] player. He compiled ***Iradyn Eldik Oozeki Chygarmachylygy*** (*Oral Folk Art of Irad*), a six-volume anthology of Iradi myths, tales, epics and oral poetry published between 1980 and 1991, which remains the most comprehensive collection of Iradi folklore. Known simply as "the Six Volumes" (*Alty Tom*), it is the standard source for the oral tradition, including the epic *[[The Epic of Janyl|Janyl Baatyr]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

Jusupbekov taught at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) for more than thirty years and was a colleague of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. He supported the [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government]] in 1992 and was killed by shellfire during the siege of [[Talas]]. His son, Erlan Sagyn, is a journalist with the *[[Irad Times]]*.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Early life and education
Jusupbekov was born on 3 February 1936 into a family of horse herders in the upper Chatkal valley. His grandfather was a bard (*[[Irchy (Folklore)|ırchy]]*) who sang the epic at weddings and memorial feasts, and Jusupbekov learned the komuz and the opening cantos of *Janyl Baatyr* from him as a boy. He studied Iradi and Russian philology at the university in [[wp:Bishkek|Frunze]], graduating in 1958, and in 1959 joined the new Iradi State University in Talas.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Academic career
Jusupbekov defended a candidate of sciences dissertation on the formulaic language of *Janyl Baatyr* in 1966 and a doctoral dissertation on the genres of Iradi oral poetry in 1979. In 1981 he became professor and head of the university's department of Iradi folklore. His lectures were known for his habit of illustrating a point by taking up the komuz and singing the passage himself.<sup>[3]</sup>

From 1959 to 1990 he led student expeditions every summer to the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley, the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and the northern steppe, writing down tales, songs, genealogies (*sanjyra*) and blessings (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) from herders, bards and elderly women. He worked alongside the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]], whose tape recordings preserved the music of many of the performances whose words he transcribed. In 1988 he joined Alimbekov's *Ene-Til* society, and he spoke in favor of the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## The Six Volumes
*Oral Folk Art of Irad* was published in [[Nurzhan|Kobozev]] by Ilim, the press of the Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR, in Cyrillic-script Iradi with commentary in Russian. Its six volumes run to about 6,400 pages and contain some 4,100 texts from about 900 performers:<sup>[1]</sup>
- I. *Myths and Legends* (1980): creation stories, the sky and ancestor cults, the goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]];
- II. *Tales and Fables* (1982);
- III. *Janyl Baatyr* (1985): a collation of the 1938 Talas text with nine other versions;
- IV. *Shorter Epics and Historical Songs* (1987);
- V. *Lyric and Ritual Poetry* (1989): horseback songs (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*), laments (*koshok*), blessings, genealogies, and wedding and work songs;
- VI. *Legends of Saints and Holy Places* (1991): stories of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] and the White Rider, and excerpts of *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*.

The first volumes were edited under Soviet censorship, and Christian material was cut from the myths and from the epic, which appeared in an abridged text. Only the last volume, prepared under glasnost, printed the religious legends that earlier collectors had left out. It was printed in Kobozev in December 1991, but the government of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] impounded the print run as "nationalist", and most copies were pulped. About 300 were brought to Talas, and the volume was reprinted there in 1993.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

Jusupbekov's full collation of the 1938 text of the epic, which he had kept back from the 1985 volume, was the basis of the complete Latin-script edition of *Janyl Baatyr* published by [[Talas State University Press]] in 2001, edited by his former students.<sup>[4]</sup> A Latin-script reissue of the whole anthology in the press's Library of Iradi Folklore (*Eldik Muras*) series began in 2008 but stopped after the third volume in 2012; it resumed in 2025, and volume IV, *Shorter Epics and Historical Songs*, is due in 2027. Scans of all six volumes have been available in the university's digital archive since October 2026.<sup>[5]</sup>

## Siege of Talas and death
During the siege of Talas in 1992, Jusupbekov took part in the nightly broadcasts of the Provisional Government from the city's radio studio, singing passages of the epic and playing the komuz between news bulletins. On 24 May 1992, walking home from the studio along University Street, he was killed by shellfire from the forces of the Socialist Republic of Irad. He was 56. He was buried in Talas.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Legacy
Jusupbekov's notebooks and correspondence are held in the [[State Archives of Irad]] in the ethnography fonds. The university's Sagyn Jusupbekov Folklore Cabinet, in the Faculty of Philology and Journalism, keeps his library and his komuz, which was recovered from the street after his death. Radio Irad's evening program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales", 1994–2020), presented by [[Baktygul Omur]], is often said to have been modeled on his siege broadcasts.<sup>[3]</sup>

His son, Erlan Sagyn (born 1971), served in a student militia during the siege. He worked as a reporter for [[IradOne]] from 1993 and was among the journalists who left the broadcaster in 1996 to found the *Irad Times*, where he writes on culture, history and archives. Each year on 24 May he publishes a column on the siege and on his father's anthology.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 4.119. Jarysh
*Quality Assessment: C-Class Article | Category: Media*

{{More citations needed|date=October 2026}}

**Jarysh** (Iradi: *jarysh*, "race, contest"; jarysh.com) is an Iradi website about the horse games of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], run from [[Talas]] by Jarysh Entertainment Group, which describes it as "Irad's #1 horse games portal". Launched in 2017 by the promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]], it publishes scores and tables of the ulak leagues, odds on matches, ticket sales for Aigyr Ulak Nights at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], and pages of models and fashion aimed at young city fans.<sup>[1]</sup> Its sponsor is the [[Kara-Bulak]] brewer [[Aigyr Lager|Aigyr]].

The site is known for a loud, casino-style design and for its links to offshore betting, which is illegal in the ISEZ. Its betting subdomain has been blocked since 2023.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Baisalov, a nightclub promoter who had run Club Doran in Talas since 2004, returned to the city in 2014 after several years in Turkey and Kazakhstan and set up Jarysh Entertainment Group to promote equestrian events. The website opened in 2017 with live scores of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* matches, which [[IradOne]] then covered only in highlights.<sup>[1]</sup>

In June 2018 the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] gave the company a seven-year concession to run the bars, stage and VIP boxes at the State Hippodrome on league Saturdays, without a public tender. The Directorate said no other company had applied; opposition councilors in Talas called the award "a gift" and asked for the contract to be published.<sup>[3]</sup> The concession was renewed for ten years in June 2025, again without a tender; the renewal was not announced and came to light in the Directorate's annual report. The company has since run the Saturday-night events as **Aigyr Ulak Nights**, with beer decks, live music, a half-time "Fan Pull" for amateurs and buses to Club Doran after midnight. Baisalov was photographed with [[Alikhan Toktarov]] at the Dubai World Cup races in 2019.

## Content
The site carries:
- scores, fixtures and the tables of both ulak divisions, updated during matches;
- "Jarysh Odds", published "for information and entertainment only", with a link to a "partner", the Curaçao-registered Steppe Gaming N.V.;
- ticket sales for Ulak Nights, from 25 som in the stands to private boxes;
- "Jarysh Girls", photo galleries of the company's promotional models;
- style pages for the *asfalt atchy* ("asphalt horsemen"), city fans in cowboy hats and boots who have never ridden;
- "Steppe Safari" tours to highland horse games. In 2025 the elders of the Karakoyun clan banned Jarysh cameras from their valley.

## Betting
Under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011, wagers in the ISEZ may be placed only at the Directorate's licensed tote windows; bookmaking and online gambling are illegal. In November 2023 [[Attelkom]] blocked bet.jarysh.com, a betting site run for Steppe Gaming, at the Directorate's request. Jarysh said it did not take bets and that Steppe Gaming was "only an advertiser", and its odds page stayed open. Bookmakers told the *[[Talas Herald]]* that bets had moved to channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app.<sup>[2]</sup>
